docs.title: Agentic Software Engineering: Build, Verify, Evaluate
docs.text:
Agents generate. You verify, decide and explain.

Over fourteen weeks you learn to enter an unfamiliar repository, turn a user need into an executable specification, delegate a bounded task to a coding agent, check the result and explain the decision yourself. The course is taught in English.

Read the syllabus How this course works Start with Week 0

docs.title: How this course works
docs.text:
• Generate, then verify

    Every example shows both steps. A check you can rerun is evidence; an agent saying "done" is a claim.

  • Predict before you look

    Each class opens with a decision you can get wrong. Save your prediction, run a check that tells the answers apart, then revise.

  • Decide, don't regenerate

    When a candidate passes, accept it, narrow the task, recheck something specific or stop.

  • Explain it without the agent

    Two checkpoints and an oral defense, 40 of 100 points, are done without AI.

docs.title: One case, fourteen weeks
docs.text:
The teacher follows one CI dashboard case. From week 3 you carry one path through your own copy of ci-dashboard, and you build a complete feature in a real open-source project through two or three approved contributions.

Weeks Question 1-3 What happened, and where should a bounded agent act? 4-8 What does the user need, and does the change keep required behavior? 9-11 Can the experiment, the evaluator and the running service be trusted? 12-14 What survives another person's review and actual use?

docs.title: Agentic Software Engineering: Build, Verify, Evaluate
docs.text:
English is the first teaching language. Over fourteen weeks, you will learn to enter an unfamiliar repository, clarify a user need, delegate a bounded task to an agent, verify the result and explain the decision yourself.

The teacher uses a continuing CI dashboard case. Each student enters their own copy of the supplied ci-dashboard repository in week 3 and uses it alone to practise testing, security, evaluation, incident recovery and audit verification on one path. You build a complete feature in a real open-source project instead, through two or three approved contributions. Optional features and advanced tool integrations are not required for the highest rubric band.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• LO1: Explain model and agent behavior, including context, tools and stopping failures.
  • LO2: Design a bounded agent workflow with relevant context, permissions and resource awareness.
  • LO3: Turn user discovery into executable requirements and acceptance criteria.
  • LO4: Understand and improve an existing repository while preserving required behavior.
  • LO5: Verify generated code and independently explain tests, reviews and merge decisions.
  • LO6: Design and audit evaluations, interpret traces and calibrate evaluators.
  • LO7: Reproduce and mitigate local agent and application security failures.
  • LO8: Deploy, observe and recover a product and explain incident decisions.
  • LO9: Work responsibly, attribute assistance and calibrate claims against evidence.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Component Points When CP1: individual AI-off diagnosis, test and repair 10 Week 5 CP2: individual AI-off unfamiliar-code review and recovery reasoning 10 Week 11 Individual oral defense 20 Weeks 13-14 Open-source contributions 30 C1 weeks 3-6, C2 weeks 7-13 Individual project 20 M0-M4 Individual practice portfolio 10 P1 week 2, P2 week 6, P3 week 9

Passing requires at least 60/100 overall and 20/40 across the two independent checks and oral defense. Missing components remain missing until resolved; they are not treated as zero or passing. There are no bonus points.

P1 (agent explanation), P2 (specification-constrained review) and P3 (evaluation audit) are the only separate personal practice submissions, worth 4, 3 and 3 points. Keep the artifact, verification, your own short explanation and feedback-based revision. Repository context and discovery feed M0, testing and security feed M1, and the evaluator workshop feeds M2. In the repository-context workshop each student also writes one standard skill for the tracing method, checks when it triggers, uses it once on ci-dashboard and once read-only on your candidate contribution project, and revises and tests a small MCP tool server. Weekly self-checks replace a separate quiz system; there is no CP3 or extra reflection report.

The oral defense uses four integrated domains: requirements and code paths, verification and evaluation, security and incident recovery, and a changed-input responsibility decision. LO3, LO6, LO7 and LO8 are required; the defense transfers rather than repeats every outcome one by one. The project demonstration cannot replace it.

docs.title: Feedback and reassessment
docs.text:
Each independent component below 50% is eligible for one equivalent resit after feedback, covering the same outcomes, duration and difficulty. The effective score is the larger of the original score and the resit score capped at half that component's maximum. Preserve both records. A valid passing sitting cannot be repeated to improve the mark. Approved technical-fault or accommodation equivalents replace invalid sittings without consuming the resit. Projects and portfolio samples use the published feedback/revision window.

Model access depends on safety admission and the approved model route, never on exam scores. Real model calls use one approved hosted API configuration with a domestic and an overseas option; you choose one, and comparisons such as P3 stay within that option. You use your own API key and pay for your own usage. The key stays on your machine and only the launcher reads it. Each run has request and token limits, and a run that reaches its limit stops. We recommend setting a spending limit with your provider.

If you cannot or prefer not to pay, cannot register in your region, or do not want to give personal data to a commercial provider, you may choose the replay route without giving a reason. You replay teacher-verified recordings of real runs through course_llm, still predict, check, recompute and explain the result yourself, and label the work as replay. You still declare one option in P1 and replay that option's recordings. The mark ceiling is the same, and choosing replay is never a negative factor in any mark. M3 is unaffected: the teaching team runs every student's model audit (see the project section). Never share, borrow or pay for another student's key.

After you build the small controller, you drive one mature coding agent on ci-dashboard inside the course launcher sandbox. The tool has no general network access; its only egress is the host-mounted relay, which is part of the launcher's host-side broker, allows only the approved endpoint and adds your key outside the sandbox, so you need no separate tool subscription. On the replay route you work from teacher recordings of the same tool. See Week 0 setup for the supported execution route. Until that relay passes its independent security review, use the course mini-agent and teacher recordings instead.

docs.title: Individual project
docs.text:
Milestone Points Evidence M0: discovery and specification 2 One user need, one agreed small change and executable acceptance M1: reliable change 6 Reviewed PR, tests, security regressions, an AGENTS.md, one hook gate and an agent-readiness scorecard before and after M2: evaluation and operation 6 Evaluator, preview and incident recovery for the same path M3: model audit and verification 3 Model audit record and evidence for every finding M4: repair and delivery 3 Response to verified findings, tested iteration and expo demonstration

You complete the project on your own; there are no groups and no contribution adjustment. Your project score is your own 0-20, with the published project rubric, written reasons, appeals and human review. Agree one small change in M0 and carry the same path through M1-M4.

M3 works like this. Tag a frozen snapshot of your repository and submit the tag by the published deadline. The teaching team runs the course model audit on it once with the teaching-team key, keeps the original output and run record, and sends you a copy; you need no key of your own. The audit covers evaluation, security and maintenance. The snapshot must contain only your own work in the course repository: no participant material, credentials or anyone else's private code. For every finding, either confirm it with a test that fails before the fix or a repeatable reproduction, refute it with runnable evidence, or say what is missing and why you cannot decide. Then check one place yourself: add a problem the model missed, or state what you checked and found nothing. Marks depend only on your verification: whether the evidence runs, whether it supports your conclusion and whether you claimed more than you checked. The number or severity of model findings earns nothing, and model output never enters a grader. Confirmed findings carry into M4.

docs.title: Open-source contributions
docs.text:
You submit two or three pull requests to approved public open-source projects, worth 30 points in two samples:

Sample Weeks Work Points C1: warm-up contribution 3-6 One small, complete fix (a defect, a test or documentation) 8 C2: substantial contribution 7-13 One approved feature or non-trivial fix, in one or two pull requests 22

The contributions rubric gives the criteria and points for C1 and C2.

The teaching team publishes the approved project list before week 3. It includes public open-source projects maintained by partner companies and other active projects. Each listed project has an OSI-approved licence, a contribution guide, maintainers who have responded recently, AI-use rules that allow your planned use, a build and tests that run offline within the launcher's limits, and maintainers who have agreed to receive course contributions. At most five students work on one project at a time. You may propose another project; it is approved on the same conditions. Submit the C2 proposal at the end of week 6; the teacher approves the project, issue and scope before week 7.

Contributions are marked with the same explanation check, verification evidence and AI-use note as other open work, plus your upstream collaboration: issue discussion, revisions after review and following the project's rules. A merge or a maintainer reply is not required. Contribute only to public repositories. Never use code from your residency, employer or a partner company's internal systems, and never send it to a model. If a project bans AI-generated contributions, choose another project or work on it without a model. Model-generated or suggested code runs only through the course launcher; prefetch upstream dependencies at locked versions and hashes before the launcher goes offline, and push to the upstream project from your own machine, outside the sandbox. Contributions without any model, or on the replay route, have the same mark ceiling.

You may use a pseudonymous account where the project allows it; the teaching team keeps the mapping privately. You are never asked to sign a CLA that assigns your copyright to a company, and signing a CLA that only grants a non-exclusive licence is your informed choice. If you cannot or prefer not to publish publicly, or do not want to sign a CLA or DCO, you may take the course-hosted route without giving a reason: you submit C1 and C2 of the same scope to a non-public course practice repository, where a TA reviews them as an upstream maintainer would. The rubric and maximum mark are the same, and the choice is never a negative factor in any mark.

The week 14 demonstration is an expo: everyone demonstrates at the same time while staff and classmates move between stations and ask questions, and each student answers at least one staff question.

docs.title: Workload and participation
docs.text:
Each week has a published hour estimate that covers Week 0 installation, safety admission and API key setup, classes, waiting, help, exams, project work, user recruitment, feedback and revision. The estimates are planning guidance, not a cap: they are updated when a week's required work changes and recalibrated from timed pilot runs. If you go over an estimate, ask for help first; you are never marked down for exceeding a time box. Week 2 includes a required session dissection of about two and a half hours. Rounded up for the published planning value, current estimates are: Week 0, 3; Weeks 1-14, 9, 12, 16, 14, 14, 13, 12, 12, 12, 12, 13, 11, 12 and 11. Weeks 3-13 include work on the open-source contributions; all estimates will be recalibrated from timed pilot runs. P1/P2/P3 are estimated at 11/3/4 hours including workshop time; the session dissection is part of P1, not a second submission. Project workshops are already part of their milestones. Use one principal work entry per week and reference the same evidence across related assessment items.

In weeks 3, 6, 10 and 13 a practitioner from a partner organization joins the first class for up to 45 minutes. Bring one question, and afterwards write one sentence comparing what you heard with that week's evidence. Guest talks are not assessed.

Run two discovery activities of your own for M0. Complete three usability sessions of your own across weeks 11-13. Obtain informed consent before participation, collect minimal data and honor withdrawal; use an actually approved equivalent activity when participation is unavailable. Text rehearsal is not a participant session. Keyboard and approved accessible participation preserve the same learning outcomes and attainable marks.

docs.title: AI use and responsibility
docs.text:
Use approved assistance for open work. Complete checkpoints, oral answers, initial personal review, discovery notes and personal reflection independently. Attach AI use once to the artifact and reuse its ID; submit only task-relevant traces, not unrelated chat history. Never include private records or credentials in prompts or submissions. Every real model call goes to an approved external provider. Participant material, including raw interview and test material and anything derived from it, is never sent to a model, whatever the consent. Participant material means the notes, records, quotations, observations and media produced in interviews and tests, and their de-identified versions. Requirements, acceptance criteria, tests and hypotheses you write yourself are not participant material if they neither quote a participant nor describe what a particular participant said or did, and you may use them with the approved model route; citing only an activity ID such as [interview:…] does not change this. Never send private code or personal data to a model without proper authorization. Keep your API key out of prompts, the repository, submissions, traces, screenshots and logs.

Explain what changed, why, which inputs are most likely to fail and what you verified yourself. Grading uses observable work and explanation; writing style is not an AI-authorship verdict. Evidence conflicts require a human process and an opportunity to respond.

docs.title: Check your starting point
docs.text:
These twenty course-authored questions cover Python, Git, testing and HTTP. Questions, answers and explanations are public student assets. This diagnostic is practice feedback, not a quiz bank, admission decision or official course grade. It has no pass threshold. Try it without AI first so the result helps you choose what to review; checking the public answers afterward is encouraged. No personal information is needed.

Use the Week 0 launcher setup. Copy this directory's public files into a separate workspace. In that sandbox, python run.py prints questions; python run.py --show-answers also explains the answers. Record your choices in a JSON object such as {"P1": "C", "G1": "C"}. Omit unanswered questions.

Run python run.py --answers answers.json through the same launcher to receive a deterministic JSON result. Incorrect and omitted answers receive no correct-answer point; each question counts once. Unknown IDs, duplicate IDs and values outside A-D fail input validation. The script reads data and never executes submitted code. Answers shipped with the questions make this unsuitable for summative grading.

Read the explanation for each missed question. Explain one correction in your own words and try that concept on a small example through the launcher. Bring the topic and safe error category to course support if still stuck. This fits within the Week 0 time budget; it does not create another scored submission or a requirement to export a conversation.

docs.title: Explain a PR and verify its evidence
Purpose
docs.text: Give an approved model enough information to review your diff in a fresh context with a bounded scope. Mark each finding confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with your own evidence, and record what you checked; if model review is unavailable, ask a TA. Answer four questions in one PR: what changed, why, which inputs are likely to fail, and what you personally verified. A complete structure is feedback about the explanation's shape. A teacher still checks the work and your understanding. The structural check itself makes no model call and has no authorship detector, score or automatic merge decision.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
Copy the body under ## Explain gate from the PR template into your PR. Replace each placeholder with a short, concrete answer. Keep the four level-three headings exactly as written. There is no word-count requirement. Put commands and results in explanatory prose; code fences, quoted text, indented code and HTML comments do not count as answers or headings. Use a blank line or a fence to separate code examples from prose; indentation alone does not end an existing paragraph. Empty answers, duplicate headings, standalone TODO/TBD/FIXME markers, known angle-bracket prompts and answers consisting only of N/A, none, pending or answer fail the deterministic check. The checker cannot tell whether arbitrary prose is true or meaningful; staff review resolves that. Angle-bracket detection recognizes the supplied template prompts and a fixed set of short placeholder forms. Technical notation such as List<Foo>, Future<State>, HTML tags and paired comparison operators is allowed, including on separate lines. It is not classified by its first word. Prose discussing a removed TODO or a UI placeholder is allowed; a line containing only a reserved marker still fails, including Markdown emphasis, bullet/numbered lists and list checkboxes. Indented child list items also count as answer text; code indentation is measured relative to the containing list item. Quoted lines and fenced code within a list remain excluded. Unprefixed continuation lines in a quoted paragraph are excluded too. Separate your own answer from quoted material with a blank line. A heading inside a list does not end the active answer.

Each individual PR has one explanation record. A correction may be posted in a comment beginning with the exact line ## Explain gate and using the same four headings. Explain only your own change and verification. The Action uses the authenticated GitHub account on the PR or comment and the instructor's restricted pseudonym mapping. The latest marked comment by an account replaces that account's earlier explanation for the current check; retain the earlier version in the existing record when correcting it. The PR opener's body supplies their record unless they post a marked comment. Unmapped accounts do not supply course evidence. Staff must verify account attribution and resolve third-party edits; API attribution does not prove personal mastery.

The Action creates one stable evidence_id per repository/PR/person, for example eg:course-example/project:17:student-01. Reuse this ID in the existing AI-use note. If you already have a work/evidence ID, link it once from that note. Do not copy the diff, logs or explanation into another form. Keep the AI-use note once per work item, updating it when the use changes. No unrelated chat export is required. Model-generated code and commands still run only through the task's already verified course launcher.

A minimal record follows evidence.schema.json: PR location, pseudonym, milestone, base/head commits, SHA-256 of the fetched diff bytes, explanation source and SHA-256, and the structural result. It contains no explanation body, account map, raw diff, test logs, grade or authority claim. An edit to the explanation, base, head or diff invalidates an old review. Even an unrelated code change requires refreshing the PR record. Preserve historical reviews in the existing restricted record; use only a fresh current export for this check.

docs.title: Generate, then verify: a synthetic example
docs.text: A generated change rejects an empty list before selecting its first element. You personally run the allowed launcher tests and discover that a one-item list was also rejected. After correcting the condition, record the empty-list failure case and one-item success case in your fourth answer, with a reference to the existing verification result. Do not describe the generated tests as personally executed until you actually run and inspect them. This example is course-created and does not claim any real student's work or model run.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
The teacher checks every structural problem and at least one available record for each student, then 20% of the remaining individual PR records, rounded up. For M1, a TA checks the student's bounded model-review evidence. Students without evidence are explicitly listed for follow-up. Missing evidence is not an automatic zero or an integrity decision. Explain or correct the gap through the existing course process.

Staff record the reason, evidence reference and correction in their existing checklist. The same evidence may support different claims but must not be scored repeatedly merely because it is referenced again. If a reviewer asks for more evidence, add the missing reproduction or limitation to the same explanation record. Grading and appeals use the course's published process; this page only describes the four-question structure and how to record what you checked. Staff instructions are distributed separately to instructors.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Copy the Explain gate section into your PR body. To correct it later, post a comment whose first line is ## Explain gate and that uses the same four headings. Copy no front matter or template-maintenance sections. Replace placeholders with your own explanation and evidence.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
## Explain gate

### What changed?
<Describe the observable behavior that changed.>

### Why?
<Explain the cause, chosen approach and relevant assumption.>

### Which inputs are most likely to fail?
<Identify concrete boundary or adversarial inputs and expected behavior.>

### What did you personally verify?
<State what you actually ran and observed, referring to the existing verification result.>

## AI-use note reference
<Link the existing work item's one AI-use note and evidence ID, or write it here once.>

docs.title: Review
docs.text: Respond to feedback and record the correction and re-verification in the same PR. The Action checks structure; a teacher verifies the reasoning and personal evidence. A new revision needs a fresh check. Optional extensions do not raise the requirements for full marks.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Map one request path in ci-dashboard, rehearse a paired context comparison on one fixed task and check one permission boundary. Write a SKILL.md for your tracing method, use it once on ci-dashboard, test when its description triggers and use it read-only on your candidate contribution project (or a listed repository if you have no candidate yet). Revise a small ci-dashboard tool server against five agent-ergonomics rules and test it through the protocol (LO2, LO4).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Use Week 0 setup and the week 3 activity. Copy only the public student/ files into a new workspace.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text: Follow the student guide: request map, context pair, hook check, skill and trigger test, tool-server revision and protocol test, then a short explanation. The exact tool and skill contract is in SPEC.en.md.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text: Call-path map, context comparison, boundary evidence, skills/trace-request/ with its three before/after lines, trigger-test.yaml, skill-transfer.yaml, the revised tool_behavior.py, test_protocol.py and its launcher output. Reuse the existing work record; include verification and your own short explanation, not an additional report.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: This workshop is part of M0. Keep its evidence in that milestone; there is no separate submission or course mark. Public checks and workshop feedback do not set a grade. See the syllabus.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Use approved assistance for open work. Write predictions and your explanation yourself. Record what a trigger observer actually did. Attach AI use once and reuse its ID.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: About ten hours in Week 3, including the class time spent on Part A, verification, waiting and revision.

docs.title: Optional extensions: the HTTP adapter and three A/B pairs
docs.text: Neither extension is needed for the workshop or for the highest M1 band. Do them only after the workshop is complete, if you want more practice with the same boundary and comparison methods.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Apply one input boundary in two adapters (LO2): implement label normalization once, check that the HTTP adapter rejects the same invalid inputs, and extend the fixed A/B comparison from one pair to three.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: The workshop's prerequisites and placeholders apply unchanged. The HTTP adapter needs Flask, which you install offline from hash-locked wheels inside the launcher.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Label normalization (60 minutes). Implement normalize_label in label_behavior.py, following the starter application: trim, lowercase ASCII letters, join words with one hyphen, accept 1-32 characters of ASCII letters, digits and spaces with at least one letter or digit, and reject everything else. Predict a normal and three invalid inputs before you run anything.
  2. Check the HTTP adapter (40 minutes). The acquisition helper downloads only hash-locked public wheels; installation happens inside the launcher without network. Do not add downloaded wheels to your submission or copy an installed environment.

sh uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python capstone/context-workshop/student/prepare_app.py LAB_WORK/wheels sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace LAB_WORK -- bash -c 'python -m pip install --no-index --no-compile --target deps --find-links wheels flask==3.1.2 && python -B starter-app/check_app.py'

  1. Three A/B pairs (60 minutes). Run the controller without --core. It runs the health, invalid and label tasks once without and once with your context:

sh uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python capstone/context-workshop/student/ab_collect.py LAB_WORK --output LAB_EVIDENCE

Failed model answers are valid observations; analyze them without rerunning until scores improve. A controller or runtime failure stops collection and keeps attempt.json; preserve it and ask for help before a new, labelled attempt.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text: Add label_behavior.py, the check_app.py output and, if you ran it, the version-1 ab-report.json with its report Markdown to your existing work record. Point ab.entry at whichever report you want feedback on.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: No extra points. The workshop's A/B check accepts either the one-pair or the three-pair report with the same evidence rules.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Same as the workshop: approved assistance for code; predictions and explanation are your own; one AI-use note reused by ID.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: About two hours and forty minutes, on top of the workshop.

docs.title: repository-context workshop: Find the relevant context
At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: finish the class map of one ci-dashboard request by hand, choose context for a fixed question and rehearse the paired collection, check one permission boundary, package your tracing method as a SKILL.md, test when it triggers and use it once read-only on your candidate contribution project, then revise a small ci-dashboard tool server until an agent could use it safely, and prove that with a test that speaks the protocol.
  • Hand in: one work record holding the call-path map, the A/B report, both boundary results, your skill directory, trigger-test.yaml, skill-transfer.yaml, the revised tool_behavior.py, test_protocol.py and your own explanation.
  • Done when: skill_check.py, transfer_check.py and public_check.py report no problems, test_protocol.py passes through the launcher, and every prompt in explanation.en.md has an answer that points at something you actually observed.
  • Time: about ten hours in Week 3, including the Week 3 class time spent on Part A, which begins with the class map. This is practice inside M0, not a separate mark.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Trace one request across files in ci-dashboard (LO4). Choose the context an agent needs, verify one permission boundary, package a repeatable procedure as a skill whose description fires when it should, and design tools for a reader that sees only their names, schemas and descriptions (LO2). Each part has the same rhythm: generate or write something, check it against an expectation you set first, then change one thing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Complete Week 0 setup; its launcher and profile resolver are the only supported way to run the commands below. Commands run from the supplied course root. Copy only this public student/ directory into a new workspace outside the private repository; exclude .git, caches, wheels, teacher assets and credentials. On macOS use an absolute path under /private/tmp, since /tmp is a symlink the launcher rejects. Replace LAB_WORK with your workspace path. Resolve VERSION and DIGEST using:

uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json

docs.title: Part A: context and boundaries
docs.text:
1. Map the project-list path (50 minutes, the first 15 in class). Finish the map you started in the Week 3 class activity, in your own ci-dashboard repository (get it first if you have not). Follow GET /domains/ci_dashboard/ from the route to what the visitor sees, reading the source; the application does not need to run. In your work record, keep:
  2. the commit you read (git rev-parse HEAD);
  3. the path as a text list of arrows, each labelled confirmed (file:line at that commit), refuted (what the code does instead) or cannot tell;
  4. every branch the arrows hide: what a visitor without a session receives, and what the page shows to a user with no projects;
  5. one open behavior question with the test you would look for before editing, and a bounded edit with what a caller would observe after it.

Then ask a classmate or a TA to pick one arrow you labelled confirmed and try to show from the code at your commit that it is wrong. Record whether it held. You reuse this map in step 5 and when you choose your M0 scope. 2. Select context (40 minutes). Read the starter application and starter-app/app.py; the fixed task asks which path checks this app's health. Edit context.py as text. Keep its Project, Commands and Boundaries sections; replace placeholders with relevant facts from the starter application and check each fact against a line of app.py or its README. Packet A will contain only the fixed task; packet B adds this context. Predict which packet would let a model answer the health-path question, and why. The collector enforces the approved model's combined prompt-byte limit before generation. Shorten context when told to; do not change model parameters. 3. Verify a boundary (30 minutes). Read the supplied hook.py. Predict both results, then run each command separately. Keep the hook unchanged.

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace LAB_WORK -- python -B hook.py '{"event":"before_write","path":"src/app.py"}' sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace LAB_WORK -- python -B hook.py '{"event":"before_write","path":"../outside.py"}'

The first should exit 0 and the second 2. Explain why an allowed ordinary edit and a rejected escape are both necessary. The hook illustrates policy; the launcher's isolation is the actual execution boundary. 4. Collect one fixed pair (45 minutes). Run the course controller from the course root. It runs the health task once without context and once with it, with fresh execution and identical approved configuration. Use a new output directory outside the workspace.

sh uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python capstone/context-workshop/student/ab_collect.py LAB_WORK --core --output LAB_EVIDENCE

The pair runs on the FAKE practice route: both rows receive the same fixed practice reply, so both fail the health task whatever your context says. It rehearses the workflow only (two fresh runs, identical configuration, one call each, metrics and a receipt) and is not real-model evidence. It cannot confirm or refute your step 2 prediction, so record that prediction as cannot tell. Check instead that ab-report.en.md says Mode: fake and has one without and one with row. The course replay in the Week 3 notes is where you see two packets change an answer. A runtime failure keeps its attempt record: preserve it and ask for help before a new, labelled attempt.

docs.title: Part B: a skill that fires when it should
docs.text:
A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md file: YAML front matter with a name and a description, then a Markdown body with the procedure. An agent that supports skills sees only the name and description until it decides to load one, so the description decides whether the skill is ever used. The body is loaded only after that, and everything in it then costs context, so hold the procedure itself there and leave longer background in a separate file in the same directory. A skill grants no permission and does not replace the launcher.

  1. Write the skill (45 minutes). In step 1 you traced the project-list path by hand across three files and checked each arrow at one commit. Write that procedure as skills/trace-request/SKILL.md, so an agent or another developer can repeat it on another request. The supplied skills/verify-change/SKILL.md shows the format for a different job; do not copy its content.
  2. name: trace-request, matching the directory name.
  3. description: both the job the skill does and the situation that should trigger it, phrased the way a person would ask for it ("Use when ..."). At least eight words.
  4. ## Steps: at least two concrete steps; give the exact command for any step a command can do.
  5. ## Judgement: the decisions a step list hides: which way to go when more than one reading fits ("If two routes match, ..."), and the moves to avoid.
  6. ## Verification: the exact command or check, in backticks, that shows the trace was right.

Check the structure from the course root; it reads your files as data:

sh uv run --locked python capstone/context-workshop/student/skill_check.py LAB_WORK/skills/trace-request/SKILL.md LAB_WORK/trigger-test.yaml

The trigger-test problems it reports are for step 7. 6. Use it on ci-dashboard (30 minutes). Choose a different request in your ci-dashboard repository from the one in step 1. Follow your own skill, with or without an approved agent, and write three lines in your work record: what you did by hand in step 1, what the skill made you do differently, and one step, judgement or verification you changed after using it. The Week 3 activities explain the observe, adjust, recheck loop for that change. A skill nobody has used is a draft.

Then carry it to your candidate contribution project (about 60 minutes). A skill written beside one repository quietly assumes its layout. Use yours once more, read-only, on the project you have picked as a candidate for your contributions, and record that run in skill-transfer.yaml. If you have no candidate yet, use one of the repositories listed below or another that meets the same criteria.

  • Choose the repository and one request you can trace: an HTTP route, a command-line command or a message handler. The repository must be public, on any forge, under a licence the Open Source Initiative has approved (MIT, Apache-2.0, the BSD licences, GPL, LGPL, AGPL, MPL-2.0 and many more; transfer_check.py holds the full list), which every approved contribution project meets. If you chose the course-hosted contribution route, use the course practice repository and add route: course-hosted under repository in your record. Export only the part that holds the request: at most 200 files and 1 MB. Any of the repositories below also fits; their licence and size were read from each repository at the commit shown.

    Repository Commit Licence (file) Export these paths Files A request to trace https://github.com/miguelgrinberg/microblog a975ef64864354867c88e0ed3a17ba7d17dca752 MIT (LICENSE) app microblog.py config.py tests.py LICENSE 47 GET /api/users/<id> https://github.com/pallets/flask d73fa1cdcbd8b1465c151db8924ba58b1dd14e35 BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt) examples/tutorial LICENSE.txt 23 POST /auth/register in the tutorial app https://github.com/bottlepy/bottle cbd569c447b3fd53f194cef9a306146ce6a07a59 MIT (LICENSE) bottle.py test LICENSE 45 how a route's return value becomes the response body

    Whichever repository you use, your record names it and the commit you exported. - Export one pinned commit on your own machine with plain git. Type these commands yourself and never run a model-suggested command outside the launcher. OSS_CLONE is a new folder outside your workspace and LAB_OSS a new, empty one; the example uses the first row:

    sh git clone --no-checkout https://github.com/miguelgrinberg/microblog.git OSS_CLONE mkdir LAB_OSS git -C OSS_CLONE archive a975ef64864354867c88e0ed3a17ba7d17dca752 app microblog.py config.py tests.py LICENSE | tar -x -C LAB_OSS find LAB_OSS -type f | wc -l cp -R LAB_WORK/skills LAB_OSS/skills

    git archive writes exactly that commit's files without .git, which the launcher refuses anyway. Do not install the repository's dependencies or run its code on your machine. If the launcher reports the folder as too large, export fewer paths. - Run the skill on LAB_OSS through the launcher only, with an approved agent that loads SKILL.md skills or by following it yourself. The launcher copies LAB_OSS into a container with no network and discards every change, so your export stays exactly as exported. Run each command the skill names as sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace LAB_OSS -- COMMAND. With an agent, ask the way a user would, without naming the skill, and record whether the session loaded your skill. Never fill that in from what a model says it would do. The container has no network, so the repository's own dependencies are usually missing: a verification step that cannot run there is a misfit worth recording. - Record in skill-transfer.yaml the repository, the commit and what you exported, how you ran the skill, the path it traced (files and functions), one step, judgement or verification that did not fit this repository, and the change you then made to LAB_WORK/skills/trace-request/SKILL.md, with what you saw when you used the changed skill on the same request. If the skill did not trigger, change its description first. Point skill.transfer in agent-capabilities.yaml at the record and check it from the course root:

    sh uv run --locked python capstone/context-workshop/student/transfer_check.py LAB_WORK/skills/trace-request/SKILL.md LAB_WORK/skill-transfer.yaml

    It reads both files as data. It checks that the record is complete and agrees with your skill, never whether the skill fired or traced well. 7. Test when it triggers (45 minutes). Fill trigger-test.yaml. Write at least three requests that should load your skill, worded the way people ask (do not name the skill), and at least one near miss that sounds similar but needs something else, such as a request verify-change should answer. Set should_trigger and write your predicted value for every prompt before you observe anything. Then observe with one of two routes and record which in observer and observer_detail: - peer (the template's default): a classmate who sees only the two skills' names and descriptions, then one prompt at a time, and says which skill they would load, or none. - agent, when your course provides an approved agent that loads SKILL.md skills: install both verify-change and your skill where that agent looks for skills. Use a fresh session per prompt and record whether it loaded your skill.

Both routes earn the same feedback. If any observed value differs from should_trigger, change the description once, observe only those prompts again and record the result under revision. The feedback checks that your record is complete and consistent; it does not reward or penalize what the observer chose. Run the skill_check.py command again until it reports no problems. Its advisory table lists the words each prompt shares with your description; a should-trigger prompt that shares none is a common reason a skill never fires.

docs.title: Part C: a tool server an agent can use
docs.text:
The supplied server exposes ci-dashboard records through four tools. protocol.py is the course scaffold: it speaks the stdio protocol, checks every call's arguments against the tool's published inputSchema (including enum, minimum, maximum, required and additionalProperties), fills schema defaults, limits each session to 12 accepted calls a minute and turns an unexpected exception into a structured error. Leave it unchanged. tool_behavior.py is a working first draft for you to revise. ci_snapshot.json is a small synthetic export with ci-dashboard's projects, pipelines, builds and build statuses. The exact contract is in SPEC.en.md.

An agent chooses and calls tools from their names, schemas and descriptions alone, so review the draft against five rules:

  1. Put every limit in the schema. Write the allowed statuses as "enum": [...]: the scaffold rejects any other value before your code runs, and the agent can read the full list of valid values. A limit stated only in the description is invisible to that check. When the two disagree, the agent meets rejections that nothing it read accounts for.
  2. Return only what the next step needs. Hand back the fields an agent will use, not the stored record. Every extra field is paid for again at each later step, and mirroring the storage layout breaks your tool when that layout changes. If you cut a list short, say so.
  3. Report a failure as a result the agent can read. Return a structured error naming what failed and whether trying again could succeed: an unknown ID fails every time, a rate limit clears. A raw exception gives the agent nothing to act on; a structured error tells it whether a retry is worth making.
  4. Say what comes back and where each input comes from. State what each tool returns and which tool produces each ID it accepts ("the pipeline_id returned by list_pipelines"), so the agent can call them in sequence. Guidance that spans several tools goes in the server INSTRUCTIONS.

  5. Guard every irreversible action. Mark the read-only tools with readOnlyHint: true. Give the irreversible tool destructiveHint: true and a dry_run argument that defaults to true, so a call that leaves it out only previews the effect.

  6. Review the draft (30 minutes). Before running anything, list in your work record which rule each part of the draft breaks and what an agent would do wrong because of it. Then run the public check and compare its report with your list:

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace LAB_WORK -- python -B public_check.py

It checks the hook and the static half of rules 1, 4 and 5 through tools/list. It cannot see rules 2 and 3 or the brake's behavior; those need calls.

Optional: watch an agent use your server (about 15 minutes, not in the estimate). server_replay.py gives your server one request: "Cancel the running build on the unit-tests pipeline. An old ticket gives its build_id as 103." The agent is a short course-written policy, not a model; its six rules are listed in the script. For the draft, predict whether the agent carries an ID from a result into its next call, recovers when the ticket's ID is wrong, and previews before it cancels. Then run:

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace LAB_WORK -- python -B server_replay.py --summary

On the draft, the first call cancels build 103, which had already passed, and the running build keeps running; the last line gives the three observations. Run it again after step 9, and once with --ticket-id 999, and mark each prediction confirmed or refuted. The policy reads only the field names in the contract and never sends a bad argument, so it shows what your result shapes, errors and brake allow, not how a model reads your schemas and descriptions. It calls the scaffold inside its own process, which is why it cannot serve as your protocol test. Nothing in feedback reads its output. 9. Revise the tools (120 minutes). Edit tool_behavior.py until the server meets the contract. Keep the tool names and read data only from the store the scaffold passes in: feedback runs your server against a different snapshot with the same shape. Change one rule at a time and rerun the public check. Ask for feedback once your schemas pass, before you start on shaping and errors. 10. Test through the protocol (45 minutes). Write test_protocol.py: start protocol.py as a subprocess (from the test file's own directory), send JSON-RPC lines, read the responses and assert on them. Cover at least one chain (list_pipelines to search_builds to get_build), one error with its retryable value, and the brake (omitting dry_run previews and leaves the build running). Importing tool_behavior and calling functions does not count: a protocol test must fail when the protocol layer is broken. The feedback runs your test against the supplied protocol.py, against a server that answers identically but is written differently, and against a broken copy of each, so assert on the responses, not on the server's source text or file digest. Run it through the launcher:

```sh
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace LAB_WORK -- python -B test_protocol.py
```

docs.title: Part D: explain
docs.text: 1. Explain and revise (45 minutes). Compare your predictions in steps 2, 7 and 8 with what you observed, including the replay if you ran it. Explain one useful context fact, one limitation of the two-observation experiment, the trigger prompt you predicted wrongly and why, and the rule whose fix changed the most agent-visible behavior. Discuss feedback and revise once.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text: Keep the project-list map with its commit, the two context packets (reference the fixed task and context.py), the generated ab-report.json and ab-report.en.md with their two traces, both boundary results, skills/trace-request/ with its three before/after lines, trigger-test.yaml, skill-transfer.yaml, your revised tool_behavior.py, test_protocol.py with its launcher output, the replay output if you ran it, and your short independent explanation. Keep agent-capabilities.yaml pointing at these files. Use the existing work record. The teaching team keeps the controller receipt separately; do not place private receipts or unrelated conversations in your work. Incomplete runs stay incomplete.

docs.title: Work record outline
docs.text:
Project-list map (step 1): commit, labelled arrows, branches, open question and test,
  bounded edit and prediction, peer challenge and whether the arrow held -> TODO
Context facts checked against the starter app, prediction, FAKE pair (steps 2, 4) -> TODO
Hook results and why both matter (step 3) -> TODO
Skill: three before/after lines from using it on ci-dashboard (step 6) -> TODO
Skill on your candidate contribution project: misfit and change (step 6) -> skill-transfer.yaml
Trigger test: predicted vs observed, and the revision if any (step 7) -> TODO
Draft review: rule broken -> what an agent would do wrong (step 8) -> TODO
Optional replay: predictions, draft and revised observations (steps 8, 9) -> TODO or none
Protocol test output from the launcher (step 10) -> TODO
Explanation and one revision after feedback (step 11) -> TODO
Predicted and actual hours -> TODO
AI-use note ID -> E-01

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
Check Points Context output has the three sections and fits 2,000 characters 10 SKILL.md structure: name, description with "when", steps, judgement, verification 10 Trigger test and candidate-project run recorded completely and consistently 10 Tools discovered and chained correctly on unseen data 10 Rule 1: schema constraints, and the handlers accept exactly what the schema says 10 Rule 2: documented fields only, bounded size, truncation reported 10 Rule 3: structured errors with the right retryable value, and the call allowance 10 Rule 4: descriptions name ID sources, agree with the schema; server instructions 5 Rule 5: annotations, dry_run default, preview leaves state, commit changes it 10 Your protocol test passes, and fails when the protocol layer is broken 5 Hook allows the ordinary edit and rejects every unsafe event 5 A/B report complete with controller evidence 5

These points show which checks pass; the workshop has no separate course mark and its evidence counts towards M0. A higher model pass rate is not required, and the trigger check never rewards what the observer happened to choose. Feedback calls the files your manifest declares, so relocated files earn the same points; it runs your server on a different snapshot, so answers recorded from ci_snapshot.json earn nothing. See the syllabus for the portfolio and project allocation. The optional extension has the HTTP adapter and the three-pair comparison; it adds no requirement.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text:
• Green: context text, the skill body, tool revisions and the protocol test may use approved assistance. Generated code and commands run only through the launcher.
  • Yellow: if an agent is your trigger observer, record what the session actually did; never fill observed from what a model says it would do.
  • Red: write the predictions (steps 2, 7, 8) and the final explanation yourself.

Attach one AI-use note to the work and reuse its ID:

E-01: tool/model and purpose, or "none"; what I verified myself; evidence references.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: About ten hours: Part A 2 h 45 min, Part B about three hours, Part C 3 h 15 min, Part D 45 min. These are planning estimates for Week 3, not limits. Record your predicted and actual time in the existing calibration log. Ask for help at the first boundary check, after your schemas pass, or whenever the plan stops fitting.

docs.title: Capability contract, version 2
docs.text:
agent-capabilities.yaml is the one discovery file. Feedback reads its own copy of agent-capabilities.schema.json, skill_check.py and tool_rules.py; changing the copies in your workspace changes no check. All entries are relative regular files inside your workspace: no symlinks, parent traversal, private paths, credentials or host mounts. An entry's location is free, so files moved into an adapter directory earn the same feedback. Entries cannot start with a dot. The launcher refuses any directory named grader or instructor anywhere in your workspace.

Capability Manifest key How it is checked Context context.entry python -B ENTRY exits 0 and prints at most 2,000 Unicode characters with nonempty ## Project, ## Commands and ## Boundaries sections, in that order Skill skill.entry, skill.triggers, skill.transfer Read as data with skill_check.py and transfer_check.py; see Skill Tool server mcp.entry Started as python -B ENTRY in the launcher and driven over stdio by an MCP client; see The four tools Protocol test tests.entry python -B ENTRY exits 0 against your server and against an equivalent server written differently, and exits nonzero when only the stdio tools/call path of either one is broken Hook hook.entry python -B ENTRY EVENT_JSON exits 0 for before_write of src/new.py and 2 for traversal, absolute host paths and hidden environment files A/B ab.entry The fixed pair (or the optional three pairs), each once without and once with context, matching profile, configuration and controller evidence

Every capability also names an evidence file, normally explanation.en.md.

docs.title: Skill
docs.text:
SKILL.md starts with YAML front matter between two --- lines:

  • name: 1-64 lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, equal to the directory name, and not verify-change (the course example).
  • description: 1-1,024 characters, at least eight words, containing "when".
  • Optional fields: license, compatibility, metadata, allowed-tools. No others.

The body has at most 500 lines and contains ## Steps (at least two list items), ## Judgement (at least one decision: "if", "unless" or "when") and ## Verification (an exact command or check in backticks). A link to a local file is relative to the skill directory (notes.md or ./notes.md), stays inside it and names a file that exists there. A body copied from the course example fails. LF or CRLF line endings and a leading byte-order mark are all accepted.

trigger-test.yaml records one observation round:

  • skill equals the skill's name; observer is agent or peer; observer_detail says which tool and model, or who, made the selection.
  • prompts has 4-12 entries, each with exactly id, prompt, should_trigger, predicted and observed. Ids and prompts are distinct; a prompt is 1-300 characters and does not paste the description.
  • At least three should-trigger prompts do not contain the skill's name, written with hyphens, spaces, underscores or nothing between its words; at least one prompt is a near miss with should_trigger: false.
  • If any observed differs from should_trigger, revision has a nonempty description_change and rechecked lists exactly those prompt ids with their new observed value.

skill-transfer.yaml records one read-only run of the skill on your candidate contribution project, or on a listed repository if you have no candidate yet:

  • skill equals the skill's name.
  • repository has url, commit (the full 40-character SHA you exported), license (the SPDX ID of an OSI-approved licence; transfer_check.py lists every accepted ID), license_file (inside one of paths), paths (the relative paths you passed to git archive, no .git) and files (1-200), and optionally route.
  • url is a plain https:// URL with a host name and at least an owner and a name: no credentials, port, query, fragment or ./.. parts, not an IP address (in any notation) and not a name reserved for examples, tests or local networks. No path part may start with ci-dashboard or agentic-se-course: neither your own project nor the course materials, nor a renamed copy of them, counts.
  • route is public when left out; then url is a public repository on any forge, outside the course organization.
  • route: course-hosted is for students on the course-hosted contribution route; then url is the course practice repository you were given, which may be non-public and may sit in the course organization.
  • request is the request you traced (1-200 characters).
  • run.route is agent or self, with run.detail. The agent route also records prompt (1-300 characters, not naming the skill) and triggered (true or false, as observed); the self route records nothing else.
  • traced lists at least two distinct steps, each a file inside paths and a symbol.
  • misfit has a nonempty step and observed.
  • change has part (description, steps, judgement or verification), before, after and recheck; after differs from before and appears in the submitted SKILL.md. If triggered is false, part is description.

Feedback checks these records' structure and consistency. It does not judge whether the observer chose correctly or whether the skill traced well, and no model output is used to compute it. The trigger test and the transfer record together earn one item.

docs.title: The four tools
docs.text:
The scaffold reads ci_snapshot.json beside the server entry. Feedback replaces that file with a different snapshot of the same shape (other IDs, branches and messages), so read records only from the store argument. Every result is one JSON object in one text content block.

Tool Arguments Success result list_pipelines none {"pipelines": [{"pipeline_id", "title", "enabled"}]} in ascending pipeline_id order search_builds pipeline_id (integer, required), status (one of passed, failed, canceled, running), limit (integer 1-20, default 5) {"builds": [{"build_id", "branch", "status", "attempt", "started_at"}], "total", "truncated"} get_build build_id (integer, required) {"build_id", "pipeline_id", "branch", "status", "attempt", "started_at", "summary"} cancel_build build_id (integer, required), dry_run (boolean, default true) Preview: {"dry_run": true, "would_cancel": {"build_id", "pipeline_id", "branch", "status"}}. Commit: {"dry_run": false, "canceled": {"build_id", "status": "canceled"}}
  • search_builds returns the pipeline's builds newest first (by started_at, then higher build_id), filtered by status when given. total counts every match before the limit; truncated is true when fewer builds are shown than total.
  • summary is the first line of the build's message, cut to 120 characters. Logs, runner details and artifacts are never returned.
  • Size bounds, counted as the UTF-8 bytes of the result's text block: a get_build result is at most 400 bytes; a search_builds result is at most 60 + 160 × n bytes, where n is the number of builds it returns. Results with exactly the fields above fit.
  • cancel_build changes state only when dry_run is false. A build that is not running cannot be canceled, in a preview or a commit.
  • Each tool sets additionalProperties: false, describes every argument, and names where each ID comes from: pipeline_id from list_pipelines, build_id from search_builds. The three readers carry annotations.readOnlyHint: true; cancel_build carries readOnlyHint: false and destructiveHint: true.
  • INSTRUCTIONS describes the workflow across tools and mentions list_pipelines, search_builds and dry_run. A description must not state a status or a limit that the schema does not have.

Errors use one shape, sent with isError: true:

{"error": {"code": "not_found", "retryable": false, "message": "No such build; ..."}}
Code When retryable invalid_argument Arguments break the published schema (the scaffold reports these) false not_found An unknown pipeline_id or build_id false conflict cancel_build on a build that is not running false rate_limited More than 12 accepted calls in a minute in one session (the scaffold adds retry_after_s) true internal Your handler raised or returned a non-object (the scaffold reports these) false

The message is 1-300 characters, says what to do next where it can, and never contains a traceback. Keep stdout for protocol messages only and do not open network ports. The scaffold is a teaching subset of MCP, not a complete implementation; feedback drives it with the course's locked MCP Python client inside the launcher, which bounds input, output and lifetime. A hang or an oversized session voids all tool-server feedback, because no session completed within its bounds.

docs.title: A/B report
docs.text:
The A/B task is API-context retrieval: generate one JSON request-plan value and verify it against the public app contract. It does not measure patch-generation quality. The expected values are public in ab_tasks.json so the comparison is reproducible. Never describe these course-authored observations as industry statistics or a representative benchmark. Report failures, including ties or worse results with context.

ab_run.py runs only inside the launcher and uses sandbox_model.chat; the broker calls course_llm outside your workspace. ab_collect.py is the course controller on the host: it owns profile resolution, trace metrics, report assembly and the receipt. The report stores the resolved profile ID, version and digest, the frozen sampling configuration, task and context digests, paired pass flags, token counts, configured cost and latency, bound to one minimal course_llm trace per observation. Answer checking strips one leading <think>...</think> block and an optional whole-answer Markdown fence, then accepts an exact {"value": ...} object or a bare scalar of the expected type and value. It never searches prose for a correct substring or executes model text.

A JSON or schema check cannot prove where a file was produced, so the teaching team keeps the controller receipt outside your workspace and passes it to the feedback run. Copying or editing your own receipt does not establish provenance. A missing receipt leaves only the A/B item unverified; other verified capabilities keep their points.

docs.title: Explain your work
docs.text:
Keep these short answers with the work product and verification results.

  • Which files and functions decide what GET /domains/ci_dashboard/ shows at your commit? Name one branch the route function alone hides, the arrow a classmate or TA challenged and whether it held, and your bounded edit.
  • What did you predict context would change for the starter application's health question, and why? Say what the FAKE pair showed about the workflow and why it cannot confirm or refute that prediction.
  • How did you verify the supplied hook? Show the allowed edit and rejected traversal, and explain why the hook does not replace the sandbox.
  • Which other ci-dashboard request did you trace with your skill? Give three lines: what you did by hand, what the skill made you do differently, and the step you changed after using it and what the recheck showed.
  • What did your skill assume that the open-source repository did not do? Quote the step before and after your change and say what the recheck showed.
  • Which trigger prompt did you predict wrongly, if any? Quote your description before and after any revision and say which words made the difference.
  • Which rule did the draft tool server break in the way most likely to mislead an agent? Show the call and response before and after your change.
  • What does test_protocol.py check that public_check.py cannot?
  • What did feedback reveal, and what changed after one revision?
  • AI-use note E-01: state no AI, or the actual tool/model and purposes. Reuse E-01 elsewhere.
  • Unaided reflection: describe one prediction error, its evidence, and a next improvement.

Replace the prompts with your own concise answers. Do not include keys, personal data, unrelated chats or author/reviewer metadata.

docs.title: Label service
docs.text:
This course-authored Flask app has a health check at GET /healthz. POST /labels accepts exactly one JSON field, label. Invalid labels return status 422 and {"error":{"code":"invalid_input"}}. Valid labels return {"label":"normalized-label"}.

In the workshop, read this app in step 2 to choose context for the fixed health question and check each fact against app.py. Step 1 maps ci-dashboard, not this app, and no normalization implementation is required.

For the optional extension, complete label_behavior.py in the parent directory. Trim leading/trailing spaces, lowercase ASCII letters, and join words separated by spaces with one hyphen. The input must have 1-32 characters before trimming and consist only of ASCII letters, digits and spaces; at least one letter or digit is required. Reject all other inputs. The HTTP adapter uses this behavior.

Use the HTTP preparation and launcher commands in the optional extension. check_app.py uses Flask's in-process test client; no HTTP server needs to be exposed. The app defaults to loopback with debug disabled. The workshop's tool server is separate and does not use Flask.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text: Use your ci-dashboard repository to complete two safe discovery activities, choose one bounded need, write executable acceptance criteria, and verify the first implementation for M0 (LO3). Use the synthetic persona route when real discovery is unavailable; it has the same learning outcome and evidence ceiling.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:

docs.title: Discovery workshop: write and freeze an executable M0 specification
Objectives
docs.text:
Work independently in your supplied ci-dashboard repository. Use two small discovery activities to choose one useful, bounded need, write an executable specification, and check the first implementation with independent tests (LO3). The resulting specification and acceptance evidence stay in M0 and travel with the same repository into the later project workshops.

Keep a short personal work record for your decisions and verification, but do not create a second submission or a separate workshop mark. Personal understanding is checked through the course's independent components and defense.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Read Week 0 setup and the project kit. Use a fresh copy of the public student/ bundle inside your ci-dashboard workspace. Never copy the instructor, grader, Git metadata, caches, credentials, participant records, or a complete private checkout.

Run generated code, tests, and model requests through the approved route in Week 0 setup. Do not put credentials, raw prompt logs, or participant material in the repository.

docs.title: Discovery input and privacy
docs.text:
The default first-run input is the two supplied, clearly marked synthetic personas. They are teaching material, not evidence of real users. You may instead use two new or reused activities only when the teacher has checked the current notice, consent or approved equivalent, scope, de-identification, withdrawal state, and accessibility route. Keep only opaque activity IDs and the teacher's confirmation reference in interviews/index.yaml. Do not copy names, contact details, signatures, raw audio/video, quotes, identifying combinations, or unrelated sensitive details.

Participant material, including de-identified notes and derived quotes, must never be sent to a model. You may send your own problem statement, hypotheses, acceptance criteria, and test code through the approved broker when permitted by the course policy; refer to an activity by ID only. If an activity is withdrawn, stop using it, remove its notes and derived references, and replace it through the same route. A refusal or withdrawal never lowers the available M0 ceiling.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Choose a bounded need. Enter your ci-dashboard checkout and use the repository-context workshop's call-path map. Choose one user-visible behavior, one non-goal, and an independent expected result. Record the decision in the existing work record.
  2. Prepare the activities. Use the two synthetic personas, or the two teacher-approved activities, and fill the two note templates yourself. Keep observations separate from assumptions. Complete interviews/index.yaml with the format below; each row must have a unique activity ID, source, current notice/confirmation references, de-identification status, and scope.
  3. Write the specification. Fill spec/feature.en.md with the problem, target users, non-goals, risks, and at least three independent Given/When/Then acceptance criteria. Every criterion names exactly one [interview:ACTIVITY-ID] from the index. State boundary cases and the expected result a reviewer can check.
  4. Review the boundary. Ask the approved model for a bounded review of one concrete input/output example, including equality, zero, and a rejected or unavailable case where relevant. Mark each finding confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with your own evidence, or ask a TA to check it when model review is unavailable. Send only your own criterion and example; never send participant notes, quotes, or descriptions of what a participant said or did. Resolve one ambiguity in the same specification and record what changed and why.
  5. Implement and verify. Ask for a bounded candidate through the approved hosted route or labelled FAKE mode, inspect the diff, and implement the chosen behavior in your ci-dashboard branch. Add at least five distinct acceptance tests that can fail for different reasons and check them against the specification yourself or with a TA. Run the M0 smoke command below and retain its observed result. Record the additional acceptance suite as not executed until a reviewed test action is supplied; identify an additional edge case not used as an example and its expected result.
  6. Hand off to M0. Keep the map, two activity records, specification, tests, result, short explanation, and one AI-use note together in your M0 evidence. You should be able to reproduce the checks from a clean public checkout.

docs.title: Activity index
docs.text:
The index deliberately accepts JSON-compatible YAML only (no aliases, tags, or duplicate keys). The row order matches interview-1.en.md and interview-2.en.md.

{"activities": [
  {"activity_id": "L3-A01", "source": "controlled_persona",
   "notice_version": "L3-PRACTICE-V1", "confirmation_ref": "SYN-C01",
   "deidentified": true, "scope": "discovery-workshop", "current": true,
   "persona_id": "L3-P1-V1"},
  {"activity_id": "L3-A02", "source": "controlled_persona",
   "notice_version": "L3-PRACTICE-V1", "confirmation_ref": "SYN-C02",
   "deidentified": true, "scope": "discovery-workshop", "current": true,
   "persona_id": "L3-P2-V1"}
]}

The supplied values are synthetic references. Do not copy them as teacher confirmations. For new_live or m0_reuse, use the opaque references supplied by the teacher and set persona_id to null. The same activity may support M0 and this workshop when the teacher has checked that the original scope still applies; do not count one activity twice inside this pair.

docs.title: Optional warm-up
docs.text: The starter app/ contains the bounded arithmetic interface remaining(capacity, requested). The acceptance/test_acceptance.py file is a blank starting point for this warm-up's tests; add at least five tests using the literal assertion form described in its docstring. Use it only as a ten-minute rehearsal of writing a failing and a passing test when your teacher enables the warm-up. It is not your M0 feature, does not replace discovery, and does not create a separate score. Your feature and its checks belong in the ci-dashboard workspace.

docs.title: Generate, then verify safely
docs.text:
The optional generator requests only a synthetic interface proposal; it does not read the interview notes and does not replace your own M0 implementation. Use the profile, version, and digest printed by Week 0. Until the hosted route is enabled in this checkout, use the following command for deterministic FAKE practice:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace m0-work --model fake --output m0-proposal -- python generate.py

Record this run as FAKE, not a real-model observation or a teacher-frozen replay. For the no-key replay route, follow Week 0 setup. Inspect candidate.txt before adapting any code; never execute exported code on the host.

For the optional warm-up, run its acceptance checks through the same launcher:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace m0-work -- python verify.py

For M0, copy the public ci-dashboard checkout into m0-work and run its own locked smoke launcher. The checkout's launch.py uses the teacher-provided course-legacy-runtime:local image; from the copied project directory, run:

(cd m0-work && python3 -I launch.py smoke)

This smoke command is the runnable execution check for M0. Keep your additional acceptance tests in ci-dashboard, check them against the specification, and record them as not executed until a reviewed test action is supplied. The optional verify.py script checks only the arithmetic warm-up; its output does not establish that the M0 feature passes acceptance.

docs.text: Plan about five hours for your discovery work, including setup, two activities, criteria, implementation, verification, feedback, and one revision. Reused discovery time counts once. This is a planning estimate, not a cap; if you go over it, ask for help first. You are never marked down for exceeding it. Record predicted and actual time in the existing calibration log. Ask for help when a privacy check, boundary check, or launcher failure blocks you.

docs.title: Original synthetic course exercise: L3-DISCOVERY-V1
docs.text:
Every role and event in personas.json is invented for this teaching exercise. There are no real participants, approvals, user-research findings, or restricted assets in this package. Keep version L3-DISCOVERY-V1 and IDs L3-P1-V1/L3-P2-V1 fixed when citing the package.

Use both roles for your two discovery activities. Act as interviewer and note taker yourself: read one event, ask what happened previously, and inspect the supplied obstacle and counterexample before forming a hypothesis. Repeat with the other role. The persona file supplies the answers; do not ask anyone to supply personal experiences. Any real personal data or participation still needs the applicable notice and consent. Do not invent an AI conversation and call it a real interview.

Ask "What happened on the last request?", "What did you do when the form rejected it?" and "Which outcome would show that our interpretation was wrong?" If the script does not answer a question, record it as unknown. Manually write your notes, separating what the script says from your explanation. Generate a requirement hypothesis, then verify it against a counterexample and an executable input/output pair.

This text route supports practice when recruitment fails, private data would be exposed, or a synchronous/audio activity is inaccessible. It requires no audio, timed interaction, personal disclosure or purchase. Actual reasonable accommodations and formal equivalence approval remain teacher decisions. Use this route for formal work only after the teacher has approved the arrangement and its equivalence. All three discovery sources use the same specification and verification standard.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Use Week 0 setup and the week 10 activity. That activity identifies the public starter files and exact supported launcher commands. Copy only public files into a new workspace.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
Define request/environment/stop/score, verify a code scorer, compare your labels with the teaching team's private anchor set, calibrate a judge and run the evaluator's local regression gate.

Use the supplied student bundle and evaluator kit. Label the supplied 30-case anchor-cases.json independently, submit the matching human.json once for comparison with the private teaching anchor set, freeze the development/holdout split before tuning, verify the code scorer and keep the calibration and local-gate evidence in the same M2 repository. The teaching team retains item-level anchor labels and recording provenance; FAKE replays only verify the pipeline.
