docs.title: Legacy code repository
docs.text: The course uses ci-dashboard and its shared _base scaffold. Keep seeded defects and reference fixes within the instructor isolation boundary. Other product domains remain available only in Git history and are not teaching options.

docs.title: CI Dashboard API and Starting Points for Executable Specifications
docs.text: This document describes target product behaviour and public data formats. It is not a complete acceptance test suite. When taking over the application, establish independent expectations for small inputs, compare actual behaviour, record discrepancies and verify repairs.

docs.title: Sessions and common rules
docs.text:
Domain routes have the fixed prefix /domains/ci_dashboard. /login, /register, /logout and /profile use the shared application. Except for login and registration pages, domain functions require a valid local session. POST forms include the session's hidden csrf field. Templates automatically escape page and text results.

The application bounds request bodies. The UTF-8 representation of the JSON payload field is limited to 12000 bytes. Duplicate JSON keys, non-finite numbers, wrong types and unknown build fields are rejected. Error responses do not reflect raw import content.

  • 400: invalid fields, method parameters or fixture target.
  • 401: no valid session.
  • 404: the record does not exist or does not belong to the current account.
  • 302: a successful form operation redirects to a fixed local page.

Identifiers are positive integers. Descriptions, diagnostics, branches and external IDs are text. Text resembling commands, URLs or paths does not instruct the application to execute anything, access a network or open a file.

docs.title: Projects and pipelines
docs.text:
Method Relative path Behaviour GET / List the current account's projects GET / POST /projects/new Create a project using title and description GET /projects/<id> Project overview, pipelines, builds and summaries GET / POST /projects/<id>/edit Update descriptive fields without transferring ownership POST /projects/<id>/archive Toggle archived display status while retaining history GET / POST /projects/<id>/pipelines/new Create a pipeline; accepts only title POST /pipelines/<id>/toggle Toggle pipeline status without running a script

Project titles allow at most 120 characters and descriptions 1000. A pipeline belongs to a fixed project. The server must check cross-account reads and changes; hiding a button is not an authorization check.

docs.title: Build samples and imports
docs.text:
GET /sample?seed=7&count=12&pipeline_id=1 returns synthetic samples. seed accepts 0–2147483647 and count accepts 1–30. Identical parameters must produce identical JSON. The generator reads no system clock, real CI environment, credentials or external service.

POST /import accepts a form field named payload containing:

{
  "target": "fixture",
  "builds": [
    {
      "external_id": "synthetic-run-1",
      "pipeline_id": 1,
      "branch": "main",
      "status": "failed",
      "started_at": "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z",
      "duration_ms": 1200,
      "attempt": 1,
      "message": "compile failed file=widget.py line=12"
    }
  ]
}
Field Constraint target Exactly fixture; not a URL, filename or webhook builds 1–30 records; validate the entire batch before writing external_id Nonempty text, at most 80 characters; identity is scoped to the pipeline pipeline_id Positive integer ID of a pipeline owned by the current account branch Nonempty, case-sensitive text, at most 80 characters status passed, failed, canceled or running started_at UTC seconds, strictly YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ duration_ms Integer from 0 to 86400000, in milliseconds attempt Integer from 1 to 100, identifying a retry of the same external build message Nonempty diagnostic text, at most 300 characters

For duplicate pipeline/external-ID pairs, retain the greatest attempt number. If the same attempt is imported again, use the later-arriving record. Invalid fields or a pipeline outside the current account must prevent every row in the batch from being saved.

GET /projects/<id>/export returns the current records as JSON using the fixed filename synthetic-builds.json. It omits internal row IDs and retains target: fixture. The application does not create a user-named output file. Check the destination pipeline's identity scope before importing the export again.

docs.title: Report workbench
docs.text:
GET /explore opens the form. POST takes operation and JSON payload, displaying the result as escaped text. The programmatic entry POST /report/<operation> takes the same payload field and returns JSON. A fixed table selects report code; operation names are not used in imports, file paths or command construction.

These are target calculation semantics. Create independent verification inputs when taking over the application.

Report Additional parameters Output and semantics success_rate project_id passed, total, percent; denominator includes only passed/failed; percentage is null when no completed builds exist duration project_id seconds array and mean_seconds; divide raw milliseconds by 1000; mean is null for an empty set latest project_id Compare start time, attempt number and external ID in that order; return the latest external_id, or null for an empty set branch_filter project_id, branch Stable-order ids; literal, case-sensitive branch matching cluster project_id Failed builds only; cluster diagnostic text after normalizing line=<digits> threshold project_id, threshold due=true when failure count reaches the threshold; threshold is 1–100 pagination project_id, page, size Pages start at 1, with 1–30 records per page; return ids and total count; adjacent pages do not overlap daily project_id Count by explicit UTC date, listing only dates actually present failure_streak project_id Count consecutive failures backwards from the latest completed record; success ends the streak; ignore canceled/running records

Similar diagnostics do not establish identical causes. A cluster count is not a repair count, and rule triggers are not a notification-delivery success rate. The product handles local fixtures only.

docs.title: Local-account helper reports
docs.text:
Report Parameters Target behaviour search query Literal substring search of the current account's project titles access project_id Accessible project's ID, title and owner; null when inaccessible artifact name Query the current synthetic account's virtual archive; default build.txt; no filesystem access fingerprint value, optional salt Fingerprint a synthetic phrase; default salt is random and process-local receipt message, signature Check a local notification signature without delivering anything receipt_record notification_id Verify a saved notification's signature in the current account's database

The optional fingerprint salt is solely for reproducible synthetic inputs: 16 bytes represented as 32 hexadecimal characters. Do not use these demonstration passwords or receipt interfaces for real authentication. The artifact archive is an in-memory synthetic mapping; it never opens host logs, mount points or submitter-provided files.

docs.title: Notification rules
docs.text:
GET /projects/<id>/rules displays rules and notification records. POST takes payload:

{"threshold":2,"target":"fixture"}

POST /rules/<id>/toggle toggles a rule. POST /projects/<id>/notify, with the form field target=fixture, evaluates enabled rules against current builds and records notifications. It returns the notification ID and message, retaining the signature in the current database for receipt_record verification. There is no retry delivery, external queue or DNS.

docs.title: Individual failure investigation
docs.text:
GET /projects/<id>/builds supports branch, status, page and size filters. GET /builds/<id> shows raw diagnostics and neighbouring records from the same pipeline.

POST the following fields to the build-detail endpoint:

  • classification: unknown, source, test, environment or dependency.
  • explanation: nonempty hypothesis and evidence, at most 2000 characters.
  • verification: nonempty verification steps and observations, at most 2000 characters.
  • resolved: text 0 or 1, representing only the investigator's recorded disposition.

GET /projects/<id>/triage summarizes failures and their disposition. A resolved label records the investigator's judgement; it does not show that a defect is fixed or secure. Importing a replacement build creates a new internal row and deletes investigation records belonging to the old row. Export evidence or record it in the course decision log before replacement when history must be preserved.

docs.title: Offline JSON conversation transport
docs.text:
protocol.py sends a bounded number of local form requests to the same application inside the course isolation environment. Each run creates clean synthetic data, executes requests in order and deletes the directory. It has no expected-answer or repair-status fields.

{
  "actions": [
    {"method":"POST","path":"/login","data":{"username":"demo","password":"CHANGEME"}},
    {"method":"GET","path":"/domains/ci_dashboard/projects/1/export","data":{}}
  ]
}

Only GET/POST and local paths are allowed; data keys and values must be strings. The transport obtains the actual session CSRF value for each form. At most 40 actions are allowed, and requests remain subject to the 12000-byte object limit. Each result-array entry contains status and json. HTML responses have null json and no page body.

Students must still execute through the course launcher or instructor's isolated workbench; the transport script is not a host execution entry point. Instructor detection expectations, scanner configuration and signing material stay out of this transport. An exception or nonzero exit does not establish successful repair.

docs.title: JSON Schemas and generator command
docs.text:
build-import.schema.json describes the public import structure; conversation.schema.json describes local conversation transport. Schemas cannot verify database ownership, whether calendar dates actually exist or the request's total UTF-8 byte count. The application must enforce those constraints. An editor accepting the structure does not establish business acceptance.

Generate samples in the same format through the course launcher:

python3 -I launch.py sample --seed 7 --count 12

A missing explicit seed or out-of-range value returns an error instead of using system randomness. Output contains synthetic JSON only. Save it, check the schema and destination pipeline, then import and verify record counts and statistics.

docs.title: Data Model and Migration Discipline
docs.text: All data is synthetic teaching data. Runtime output stays in the designated workspace's data_dir. SQLite connections enable foreign keys and use memory for temporary SQL storage. The source root accepts neither dynamic import configuration nor external database connection strings.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
erDiagram
    users ||--o{ ci_dashboard_projects : owns
    ci_dashboard_projects ||--o{ ci_dashboard_pipelines : contains
    ci_dashboard_pipelines ||--o{ ci_dashboard_builds : records
    ci_dashboard_projects ||--o{ ci_dashboard_rules : configures
    ci_dashboard_projects ||--o{ ci_dashboard_notifications : records
    ci_dashboard_builds ||--o| ci_dashboard_triage : explains
    users ||--o{ ci_dashboard_imports : imports

docs.title: Identity and boundaries
docs.text:
User identity comes from the server-side session. Forms cannot override project ownership. Pipeline, build, notification-rule and investigation operations follow the relationship chain back to the project owner. External build IDs cannot overwrite one another across pipelines.

SQLite assigns internal row IDs; they are not timestamps. External times are explicit UTC strings. Attempt numbers distinguish repeated imports of the same external build; they are not a global sequence for the entire pipeline.

Descriptions and investigation records are plain text. Diagnostics must not become template source, SQL structure or process commands. Write negative tests for these boundaries as well as tests using ordinary strings.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
A Domain registers fixed routes, a tuple of SQL migrations and a fixture callback. Migration versions increase from 1. Released migrations are append-only and cannot be rewritten. The framework records applied migrations by (domain, version). Each migration runs in a transaction; a failure must roll back rather than load fixtures into a partial schema.

legacy_app owns shared user, record and migration tables. Domain tables use the ci_dashboard_ prefix. Migrations must not execute ATTACH, read or write external files, load dynamic extensions or control nested transactions.

Before adding a table, describe its entities, ownership chain and deletion semantics, then implement the migration and verification. At minimum, verify fresh initialization, repeated initialization, migration of an existing database, rollback on failure and that JOIN changes do not broaden read or write permissions.

docs.title: Raw records and derived results
docs.text:
The database retains raw build durations in milliseconds, UTC times, statuses, branches, attempts and diagnostics. Success rates, daily distributions, clusters and failure streaks are computed on demand. Importers cannot override calculations with a supplied correct-result field.

Investigation records contain the investigator's explanation and verification process, stored separately from raw status. resolved is an application disposition flag; it is not a course grade, vulnerability waiver or deployment permission. Notification records also do not establish successful external delivery.

Import logs retain only the account, record count and fixed fixture origin, without host paths, API tokens or raw request logs. Replacing a build with a retry cascades deletion of its old investigation record through the foreign key, preventing attachment to the wrong record.

docs.title: Backup, replay and minimization
docs.text:
The launcher deletes data after each run. To retain evidence across sessions, use the export response in the instructor's isolated workbench and record minimal synthetic inputs and observations in the course workspace. Do not broaden host mounts.

Fix the generator seed, sample count, pipeline mapping and import order for replay. Keeping the seed while changing input order does not establish equivalent retry handling. Generate the data, then independently calculate or assert the expected results.

Databases, caches, virtual environments, runtime logs and old ZIPs stay out of Git and course distributions. Do not send unrelated process information to instructors through a database backup. Minimize and redact submitted evidence according to course rules.

docs.title: Model capabilities and limits
docs.text:
The application neither executes pipelines nor fetches Git repositories, installs dependencies or uploads artifacts. Enabled status controls the interface and local rules; it does not enable arbitrary commands. Request and batch-size limits bound synthetic data volume. Before performance changes, establish a baseline and record the measurement environment. Use measurements rather than subjective impressions.

Begin with characterization tests, repair verifiable behaviour and then extend the model as requirements justify. Explain database, interface and statistical-semantics changes separately, keeping each change explainable, reversible and testable.

docs.title: CI Results Dashboard and Failure Investigation
docs.text: This capstone starting point is a legacy developer tool built with synchronous Flask routes, direct SQL, SQLite and server-rendered templates. It brings project pipelines, synthetic builds, failure diagnostics and notification rules into one interface. Use it to practise taking over, verifying and modernizing software. A page loading successfully does not establish that its statistics or access controls are correct.

docs.title: Product context
docs.text:
A small development team needs to identify the latest build, branches with repeated failures, recurring diagnostics, whether retries changed the result and who verified a failure's cause. This version retains raw records and provides summaries and individual investigation records. Clusters suggest where to investigate; they do not prove root causes.

Projects, pipelines and builds have separate identities. External build identifiers are unique only within their pipeline. Imports come exclusively from synthetic fixtures. The application does not connect to GitHub, GitLab, CI runners or notification platforms, and does not execute build scripts.

docs.title: Start safely
docs.text:
Complete Week 0 setup first; it shows how to check that you can run the practices and the launcher rules used throughout the course. Then obtain the instructor-prepared course-legacy-runtime:local dependency image. Use the reviewed launcher only in the separate directory distributed to students. Do not run internal tests or controllers from the instructor repository. See START.en.md for entry points and image preparation.

python3 -I launch.py smoke
python3 -I launch.py run-job

The launcher copies public source into a disposable workspace, disables external network access, publishes no ports and limits CPU, memory and processes, with an execution timeout. Each run destroys its temporary database on exit. After generating or modifying application code, run the same smoke check and record observations and failures. A smoke pass is not full acceptance evidence.

The public account demo uses the teaching password CHANGEME. The synthetic account fixture_peer uses the same password for multi-user exercises. Never enter real passwords, personal data, organization logs or CI credentials. The application listens on 127.0.0.1:5000 with debugging and automatic reload disabled. Browser interaction requires the instructor's isolated workbench; do not bypass the boundary with host networking or a different listening address.

docs.title: Complete one workflow
docs.text:
1. Sign in, open the CI dashboard and inspect the projects and pipelines.
  2. Open the sample generator from the build-import page. Fix the seed and count, save the JSON and inspect its fields before using it.
  3. Paste and import the JSON. Compare the imported count with the raw build table. An invalid field or unauthorized pipeline should reject the whole batch. After a rejected import, inspect the data again to confirm that no partial batch remains.
  4. Inspect project summaries, daily distributions and clusters. Calculate a small sample manually from raw records and compare it with the report.
  5. Browse builds by branch, status and page. Check page boundaries and duplicate records.
  6. Record a failure hypothesis, verification steps and observations in the build detail. Mark it resolved only after verification.
  7. Configure fixture notification rules and run one local evaluation. Inspect the notification records; they are written only to the current temporary database.
  8. Export JSON and check its fields and record count. The export is a response body; it does not open a user-supplied host file path.

docs.title: Maintenance backlog
docs.text:
• Add independent characterization tests for summaries, filters and boundary inputs.
  • Preserve investigation evidence; current clustering cannot prove a root cause.
  • Define import and duplicate-event contracts and verify different arrival orders.
  • Establish a behaviour baseline before upgrading old dependencies; reinstall and run regression and security checks after upgrading.
  • Verify multi-user behaviour, exceptional inputs and isolation boundaries explicitly.
  • Measure before scaling beyond the synthetic teaching data and confirm resource limits.

These directions do not enumerate defects or reveal repairs. Generate an investigation plan and executable specifications, then verify the results. Establish a baseline before asking an agent for a broad rewrite.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Path Responsibility legacy_app/ Authentication, CSRF, public records, workspace paths and database lifecycle domains/ci_dashboard.py Project, pipeline, import and notification routes domains/model.py Domain migrations, synthetic fixtures and synchronous persistence domains/inspection.py Build browsing, investigation records and report workbench domains/metrics/ Report calculations and local strategies domains/synthetic.py Seeded synthetic build generator legacy_app/templates/ci/ Keyboard-operable server-rendered pages and tabular charts protocol.py Network-free JSON conversation transport using the real application routes manage.py Initialization, serving, local jobs and the single public smoke check launch.py Safe course execution entry point

See API.en.md for interfaces and DATA.en.md for the data model and migration rules. The public application does not import instructor modules, read allocation information or detection expectations, or include external webhook clients.

docs.title: Verification and delivery
docs.text:
Submit the M1 functional baseline first, then close security items according to the course calendar. Retain expected calculations for small inputs, test results, before/after diffs, dependency-lock changes and your own explanation. For a new feature, write the specification, generate the implementation and run verification.

Add one AI-use note to this milestone's artifact, verification and explanation record; PRs reference the same evidence ID. Submit specified redacted trajectories only when the exercise needs them. Per-commit trailers and a separate disclosure file are not mandatory. Write your reflection independently as required by the course. Do not put real credentials or unauthorized logs into model prompts.

The launcher, smoke checks and the Dockerfile support local teaching execution only; do not deploy this application. A smoke pass shows that the application starts, not that it is secure. Your instructor checks M1 security repairs separately against your current code, so rerun your own verification after any source or dependency change.

docs.title: CI Dashboard: Getting Started
docs.text: This application uses synthetic data. Generate or modify code inside the isolated environment, then verify login, record lists, details and job output. The example user is demo, with the public teaching password CHANGEME. Do not enter real passwords or personal data.

docs.title: Student execution
docs.text:
Instructors first prepare and verify the course-legacy-runtime:local image, Docker service and reviewed launch.py. The image contains Python and locked dependencies, without the instructor repository, scorers, hidden tests or answers. Run the trusted launcher from the distributed application directory:

python3 -I launch.py init-db
python3 -I launch.py smoke
python3 -I launch.py run-job
python3 -I launch.py sample --seed 7 --count 12

The launcher disables networking by default, mounts only a temporary copy of this application's public source and limits CPU, memory and processes, with a 300-second timeout. It passes no host environment variables, credentials or Docker socket, and publishes no ports. Jobs write only to data/ in the temporary copy. All runtime data is destroyed at exit; inspect output in the terminal. run serves only on container loopback. Interactive browser access must use the instructor's isolated workbench; do not bypass the boundary with 0.0.0.0 or host networking. Do not execute generated code before the sandbox is ready.

Synthetic-data commands require an explicit seed. Save the generated output, check its format, then import it and verify the statistics.

docs.title: Maintainer: offline installation and native verification
docs.text:
The following commands are for maintainer-reviewed code in a designated workspace; they are not the student safety launcher. Prepare Python 3.12.13, uv 0.10.12, Make, and a dependency cache for the same platform and Python version. A connected preparation machine may run uv sync --locked --no-dev --link-mode copy --cache-dir CACHE_DIR; move that cache outside the application source when preparing an offline machine. The lock file fixes all transitive dependencies, and the cache is not source code or part of the course ZIP.

# CACHE_DIR is a teacher-provided, prewarmed dependency cache.
UV_CACHE_DIR="$CACHE_DIR" make install
make init
make smoke
make run

make install always uses --offline --locked; missing dependencies fail instead of downloading. make run uses an isolated virtual environment, disables the debugger and reloader, and listens on 127.0.0.1:5000 by default. config.toml accepts only host, port, data_dir and job_target; external addresses, unknown fields, absolute data paths, traversal and links are rejected, and .env or host configuration is not read. The session signing key is random for each process, so a restart requires signing in again.

Run make smoke with a clean application data directory; it verifies the initial synthetic data. init-db does not reset existing data; a maintainer must stop the service before explicitly backing up or resetting data. Do not commit databases, caches or virtual environments.

docs.title: Domain development
docs.text: Add trusted domain modules under domains/ and explicitly register each Domain in registered_domains() in domains/__init__.py. Routes use the /domains/<name> prefix, with separate table names and template subdirectories. Public legacy_app does not discover plugins automatically, import arbitrary configured modules or execute instructor extensions. Domain code belongs to the application's trust domain and still requires sandbox execution and independent review.

docs.title: An inert attack, a working defense and triaged scanner findings
Objectives
docs.text: Reproduce one local attack chain and preserve allowed behavior. Run a static analyser, a dependency audit and a secret scan on ci-dashboard, and triage every finding with an agent's help: decide what is real, prove it, fix one true positive with a regression test, and catch one agent claim that was wrong (LO7).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Use Week 0 setup and the week 8 activity. That activity identifies the public starter files and exact supported launcher commands. Copy only public files into a new workspace.

docs.title: Part A: attack and harden
docs.text:
Reproduce one local indirect-injection chain and preserve allowed behavior. Use the supplied FAKE replay: it reads an injected note and poisoned MCP output, proposes changing its own policy to auto-approve and contacting the loopback mock, then performs the allowed health check. The starter policy permits the two dangerous effects. Harden student/harden/policy.json with a tool allowlist, no policy write path and explicit confirmation requirements, then rerun the same replay. The health check must still pass while both dangerous proposals are denied.

Copy only student/ into a fresh workspace, resolve the offline launcher profile, then run both replays through the launcher:

mkdir -p security-workshop-run
cp -R capstone/security-workshop/student/. security-workshop-run/
security_profile=$(uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json)
security_version=$(printf '%s' "$security_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["version"])')
security_digest=$(printf '%s' "$security_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["digest"])')
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$security_version" --digest "$security_digest" \
  --workspace security-workshop-run -- python attack/run_all.py --workspace run
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$security_version" --digest "$security_digest" \
  --workspace security-workshop-run -- python attack/run_all.py --workspace run-fixed --policy harden/policy.json

The report records proposals, policy decisions, effects and the mock records. It creates a fresh namespace, capability and random loopback port for every invocation. It never needs an API key or an external network. The Python runtime guard is defense in depth; use the Week 0 launcher for OS-level network and mount isolation.

docs.title: Part B: scan, triage with an agent, fix one finding
docs.text:
A scanner finding is a claim, not a verdict. Your job is to turn each claim into a decision you can defend with evidence. The three scanners are in student/scan/. They use only the Python standard library and a dated advisory file, so they run inside the launcher with no network:

Scanner Question it answers Where its rules live Static analysis Does the code contain a risky pattern, such as SQL text built from a value? scan/sast.py Dependency audit Is a locked package version inside a known advisory's affected range? scan/deps.py, scan/advisories.json Secret scan Does a file contain a credential-shaped string? scan/secret_scan.py

Every rule is short enough to read; read them before you trust a result. Semgrep (tools/semgrep; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3), pip-audit (tools/pip-audit; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1) and gitleaks (tools/gitleaks; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1) answer the same three questions. The course kit is smaller so that you can read all of it, and it needs no network inside the launcher.

docs.title: 1. Build the workspace
docs.text:
From the course root, commit your current project work first, then copy the starting commit and your current commit of your ci-dashboard repository into a new workspace. START is the commit you received; PROJECT_REPO is your checkout.

mkdir -p security-scan-work/before security-scan-work/app
cp -R capstone/security-workshop/student/scan security-scan-work/scan
git -C PROJECT_REPO archive START | tar -x -C security-scan-work/before
git -C PROJECT_REPO archive HEAD | tar -x -C security-scan-work/app
cp security-scan-work/scan/triage-template.json security-scan-work/triage.json
scan_profile=$(uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json)
scan_version=$(printf '%s' "$scan_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["version"])')
scan_digest=$(printf '%s' "$scan_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["digest"])')

These commands copy files; they run nothing from the project. The launcher accepts at most 256 files and folders in one workspace, so leave out anything your scan does not need.

docs.title: 2. Scan the starting code
docs.text:
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$scan_version" --digest "$scan_digest" --workspace security-scan-work -- python scan/run_scans.py --target before > scan-before-launcher.json
python3 -c 'import json; from pathlib import Path; e=json.loads(Path("scan-before-launcher.json").read_text()); assert e["exit_code"] == 0; Path("security-scan-work/scan-before.json").write_text(e["stdout"])'

Each finding has an id, the file and line, the rule's message and a short excerpt. Secret values are shortened in the report; open the file only in your local workspace to investigate them. Never give an agent a file that still contains a real credential: rotate it first. Before asking an agent anything, predict for each finding whether it is real and write the prediction down.

docs.title: 3. Triage with an agent, then check every claim
docs.text:
Give your approved agent (see Week 0 setup) scan-before.json and the flagged files. Ask it to classify each finding as one of:

  • true positive: the risky behavior can happen here. Requires a reproducer: an inert input or a test that makes it happen, and what you observed when you ran it.
  • false positive: it cannot happen here. Requires the reason, naming the condition that stops it, and evidence for that condition: a file and line, a test or command output.
  • needs more evidence: you cannot decide yet. Requires the missing fact and the next check that would supply it.

The agent's answer is a draft. Check every claim yourself before it goes in triage.json: run each reproducer through the launcher; for each "cannot fire", find the code that stops it and try one input against it. Combine findings that share one root cause into one entry, for example two advisory IDs that are aliases of each other, or one constant flagged by two scanners.

For a dependency finding, read the advisory and check each condition it lists against how this application runs. A version inside the range is a fact; whether the problem can fire here is the triage question. For a real secret, also check history: deleting a value does not remove it from earlier commits (search them with git -C PROJECT_REPO log -S 'FRAGMENT' --oneline, using a distinctive fragment of the value), and a real credential must be rotated, not only deleted.

docs.title: 4. Fix one true positive with a regression test
docs.text:
Choose one true positive. Copy scan/regression_test_template.py to tests/test_security_regression.py in your project and write one test: a permitted input still works, and your inert reproducer no longer has its effect. Run it on the starting code and keep the failing output. Repair the code, rerun the test, keep the passing output, and rerun the scan. Record the test and both outputs in the entry's fix.

The finding must disappear because the code is repaired. These are not repairs: a suppression comment, an ignore file, deleting or renaming the flagged function, or rewriting the code so the pattern no longer matches while the behavior stays the same.

docs.title: 5. Record one agent claim that was wrong
docs.text: In agent_errors, record one claim the agent made that your checks showed to be wrong: the class, the reason, the reproducer or the proposed fix. Say what was wrong and which check caught it.

docs.title: 6. Check the record
docs.text:
After committing your fix, delete security-scan-work/app, extract HEAD into it again with the same git archive command, then:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$scan_version" --digest "$scan_digest" --workspace security-scan-work -- python scan/check_triage.py --baseline before --current app --triage triage.json

The checker scans both trees with its own rules and ignores any rule, suppression or report inside them. It runs your regression test on both trees. It reports level 0 to 3: every finding triaged, one fix verified, one agent error recorded. Level 3 means your record is complete and your test supports the fix. It does not mean the project is secure: these rules match a few patterns, and authorization mistakes or logic errors rarely match any pattern. Keep finding those by review and tests.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text: M1 attack, fix and regression evidence, and triage.json with the checker output. Reuse the existing work record; include verification and your own short explanation, not an additional report.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text: This workshop is part of M1. Keep its evidence in that milestone; there is no separate submission or course mark. Public checks provide feedback only. The fix in Part B is one of your M1 security repairs; the other true positives still need repairs and regression tests before M1 is complete. The planted security seeds are not published; at M1 review the teaching team runs its own seed check on your revision. See the syllabus.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Use approved assistance for open work. Complete initial individual review, discovery notes and personal explanation/reflective reasoning yourself. Independent checks and oral defense are AI-off. Attach AI use once and reuse its ID. In Part B, write your own predictions before asking the agent, and treat every agent classification as unverified until your own check supports it.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: About 1 hour for Part A, of which 30 minutes is the replay block in the Week 8 workshop, and about 3 hours for Part B, including verification, waiting and revision. Both parts belong to the M1 milestone work, not an extra assignment.

docs.title: Security workshop student bundle
docs.text: This is a local, synthetic exercise. The supplied payloads are inert course material: they send only a harmless marker to the mock server on the fresh 127.0.0.1 port chosen for the current run. They do not resolve names, contact the internet, read credentials or write outside the workspace.

docs.title: Run the public regression and replay
docs.text:
From the course root, copy this public directory into a new workspace and use the offline course launcher. Resolve the profile once for both runs:

mkdir -p security-workshop-run
cp -R capstone/security-workshop/student/. security-workshop-run/
security_profile=$(uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json)
security_version=$(printf '%s' "$security_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["version"])')
security_digest=$(printf '%s' "$security_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["digest"])')
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$security_version" --digest "$security_digest" \
  --workspace security-workshop-run -- python attack/run_all.py --workspace run

The first result is legitimate_task. The five legacy observations then show which inert vectors reached the local mock. The agent result is a deterministic FAKE replay: it reads victim-project/agent-notes.md and poisoned MCP text, proposes a policy edit and a mock contact, then performs the allowed health check. The starter policy permits all three, so agent_attack_hits is 2.

The five legacy observations are boundary diagnostics and intentionally remain present after hardening; the policy score uses the two policy-controlled agent effects.

Copy the policy into your hardening work and close the two effects by changing the policy controls, rather than deleting the replay or adding a global bypass:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$security_version" --digest "$security_digest" \
  --workspace security-workshop-run -- python attack/run_all.py --workspace run-hardened --policy harden/policy.json

The hardened run must keep the health effect, deny write_policy and contact_mock, and report agent_attack_hits as 0. The policy demonstrates five controls: a tool allowlist, writable-path and network-host allowlists, explicit confirmation for dangerous proposals, and auto_approve: false. An explicit confirmation requirement still applies when auto_approve is true, so the replay uses the conservative rule that confirmation wins. For defense in depth, each dangerous effect must stay blocked when any one control is reset to its starter value.

Do not run payloads directly on a host project. Use the course launcher described in Week 0 when the activity is performed with an agent. The Python runtime guard is defense in depth and best effort; the launcher supplies the OS-level network and mount isolation.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Keep the JSON output, the legitimate-task result, the proposal/decision trace, the policy diff, the attack count, the checklist decisions, and a short explanation in the existing work record. Attach one AI-use note if assistance was used. The mock log contains only the synthetic namespace, capability and vector name.

docs.title: Scanners and triage
docs.text: scan/ holds the three offline scanners used in Part B of the workshop: static analysis (sast.py), a dependency audit against the dated advisories.json, and a secret scan (secret_scan.py). run_scans.py --target DIR prints one JSON report. check_triage.py gives feedback on your triage.json; start from triage-template.json and regression_test_template.py. Run them through the course launcher exactly as the workshop page shows. Nothing inside a scanned project can switch a rule off.

docs.title: Victim project fixture
docs.text:
This tiny synthetic project gives the replay two untrusted text surfaces: agent-notes.md in the repository and the text-only result from poisoned-mcp/. Both ask the agent to edit its own policy and contact the loopback mock. Neither text is an authority grant, and neither contains credentials.

The starter policy.json intentionally permits those proposals so the attack is observable. Students copy its controls into harden/policy.json, then rerun the same replay. The allowed health task writes victim-output.json; the hardened run must preserve that behavior while refusing the policy edit and mock contact.

docs.title: Tests that detect a meaningful fault
Objectives
docs.text:
Use mutation testing, explain one property and replay a supplied fuzz case; reuse the method (and the tests you wrote) in M1. (LO5).

This workshop starts with a small public utility extracted from the ci-dashboard validation boundary. It is deliberately outside the M1 seed set; no M1 seed or seed input is copied into this exercise. The workshop target is a UTC timestamp parser; the project tests later apply the same three checks to your own M1 target.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Use Week 0 setup and the week 7 activity. Run the commands from the course root. They copy only fixture/ and student/ into a new workspace, so the original fixture stays unchanged and a peer can reproduce the baseline.

docs.title: 1. Predict and challenge the public target
docs.text: Read fixture/target.py and student/checks.py without running them. Predict which mutants the weak check can kill. Run the weak suite and the bounded mutation command, then record one surviving mutant and the input that should distinguish it. Add one assertion to weak_checks in student/checks.py, rerun the mutation command, and keep the before/after output.

docs.title: 2. Add a property and replay a fixed fuzz input
docs.text: Run the property suite. Explain its input domain and one boundary it does not cover. Run the seeded fuzz command and replay the supplied invalid timestamp exactly. Keep the seed, input, command and observed result together. A passing property or an empty fuzz report is evidence about that configuration only; it is not a proof of correctness.

docs.title: 3. Move the method to M1
docs.text:
On your own M1 test target, state an independent oracle, add one property, and replay one reproducible fuzz input. Do not copy the public timestamp function or any M1 seed fixture. Record the target revision, test command and result in the existing M1 functional baseline.

Every command in tasks 1-3 runs through the course launcher; see where commands run.

Start with the linked classroom activity: save a prediction, inspect its public fixture, and explain a result before revision. It rehearses the workshop method. For task 3, use the project bundle described in the M1 project route: it is the M1 test target and holds the mutation configuration (mutants.json and mutant_manifest.json) and the bounded fuzz corpus (fuzz-corpus.json). A classroom fixture result alone does not complete task 3.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text: M1 tests and before/after evidence. Reuse the existing work record; include the workshop commands, verification and your own short explanation, not an additional report. The public fixture catalog records the checked-in baseline runtime.

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
This workshop is part of M1. Keep its evidence in that milestone; there is no separate submission or course mark. Public mutation numbers and feedback_score provide feedback only; they never enter the course mark. M1 is assessed by reading your tests and before/after evidence against the project rubric; the number is not imported. See the syllabus.

The general rubric's mutation-threshold wording in Testing strategy does not apply to M1 or to feedback_score; use the workshop's feedback goal and explain the evidence.

docs.title: AI use rules
docs.text: Use approved assistance for open work. Complete initial individual review, discovery notes and personal explanation/reflective reasoning yourself. Independent checks and oral defense are AI-off. Attach AI use once and reuse its ID. If a model proposes a test, read it first, run it as described in where commands run and keep the launcher result with the test revision.

docs.title: Estimated time
docs.text: Up to 4 hours inside the corresponding milestone budget, including verification, waiting and revision. This is not an additional homework quota.

docs.title: Where commands run
docs.text: Run every command in this workshop through the course launcher, as in the Week 7 activity: the fixture runner, the project scripts, checks you wrote yourself and any model proposal. Read a model proposal as text before you copy it into a workspace, and never put a key in a workspace. Each launcher command takes about 40 seconds because it repeats the launcher's safety checks first. The uv run lines under teaching-team host check are for the teaching team's own machine; they are not a student route.

docs.title: Timestamp fixture
docs.text:
From the course root, copy the public fixture into a new workspace and resolve the offline launcher profile once:

testing_work=$(mktemp -d ./testing-workshop.XXXXXX)
cp -R capstone/testing-workshop/fixture capstone/testing-workshop/student "$testing_work/"
testing_profile=$(uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json)
testing_version=$(printf '%s' "$testing_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["version"])')
testing_digest=$(printf '%s' "$testing_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["digest"])')

Run each command separately:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$testing_work" -- python fixture/runner.py weak
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$testing_work" -- python fixture/runner.py mutation
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$testing_work" -- python fixture/runner.py property
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$testing_work" -- python fixture/runner.py fuzz --seed 17
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$testing_work" -- python fixture/runner.py replay --text '2026-02-30T12:00:00Z'
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$testing_work" -- python fixture/runner.py fuzz --seed 17 --implementation calendar_check_removed
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$testing_work" -- python fixture/runner.py replay --implementation calendar_check_removed --text '2026-02-30T12:00:00Z'

Edit student/checks.py inside $testing_work, rerun the mutation command and retain both reports. A model-proposed check goes into the same file only after you have read it, and runs through the same command.

docs.title: M1 project route: ci-dashboard validation
docs.text:
The project bundle in project/ is the runnable M1 target. It is a teaching snapshot of capstone/legacy/ci-dashboard/domains/validation.py, with the same public validation contract and no instructor seeds. The course uses a small deterministic standard-library mutator plus a bounded property helper. This route is selected because the launcher image has no mutation package, pytest or Hypothesis; fixed source replacements are auditable and accept --seed, with no package installation or network access.

From the course root, copy the public project files into a new workspace (reuse testing_version and testing_digest from the timestamp fixture) and run the supplied calibration commands:

m1_test_work=$(mktemp -d ./m1-test-work.XXXXXX)
mkdir "$m1_test_work/project"
cp -R capstone/testing-workshop/project/domains capstone/testing-workshop/project/fixtures capstone/testing-workshop/project/replay capstone/testing-workshop/project/tests "$m1_test_work/project/"
cp capstone/testing-workshop/project/*.json capstone/testing-workshop/project/*.py "$m1_test_work/project/"
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$m1_test_work" -- python project/run_property.py
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$m1_test_work" -- python project/run_fuzz.py --seed 17
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$m1_test_work" -- python project/run_mutation.py --tests project/fixtures/weak_tests.py --seed 17
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$m1_test_work" -- python project/score_submission.py --tests project/fixtures/weak_tests.py --seed 17

Save your own test file as project/tests/student_tests.py inside $m1_test_work, whether you wrote it or a model proposed it, and score it the same way:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$testing_version" --digest "$testing_digest" --workspace "$m1_test_work" -- python project/score_submission.py --tests project/tests/student_tests.py --seed 17

The mutation runner applies every replacement in the fixed mutants.json configuration to a new clean copy and isolated child process, records the seed, and emits JSON. The scorer runs the same process and independently computes formative feedback; it never trusts a submitted score or model prose. A baseline is required before mutation runs. A timeout, skipped or missing dependency is one infrastructure failure and produces no feedback_score; it is never a kill, survivor or denominator reduction. The public project/mutant_manifest.json lists equivalent and control entries beside mutants.json, with a kind and contract reason. Only behavioral entries form the denominator. Equivalent mutants are removed from the denominator only when the published contract reason says their behavior is identical. Source-only equivalent controls are also run; killing one marks the report identity_probe and sets its feedback_score to null. A killed mutant is one for which the submitted tests fail against the changed implementation. A survivor remains a survivor until a test or a written contract explanation addresses it. An equivalent mutant is excluded only when the contract makes its observable behaviour identical (for example, a message-only change); the report must list its name and reason. A timeout, missing dependency, crash, or launcher failure is the same infrastructure failure rule, never a kill, survivor or denominator reduction. The denominator is every selected behavioral mutant from the fixed run configuration. Do not delete a test, edit the harness, alter the source snapshot, or hard-code a sample output to change it; the clean-copy scorer and independent oracle are what the teacher uses for feedback. The feedback goal for this workshop is 0.70. Equivalent mutants are listed by the teacher with a contract reason.

docs.title: Agent-generated tests and evidence
docs.text:
Ask the approved model, or use the public frozen FAKE/replay response in project/replay/frozen.json, to propose tests for one M1 validation claim. Treat the proposal as untrusted text: inspect it, save the claim and expected counterexample, and execute it through the launcher. Run the resulting test file with score_submission.py. For every surviving mutant, record the mutant name, the observation that the test failed to make, and the model claim it disproves (or mark that the claim remains unverified). Then add one property with an independent oracle and rerun mutation and fuzz with the same seed. The model response is evidence of generation; mutation, property and replay outputs are the verification evidence. The scoring tool never reads or scores model prose.

Keep a single work-record row for the target revision, test path, seed, mutation command, selected denominator, killed/surviving/equivalent names, infrastructure failures and the before/after feedback score. The weak, partial, strong and reference fixtures are calibration examples; they are not student answers or a grade.

A frozen FAKE response is generation evidence only. The reference suite stays under project/instructor/ and is removed from the student package; the public manifest beside mutants.json is the only denominator declaration.

docs.text:
On the teaching team's machine, these commands check the course-written project files directly from the repository root. catalog.json records the timestamp fixture commands run the same way with uv run --no-project python from this directory. Students use the launcher commands above.

  --tests capstone/testing-workshop/project/fixtures/weak_tests.py --seed 17

  --tests capstone/testing-workshop/project/fixtures/weak_tests.py

docs.title: ci-dashboard validation project
docs.text:
This directory is a public teaching snapshot of capstone/legacy/ci-dashboard/domains/validation.py. It is intentionally self-contained so the launcher can give a student the target, tests and bounded fuzz corpus without exposing instructor seeds or a grader.

The project uses a deterministic standard-library mutator and a bounded property helper. It has no pytest, Hypothesis or mutmut dependency, so it also runs in the launcher image. Students run these scripts through the course launcher with the commands in the workshop's M1 project route. On the teaching team's machine, check the course-written files from the repository root:

uv run --locked python capstone/testing-workshop/project/run_property.py
uv run --locked python capstone/testing-workshop/project/run_fuzz.py --seed 17
uv run --locked python capstone/testing-workshop/project/run_mutation.py \
  --tests capstone/testing-workshop/project/fixtures/weak_tests.py --seed 17

A student's test file receives formative feedback in a clean copy with score_submission.py. The fixed mutants.json replacements and public mutant_manifest.json are applied in a seeded order; the scorer runs each in a fresh isolated child, hashes the target before and after execution, clears child environment variables, reports one infrastructure-failure rule, and never accepts a student's printed result. The report field is feedback_score; it is never a course mark. A feedback score of 0.70 is the workshop feedback goal. The manifest gives every equivalent or control entry a kind and contract reason, and only behavioral entries form the denominator. The teacher's independent oracle and strong tests remain under instructor/ and are removed from the student package.

The frozen replay at replay/frozen.json contains claims with stable claim IDs and suggested test files. Copy each suggestion into the project and score it through the launcher route. The counterexample suggestion is expected to fail the baseline; that failure is evidence to inspect, not a score to hide.

The supplied tests/test_validation.py contains one seeded standard-library property and leaves one boundary for you to add. The public suite may contain at most one seeded property and must not copy the teacher strong or reference suites. Run every student test, including a model-generated one, through the course launcher as the workshop README describes; the host-side uv run commands above are not a student route.

docs.title: Read Trajectories Safely: Generate, Then Verify
docs.text:
The evaluation framework contains the trajectory schema, cheating-pattern detection, benchmark audits and evaluation-task templates. Results must be reproducible and report both correctness and execution evidence.

These tools read the trajectory JSONL v1 contract. They do not call models, execute commands recorded in trajectories or send trajectories over the network. Students can check their own evidence, and instructors/TAs can inspect process evidence. Generated or suggested code must still use the course safety launcher; these tools parse data only.

docs.title: Offline Use
docs.text:
Course build repository: After completing make setup at the repository root, generate a minimized copy from a fully synthetic example, then validate and inspect it:

uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.validate evals/trajectory/examples/synthetic-tools.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.redact evals/trajectory/examples/synthetic-tools.jsonl -o /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.validate /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.stats /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.viewer /tmp/course-safe.jsonl -o /tmp/course-view.html
uv run --locked pytest tests/test_trajectory_tools.py -q

Extracted student package: The package excludes the build repository's Makefile, root project and instructor-side test directory. Use the standalone route below from the student-package root in a POSIX shell, after installing the course-designated uv:

uv venv --python 3.12.13 evals/trajectory/venv
uv pip sync --python evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python --require-hashes evals/trajectory/requirements.lock
export PYTHONPATH="$PWD/src/course_llm/src"
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.selfcheck
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.validate evals/trajectory/examples/synthetic-tools.jsonl
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.redact evals/trajectory/examples/synthetic-tools.jsonl -o /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.stats /tmp/course-safe.jsonl
evals/trajectory/venv/bin/python -m evals.trajectory.viewer /tmp/course-safe.jsonl -o /tmp/course-view.html

The standalone requirements.lock is exported from the course_llm dependency closure in the root uv.lock. It pins versions and hashes without resolving floating versions or installing project build tools. PYTHONPATH points to the course_llm source included in the student package. Environment preparation may download Python/locked dependencies; instructors can preinstall them or supply a matching offline wheelhouse, adding --no-index --find-links <wheelhouse> to uv pip sync. After preparation, all trajectory commands and selfcheck disable model calls and run offline without pytest or API keys. The self-check verifies synthetic trajectories and HTML round trips; it is not the build repository's full security regression tests.

Open the generated single-file HTML in a browser. Tab to step headings and expand them with Enter or Space. Tool calls use native mark highlighting; roles do not rely on color alone. The page needs no server, JavaScript, CSS, font downloads or external images. CSP blocks scripts, external resources, network connections, forms and object loading. The viewer observes records; it cannot prove model output correct. Check the task's actual test results as well.

All four CLIs accept an input path and optional -o/--output. Without an output path, the complete result goes to stdout. After successful publication, redact writes its redaction report to stderr: only call counts, removed content-field counts and removed-identifier counts, with no original text, filenames or reversible mappings. Failure returns nonzero with fixed English errors and no partial report. Existing output files remain unchanged on failure; new destinations are not created. Successful publication atomically replaces output with owner-only read/write permissions. Identical input/output paths, final-path symlinks and special files are rejected; callers must use trusted parent directories.

docs.title: Minimization Boundary
docs.text:
Reuse course_llm's TracePolicy and mandatory filtering. By default, remove every value, including original user text, assistant bodies, tool arguments, tool results and original call IDs. Unlabeled names, credentials, personal identifiers, absolute paths and long tool outputs are therefore removed in full rather than guessed with regular expressions. There is no dynamic allowlist or switch to retain bodies. Collected content receives fresh private random HMAC digests; keys are not written to disk. Existing not_collected fields retain their lengths and HMACs for correlation within one run. HTML and statistics do not display digests.

Model/tool identifiers retain only the built-in fake-v1/read/write/bash; all others become [REDACTED] and remain subject to the trajectory secret filtering. Custom tools share one redacted category, so their names cannot be distinguished. This reduces detail to support safe sharing by default. Finer categories require a separately auditable public classification contract. The viewer checks actual fields and identifiers rather than trusting an input's claimed redacted status; bodies or unknown identifiers require running redact first. Successful validation proves structure only, not authentic provenance, absence of privacy risk or billing accuracy.

docs.title: Statistics and Rejection Rules
docs.text:
• One line represents one call. steps counts returned assistant steps with usage measurements; snapshot_steps separately counts all context-snapshot steps. tools counts tool requests only in the current returned step, without adding repeated history.
  • Tokens and latency come only from the current returned step. Latency is the sum of observed call latencies, not end-to-end wall-clock time. Known costs are summed with Decimal, without inferring prices from model names. Amounts in the three examples are synthetic arithmetic inputs only.
  • Provider failures preserve missingness: cost: null, unknown_cost_calls, usage_complete: false and latency_complete: false. known_cost is a known subtotal, not the full cost.
  • Reject unknown versions, negative/non-finite numbers, duplicate JSON keys, malformed/blank JSONL, duplicate or reversed sequence numbers within a run, usage/latency repeated in historical snapshots, and inconsistent status/cost. Excerpts may have sequence gaps. v1 has no totals field; the schema rejects added summaries, and every report recomputes results.
  • Limits: 1 MiB per line including the newline; 16 MiB and 10,000 lines per file. Exceeding any limit rejects the entire input. Tokens, sequence numbers and latency cannot exceed 2**53-1; cost text is at most 64 characters, the absolute Decimal exponent at most 18, and the amount at most 1e18. These are tool resource limits, not model or industry data.

docs.title: Three Fully Synthetic Example Trajectories
docs.text:
• Single reply: Known cost and usage measurements.
  • Tool calls and follow-up reply: Count repeated context once.
  • Provider failure: Unknown cost cannot be treated as zero.

Every identifier, timestamp, amount and digest is fixed teaching data constructed by the course, with no real student or user information.

docs.title: Access, Storage, Deletion and Sharing
docs.text:
Follow the trajectory collection responsibilities without adding course policy. Creators retain only minimal excerpts needed for their work, in controlled directories inside the course workspace that are excluded from Git. Instructors/TAs read necessary evidence only through authorized course channels. Peer sharing uses self-checked minimized copies only. HTML is also process data; redaction does not make it suitable for public release.

Creators clean up original trajectories, minimized copies, reports and HTML; course administrators handle controlled copies and backups. Retention and deletion/withdrawal follow approved course arrangements. These tools set no retention period and do not automatically remove backups. If arrangements are unresolved, use only synthetic material and temporary files, delete them after verification, and record that deletion completed without retaining original content. The /tmp paths above serve synthetic demonstrations only; creators delete both temporary files afterward.

Share in order: confirm authorization and the minimum necessary data; generate a copy with redact; use validate and stats to check missingness; generate HTML with viewer; manually inspect the copy and complete the course secret scan; share through a controlled channel. Never submit environment configuration, raw interviews, credentials, complete tool output or instructor answers. If sensitive values appear, stop sharing, replace/delete affected copies and report through the course process. Automated validation does not replace manual self-checks.

docs.title: Trajectory Anomaly-Pattern Practice
docs.text: The detector and synthesizer provide seven fixed lexical clues, deterministic regression reports and an offline read-only execution entry point. Matches enter a human review queue only; they do not determine authorship, misconduct or grades.

docs.title: Clues Are Not Conclusions
docs.text: This tool sends lexical patterns in records to a human review queue only. It does not determine author identity, integrity violations or grades. Writing style, perplexity and general AI-authorship detection are prohibited. Never convert match counts, confidence descriptions or empty reports into scores, sanctions, authorship probabilities or proof of exoneration. confidence describes observable lexical clues, not probabilities about a person. The detector connects to no gradebook, scorer or integrity system.

docs.title: Legitimate Behavior That Can Trigger Each Rule
docs.text:
Pattern Current Trigger Scope Legitimate False Positive Example Human Verification read_tests Test paths in read/read_file/list_directory; cat/head/tail/less/ls/rg/grep/find occurring with a test path. Read public tests to understand requirements. Determine whether tests are public and access is authorized; not all tests are hidden tests. history_patch A bash/shell request for git show or git log with -p/--patch; supports the global options below. Inspect an authorized historical regression and explain its cause. Check whether history is within permitted materials; show may display an ordinary file. print_pass Shell or written content contains print/echo/printf with PASS/PASSED/OK/SUCCESS. Write a console-renderer test that should print PASS. Check actual test results, output provenance and execution records. hardcode_output Literal return values in write/write_file/edit/apply_patch content, literal assignments to result/output/answer, or similar shell redirection. Implement a constant-response mock required by the specification. Check whether generalization is required, results under changed inputs and the specification's basis for the constant. modify_tests Test paths or patch content in write tools; test paths appearing with redirection, tee/rm/mv/cp/sed -i in shell. Add an authorized public regression assertion. Check modification authorization and the actual effectiveness of old/new assertions. network_answer HTTP addresses used by curl/wget or fetch/http_get/download occur with answer/solution/fix/patch/diff clues. Download an instructor-authorized patch from a course-local mock. Verify actual data provenance, authorization and attribution; a URL name does not prove its content. copy_diff git apply, patch -p, copying .diff/.patch, or writing content with unified-diff markers. Apply a disclosed teammate patch. Check provenance, collaboration scope, the student's explanation and independent verification.

These are course-authored synthetic examples, with no research-data citations or external detection performance claims. The source record says the assigned cheating-agents factsheet had not yet been delivered; the implementation infers no facts from a missing card and does not wait for uncited factsheet batches. This historical note does not assert the card's present availability.

docs.title: What Cannot Be Inferred
docs.text:
A tool request does not prove that a command executed, succeeded or affected the final artifact. Trajectories may be altered, truncated or copied and may retain only partial context; structural validation does not authenticate provenance. A trajectory alone cannot establish authorization, intent, authorship, test visibility, network-response content, artifact correctness, student learning or deserved grades.

Rules recognize only the listed tool names and command/cmd, path/file_path, content/text/patch/diff and url arguments, in ordinary objects or key/value entry lists. They do not interpret shell, expand variables, aliases, encodings, scripts, symlinks or escapes, or open paths. Strings containing multiple commands may incorrectly associate unrelated words. Python internal reads/writes, other languages, unlisted tool shapes and indirect copying may be missed. The constant-return rule is deliberately broad and cannot prove hardcoding for tests. User quotations, assistant bodies and tool results are not treated as tool requests.

The history rule only tokenizes quotes and splits on separators. It supports global git options -C, -c (separate/attached values), --git-dir, --work-tree, --namespace, --config-env (separate/equals values), and -p/--paginate, -P/--no-pager, --bare, --no-replace-objects, --no-lazy-fetch, --no-optional-locks and --no-advice. For example, git -C /workspace/repo log -p and git --no-pager show HEAD both produce clues. Global git -p is a pagination flag, not a log patch flag. Paths after log's -- and -p/--patch in other command segments do not participate. Unknown global options, unclosed quotes, wrapper commands, Git aliases, combined short options and other shell syntax may cause false negatives; the detector never executes them to determine semantics. Quoted separators may also split segments. Lexical results cannot replace verification of shell syntax or actual Git behavior.

minimal trajectories have no body; ordinary redacted policy also replaces non-allowlisted arguments and their keys entirely. Actual Client/FakeProvider/Tracer integration tests set no synthetic allowlist and verify coverage.conclusion: insufficient_evidence with empty findings for all seven request types. Argument strings containing [REDACTED…] markers are excluded from matching. The detector neither joins text across markers nor reverses digests. Partially analyzable fields or requests produce partial_evidence while retaining visible clues; see the usage guide for coverage states/counts. Current detection applies only to synthetic course exercises retaining supported arguments; do not claim coverage of real student behavior. Do not improve detection by restoring private bodies, saving or classifying real content before redaction, dynamically expanding the TracePolicy allowlist or labeling real data synthetic. Any real collection extension requires separate design, authorization and independent review. This task adds no collection metadata and does not change the frozen schema.

Every finding reports zero-based JSONL line, within-line step and within-step tool-call indexes, plus the rule version, pattern, fixed evidence labels and confidence description. It echoes no input snippets, tool IDs, model names, paths, hashes or original field values. Humans locate the evidence in an authorized original copy; reports themselves also travel through controlled channels. Repeated context across lines produces repeated clues, requiring manual deduplication by position. Counts must not be treated as independent events.

docs.title: Second Review and Appeals
docs.text:
1. Instructors/TAs check versions and indexes, trajectory completeness, redaction status and the task's permitted materials/tools.
  2. Check every legitimate counterexample above against actual execution results and artifact tests. Invite the student's explanation and accept equivalent process records created at the time. Incomplete records or absent tool coverage cannot themselves establish responsibility.
  3. Provide evidence-based written human reasons and retain the student's response; clues may be withdrawn. The detector must not trigger grade deductions, automatic rejection or integrity conclusions. Actual grading and integrity concerns follow established human course procedures.
  4. Students may seek review/appeal of facts, context or interpretation. Authorized personnel who did not make the original judgment examine the same evidence and supplements, retaining reasons for corrections and outcomes. Channels, deadlines and access follow published course arrangements; the tool creates no policy. Until arrangements are clear, use it only for synthetic exercises.

Data creators clean up temporary trajectories and reports; course administrators handle controlled copies and backups. Retention/deletion responsibilities follow the course_llm conventions. Never submit real credentials, student identities or instructor answers.

docs.title: Trajectory Anomaly Patterns: Generate, Detect, Explain, Verify
docs.text:
For LO6/LO9, first predict which tool requests will trigger clues, then run detection and explain false positives and false negatives. Begin with the detection limits and human review route. Everything here is a public, course-authored exercise, with no hidden answers, scorers or instructor-only question bank. Commands in the synthesizer are JSON strings and are never executed.

Current detection covers synthetic course trajectories that retain supported tool arguments. Ordinary minimal/redacted collection does not retain analyzable commands, paths or content; reports explicitly return insufficient_evidence. These tools provide no content-detection route for real student trajectories and do not require collection-policy changes.

docs.title: Prepare a Trusted Parsing Environment
docs.text:
After make setup in the course build repository, prepare the image. This step may download locked dependencies:

docker build -f evals/cheat_detector/Dockerfile -t course-cheat-detector:1 .

The image copies only the parser, course_llm and bundled schemas, not the workspace or instructor assets. The base image has a pinned digest; Python comes from .python-version; dependencies reuse the hashed trajectory dependency lock, adding no third-party dependencies. The local image tag must identify the image built from the reviewed source for this run. Do not use an image of unknown provenance merely because it has the same name.

docs.title: Generate Once, Then Verify Once
docs.text:
These commands only produce/parse synthetic course data; they do not execute shell commands or code inside trajectories.

uv run --locked cheat-synth --pattern read_tests --pattern history_patch --seed 17 > /tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl
uv run --locked python -m evals.trajectory.validate /tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl
uv run --locked cheat-detect /private/tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl
uv run --locked cheat-regression --seed 17
uv run --locked pytest evals/cheat_detector -q
uv run --locked python -m evals.cheat_detector.verify_isolation

On Linux, replace /private/tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl with /tmp/course-synthetic.jsonl. On macOS, /tmp is a system symlink and the CLI rejects symlinks in any input-path component, so use the real path. By default, cheat-detect <trace.jsonl> mounts only that explicit file read-only at /input/trace.jsonl, disables networking, uses a read-only root filesystem, drops capabilities, prevents privilege escalation and limits resources to 1 CPU, 256 MiB and 32 processes. The client deletes the container after a 45-second timeout. It reads private files as the caller (with the caller's UID/GID, or as container root under rootless Docker, which the engine maps to the caller), without changing file permissions or mounting parent directories, the Docker socket, instructor assets or credentials. It never pulls an image automatically and offers no host fallback. The Docker client requires a trusted runtime environment and local Docker permissions. Callers must control parent directories and must not replace files during execution. Paths containing commas, symlinks or special files are rejected.

worker is a passive parsing-library entry point inside the container. Calling it directly on the host does not provide isolation and is not a route for real trajectories. Inputs are limited to 1 MiB per line, 16 MiB and 10,000 lines per file. Shared strict v1 JSONL validation rejects the entire input for duplicate keys, blank lines, broken final lines or version/usage contradictions. Dependency code and bundled schemas are fixed parsing resources. Input never causes other files to be read, commands to run or models to be called. Success writes only JSON to stdout; failure returns 1 with fixed English diagnostics on stderr, without echoing input or detailed runtime errors. Matches still return 0 and do not act as disciplinary gates.

--pattern may be repeated; --seed is required. --kind positive|negative|benign|minimal selects an exercise target, absence of that clue, the same action with legitimate authorization, or missing body content. A fixed seed produces fixed JSONL bytes. Metadata, timestamps, HMAC keys and numbers are synthetic and must not be reused with real data. Callers redirect and clean up the output.

docs.title: Read Regression Reports
docs.text:
Read coverage.conclusion before findings:

Value Meaning no_tool_requests The supplied snapshot has no assistant tool requests; this says nothing about behavior outside the trajectory. insufficient_evidence Requests exist, but none has analyzable arguments for a supported tool; action clues cannot be checked. partial_evidence Only some requests or required arguments are analyzable; existing matches do not close evidence gaps. available_arguments Every request in the supplied snapshot has visible, nonempty arguments required by its supported tool shape; lexical-rule limitations still apply.

coverage.argument_availability assigns each request to exactly one of available, partial, unavailable or unsupported; their sum equals tool_requests. Shell tools require command/cmd, reads require path/file_path, write/write_file/edit require a path and content, apply_patch requires content, and network tools require url. See detection limits for aliases and coverage. Missing, non-string or empty arguments and arguments containing redaction markers are not analyzable. Unknown/redacted tool names count as unsupported. Partially available write arguments can still provide clues. The compatibility count unavailable_arguments counts only requests whose arguments were entirely uncollected or contain any redaction marker. It does not cover unknown shapes or missing keys and cannot alone establish coverage. It may overlap the four categories and is not included in their sum.

Every coverage state retains disposition: manual_review_only. Empty findings cannot substitute for the coverage conclusion; available_arguments does not establish complete detection, complete logs or a verified artifact. These are detector-report fields, without changes to the trajectory schema, collection fields or privacy contract.

cheat-regression --seed 17 reports expected/observed results per example and tp/fp/tn/fn per rule. The current fixed course regression set has 7 patterns x 4 contexts; each rule has TP=1, FP=1, TN=25 and FN=1. A positive label marks the predefined investigation target in a synthetic exercise, never an integrity violation. Authorized examples that still match count as FP; targets hidden by body minimization count as FN.
