docs.title: Who does what during a repair?
docs.text:
Model:       requests read("contract.md")
Controller:  permits this read
Tool:        returns the file's bytes
Model:       proposes a patch using those bytes

The model proposes; the controller decides permission; the tool performs the allowed operation.

A file read supplies information. A patch still needs a completed check.

Schematic event sequence, not a recorded session.

docs.title: An agent connects generation to an environment
docs.text:
The controller also enforces limits and decides when execution stops.

Week 2 makes this loop explicit in a small implementation.

docs.title: Where is the test result?
docs.text:
I updated the function and all tests pass.

The record contains a file write, followed by that message.

Name the missing observation and one useful next action.

30 seconds alone, then compare explanations.

docs.title: Generation uses the available context
docs.text:
A token can be a word fragment, punctuation or part of a program.

A generated algorithm still needs to be executed to observe its behavior.

docs.title: Reading a file supplies context
docs.text:
Training → changes learned parameters Reading a contract → changes the current input

A file on disk contributes no content until the workflow supplies it.

Missing rules and stale test results can change the next proposal.

docs.title: Where does the learned ability come from?
docs.text:
Pretraining: learn patterns from text and code.

Supervised fine-tuning: learn from examples of desired responses.

Reinforcement learning: adjust behavior using reward or feedback.

These change learned parameters. Reading today's contract supplies current context; it does not retrain the model.

High-level background. No training implementation or ML prerequisite.

docs.title: The function is only one part of the task
docs.text:
The developer also needs the dashboard's failed-build count.

sample.json → dashboard.py → visible rows + summary

A correct label does not guarantee a correct summary.

Repository walkthrough: a hand trace, not a recorded agent run.

docs.title: Define what the repository change must preserve
docs.text:
For build records with string statuses:

  • Normalize labels according to the status contract.
  • Count the rows whose label is failed.
  • Keep every build ID in its original order.

Which files would you inspect before proposing an edit?

docs.title: Read the caller as well as the helper
docs.text:
From dashboard.py:

rows = []
for b in builds:
    label = status_label(b["status"])
    rows.append({"id": b["id"], "label": label})
failed = sum(b["status"] == "fail" for b in builds)

The label and the count interpret the same status differently.

docs.title: Delegate a bounded investigation
docs.text:
Read the contract, sample, helper, caller and checks. Explain where labels and counts can disagree. Propose the smallest repair and regression checks. Preserve all build IDs and their order.

An agent can gather context and carry observations into its next step. The engineer still decides whether the proposed checks cover the request.

Teaching prompt, not run. Next: two frozen recorded attempts that used a shorter prompt.

docs.text:
Hand trace after adding strip().lower() in labels.py:

Build 17: "\tfAiL\n" → label failed
Build 18: "ok"       → label passed
Build 19: "cancelled"→ label unknown

Summary: failed = 0       Required: 1

docs.text:
In dashboard.py:

- failed = sum(b["status"] == "fail" for b in builds)
+ failed = sum(row["label"] == "failed" for row in rows)

The helper normalizes a status once. The count uses that label.

Check the complete dashboard result, including all IDs in order.

docs.text:
labels:  failed, passed, unknown
failed:  1
IDs:     17, 18, 19     (same order, none removed)

These are the expected results for the sample, not an observed pass.

An actual decision also needs completed checks on the current files, retained regressions and a review of the changed scope.

docs.title: Compare your own prediction with one attempt
docs.text:
20 minutes. Use the existing P1 calibration record.

Save a time estimate and binary pass prediction for task 001. After the task is revealed, derive a check, generate once and verify.

Inspect the result with a peer. Revise one claim independently.

Activity steps include timing, commands and text participation.

docs.title: Explain the behavior you can support
docs.text:
I predicted . The requirement says . For input , I expected ___ and observed . That supports ___, but leaves ___ unchecked.

If execution did not complete, name the missing observation.

A correct first candidate can still teach you something about your prediction.

docs.title: A nearby task changes the constraint
docs.text:
001 Signed sum: negative values and empty input.

002 Stable unique strings: first-occurrence order and case.

003 Inclusive clamp: behavior at both endpoints.

005 Whitespace and word order: separators and sequence.

The workshop completes these four attempts. The rest are optional practice.

docs.title: Compute the error before explaining it
docs.text:
Two invented reporting rows:

              Time prediction → record     Pass prediction → record
Attempt A          5 → 7 min                      yes → yes
Attempt B          5 → 7 min                      yes → no

Mean signed time error: +2 minutes. Binary pass-prediction error: 1 mismatch out of 2.

Invented rows; arithmetic only.

docs.title: Keep a missing outcome visible
docs.text:
2 successes · 1 failure · 1 unknown

Completed coverage: 3 of the 4 required first attempts.

A later repair does not replace the original failure.

A model error, an execution failure and time spent waiting need different explanations.

docs.title: A correct count, but where did the builds go?
docs.text:
A new patch filters the rows to keep only failed builds. The count is now correct. Its only check asserts failed == 1.

Accept or revise? Write a distinguishing expected result.

Use the original contract. Answer independently before comparing with a peer.

docs.title: A new service sends completed
docs.text:
The current rule maps unknown strings to unknown. The new request does not say whether completed means success.

What can you test now? What must you learn before changing the mapping?

A representation change and a new product meaning need different evidence.

docs.title: Exit question
docs.text:
The model reads a contract and writes a patch. The controller denies its test request. The model then says “all tests passed.”

Explain what happened, what is unknown, and one permitted next action.

Answer without AI. Identify the responsible components.

docs.title: What a production harness adds
docs.text:
The same loop, with more around it:

Added around the loop Week Tool definitions, argument checks, budgets, stop rules 2 A compacted record of earlier steps 2 Repository context selection, context files, skills, tool servers 3 Hooks and a sandbox around tool effects 3 A specification and a staged plan with checkpoints 4

Each layer changes what the model sees or may do. None checks the result for you.

docs.title: Next: build the loop you can now explain
docs.text:
Week 2: implement the small controller and inspect its observations and stopping.

P1 continues with the same four calibration attempts and adds five controller tasks. It reuses your work, verification, explanation and revision.

Worked notes · Activity · Self-check

Course case · Week 0 execution route

docs.title: Dashboard status demonstration
docs.text: This public example supplies an authored candidate, its worked repair and a demonstration runner. The runner executes both functions on the same six contract cases. It makes no model calls. Its scripted candidates let you inspect one complete repair repeatedly without treating the result as a model capability measurement.

docs.title: Contract and prediction
docs.text:
The input is a Python string. Ignore surrounding whitespace and letter case in the ASCII status names. Map ok to passed, fail to failed, and every other string to unknown, including the empty string. Behavior on a non-string input is outside this exercise's contract.

Before opening the repair, predict Candidate A's output on " OK " and write the required output. Explain which operation can make them differ. Then compare the six-case matrix in the notes. These are worked teaching examples, not answers to the four P1 calibration tasks.

docs.title: Repository walkthrough
docs.text: This second example extends the same dashboard from a helper function to its caller. It is a course-authored hand trace, with a frozen source snapshot below. The proposed actions, patch and outputs are authored teaching material. No model selected these actions, and no repository test run is being reported. Read the snippets as text; the runnable six-case helper demonstration in the next section is a separate artifact with its own execution evidence.

docs.title: Request and frozen files
docs.text:
A developer needs reliable labels and a matching failed-build count. Each build has an integer ID and a string status. Preserve every record's ID and its input order. The count must equal the number of displayed rows labeled failed. Use the existing status contract for all labels. Storage, input validation and additional service statuses are outside this change.

These five named files form the entire teaching snapshot. They are printed here, not taken from a project repository or its instructor solutions.

contract.md:

Ignore surrounding whitespace and ASCII letter case in string statuses.
ok -> passed; fail -> failed; every other string -> unknown.
Keep every build ID in its input order.
failed equals the number of displayed rows labeled failed.

sample.json:

[
  {"id": 17, "status": "\tfAiL\n"},
  {"id": 18, "status": "ok"},
  {"id": 19, "status": "cancelled"}
]

labels.py (the same initial helper as Candidate A):

def status_label(raw):
    labels = {"ok": "passed", "fail": "failed"}
    return labels.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")

dashboard.py:

from labels import status_label


def dashboard(builds):
    rows = []
    for b in builds:
        label = status_label(b["status"])
        rows.append({"id": b["id"], "label": label})
    failed = sum(b["status"] == "fail" for b in builds)
    return {"rows": rows, "failed": failed}

test_dashboard.py (the existing check):

from dashboard import dashboard


def test_ordinary_failure():
    assert dashboard([{"id": 1, "status": "fail"}]) == {
        "rows": [{"id": 1, "label": "failed"}],
        "failed": 1,
    }

docs.title: Pause 1: choose context and define the change
docs.text:
Before reading the proposed sequence, identify which files establish the desired behavior, current implementation and existing observations. The printed test supplies a check, not an observed test result. Derive the required full output for the sample from the contract before examining the patch.

A bounded delegation prompt could be:

Read the contract, sample, helper, caller and checks. Explain where labels and counts can disagree. Propose the smallest repair and regression checks. Preserve all build IDs and their order. Report the files changed and the actual checks completed; identify any missing result.

An agent could perform the repeated context gathering, file edits and permitted checks, using returned observations to decide what to inspect next. That is the workflow this example makes concrete. It is not a measured speedup or an observed model success. The engineer still owns the contract and acceptance decision.

docs.title: Pause 2: follow a helper-only proposal
docs.text:
In the authored sequence, a proposed read of dashboard.py would be checked by the controller before a tool could return its bytes. Those bytes reveal two separate interpretations of the status: the helper supplies a row label, while the summary compares the raw string directly. A model could overlook the second interpretation.

Suppose the first proposed edit changes only labels.py:

-    return labels.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")
+    return labels.get(raw.strip().lower(), "unknown")

The hand-derived sample result is:

{
  "rows": [
    {"id": 17, "label": "failed"},
    {"id": 18, "label": "passed"},
    {"id": 19, "label": "unknown"}
  ],
  "failed": 0
}

The required count is 1. The helper's six cases do not call dashboard, and the existing dashboard test uses the exact raw string fail. Those checks would miss this disagreement. This conclusion follows from the printed code; it is not a recorded pass or failure. What check should be added before another proposal?

docs.title: Pause 3: use one interpretation and protect the caller
docs.text:
Keep the helper repair and propose this additional change in dashboard.py:

-    failed = sum(b["status"] == "fail" for b in builds)
+    failed = sum(row["label"] == "failed" for row in rows)

For the sample, independently expect all three rows above in the same order, with failed: 1. A full-output assertion checks the labels, count, retained IDs and order. Also retain the original ordinary-failure check and the helper's ordinary, padded, unknown and empty-string regressions. An empty build list should produce {"rows": [], "failed": 0} under the same row/count rules.

At this point the authored sequence contains a proposed repair and hand-derived expectations. Accepting an actual implementation would additionally require completed checks on the exact changed files, inspection of the diff and a review of remaining scope. A successful file write, test request or final message cannot fill that gap. Do not enter any of these hand-derived values into your model-calibration record.

docs.title: Pause 4: decide what to delegate next
docs.text: Name one useful bounded next action for an agent and one judgment you must make yourself. For example, the workflow can collect the relevant files and execute an allowed full-output regression; you must decide whether its expectations preserve the stated product behavior. If the new status completed has no supplied meaning, neither more code generation nor a green test invented by the agent settles that rule.

docs.title: Supported execution
docs.text:
Use the approved hosted or replay route in Week 0 setup. The following preparation copies only the three public Python files. It does not execute them. Run from the reviewed course root in one shell and choose new workspace and output directories for another demonstration.

mkdir week01-demo-work
cp lectures/week-01/fixture/candidate.py lectures/week-01/fixture/repaired.py lectures/week-01/fixture/demo.py week01-demo-work/
week01_profile=$(uv run --locked python scripts/hosted_profile.py --profile approved-hosted --json)
week01_version=$(printf '%s' "$week01_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["contract"]["version"])')
week01_digest=$(printf '%s' "$week01_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["models_sha256"])')
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version "$week01_version" --digest "$week01_digest" --workspace week01-demo-work --output week01-demo-result -- python demo.py

Inspect the launcher's JSON and week01-demo-result/observations.json as text. Expected successful launcher result: exit_code: 0, model_requests: 0, with this transcript inside stdout:

generation: scripted-course-candidates
candidate / ordinary: 2/2 passed
candidate / contract: 4/6 passed
repaired  / contract: 6/6 passed
regression: original cases retained

Candidate A's two failed checks are expected observations. The demonstration succeeds only when those failures and the repair's six successes match the specified matrix. An unexpected result raises an error. The exported JSON contains each input, expected and actual output, and SHA-256 hashes of the three executed source files.

The hashes bind this public record to source bytes for inspection. An editable local record is practice feedback, not an authoritative grade or proof of a model run. This demonstration makes no model request and supplies no new profile.

The public regression verifier also checks that a broken repair, an unexpectedly changed candidate or an exception cannot produce the success transcript. In the same prepared shell, copy this public file and run it through the launcher:

cp lectures/week-01/fixture/verify_demo.py week01-demo-work/
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version "$week01_version" --digest "$week01_digest" --workspace week01-demo-work -- python verify_demo.py

Expected: five passing checks (Ran 5 tests, OK) in the launcher's captured output, zero exit status and zero model requests. These checks support the teaching demo; they add no student submission requirement.

docs.title: Inspection and continuation
docs.text:
Read the original two checks and the two previously failing cases. Explain why each added case distinguishes Candidate A from the repair. Describe a behavior the six cases do not test. You can trace the same table without executing code; label that work as a hand trace and use the supplied transcript as a reference expectation.

The launcher performs its normal safety checks before execution. If it reports a safety failure, stop and use Week 0's support route. Keep an absent or unexpected execution result as such; do not present the reference transcript as the output of that failed invocation. Continue the classroom discussion from the written contract and code while support is arranged. Further actual runs use the approved route.

docs.title: Week 2: Build and inspect a small agent
docs.text: This directory holds Week 2 materials. You trace request validation, tool effects, observations and stopping in a small controller, then finish P1 with a bounded read/write/bash loop. The instructor builds the first steps of that loop as a live demonstration. An optional activity compares the system prompts and tool definitions of two open-source coding agents.

docs.title: A short loop you can explain
Purpose
docs.text:
Duration: 60 minutes within the workshop, including verification and revision. Materials: notes, a keyboard-accessible editor/terminal, the three public fixture files, and a device that passed the Week 0 setup check. Grouping: pairs, or individual work with the same feedback checkpoint. Everyone writes all five steps of run() in their own loop.py, and their own prediction and explanation. In a pair, the partner only observes: they read along against the contract and may name a failing check, but never type in the other person's file. Output: your loop.py with the run() you wrote, its actual verification result, and a short explanation of one failure and repair. Reuse these in the P1 record where relevant, with one AI-use note. This is formative practice, not a pair assessment or a new grading formula.

Use the approved hosted or replay route in Week 0 setup. Run code only after that page's check shows you can run the practices. Independent assessments remain AI-off.

docs.title: Activity sequence
docs.text:
Minutes What to do Evidence and feedback 0-5 Confirm you can run the practices (Week 0 setup). Predict the tool messages and the check for read, a wrong write and verify. Each person writes the predicted result under each call ID, the stop reason and the check (LO1). 5-20 Read the supplied tool and checked, naming the accepted arguments. Live demonstration: the instructor builds contract steps 1-3 of run() on screen while you type the same three in your loop.py; in P1 you build the whole controller yourself. You type in your own loop.py; in a pair, your partner checks each step against the contract (LO2/LO7). Run the public checks: until run() exists they stop with "Write run() in loop.py first"; after step 3, four checks pass and eleven still fail. 20-30 Finish steps 4-5 yourself: every call answered by one tool message under its own ID, and the step_limit stop. Rerun the checks until all fifteen pass, then run scripted generation. Compare the actual written result with the actual verified result in completion.json (LO1/LO2). Your partner watches and may name the failing check, never the code. 30-40 In demo.py, change CANDIDATE from "4 " to "5 ". Predict, run and inspect the failed check. Restore "4 " and rerun. Keep both results. Explain why the run still stops with final and why that is not success (LO1). 40-50 Read the public check that shows the proposer receiving each result. Design a short context record preserving the goal, refused calls and the last failed check. Peer names one omitted constraint. Revise the record and explain its budget (LO1/LO2). 50-60 Run the model route if you have access, or follow the walkthrough below. Compare the model's calls with the scripted ones, then answer self-check Q2 and Q4 individually. Keep the actual mode and request evidence. Replay is labelled separately from a hosted API run.

At minute 25, stop to offer help if anyone's steps 4-5 do not pass the public checks yet. Hint 1: read the first failing check's name; it names the behavior that is missing. Hint 2: decide where in run() the only call to tool belongs: after step 3's final branch, once per call in the reply. Hint 3: work from the failing names, one at a time. test_generate_then_verify and test_the_proposer_receives_each_observation want one role: "tool" message per call, under that call's ID, before the next request. test_two_calls_in_one_reply_are_answered_in_order wants that for every call in a reply that holds two, in the order the reply lists them. test_denied_calls_become_observations_without_effects, test_a_missing_file_is_an_observation and test_a_check_timeout_is_an_observation want every result, including refusals and failures, sent back as a message. test_a_repeated_read_runs_until_the_turn_budget_ends wants the step 5 stop. No code is shown; the instructor's steps 1-3 stay on screen. At minute 50, a peer identifies one unsupported success claim or lost constraint and the author visibly revises it. More time or an approved interaction accommodation does not reduce attainable marks. If startup consumes the time box, arrange supported continuation instead of running on the host or adding an unplanned homework quota.

docs.title: Execution route
docs.text:
Run only once Week 0 setup shows you can run the practices: complete its trusted preparation and actual launcher checks first. If any safety check fails, stop and report the safe failure category. Do not change networking, mounts, privileges, image or resource caps.

From the reviewed course root, use these trusted preparation commands. They copy only public synthetic exercise files to a new directory and resolve the shared profile. They do not execute the fixture on the host. Use a fresh shell for the sequence, and keep the variables in that shell for every launcher command.

mkdir week02-work
cp lectures/week-02/fixture/*.py week02-work/
week02_profile=$(uv run --locked python scripts/hosted_profile.py --profile approved-hosted --json)
week02_version=$(printf '%s' "$week02_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["contract"]["version"])')
week02_digest=$(printf '%s' "$week02_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["models_sha256"])')

The profile identity is public configuration. Do not print environment overrides or credentials when diagnosing a resolver refusal. week02-work must contain only these public files and your exercise edits, never .git, teacher tests/answers, keys or the whole private course tree. Make edits with your editor. The launcher copies input into a temporary bounded workspace and does not mount your host workspace.

The public checks of your run(), then scripted generation and verification:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version "$week02_version" --digest "$week02_digest" --workspace week02-work -- python verify_loop.py
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version "$week02_version" --digest "$week02_digest" --workspace week02-work --output week02-result -- python demo.py

Expected: before you write run(), the checks exit nonzero with "Write run() in loop.py first" and the demo prints "error": "write run() in loop.py first"; neither makes a model request. With your run(), the fifteen public checks report OK with zero exit status in the launcher's result. The demo then exits zero and prints generation: scripted-practice, stop_reason: final, check: verified and eight messages, with zero model requests. The new week02-result directory receives only result.txt and completion.json. Inspect both as text: the tool messages answer c1, c2 and c3 with 5\n, written and verified. Every invocation reruns the launcher safety checks, including intentional exhaustion probes. Allow time for those checks. These are public practice checks, never authoritative grades.

For the wrong-write experiment, edit only the CANDIDATE line in week02-work/demo.py, leaving the initial file value and the check unchanged. Use this command for both the failing run and the restored run:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version "$week02_version" --digest "$week02_digest" --workspace week02-work -- python demo.py

The wrong candidate yields check: check_failed, stop_reason: final and a nonzero exit. The restored candidate yields check: verified. Use the command without --output for repeats, or a new output directory. The launcher refuses overwriting an existing output directory. Each invocation resets the synthetic file inside its temporary workspace. The budget experiment in the notes edits only the MAX_STEPS line the same way and uses the same command; keep it at 4 or below. Exported code remains untrusted and must go through the launcher again before execution.

For an API run, first make the public checks pass on your run(); the model route uses it. Use the resolver output and host key described in the Week 0 setup. A student without a key chooses the replay route; both routes use the same task and verification.

mkdir -p -m 700 ~/course-traces
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version "$week02_version" --digest "$week02_digest" --workspace week02-work --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key --trace ~/course-traces/week02-model-trace.jsonl -- python demo.py hosted

The trace goes to ~/course-traces, a directory only you can read, outside Git and outside every course workspace. The launcher adds one record per model request to the file but does not create the directory, so run the mkdir line first.

Each turn sends one prompt through sandbox_model.chat: the tool contract and the whole message history so far, including every tool result. The launcher calls course_llm through the existing broker; at most four requests are made. The student process receives text, no endpoint, credential, network exit or provider credential. The model chooses calls only from read, write and bash as tool accepts them; anything else comes back to it as a refusal. Expect one request per turn in the launcher's result and trace, and the summary line generation: hosted-api-or-replay with the actual stop_reason and check. Report a refusal, an unusable_reply, a wrong write or a step_limit as such. Do not substitute scripted text and label it model output. Keep the minimal model-call JSONL in ~/course-traces while checking it, then include only assignment-required, reviewed evidence.

Without a key, use the same task with the replay record your instructor names:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version "$week02_version" --digest "$week02_digest" --workspace week02-work --model replay --replay-file REPLAY_FILE --replay-digest REPLAY_DIGEST -- python demo.py replay

docs.title: Records
docs.text: Keep your own candidate change, actual mode and verification result, and explanation under the same exercise evidence ID. completion.json is a small inspection aid. It does not replace the broker JSONL required for actual model-call evidence.

docs.title: Review
docs.text: Use peer feedback to revise one claim, then compare both cases again. Independent content review and actual classroom rehearsal are separate from this activity record.

docs.title: Keyboard and text participation
docs.text:
All code, tables and messages are plain text. An editor and terminal operated by keyboard are sufficient. The live demonstration uses the same files, with the instructor reading call names and results aloud. No drag gesture, color distinction or diagram is required. The slide diagram has an adjacent text description.

If you cannot run the practices yet or have no approved device, work through this course-authored synthetic walkthrough, with no execution: initial file 5 ; call c1 read returns 5 ; call c2 write 4 returns written; call c3 verify returns verified; the next reply has no calls, so the loop stops with final and the check is verified. For the failure variant, replace the write with 5 : c3 returns check_failed, the next reply still has no calls, the stop is final and the check is check_failed. On the model route the same results go back to the model as tool messages before it chooses its next call. Explain which result changes and why nobody may claim success. This is learning support, not evidence that a model or sandbox ran.

The course team can approve equivalent equipment, a supported replay/interaction path or additional time with the same LO, task, verification and individual evidence requirements. Consult the actual course support route and fallback status. Choose replay without giving a reason when the hosted route is unavailable; it keeps the same task, verification and evidence requirements and the same score ceiling.

docs.title: Optional extension
docs.text: After the workshop, compare two production prompts: read the instructions and tool definitions of two open-source coding agents, and sort which rules a schema, tool code or runtime enforces and which only ask, as you did for your own tool and CONTRACT.

docs.title: Return to the dashboard
docs.text:
Write run() until the public checks pass, reproduce one failed verification and explain how the proposer's next call depends on the result it received.

Submit P1 from the existing P1 code, trace, verification and your independent explanation.

Before leaving, decide whether to accept the change, narrow the task, obtain one missing observation or stop. Explain what evidence could change that decision.

docs.title: Dissect a recorded agent session
docs.text:
The loop you write from the notes shows the idea in miniature. A mature coding agent runs the same loop, but every request carries far more: long instructions, a set of tool definitions and the whole conversation so far. In this activity you read one recorded session request by request. You predict first, check each prediction against the record, and then compare what you saw with your own P1 controller.

The session shipped with this page, sample-session.jsonl, is course-made: the course team wrote it by hand in the same format a recording of a real agent uses. It shows what to look for. It does not describe how any product behaves, and it contains no measured numbers.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Required. Everyone completes this activity in Week 2. It is part of P1, not a separate submission.

Estimated time: about two and a half hours in total: predictions, the request-by-request reading, the comparison with your controller and the short write-up. This is an estimate, not a limit; ask for help at the workshop if it is running far over.

Order:

  1. After the Week 2 class and before its workshop, do steps 1-4 and bring your request table and answers.
  2. At the workshop, swap tables with a partner as described under Review, and revise.
  3. Step 5 needs a trajectory.jsonl from your own P1 runs, so do it once your Agent.run has run the P1 tasks. Then write up the records.

Materials:

  • the record: session/sample-session.jsonl, or a teaching-team recording of a real agent if one has been published beside it (see below);
  • the viewer: session/show_session.py;
  • your own P1 controller and one trajectory.jsonl from your P1 runs;
  • the notes section on reading a production agent's instructions.

Grouping: work alone or in pairs. You may discuss the record with a partner, but each person writes their own predictions, dissection and comparison.

Route: everyone dissects the same published record, so this activity costs nothing and does not need an API key. If you use the hosted route in Week 0 setup, you may also dissect one request from your own run's trace (step 5). That option earns no extra marks; students on the replay route reach the same full marks with the record alone.

AI use: red. Write your predictions, dissection and comparison without AI, as for the P1 reflection.

docs.title: Which record to use
docs.text: The header line of each record names its source. "provenance": "course-made-sample" is the hand-written sample. "provenance": "teacher-recording" is a real session that the teaching team captured with the course's approved model configuration, with the agent's name and version, the recording date and a list of what was redacted. When a teacher recording sits beside the sample in session/, dissect the teacher recording and use the sample only to practise the steps. Otherwise, dissect the sample.

docs.title: Step 1: predict before you open the record
docs.text:
Read only the task in the header line: the agent must change a status label in a small repository and keep its tests passing, which touches a source file and a test file. Then, before running the viewer, write down your answers:

  1. How many requests will the agent send to the model to finish this two-file change?
  2. Which tool will it call first?
  3. Will the instructions and tool definitions be sent once, or with every request?
  4. Will any tool call fail? If one does, what will the agent do next?
  5. How will the size of the request change from the first request to the last? Will anything sent earlier be removed or rewritten?
  6. Why will the loop stop, and what evidence will the agent have for its final message?

Keep these answers unchanged. You compare them with the record in step 4.

docs.title: Step 2: read the record request by request
docs.text:
Run the viewer from the course root. It uses only Python's standard library, reads the file and prints text. It never runs anything found in the record and never uses the network.

python3 lectures/week-02/session/show_session.py lectures/week-02/session/sample-session.jsonl

The summary prints one block per request: whether the instructions and tools were sent again, which messages are new since the previous request, which earlier messages changed, and what came back. To see everything one request sent and received, including the full instructions, every tool schema and every message, name the request:

python3 lectures/week-02/session/show_session.py lectures/week-02/session/sample-session.jsonl --request 4

Expected: the summary starts with a Session: line naming the source and ends with an End of record block. A file that is not a session record or course trajectory gives one error: line naming the problem and its line number.

docs.title: Step 3: dissect
docs.text:
Fill one row per request. Keep each cell short and cite what you saw.

Request New or changed instructions Tools offered (count; any change) What came back: text, tool calls or both How the results return What was re-sent, cleared or rewritten Continue or stop, and why

Then answer these questions. Label every answer [observed] when you can point to it in the record (give the request number and message index, for example request 5, [11]), or [inferred] when you are reasoning from what you read without having seen it happen. Both kinds are acceptable. A wrong label is the mistake to avoid.

A. The instructions. Open the instructions in request 1. Sort each sentence into the four groups from the notes: role or goal, tool contract, stopping or escalation rule, request for caution. Pick one sentence from each group and say which failure it guards against. Then say what, if anything, enforces it: a tool schema, the tool's own checks, a sandbox, an approval step, or nothing. Where does the description of the environment (working directory, date) sit in the request? Find a message that was added in the middle of the conversation rather than at the start. Who wrote it, which role does it use, and why might an agent add it there instead of repeating it in the instructions?

B. The tools. How many tools were offered, and did the set change during the session? Choose two tools that do different kinds of work, for example a file-editing tool and the planning tool, or the command tool. For each one: copy the relevant part of its schema; say which parameters are required, which are optional and what the tool deliberately does not let the model choose; find one sentence in its description that looks as if it was added because a model kept making the same mistake, and name that mistake. Which constraints does the schema enforce, and which does the description only ask for?

C. What the model returned. For each response, was it text, tool calls or both? Find a response with more than one tool call. Were those calls independent of each other?

D. How results return. How does each tool result find its call? What did the agent see when a tool call failed, and what did it do in the next request? Count the requests between the failure and the recovery, and quote the error text exactly.

E. Where and why the loop stopped. Which response ended the loop, and how can you tell from the record alone? Find the observation that supports the final message. Is the final claim verified by an observation in the record, or only stated? Would the record let you detect a final message that claimed more than the agent had checked?

F. What was re-sent, cleared or rewritten. How did the request size change across the session, and what accounts for most of it? Which earlier messages changed between two requests, what replaced them, and what information did that remove? Did the agent need that information again, and how would it get it back?

G. Plans and task state. Where does the agent keep track of which steps are done? If it records a plan or task list, list every place the plan appears: tool calls, tool results and any message added in the middle of the conversation. What does the result of a plan update tell the agent, and what does it not check? Find a request where the plan, as last recorded, is behind what the tool results already show, or say there is none. For each item marked completed at the end, cite the observation that shows the step was done. If the agent keeps no plan, say where its task state lives instead.

docs.title: Step 4: check your predictions
docs.text: Put each prediction from step 1 next to what you observed. For the prediction that was furthest off, write two or three sentences: what in the record surprised you, and what you would now expect from your own controller in the same situation.

docs.title: Step 5: compare with your P1 controller
docs.text:
Run the same viewer on a trajectory.jsonl from one of your P1 task runs (use your own output directory name):

python3 lectures/week-02/session/show_session.py lab01-repair/trajectory.jsonl

A course trajectory holds roles, approximate sizes and tool names, but not text; read the text of the same run in its completion.json. If you used the hosted route, you may instead dissect one request from the trace file your own run wrote. Both give the same marks.

Answer from the two records side by side:

  • What does your controller send as its first message, and what does the recorded agent send? Where do your tool names and argument rules live: in a schema the model sees, in your validation code, or both?
  • Does your controller send the whole history every time? Compare what your compact copy sends with what the recorded agent re-sent or cleared.
  • How does each loop decide to stop, and what evidence does each have at that point?
  • Where does each loop keep track of which steps are done, and what happens to that record when old messages are dropped or cleared?

Then choose:

  • one behaviour you would copy into your controller, and
  • one behaviour you would change if you built the recorded agent,

each with its evidence (request number and what you saw) and the check that would show it working: a test, a trace you would inspect, or a failing case that should now stop correctly. A behaviour you copy without a check is a claim, not an improvement.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
Write your dissection inside your P1 Week 2 checkpoint explanation, under the same evidence ID; see P1 deliverables. Include:

  • your six predictions as you wrote them before reading the record;
  • the request table and your answers to A–G, each labelled and cited;
  • the prediction check and your copy/change choices with their checks.

Name the record you dissected by its file name and provenance. Do not copy the whole record into your submission; cite request numbers and quote only the lines your answer depends on. If you dissected a request from your own run, quote only roles, sizes, tool names and short lines you have checked for keys, personal data and private code. Never include an API key, a header or an environment value.

docs.title: Review
docs.text: At the workshop, swap your table with a partner. The partner checks one [observed] answer against the record using its request number, and marks any place where a final message or success claim has no supporting observation. Revise that answer before you submit. The partner's check is feedback; your explanation remains your own.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake How to notice it Small correction Counting tool calls instead of requests Your request count differs from the number of Request N blocks One response can hold several calls; count model requests Treating the final message as evidence Your answer to E quotes only the last message Find the tool result that supports it, or say there is none Treating a plan item marked completed as evidence Your answer to G cites only a plan update Find the tool result that shows the step was done Assuming an instruction is enforced You cannot name what would stop the model from ignoring it Look for a schema rule, a tool check or a sandbox; otherwise it only asks Missing what the agent wrote into the conversation You attribute every user message to the person Read the message itself; an agent can add messages in any role Labelling an inference as observed Your citation points to a message that does not show the claim Change the label or find the request that shows it

All materials are plain text. The viewer output, tables and record can be read with a screen reader or keyboard-only editor; no diagram or colour is needed for any step.

docs.title: Week 2: Build a small coding agent
Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this week, you can:

  • LO1: trace an observation, a proposed action, a tool result and a stop decision, and predict how a loop fails when its context or stopping rule is wrong.
  • LO2: define narrow read / write / bash contracts, run a synthetic repair through the approved launcher, and account for its finite calls and verification evidence.
  • LO7: show that a refused call reaches the model as a result and has no effect, and name which limits the launcher enforces that your Python dispatcher cannot.

These are this week's contributions to the broader course outcomes. The activity and self-check exercise all three. P1 provides individual LO1 evidence. LO2 practice here prepares for your individual work in the repository-context workshop and the portfolio evidence specified by the syllabus. LO7 starts here with execution boundaries; Week 8 continues it with attack and defense, and CP2 and the security segment of the individual defense assess it. A pair's classroom result cannot replace either person's individual assessment.

Use the approved hosted or replay route in Week 0 setup. Run code only after that page's check shows you can run the practices. Independent assessments remain AI-off.

docs.title: The continuing dashboard case
docs.text:
An agent is asked to repair the dashboard status formatter. Its trace stops right after writing a file. No check appears.

assistant  tool_calls: c1 read {"path": "status.py"}
tool c1    (the file text)
assistant  tool_calls: c2 write {"path": "status.py", "content": candidate}
tool c2    "written"
assistant  "done", with no tool calls

Decision: Which observation is missing before anyone may report verified success?

The loop stopped with final: the model made no further calls. That ends the conversation; it says nothing about whether the file is right. The write records a side effect. Nothing observed the acceptance checks on that revision. Success needs an allowed verification call and its passing result in the history.

Specify accepted tools, arguments, allowed paths and the turn budget. Send the model its history, including every actual tool result, and let it choose the next call.

Acceptance decision: Report verified only when a passing check appears in the history after the last write. Report the stop reason (final or step_limit) separately; a summary must keep the last failed check.

The public result.txt exercise below isolates the call/result mechanism used when an agent edits dashboard code. Its small file is a teaching fixture, not the dashboard implementation. All examples on this page are course-authored; actual execution evidence comes from your own checks.

docs.title: One task, three tool calls
docs.text:
A model produces text or a structured proposal. An agent controller decides whether to call a tool, records the actual result, sends it back and lets the model choose again. Here, think means selecting a next call from the goal and the observations so far. A short explanation may help a person inspect that choice, but a claimed explanation does not prove what happened inside a model or that the call is correct.

Our synthetic task is to repair result.txt: it initially contains 5 followed by a newline, and should contain 4 followed by a newline. No private repository, personal data, service or benchmark is involved.

Turn Model's call Tool message sent back Controller 1 c1 read {"path": "result.txt"} tool_call_id: c1, 5 Continue 2 c2 write {"path": "result.txt", "content": "4 "} tool_call_id: c2, written Continue: a completed write is not a test 3 c3 bash {"command": "verify"} tool_call_id: c3, verified Continue 4 No calls; text "Verified." None Stop with final

The check result is the tool message under c3, not the model's last sentence. First predict the outcome of writing 5 instead. The verification subprocess exits nonzero, the c3 result becomes check_failed, and a final reply cannot change it.

docs.title: You write the loop; the protocol is P1's
docs.text:
Open fixture/loop.py as plain text. It supplies the tool contract (tool), the reply check (checked) and the evidence reader (last_check). The loop itself, run(), is yours. In the workshop the instructor builds steps 1-3 as a live demonstration while you type the same three, steps 4-5 you write alone, and the public checks tell you when it meets this contract, which is the message protocol of P1's controller tasks:

  1. Start with one user message holding the task.
  2. Send a copy of the whole history to the model (chat). Check the reply's shape before any tool runs (checked): text content, and a tool_calls list whose items each have an id, a name and an arguments object. A malformed reply, or an ID that an earlier call already used, raises an error: no result could be matched to it.
  3. Append the reply as an assistant message. With no tool calls, stop with final, even if the text is empty.
  4. Otherwise run each call through tool and append one role: "tool" message per call, with the call's own tool_call_id and the actual result as string content. A missing file or a timed-out check becomes a failed: ... result.
  5. When the turn budget (max_steps, four by default) is spent, stop with step_limit.

Until you write it, run() raises NotImplementedError and the public checks stop with "Write run() in loop.py first". final means the conversation stopped, not that the task is correct. last_check reads the evidence separately: the newest verify result, or not_run when a later write made it stale. Two P1 differences matter: P1 passes a compacted copy of the history through the supplied compact, and its tools come from the supplied runtime. The P1 README remains the exact contract for your own Agent.run.

The contract has no repeat detector. A reread after a write can be useful; the same read four times only spends the budget. The turn budget bounds both. A general agent may add a state-aware progress check, but it still needs an absolute budget. The launcher separately owns wall time, process, memory, output and model-call limits; the first bound reached ends the run.

Tool Accepted arguments Result read {"path": "result.txt"} The actual file text write {"path": "result.txt", "content": ...}, text of at most 32 characters written bash {"command": "verify"} Runs a fixed assertion; verified or check_failed

Any other tool, argument name, path or command, or content that cannot be written as text, gets a short refused: ... result under the call's ID, before any effect, and the model sees it on its next turn. last_check counts only the exact verify call, so a refused bash call never stands in for a check. The name bash does not grant a model an unrestricted shell: the adapter selects the literal verification program and never interpolates model text into a shell command. The 32-character write limit is a course exercise choice. The four-turn default matches the launcher's cap of four model requests per run. Neither is a product limit or a model-token budget.

This small dispatcher assumes the launcher copied a clean synthetic workspace with no links or concurrent writers. It cannot contain a hostile replacement of its own Python code. The launcher supplies the external isolation boundary. These public assertions are practice feedback, not a trusted hidden grader.

docs.title: ReAct and its limits
docs.text:
The ReAct structure discussed in the course alternates reasoning about a next action, acting through a tool, and observing its result. Our loop makes those transitions inspectable. It does not reproduce a research experiment or claim a benchmark result. A model-driven proposer can choose poorly, invent a tool or repeat a call. Neither the structure nor a fluent explanation guarantees progress, factual accuracy or safe permissions.

Once your run() passes the public checks, the demo driver puts two proposers behind it:

  • Scripted practice (python demo.py): a course-written function that reads the latest tool result and picks the next call: read, write the candidate, verify, then stop and report the last result. Its candidate is fixed text, so this is practice, not a model.
  • Model route (python demo.py hosted, or replay): each turn sends the tool contract and the whole history as one prompt through the launcher, at most four requests per run. The model therefore receives every observation: the file text, written and the check result. Its JSON reply becomes the next assistant message.

The model-route adapter numbers the model's calls (t1-1, t2-1, ...), as a provider API assigns call IDs. It removes a leading <think>...</think> block or one json code fence. It does not repair a wrong argument or add a missing call. A reply that is not one JSON object is reported as unusable_reply and the run fails; the check still decides whether result.txt is right.

docs.title: Context is a bounded working record
docs.text:
The window is a budget. Every request carries the history so far: the task, every reply and every tool result. A context window caps how much one request can carry, and each turn sends every earlier byte again. The contract resends the whole history each turn. That fits four turns over a one-line file; it would not fit a repository repair. P1 sends a compacted copy instead and keeps the full history in the returned trajectory.

What accumulates. The history grows with every call, and three kinds of content take most of the room. Tool output, such as file reads, test logs and search results, is usually the largest part and goes out of date first. Failed attempts stay, with their edits and error output. Repeated reads of the same file add a copy each time. The instructions and tool definitions are sent with every request as well. In the session dissection, find what accounts for most of the growth in request size from the first request to the last.

How a long history misleads later steps. Overflowing the window is the obvious failure. Three others come first:

  • Stale observations. An early read of a file stays in the history after the agent has changed the file. Nothing marks it out of date, so a later step can act on old text.
  • Contradictions. A failed attempt and the decision that replaced it both remain. The history holds both and does not say which one stands.
  • Buried instructions. A constraint that arrived once, for example in a file the agent read, sits under everything that came after it. Nothing in the loop makes the model give it weight many turns later, and clearing old tool output removes it with the rest.

What compaction does. Compaction replaces older turns with something smaller before the next request. Clearing replaces old tool results with a short stub, as the recorded session in the dissection does for two earlier file reads. Summarising replaces older turns with written text. A useful summary keeps:

  • the task and its acceptance check;
  • each constraint and decision, with where it came from;
  • what was tried and how it failed, so the next step does not repeat it;
  • open failures: the last failed check and the file version it ran on;
  • the paths of the files involved, and the current state of each one touched;
  • the next step.

It drops raw tool output, because the agent can read the file or run the check again.

What compaction can lose. Whatever the summary leaves out is gone for the model, and reading the summary alone will not show you the gap. The usual losses are a constraint that arrived in a tool result, the version a check ran on, a refusal, and an attempt that already failed, which the agent may then try again. If a summary says "test passed" but omits which file revision it tested, that claim cannot justify a later edit. Check a summary like any generated work: confirm each required fact against the transcript, then confirm that the next step still passes the same check. In Week 3 you run that comparison on one long session.

Compact or restart. Compact when the task continues and the newest raw results still matter. Restart with a fresh context and a written handoff when most of the history is stale or contradicts itself, when one phase of the work has ended, or when the agent keeps failing in the same way. A handoff holds the same items as a summary, written so that a new session can act on it alone. After either one, reread the files the next edit touches before editing.

P1 supplies compact, so you do not write one. It keeps the task, shortens long tool results and, while the copy is still too large, drops the oldest call/result groups whole; it writes no summary. Design a working record of your own first: the goal, permitted tools, current file state, last verification result and remaining budget, with older observations summarized as claims tied to evidence and unresolved failures kept. Then compare it with what compact keeps, and name one item of your record that the model loses when compact drops a group, such as an early refusal or a failed check. Character limits in this fixture do not measure tokens. Use the shared model contract and the actual broker trace for model limits and observed usage, without copying its parameters into a second configuration.

docs.title: Product comparison: the permission primitive
docs.text:
Read this comparison conceptually in Week 2. It is not permission to start a frontier agent or install an additional tool outside the approved setup. Product details refer only to the dated, independently reviewed cards. This lesson does not pin a product version.

Course primitive Codex Qwen Code Tool effects and permission The reviewed CLI documentation separates sandbox limits on writes/network from approval policy. Its explicit workspace-write / on-request combination permits workspace operations while other operations require approval. (tools/codex; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1) The reviewed explicit Ask Permissions mode requests approval before file edits or shell execution. (tools/qwen-code; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2) What to verify A never approval policy disables prompts without itself disabling the sandbox. Check actual boundaries, not the absence of a prompt. (tools/codex; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1) Select the intended approval mode explicitly and verify denied edits/commands have no effect. The card does not establish a default sandbox equivalent to the course launcher. (tools/qwen-code; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2)

Both comparisons help separate tool capability, permission decisions and containment. They do not assert identical read APIs, context compression, stopping behavior or full feature parity. Future actual product use needs the course-selected configuration and its verification. The course's miniature read/write/bash vocabulary is our interface.

docs.title: Reading a production agent's instructions
docs.text:
For reading purposes, a production coding agent shares an outline with your run(): a loop that sends the history, a set of tool definitions and instructions to the model, and answers each call under its ID. The outline is where the resemblance ends. Yours resends a four-turn history with no compaction, no progress check and three fixed tools, so it cannot stand in for a production controller's state, history and progress handling. When a vendor or an open-source project publishes its instructions, read them as an engineer reads a configuration file, not as a description of guaranteed behavior. Sort every sentence into one of four bins: a role or goal, a tool contract (name, arguments, when to call it), a stopping or escalation rule, and a request for caution. Then ask of each one: what enforces this? A schema validator, a sandbox and an approval prompt enforce. A sentence that begins "never" only asks. Our controller makes the same split visible in miniature: the shape and argument checks before any effect enforce, while the contract text in the model-route prompt merely proposes.

To practise on real text, the optional comparison activity puts two open-source coding agents side by side at fixed commits. The Codex CLI base instructions tell the agent, for example, to keep going until the query is resolved and not to git commit unless asked; its update_plan schema limits each step's status to pending, in_progress or completed, while "at most one step in progress" appears only in the description text. (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) The Qwen Code prompt builder asks the agent to run the project's own checks before reporting a change complete and to say so when a check failed or was not run; its edit tool rejects a relative path and fails when the text to replace matches more than once, while "at least 3 lines of context" is only asked. (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) Sort sentences from both before deciding which ones anything enforces.

Two habits carry over to P1. First, a tool definition is part of the prompt, so a vague tool description is a vague instruction. Second, long instructions are not evidence of safety: count what is enforced, not what is written.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Follow the 60-minute activity, including prediction, the instructor's steps 1-3, verification, feedback and revision. It fits inside Week 2's class and P1 work. The required session dissection is another part of P1; its page estimates about two and a half hours and does not create a second submission. Do its steps 1-4 before the workshop, swap tables with a partner there, and do step 5 once your P1 runs have produced a trajectory. Week 2's published estimate is 12 total hours and P1's combined Weeks 1-2 time box is 11 hours. These are planning and help checkpoints, not measured completion claims, penalties or automatic stops.

Type steps 1-3 of run() while the instructor builds them on screen, then write steps 4-5 yourself against the contract above. Run the public checks after each step; they are the target, and their names tell you which part of the contract a failure breaks. After step 3, four pass; all fifteen pass once steps 4-5 are right. Then generate the synthetic candidate and verify it. After the workshop, change one stopping decision: set MAX_STEPS in demo.py to 2 and then to 3, predict each run's stop reason and check, run both, explain the observed effect and restore 4. Keep your work product, relevant verification and short explanation together. Add AI use once and reuse the same evidence ID in P1 if relevant. Keep only the loop fragments required to explain a failure or verified stop. Do not export an unrelated conversation. Any required personal reflection is written without AI.

At the help checkpoint, use the activity's hint ladder, the instructor's steps 1-3 and the check names, or an approved equivalent interaction path. The model route is optional for full marks. P1's own task remains individual: a minimal agent of at most 300 lines, its five tasks, required JSONL trajectory and calibration record. This classroom fixture does not replace those tasks.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Use the exact resolver and launcher sequence in the activity. The workspace contains only fixture/ public files. Every executable example, including the public tests and your loop.py, runs through the same course launcher. It refuses profile drift and reruns its safety suite. Do not mount the private course checkout or teacher answers. The supplied tests run with Python's standard library inside that sandbox.

Until run() is written, verify_loop.py stops with "Write run() in loop.py first" and the demo prints "error": "write run() in loop.py first", both before any model request. With your run(), the scripted demo should print generation: scripted-practice, stop_reason: final, check: verified and eight messages. In the exported completion.json, the three tool messages answer c1, c2 and c3 with 5\n, written and verified. The exported result.txt must contain exactly 4\n. All fifteen public checks must pass, including: a reply with no tool calls is final; the proposer receives each result under its call's ID; two calls in one reply are answered in the order listed, each under its own ID, even when the first is refused; a wrong candidate ends final with check_failed; a write followed by a final reply leaves the check not_run; a later write makes an earlier check stale; a repeated read runs until step_limit; refused calls are returned to the model with no effect; malformed replies and reused IDs stop before any tool runs; and a missing file and a simulated timeout become results. The timeout test checks controller handling; the course runtime suite tests containment.

In the budget experiment, MAX_STEPS = 2 ends with stop_reason: step_limit, check: not_run, five messages and a nonzero exit. MAX_STEPS = 3 ends with stop_reason: step_limit, check: verified, seven messages and a zero exit: the check passed, but the budget ended before a final reply. The demo's exit status follows the check, never the stop reason.

On the model route the launcher's result and trace show one request per turn, up to four. A malformed, oversized or wrong reply is a failure to inspect, not a reason to alter the expected answer or increase resource limits. completion.json is an exercise-local view, not the shared course_llm JSONL schema. Keep the launcher's minimal JSONL separately when a model call is required. Neither scripted practice nor a FAKE broker response is real-model acceptance or proof that you can run the practices.

After peer feedback, rerun the failing case and the correct case. Explain the changed check result with reference to the call and its actual result. That explanation, plus your own self-check, demonstrates individual understanding.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake Observable symptom Small correction Treating a write or a final reply as success final with no passing check after the last write Read the check result from the tool messages before reporting verified Answering a call under the wrong ID A result sits under another call's tool_call_id, or a call has no answer Append exactly one tool message per call, with that call's own ID Retrying forever Repeated calls until step_limit with no new evidence Keep the absolute turn budget; add a progress check only alongside it Trusting an invented tool upload or a model-chosen shell string causes an effect Refuse it before any effect and return the refusal as the result Losing constraints during compression Summary forgets a denied path or the tested revision Keep constraints and failure evidence, then reread current state Trusting a summary nobody checked After compaction the next step repeats an attempt that already failed Check each required fact against the transcript, then rerun the same check Treating a prompt as containment Permission dialogue exists but process has broad access Keep external launcher isolation and test denied effects Running on the host to fix setup The Week 0 runtime check has not passed Stop execution and use the approved support/equivalent path Equating model text with a passed task Real call succeeded but assertion failed Report generation and verification separately

Low-resource and accessibility routes retain the same task, verification and evidence. Use the current fallback status when the hosted route is unavailable; replay keeps the same learning requirements and score ceiling. The course team can approve equivalent equipment or interaction arrangements with unchanged learning and attainable marks.

docs.title: Transfer to a new situation
docs.text:
An agent repairing the dashboard status formatter writes status.py, runs the acceptance tests and sees them fail, writes status.py again, and then the turn budget ends. Read afterwards, the new file looks right. What stop reason and check status does the record show, what must a summary of the run keep, and which observation would let you report the repair verified?

Write the expected behavior and the next check before comparing with a partner.

Submit P1 from the existing P1 code, trace, verification and your independent explanation.

docs.title: Compare two production prompts
docs.text:
On the model route, your loop sends the model a short tool contract. A production coding agent sends much more: a role, working rules, a permission policy, a stopping rule and a schema for every tool. Two open-source coding agents publish the code that builds that text under the Apache-2.0 licence: Codex CLI and Qwen Code. In this activity you read the same four parts in both, at fixed commits, and ask the same two questions of every sentence you pick: what does it make the model do, and what, if anything, enforces it?

You read the original files on GitHub. This page links them and quotes only a few words, always naming the project; it does not copy the files. Facts about the files come from two reading pages, one for Codex CLI (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) and one for Qwen Code (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7). Neither agent's files are the complete prompt a release sends at run time, and this page does not rank the two products.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Optional, about 45 minutes. It earns no marks. It extends the notes' section on reading a production agent's instructions and replaces the shorter single-file reading. Parts 1-4 need only a browser. Part 5 can use the Week 2 fixture through the launcher, or stay a written plan.

Before you start: your run() passes the public checks, or you have read its contract in the notes. You can name its three tools and its two stop reasons.

AI use: red. Write your answers yourself; the point is your own reading.

Output: one table for Parts 1-4 and a short Part 5 plan. If you use it in P1, keep it with your Week 2 checkpoint explanation under the same evidence ID; it is not a separate submission.

docs.title: The files
docs.text:
Part Codex CLI, commit 2351d9e Qwen Code, tag v0.25.0 (commit 6788c03) 1. Role and instructions default.md: the opening paragraph and capabilities list, "Task execution", "Validating your work" prompts.ts: getDefaultCoreIdentitySentence, "Core Mandates", "Software Engineering Tasks" 2. Tools and schemas the apply_patch example in "Task execution"; plan_spec.rs for update_plan "Using Your Tools" in prompts.ts; edit.ts for edit; todoWrite.ts for todo_write 3. Safety and permission the approval sentence in the capabilities list; "Validating your work"; the rules that begin NEVER or Do not "Denied Tool Calls", "Respect Tool Decisions", "Executing actions with care", the sandbox sections 4. Stopping and plans the first paragraph of "Task execution"; "update_plan" under "Tool Guidelines" "Final Reminder"; the todo_write description in todoWrite.ts

Open both Codex CLI files, the base instructions default.md and the tool definition plan_spec.rs, from the links on its reading page; the Qwen Code files are linked in the table and on its reading page.

default.md is Markdown: read it as it stands. prompts.ts is TypeScript that builds the prompt. Text between backticks is what the model receives, and ${...} inserts a value, often a tool name such as ${ToolNames.EDIT}; the names are listed in tool-names.ts. Which sections appear depends on the interaction mode, the sandbox configuration and whether the directory is a Git repository, and an environment variable can replace the whole default base prompt with a file. (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) Read the interactive default.

docs.title: Record
docs.text:
Use one row per sentence or rule. Pick at least two per part, one from each agent.

Part Agent Section and a few words What it makes the model do What enforces it Where you saw that

For what enforces it, choose one: the schema (a malformed call is rejected before the tool runs); the tool's own code (it checks and returns an error text to the model); a runtime permission or sandbox outside the model; or nothing visible. Write "cannot tell" when you did not open the code that would decide, and say which file you would need.

docs.title: Part 1: role and instructions
docs.text:
1. Find the sentence in each file that says what the agent is and what its goal is. Which words could change a choice the agent makes on a dashboard repair, and which only name it?
  2. Find each agent's rule for checking work after a change. The Codex CLI file ties when to run tests and lint to the approval mode; the Qwen Code file asks for the project's own checks before reporting a change complete, and for an honest report when a check failed or was not run. (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) For each, describe a run in which the agent reports a change without having run a test. Which field in your Week 2 completion.json would show that case, and with what value?

docs.title: Part 2: tools and schemas
docs.text:
1. Compare update_plan with todo_write: required and optional fields, the allowed status values, and where "one step in progress" is written. In todoWrite.ts, read validateTodos: list what it checks, and say whether it checks that limit. For Codex CLI, can you tell from the files you opened? Mark "cannot tell" where you cannot.
  2. In edit.ts, read the edit tool's description, its parameter schema, validateToolParamValues and calculateEdit. Sort each rule into required by the schema, checked by code with an error returned to the model, or only asked in the description. Start from two: "at least 3 lines of context" is only asked, while a second match without replace_all fails with an error that gives the count. (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) What does the model see on its next turn when it breaks each kind?
  3. The Codex CLI file names apply_patch and shows one call. Did you open its schema? If not, name what you would need to read before you could sort its rules the same way.
  4. Sort your own loop the same way: what does checked reject, what does tool refuse, and what appears only in the CONTRACT text of demo.py?

docs.title: Part 3: safety and permission rules
docs.text:
1. In the Qwen Code file, "Respect Tool Decisions" says the runtime enforces tool permissions, while "Denied Tool Calls" asks the model not to reach a denied action another way, through a shell, a generated script or an alias. (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) Why might a product need that request as well as the runtime check? For your loop, name one route that tool closes and one that only the launcher closes.
  2. The Codex CLI capabilities list refers to a "Sandbox and approvals" section that the file itself does not contain. (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) What does that tell you about where the rest of the prompt comes from, and what would you need to read next?
  3. Pick one sentence from "Executing actions with care" or a sandbox section in the Qwen Code file. Describing a sandbox to the model does not create one: which control outside the prompt would have to exist for the sentence to be true? Compare with the permission comparison in the notes.

docs.title: Part 4: stopping and plans
docs.text:
1. Both files ask the agent to keep going until the request is resolved; the Qwen Code file also names an exit, reporting the specific blocker. (tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) Neither sentence can stop a loop. Which code stops your run(), and what would a production agent need in place of your step_limit?
  2. A plan step marked completed is the model's own claim. Which observation would you need before you accept it? Compare your answer with question G of the session dissection.

docs.title: Part 5: change one part for ci-dashboard
docs.text:
Choose one sentence or schema rule from either file that you would change or add if the agent were repairing ci-dashboard. Examples: name the acceptance command instead of "the project's own test commands", or require a passing check after the last write before any final reply. Write three things:

  • The change and where it belongs: the product's base prompt, a repository instruction file (Week 3), a tool schema, or controller code. If a rule can be checked in code, say why you would or would not still put it in the prompt.
  • The predicted effect, as something a trace would show: which call appears, the stop reason and the check status.
  • The verification: how you would show the effect with the course mini-agent.

The Week 2 model route sends the CONTRACT text of demo.py before the history, so a prompt rule can be tried there. Copy your passing work into a new workspace and add your sentence to CONTRACT in the copy only:

mkdir week02-prompt
cp week02-work/*.py week02-prompt/

Then run the hosted command in the activity twice, each time with a new trace file name: once without the change, with --workspace week02-work, and once with it, with --workspace week02-prompt.

Compare the two traces and completion.json files: did a verify call follow the last write, and what were the stop reason and the check? One run of each version is one observation, not a rate; report it that way. A replay record returns the same frozen replies whatever the prompt says, so on the replay route write the expected trace for each version instead of running it. Either way, also say which part of your loop already reports the truth regardless of the prompt: last_check stays not_run or check_failed whatever the model writes.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake How to notice it Small correction Treating a sentence as a guarantee Your "what enforces it" column says the prompt Name a schema, a code check or a runtime control, or write "nothing visible" Guessing about code you did not open You wrote "enforced" for a rule whose checker you never read Write "cannot tell" and name the file to read Reading prompts.ts as one fixed text You quote two sandbox sections as if both were sent Pick one branch and say which condition selects it Copying long passages into your record Your table holds whole paragraphs Give the section and a few words; link the pinned file Judging one product better Your answer ranks the agents Compare what each rule does and what enforces it

All files are plain text on GitHub and can be read with a screen reader or keyboard; no diagram or colour is needed for any step.

docs.title: Week 2 readings
docs.text:
Before class, read the learning objectives and fixed contract in the notes. Attempt the first slide question before opening the worked explanation. After class, use the worked sections, activities and self-check. If you already saw a solution, mark the next attempt as informed practice.

The course case explains how this week connects to the product.

docs.title: Two focused external readings
docs.text:
• Permission claims need separate checks (about 10 minutes, optional): read Agent approvals & security, especially “Sandbox and approvals” and “Run without approval prompts”, to decide which sandbox, write and approval boundaries you must verify before running a read/write/bash loop. (tools/codex; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1)
  • Two production prompts, side by side (about 45 minutes, optional): open the Codex CLI base instructions and its update_plan tool definition, and the Qwen Code prompt builder and its edit and todo_write tool definitions, each at a fixed commit (both Apache-2.0). The comparison activity links every file and asks, part by part (role and instructions, tools and schemas, safety and permission, stopping and plans), what each sentence makes the model do and what, if anything, enforces it. Mark a rule "cannot tell" when nothing you can see checks it. Neither file is the full prompt a current release sends. The reading pages for Codex CLI and Qwen Code record what the files say.
