(tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7)

Required this week, as part of P1: dissect a recorded agent session.

docs.title: Week 2 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Use these explanations after your first attempt. Each conclusion is limited to the fixture and observation named in the prompt.

docs.title: Q1a–Q1c: Cycle and verification
docs.text: Q1a. Success requires a verify call after the write whose tool message returns verified, from a check that observed result.txt == "4\n". Q1b. written records an effect, not the required output. Q1c. final only means the reply had no tool calls; “done” is model text, not a tool observation. Neither is a check result.

docs.title: Q2a–Q2c: Stopping
docs.text: Q2a. step_limit: the contract has no repeat detector, so the turn budget ends the loop. Q2b. not_run: no verify call ever ran. Q2c. Neither stop reason proves the repair; a requirement check in the history is still needed.

docs.title: Q3a–Q3c: Tool boundary
docs.text: Q3a. Only bash with {"command": "verify"} runs. ./result.txt names the same file, but the contract accepts only the literal path result.txt: the dispatcher compares the text and does not resolve paths. The write carries an argument name, mode, that the contract does not list, and argument names must match exactly. Q3b. The fixture's tool function decides before any effect. The read and the write each get refused: tool, argument or path outside the contract under their own IDs. The refused write changed nothing, so the file still holds 5\n and the verify call returns check_failed. The model sees all three results on its next turn. Q3c. tool only limits calls that pass through it. It is ordinary Python in the same process as your run(), which you edit and the launcher runs, so code that skips or changes it is not held back by it. The launcher limits files, network, processes and resources for everything in the run, whatever that Python code does.

docs.title: Q4a–Q4c: Context and budget
docs.text: Q4a. Preserve the goal, allowed operation, artifact and tested revisions, last result, unresolved failures and remaining budget. Q4b. Reread the changed file and rerun the relevant check on the new revision. Q4c. A summary can be stale or wrong because it is not the observation itself.

docs.title: Q5a–Q5c: Safety state
docs.text: Q5a. Reading, planning and text reasoning may continue. Q5b. Code execution and model calls stop until the Week 0 runtime check passes and an approved model or replay is available. Q5c. The offline check is preparation feedback, not proof that you can run the practices, and it observed yesterday's state. The launcher reruns its safety checks on every run, and today's failed check is the current observation. Execution resumes only after those checks pass again through the Week 0 route.

docs.title: Q6a–Q6d: Boundaries
docs.text: Q6a. Approval decides whether an operation may proceed. Q6b. Containment limits what a running process can access. Q6c. A stopping rule decides when the controller ends. Q6d. A scripted driver does not prove model choice or feature parity.

docs.title: Q7a–Q7b: Call IDs
docs.text: Q7a. The model believes the read returned verified and the check returned the file text, so it may report success without having seen a check of the current file. Q7b. The public check test_two_calls_in_one_reply_are_answered_in_order: its replies each hold two calls, and it compares the call IDs, in order, with the answering tool_call_ids and checks each call's own result. A check whose replies hold only one call cannot catch the swap, because a single call has nothing to be swapped with.

docs.title: Q8a–Q8c: Asked or enforced
docs.text: Q8a. The edit fails and the file is unchanged. The error text, which gives the number of matches, comes back as the tool result, so the model can retry with more context or with replace_all. Q8b. Neither of these two rules stops it: the text matches once, so the single-match rule is satisfied, and nothing checks the three-line request. The single-match rule is enforced by the tool's own code; the three-line request sits only in the description. The tool's code makes other checks that this question does not cover. Whether the one match was the intended place is a question for the next read or test. (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) Q8c. tool refuses ./result.txt, an extra mode argument or any command other than verify, before any effect. The task's "Run the verify check, then report" only asks: nothing makes the model call verify. last_check does not enforce it either, but it makes the missing check visible as not_run.

docs.title: Q9a–Q9d: Compaction
docs.text: Q9a. The failure survives, but only in the agent's own sentence "the strip-only lookup fails"; the check output itself is cleared. The view.py constraint is lost: it arrived once, inside a tool result, and the agent never restated it. Nothing in the compacted history shows that it is missing, so the next step can edit view.py without any visible contradiction. Q9b. The six items from the notes: (1) the task and its acceptance check; (2) the constraint not to edit view.py, with NOTES.md as its source; (3) the strip-only attempt and how it failed; (4) the open failure: the last check failed on "OK", run on the strip-only status.py; (5) the paths status.py and view.py and their current state: status.py holds the edited version, so the first read is stale, and view.py is as shipped; and (6) the next step. It may drop the raw file contents and the full check output, which the agent can read or run again. Q9c. Check each required fact against the transcript, citing the message it came from, then let the next step run and rerun the same check on its result. The check alone is not enough: a summary can pass one check and still miss a fact a later step needs. Q9d. For example: most of the history is stale or contradicts itself; one phase of the work has finished; or the agent keeps failing in the same way. Reread the files the next edit touches before editing.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval
docs.text: Retrieval 1. Read the relevant contract through the permitted tool to supply the missing context, record its revision and rerun a requirement check. Retrieval 2. "OK" should map to passed; normalize with raw.strip().lower() and retain both padded and mixed-case regressions.

docs.title: Dashboard transfer
docs.text: The stop is step_limit. The check status is not_run: the failed test run checked the earlier revision, and the later write made that result stale. A summary must keep that failure and the revision it tested; "looks right" is a reading of the file, not a check. Only the acceptance tests run on the current revision, with a passing result in the history, would let you report the repair verified. That later run adds evidence; it does not change the earlier step_limit stop.

docs.title: Check your own loop reasoning
docs.text: After the workshop, use the public answer guidance.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Answer individually in your existing work record. These are formative questions, not an additional graded quiz. Use the notes after your first attempt and record one correction. No tools need to run for these questions.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
The loop reads 5 , writes 4 , and the next reply has no tool calls and the text “done.”

1a. Which observation would justify success?

1b. Why is the write result insufficient?

1c. The loop stops with final. Why is that stop, or the text “done,” insufficient?

A proposer returns the same read call, with a new ID, on every turn.

2a. What stop reason should a run() that meets the contract report?

2b. What check status does the history show, and why?

2c. Does either stop reason prove that the repair succeeded?

One reply holds three calls, in this order, while result.txt holds 5 : read with {"path": "./result.txt"}, write with {"path": "result.txt", "content": "4 ", "mode": "w"}, and bash with {"command": "verify"}.

3a. Which call does the fixture execute, and which argument decides each of the other two?

3b. Where is that decision enforced, and what does the model receive for each of the three calls?

3c. Why is the external launcher still needed?

An agent summary says “tests passed” but omits the tested revision, and the next call changes the file.

4a. Which revision evidence must the working record preserve?

4b. Which result must be rerun after the file change?

4c. Why can a stored summary be stale or wrong?

A model is approved but the workspace safety check fails.

5a. What work may continue?

5b. Which execution must stop?

5c. Your offline doctor check passed yesterday. Why does that not let execution continue today?

An approval prompt, an operating-system sandbox boundary and a verified stopping rule are all present in the workflow.

6a. What does the approval prompt decide?

6b. What does the sandbox boundary limit?

6c. What does the stopping rule decide?

6d. Does a scripted driver prove feature parity or model choice?

One reply asks for two calls: c1 reads result.txt and c2 runs verify. Your loop runs both but appends the verify result under c1 and the file text under c2.

7a. What does the model now believe each call returned?

7b. Which public check would catch this, and why can a check whose replies each hold one call not catch it?

The edit tool of an open-source coding agent (Qwen Code) asks, in its description, for at least three lines of context around the text to replace. Its code makes the edit fail when that text matches more than once and replace_all is not set. (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7)

8a. A model sends one line of context that matches twice. What happens to the file, and what does the model see on its next turn?

8b. A model sends one line of context that matches once. Does either of these two rules stop the edit? Which of the two is enforced, and by what?

8c. Name the same split in your own loop: one rule that tool enforces before any effect, and one that the task or CONTRACT text only asks for.

An agent's history holds the task; a read of NOTES.md that says not to edit view.py; a strip-only edit to status.py; a check that failed on "OK", followed by the agent's own message "the strip-only lookup fails"; and a reread of the edited status.py. Before the next request, every older tool result is cleared to a stub and the agent's own messages are kept.

9a. Does the view.py constraint survive the clearing? Does the failure? Why is a loss here easy to miss?

9b. Write the six items a summary of this history should keep, and say what it may drop.

9c. How would you check the summary before trusting the agent's next edit?

9d. Name one situation in which you would restart with a written handoff instead of compacting.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval: Week 1 mechanisms
docs.text:
R1. A model sees a function but not the repository's whitespace rule. What bounded next action supplies the missing context?

R2. A trim-only status lookup passes " ok " but not "OK". What output is expected for "OK", and what is the smallest repair?

docs.title: Dashboard transfer
docs.text: An agent repairing the dashboard status formatter writes status.py, runs the acceptance tests and sees them fail, writes status.py again, and then the turn budget ends. Read afterwards, the new file looks right. What stop reason and check status does the record show, what must a summary of the run keep, and which observation would let you report the repair verified?

docs.title: Build and inspect a small agent
docs.text:
Week 2 · CI dashboard

When is a repair actually finished?

docs.title: A write without a test
docs.text:
Last week, we separated a proposal from an observation.

assistant  c1 read {"path": "status.py"}
tool c1    (file text)
assistant  c2 write {"path": "status.py", "content": candidate}
tool c2    "written"
assistant  "done", no tool calls

What do we know? What result is still missing?

docs.title: The controller owns the stop decision
docs.text:
A completed write tells us that files changed.

A verification result tells us what the specified check observed.

Today you will trace a controller, predict its stopping behavior, and explain one limitation of its implementation.

docs.title: A file small enough to trace completely
docs.text:
The workshop isolates the loop in result.txt.

Initial bytes:   "5\n"
Required bytes:  "4\n"

The smaller fixture lets us inspect every call before returning to a dashboard repair. It does not execute the dashboard.

docs.title: The tool contract
docs.text:
Tool Accepted arguments Effect or result read {"path": "result.txt"} Read that file write path and content, at most 32 characters Replace that file bash {"command": "verify"} Run a fixed assertion

The name bash does not permit an arbitrary shell command.

docs.title: Which calls reach a tool?
docs.text:
{"id": "c1", "name": "bash", "arguments": {"command": "verify"}}
{"id": "c2", "name": "bash", "arguments": {"command": "echo 4 > result.txt"}}
{"id": "c3", "name": "read", "arguments": {"path": "../outside.txt"}}

Classify each using the contract. Point to the argument that decides it.

docs.title: A refusal is also a result
docs.text:
Only c1 matches an accepted tool and argument.

reply -> shape check -> tool/argument check
                          |              |
                      permitted     refused: ...
                          |              |
              tool message under the call's own ID

The model sees the refusal on its next turn. Nothing changed on disk.

docs.title: The bounded agent loop
docs.text: This map names the hand-offs only. Use it to orient the trace before inspecting the next fixture result.

docs.title: One successful path through the fixture
docs.text:
Turn Model's call Tool message back 1 c1 read c1: 5\n 2 c2 write 4\n c2: written 3 c3 bash verify c3: verified 4 no calls stop: final

Every request carries the whole history, so the model sees each result.

docs.title: The contract for the run() you write
docs.text:
1. History starts with one user message: the task.
  2. Each turn: send a copy of the history; check the reply with checked.
  3. Append the reply. No tool calls: stop with final.
  4. Otherwise one tool message per call, under that call's ID.
  5. Turn budget spent: stop with step_limit.

tool, checked and last_check are supplied. The public checks test your run().

docs.title: The same write, a different value
docs.text:
The proposer reads 5\n, writes 5\n, then calls verify.

What result comes back under the verify call's ID? What may anyone conclude when the next reply has no calls?

Keep the required bytes fixed while tracing the changed proposal.

docs.title: The assertion supplies the failure
docs.text:
assert Path("result.txt").read_text() == "4\n"

The wrong write returns written, but verification returns check_failed.

The loop still stops with final. The check result, not the stop reason, says the repair failed.

docs.title: Two stop reasons, one separate check
docs.text:
Field Meaning final A reply had no tool calls step_limit The turn budget ended last_check Newest verify result after the last write, or not_run

A malformed reply or a reused call ID raises an error before any tool runs.

docs.title: Is a repeated call always a loop?
docs.text:
c1 read result.txt
c2 write "4\n"
c3 read result.txt

The contract has no repeat detector. Is the third call useful? What stops a proposer that reads forever?

docs.title: The budget bounds what a heuristic cannot judge
docs.text:
The reread after a write shows the new state, so it is useful.

Four identical reads only spend the turn budget; the loop stops with step_limit.

A progress check can help, but it never replaces an absolute budget.

docs.title: A working record for the next action
docs.text:
Goal: result.txt must equal "4\n"
Latest write: "5\n"
Latest check: check_failed, after that write
Allowed next steps: still subject to tool and turn limits

Which line would be lost in a summary saying only "file updated"?

docs.title: The context window is a budget
docs.text:
Every request resends the task, every reply and every tool result.

What piles up Why it matters File reads, test logs Largest part; out of date after the next write Failed attempts Still visible next to the fix that replaced them An instruction read once Buried under every later turn

docs.title: A summary replaces the older turns
docs.text:
The history holds the task, a file that says "do not edit view.py", a strip-only fix, its failed check and two rereads.

Which lines must a summary keep? Which raw output can it drop?

docs.title: Compact, or restart with a handoff
docs.text:
Keep: the task and check, constraints and where they came from, what failed, open failures, file paths and state, the next step. Drop: raw output the agent can read or run again.

Restart when the history is mostly stale or one phase has ended. Then check the summary against the transcript, and rerun the check.

docs.title: Public code and an external execution boundary
docs.text:
The dispatcher restricts its own tool calls. Editable code could bypass that dispatcher.

The course launcher separately contains execution and resources. Use the Week 0 setup page for the supported invocation.

docs.title: A production prompt: which rules are enforced?
docs.text:
Two open-source coding agents publish their instructions and tool definitions.

Rule Asked, or enforced by what? Qwen Code edit: file_path must be absolute ? Qwen Code edit: include 3 lines of context ? Codex CLI update_plan: status is one of three values ? Both: at most one step in progress ?

docs.title: Count what is enforced, not what is written
docs.text:
Rule Enforced by Absolute path; a second match fails without replace_all the tool's code, error sent to the model 3 lines of context nothing visible: description only Three status values the schema One step in progress description and prompt text only, in the files linked

(tools/codex-base-instructions; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) (tools/qwen-code-system-prompt; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7) · Optional: compare two production prompts

docs.title: Live demonstration: building the loop
docs.text:
The instructor builds steps 1-3 on screen; you type them too. Steps 4-5 are yours: the failing check names say what is still missing. In P1 you build the whole controller yourself.

Then trace one correct write and one wrong write through your loop. The learning task is to explain its decisions and limitations.

docs.title: Feedback on the working record
docs.text:
A peer removes the last failed check from your summary.

Explain which next decision becomes harder to justify. Restore the needed observation in your own words.

Use the existing P1 record for the code and actual result.

docs.title: Exit: correct-looking code, exhausted budget
docs.text:
The file appears correct, but max_steps ends before verify runs.

Name the stop reason your run() returns, the check status, and a supported next action. Answer independently.

A later supported run verifies the current file. What can you now accept, and which earlier stop record stays unchanged?

docs.title: P1 and the next repository
docs.text:
Your P1 Agent.run uses this protocol, with the supplied compact. Your P1 record keeps its code, verification and your own explanation.

Next week, the controller is no longer the main unknown. You must discover which files give it useful context.

docs.title: Week 3: Find the change in an unfamiliar repository
docs.text: This directory holds Week 3 materials. You trace one dashboard request across files, select context for a bounded edit, compare two context packets and compare one long agent session before and after compaction; the repository-context workshop applies this to ci-dashboard.

docs.title: Required workshop path: repository-context workshop
docs.text:
The 80-minute classroom block rehearses each move of the week on fresh variants of the lecture's examples, then starts the workshop:

Minutes Activity Counts towards 0-15 Repository map of the project-list path The workshop's estimated time 15-30 Activity 1: a packet of your own Week 3 class time 30-45 Activity 2: would it fire, and could an agent use it? Week 3 class time 45-55 Activity 3: watch an agent use both servers Week 3 class time 55-80 Start the workshop's Part A The workshop's estimated time

After the block, Activity 4 practises reading a mature coding agent's run and checking its final summary, in about 20 minutes, and Activity 5 compares one long session before and after compaction, in about 25 minutes. Both are optional practice outside the published weekly hour estimate, and neither carries marks.

The workshop's own fixed health-path comparison, boundary check, skill and tool server are the required work; the activities below use different examples and add no second pair of required calls. The workshop's skill-use step ends with observe, adjust, recheck: what your skill's one use showed comes first, your P1 failure record second.

docs.title: Repository map: the project-list path (LO4)
docs.text:
Spend 15 minutes reading the public source of your ci-dashboard package; no application needs to run. If you do not have the package yet, get the student repository first. Follow GET /domains/ci_dashboard/:

  1. domains/ci_dashboard.py, function overview: where is the current user checked, which query selects the projects, and which template renders them?
  2. legacy_app/views.py, function require_user: what happens without a signed-in user?
  3. legacy_app/templates/ci/overview.html: what does the table show for no projects?

Record the checkout revision and three confirmed file/function references. Mark one unanswered behavior question and the test you would seek before editing. A peer checks each reference against the same revision.

The map may start as a drawing from the approved hosted or replay route, for example a Mermaid flowchart of the same path. Treat each arrow as a claim, not as an answer. Write the arrows as a text list and label each one confirmed (file:line at your revision), refuted (what the code does instead) or cannot tell (what you would need to read or run). A drawing can hide a condition, a data change or the order of calls, so add any branch the arrows leave out. Your peer chooses one arrow labelled confirmed and tries to show from the code that it is wrong; record whether it held. A map you draw yourself uses the same labels. Label only this path, inside the same 15 minutes. Reuse this map when selecting M0 scope.

docs.title: Activity 1: A packet of your own (LO2)
docs.text:
Design time: 15 minutes of class time. Materials: your ci-dashboard source, the "Build a packet of your own" section of the notes, question-2.txt and step 2 of the fixture guide. Grouping: pairs; each student builds, predicts and explains their own packet.

  1. Minutes 0–2: recall. Without the notes, write which field packet B's answer got wrong in the lecture, and which file decides it.
  2. Minutes 2–8: build. Read question-2.txt. From your ci-dashboard source, write packet-own.txt of at most 400 bytes: whole lines, each excerpt under a header line that names its file, as packet B does.
  3. Minutes 8–10: predict, then check. For status and limit, write whether your packet holds the lines that decide it. Then run packet_check.py through the launcher, or, without launcher access, have your partner check each line against the source with you. Mark each prediction against the result.
  4. Minutes 10–15: revise once. Change the packet once, within the same 400 bytes, and check it again. Your partner asks: "Which bytes did you trade for which lines, and what changed?" Write the answer in one sentence.

Output: the recall line, two predictions, both check results and one sentence on context choice, in the workshop work record. Running packets A and B through the model route is optional; use step 3 of the fixture guide, and keep each answer as it came.

docs.title: Activity 2: Would it fire, and could an agent use it? (LO2)
docs.text:
Design time: 15 minutes of class time. Materials: the skill and tool sections of the notes, label_tools.py and the launcher command in the fixture guide. Grouping: the same pairs. This rehearses the workshop's skill and tool-server parts on examples the workshop does not use.

  1. Minutes 0–5: trigger. Partner A reads only the name and description of the notes' check-label-tools skill. Partner B writes four requests the lecture did not use: two that should load it, one in different words that should, and one near miss. B records a prediction for each; A then says, for each request, whether they would load the skill. Compare, and rewrite one phrase of the description that caused a mismatch.
  2. Minutes 5–13: tools. The lecture showed four calls. These three are new:
Tool Arguments search_labels {"query": "re", "limit": 2} delete_label {} delete_label {"label_id": 12, "force": true}

Read the DRAFT and REVISED definitions. For each call, predict what each version returns, whether a label is deleted, and which rule the call tests. Add the three calls as rows in verify(), as step 4 of the fixture guide shows, run the example through the launcher and mark each prediction right or wrong. 3. Minutes 13–15: revise. Name the one change to the draft you would make first, and the call that would show it worked.

Output: the four trigger predictions and observations, and the six tool predictions marked against the run, in the workshop work record. The workshop then applies the same moves to your own skill and to the ci-dashboard tool server.

docs.title: Activity 3: Watch an agent use both servers (LO2, LO7)
docs.text:
Design time: 10 minutes of class time. Materials: the "Watch an agent" section of the notes, agent_replay.py and step 5 of the fixture guide. Grouping: the same pairs.

The lecture showed ticket IDs 21 and 9. Here the old ticket gives two new IDs: 12, which really is red-team, and 7, which is red-blue.

  1. Minutes 0–3: predict. For each ticket ID and each server, write yes or no for: carries an ID from a result into its next call; recovers from a wrong ID; previews before it deletes. Also write which label, if any, ends up deleted.
  2. Minutes 3–7: observe. Run agent_replay.py --ticket-id 12 --summary and agent_replay.py --ticket-id 7 --summary through the launcher. The first line says the agent is course-written, not a model. Fill the rows for each server from the calls and results, then check them against --summary.
  3. Minutes 7–10: explain. With ticket ID 12, the draft deletes the right label. Does that make the draft safe to use? Name the call in the ticket 7 run that answers it, and the rule whose fix made the difference.

Output: twelve yes-or-no predictions and the label each run deletes, the observations with the call that shows each, and your answer, in the workshop work record. When available, your instructor's recorded run with the course's hosted model shows what a model does with the lecture's request; read its calls with the same three questions, as they came, including a guessed ID, a wrong deletion or a step_limit stop. Until then, the course replay and its tables are the comparison.

docs.title: Activity 4: Dissect a mature agent's run (LO2, LO4)
docs.text:
Design time: about 20 minutes, after the classroom block. Materials: the "Dissect a mature agent's run" section of the notes, the record below, your ci-dashboard source and its launcher commands. Grouping: alone or in the same pairs. This activity is practice: it carries no marks and adds nothing you must submit. It needs no key, and it is the same for everyone.

Which record. When the teaching team publishes its frozen Codex CLI run on ci-dashboard, use that and keep its events exactly as they are. Until then, use the placeholder below. The course team wrote it by hand; no agent or model produced it. It uses the course's own layout, not any tool's output format, and says nothing about how any product behaves. The source lines it quotes are real ci-dashboard lines.

record: course-written placeholder; no agent or model produced it
task:   What does GET /domains/ci_dashboard/ return to a signed-out visitor, and what does
        a signed-in user with no projects see? Name the file that decides each. Run the
        project's smoke check before you answer. Do not change any files.
setup:  sandbox limited to the workspace, network off; the agent asks before anything else

e1   context    loaded AGENTS.md (workspace root):
                "Run `python -I manage.py smoke` before you report. Never install packages."
e2   plan       1 find the route  2 read the sign-in check  3 read the empty-list branch
                4 run the smoke check  5 answer
e3   call c1    shell: grep -rn "def overview" domains
e4   result c1  exit 0
                domains/ci_dashboard.py:29:def overview() -> str:
e5   call c2    read: domains/ci_dashboard.py, lines 28-38
e6   result c2  @bp.get("/")
                def overview() -> str:
                    """List the caller's projects in stable order."""
                    projects = (
                        get_db()
                        .execute(
                            "SELECT * FROM ci_dashboard_projects WHERE owner_id=? ORDER BY id", (require_user(),)
                        )
                        .fetchall()
                    )
                    return render_template("ci/overview.html", projects=projects)
e7   call c3    read: legacy_app/views.py, lines 50-54
e8   result c3  def require_user() -> int:
                    """Require an authenticated user for data and profile operations."""
                    if g.user is None:
                        abort(401)
                    return g.user["id"]
e9   plan       1-2 done; 3 skipped ("the route renders the list"); 4 in progress
e10  call c4    shell: pip install pytest
e11  approval   c4 needs network outside the sandbox; asked the operator; operator denied
e12  result c4  refused by the operator; the command did not run
e13  call c5    shell: python -I manage.py smoke
e14  result c5  exit 0
                PASS: login, list, detail, and local job smoke
e15  final      (no tool calls)
                A signed-out visitor gets 401: require_user() in legacy_app/views.py aborts
                when there is no signed-in user. A signed-in user with no projects sees
                "No projects yet."; domains/ci_dashboard.py decides this when the query
                returns no rows. The smoke check passed, so both behaviours are covered by
                the project's tests. I did not install anything or change any files.
stop:   final, after 5 calls; 1 approval asked, 1 denied
  1. Minutes 0–4: predict. Read only the task and e15. Split e15 into single claims; there are at least seven. For each, predict whether the rest of the record will confirm it, refute it or leave it open.
  2. Minutes 4–10: map. Copy the five rows of the notes' mapping table (context, plan, tool calls and results, approvals and containment, stop). For each row, write the events that show it, or "not in the record". Answer two questions with event numbers: which line of AGENTS.md did an approval enforce, and which did the agent simply follow? Where did the run leave its own plan?
  3. Minutes 10–14: label against the record. Label each claim confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and cite the event for every confirmed or refuted label. Mark each prediction right or wrong.
  4. Minutes 14–20: verify against the source. For every claim the record could not decide or refuted, check the source at your revision: the template the route renders and the smoke branch of manage.py. Run python3 -I launch.py smoke through the ci-dashboard launcher once and compare its output with e14. Give each claim a second label against the source, and keep it apart from the first.

Contrast. Suppose the same run had been made with Kiro CLI in a workspace you had not yet trusted. Using the notes and its documentation card (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9), name the first row of your mapping table that would look different, and the event you would expect instead. This is a question about the documentation, not a recorded run.

Output: the claim list with predictions and two labels each, the five-row map with event numbers, and one sentence on which claim you would most want an agent to stop making. Keep it with your Week 3 notes; you may cite it in the repository-context workshop if you choose.

docs.title: Activity 5: Compact a long session, then check (LO2)
docs.text:
Design time: about 25 minutes, after the classroom block. Materials: the "Compaction" section of the notes, long-session.json, compaction.py and step 6 of the fixture guide. Grouping: alone or in the same pairs; each student writes their own checklist and summary. AI use: write the summary and the checklist yourself; choosing what to keep is the skill being practised. This activity is practice: it carries no marks, adds nothing you must submit and needs no key.

  1. Minutes 0–8: read and list. Run compaction.py full --show and read the 19 messages. Copy the notes' five-row checklist and fill the second column with the message index that holds each fact. Mark which read of status.py is stale.
  2. Minutes 8–12: predict, then run auto. Predict which facts the supplied compaction keeps and which file the next edit touches. Run compaction.py auto --show, fill the auto column and mark each prediction right or wrong. Name the message that held the lost fact and its role.
  3. Minutes 12–20: write, predict, run. Write summary.txt of at most 600 bytes. Predict the next edit, then run compaction.py summary summary.txt and compaction.py fresh summary.txt. Fill the last column from your file, not from the result line.
  4. Minutes 20–25: verify both ways. For each fact, does your file keep it, and did the check notice when it did not? If the check failed, change one line of the summary and run it again; keep both outputs. Then write one sentence: for this session, would you compact or restart, and what would the next session reread first?

Output: the checklist with predictions and three columns, the outputs of auto, summary and fresh (and the revised run if you made one), and your compact-or-restart sentence. Keep it with your Week 3 notes; if a P1 compaction failure appears in observe, adjust, recheck, you may cite this record there.

docs.title: Access and repository-context workshop handoff
docs.text:
All materials are plain text and commands work from a keyboard. Diagrams have text equivalents. Students may use the course team's approved additional time, partner operation or verified-record replay route while preserving their own predictions, verification interpretation and LO2/LO7 explanation. An access failure does not authorize personal paid models or unsandboxed execution.

Reuse the map, predictions, failure analysis and AI-use note in the repository-context workshop work record. The required path is one repository map, one fixed-context comparison, one boundary check, one skill that you write, trigger-test and use once on ci-dashboard and once read-only on your candidate contribution project (if you have no candidate yet, on one of the workshop's listed repositories or another that meets the same criteria), and the ci-dashboard tool server revised against the five rules with your own protocol test. Additional skills and parallel worktrees are optional extensions; the optional reading has an in-memory permission example you may run.

docs.title: Observe, adjust, recheck
docs.text:
Start from your one use of the skill. In P1 you also explained one loop failure, its fix and the repeat check; if you draw on it, cite that record by its evidence ID rather than rewriting it. Planned time: the last 10 of the 30 minutes in workshop step 6, where you already choose one step to change. Nothing is added to the workshop's estimated time.

  1. Observe. If the use showed a weak or skipped step, that is your risk; say which P1 failure it resembles, if any. Otherwise reread your P1 failure and name the risk it matches on ci-dashboard; the table gives examples.
  2. Adjust. Change one thing only: one skill step or the skill's verification.
  3. Recheck. Follow the changed part again on the same request and revision. Record what you observed; "no difference" is a valid result.
Your P1 failure A matching risk on ci-dashboard Final answer before the check ran The trace is called done before its check was observed Ran to the step limit without finishing Reading goes on file after file with no stopping rule Tool result lost its tool_call_id A reference or test result is not tied to its file, command and revision Compaction dropped an earlier observation A shortened handoff drops a file or result read earlier that a later step relies on

When you start from P1 and have no failure record of your own, or yours matches no row, take the nearest row and say so. The workshop's third line gives the P1 evidence ID if you used one, the risk, the one change and what the recheck showed. Follow the skill with or without an approved agent; the record is the same either way.

docs.title: Practitioner guest
docs.text: A practitioner from a partner organization joins the first class this week for up to 45 minutes to describe how their organization chooses context and tools for coding agents; the rest of the class runs as usual. Before class, write one question for the guest. After class, write one sentence comparing one claim the guest made with this week's evidence, such as your two context packets or your skill's trigger test. Keep both in your Week 3 work entry. The talk is not assessed and adds no time outside class. A guest speaks about their own organization's practice; the course endorses no product. The talk is recorded only with advance notice and the consent of those present. If no guest is available, the class runs as usual.

docs.title: Your contribution project
docs.text: The open-source contributions (C1 in Weeks 3-6, C2 in Weeks 7-13) start this week. Pick a candidate project from the approved list the teaching team publishes before Week 3, or one you will propose on the same conditions, and use it for the workshop's read-only skill transfer; you confirm the choice in Week 4. The rules, including the course-hosted route, are in the syllabus.

docs.title: Dashboard transfer
docs.text: Packet B's answer gets every field right only after a second call that adds the template file. Can you attribute the result to B's content? State the comparison you would rerun and what must stay fixed.

docs.title: Week 3: Context engineering and agent workflows
Learning objectives
docs.text:
One idea runs through this week: an agent acts only on what reaches it. You choose the context it reads, the skill descriptions it chooses by, and the tool names, schemas, errors and results it acts on. Each of those choices is something you can test.

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • LO4: trace one real ci-dashboard request across files and mark each step of a map confirmed, refuted or cannot tell against the source at your revision.
  • LO2: choose the context a bounded question needs: compare two context packets of the same size by what each answer got right, got wrong or left open, then build a packet of your own under a byte budget and check it.
  • LO2 (optional practice): practise compacting a long agent session into a summary under a byte budget, checking that it kept each fact the next step needs, and saying when you would restart from a written handoff instead.
  • LO2: package the tracing method as one SKILL.md whose description you have tested: it fires on the requests it should and not on a near miss.
  • LO2: design tools for an agent that sees only their names, schemas and descriptions, using five rules; verify each rule with calls rather than by reading the definition; and watch how a tool's design changes what an agent does on one request.
  • LO7: keep a destructive tool behind a brake, check a permission before its effect, and say which layer contains a process that ignores both.

Each activity names the LO it practises; the repository-context workshop's page lists its required parts. Protocol details, a second tool shape (search, then execute), an in-memory permission example, a published MCP incident, and plans, worktrees and subagents are in the optional reading; they carry no marks.

Run every command through the route in Week 0 setup.

All examples on this page are course-authored and synthetic; actual execution evidence comes from your own checks.

docs.title: The continuing dashboard case
docs.text:
Recall the case from Week 1. The dashboard shows a build with raw status " OK " as unknown. The agreed rule ignores surrounding whitespace and case: this input should display passed, while an unfamiliar status should remain unknown. A reviewer suggests editing the template. First inspect this schematic request path:

# loader.py
raw = record["status"]
# status.py
label = {"ok": "passed"}.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")
# view.py
render(label)

Decision: Where does the value first disagree with the rule, and which file should the agent inspect before changing the template?

The loader preserves " OK ". The mapper lowercases it to " ok ", which is not the key "ok", and supplies unknown to the view. Inspect normalization in status.py: removing surrounding whitespace before lookup repairs this case. Changing every unknown display to passed would also mislabel an unfamiliar status. Check both inputs. The path above is a schematic; the next one is real.

Acceptance decision: Choose a bounded edit only when the path explains the symptom. A single paired run motivates a next experiment; it does not establish that a context style is generally superior.

docs.title: A real path: the project list in ci-dashboard
docs.text:
In ci-dashboard, GET /domains/ci_dashboard/ lists the signed-in user's projects. Trace it across three files:

  1. domains/ci_dashboard.py, function overview: calls require_user(), selects the caller's projects with WHERE owner_id=? ORDER BY id, and renders ci/overview.html.
  2. legacy_app/views.py, function require_user: aborts with 401 when there is no signed-in user, otherwise returns the user's ID.
  3. legacy_app/templates/ci/overview.html: a {% for %} over the projects whose {% else %} branch prints No projects yet.

The route function names what happens; the other two files decide what a visitor actually sees. A map of this path is a set of claims: each arrow needs a file and line at your checkout revision. The activity's repository map asks you to mark each arrow confirmed, refuted or cannot tell.

docs.title: Context is an intervention we can test
docs.text:
Now ask a model one bounded question about that path, the shared question: what does a visitor without a session receive, what does a signed-in user with no projects see, and which file decides each. It asks for one JSON object and allows null for anything the context does not show.

Two packets carry the same number of bytes, 639 each; only their content differs:

Packet What it holds How it was chosen A domains/ci_dashboard.py read on from the route, cut at the budget: overview, then the start of new_project Read more of the file you started in B The API's 401 line, the overview excerpt, require_user and the template's empty-table branch Follow the call across files

Predict, generate, then check. Before any run, write what each packet's answer will say for each of the four fields. Keep the model and profile, the question, a fresh call, one call per packet and the checker fixed. Change the packet only. Do not repair a wrong answer or rerun until it passes.

The checker labels each field correct, wrong, abstained (an explicit null) or missing. Its answers come from the dashboard itself: run with a signed-out client, the route returns 401, and a freshly registered user sees No projects yet.; the course's tests repeat that check against the running app. An abstention is not a correct answer, but it is honest; a confident wrong file is worse.

A course-written replay, not a model run. To show how the checker reads two answers, the course team wrote one plausible answer per packet by hand. No model was called.

Packet Status Deciding file Empty-list text Deciding file Correct A 302: wrong domains/ci_dashboard.py: wrong null: abstained null: abstained 0 of 4 B 401: correct legacy_app/views.py: correct No projects yet.: correct domains/ci_dashboard.py: wrong 3 of 4

Configuration: no model and zero calls per packet; packets of 639 bytes; the question and packet digests are pinned in ab-replay.json, which the checker refuses if any input has changed. Reproduce it with the offline profile:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python verify.py --replay ab-replay.json

The replay says nothing about how often any model answers either way. Its B answer still gets one field wrong: the route passes the list on, but the template decides the text. Your own pair, made with the commands in the fixture guide, is the measurement; your instructor may also show a pair recorded with the course's hosted model, labelled with its profile, version and digest. A tie, or A beating B, is a legitimate observation.

AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are context-file names discussed in this course. In this exercise we deliberately load the selected packet into the prompt ourselves: no filename has automatic behavior. When adopting a particular tool, verify its actual discovery, scope and precedence rules. A file that exists but was never loaded cannot explain a result. Do not infer that either filename reliably improves performance.

docs.title: Build a packet of your own
docs.text:
Packets A and B were chosen for you. The second question has no course packet. A signed-in user posts a 121-character project title straight to POST /domains/ci_dashboard/projects/new, not through the browser form: what status comes back, what is the longest title the server accepts, and which file decides each?

Build the packet yourself from your ci-dashboard source, in at most 400 bytes. Quote whole lines, and start each excerpt with a header line that names its file, as packet B does. Before checking, predict for each part, status and limit, whether your packet holds the lines that decide it. The packet check then labels each part without a model:

Label Meaning covered The deciding lines are there, whole and in order, under a header naming their file no_file The lines are there, but the header above them does not name their file browser_only Limit only: the packet shows the form's limit, which a direct request never meets missing A line the answer depends on is not in the packet

Revise the packet once, within the same budget, and check it again. Keep both results. The check says whether the evidence is in the packet; it cannot say what a model would answer from it.

docs.title: Compaction: what survives a shorter history
docs.text:
A packet is context you choose before the first request. A summary is context you choose in the middle of a session, when the history no longer fits. The Week 2 notes explain what accumulates and what a summary should keep; here you run one before/after comparison and check the summary twice: against the transcript, and by whether the next step still passes the same check.

long-session.json is a session the course team wrote by hand in the Week 2 message format; no model or agent produced it. The agent is repairing the continuing " OK " case. It reads NOTES.md, view.py, loader.py and status.py, runs the acceptance check, replaces the lookup with raw.strip(), sees the check fail on " OK " and "OK", rereads status.py and reads the check's source. The history is 19 messages and 5,283 bytes against a 5,500-byte budget: this request fits, and the next check result would not.

compaction.py builds the next request's context in one of four ways:

Mode The next request carries full Every message auto The task, every assistant message and the newest call/result group; each older tool result longer than 80 bytes becomes a one-line stub summary FILE The task, your summary in place of messages 1-16, and the newest group fresh FILE The task and your file only: a restart from a written handoff

A short course-written policy then picks the next edit from that context alone, and the same six-case check runs on the result. The policy is not a model. It reads every line it is given with the same care, which nothing guarantees of a model, and follows two rules written in the script: it keeps out of view.py only when a line names view.py and says not to change it, and it adds lower() only when a line says the strip-only fix failed. Without the first fact it changes view.py so that unknown displays as passed, which is the template patch the dashboard case warned against.

Predict, generate, then verify. Fill the checklist from the transcript first: for each fact, the message that holds it. Predict which facts auto keeps and which file the next edit touches, then run it. Write your own summary of at most 600 bytes, predict again, run it as summary and as fresh, and fill the last two columns.

Fact the next step needs Message in the session Kept by auto Kept by your summary The goal and the acceptance check The constraint on which file may change, and its source The attempt that failed, and how The current state of each file touched (which read is stale) The paths the next edit needs

The supplied compaction, run by the course. These are the script's own outputs, with no model involved; run them yourself with the commands in the fixture guide.

Mode Context bytes Next edit Check full 5,283 status.py: raw.strip().lower() passed, 6 of 6 auto 3,523 view.py: show unknown as passed failed: "queued" shows passed, and view.py changed

The constraint arrived once, in the middle of a tool result: the NOTES.md read in message 2. Clearing old tool output removed it. The agent's own sentence about the failed strip-only fix survived because assistant messages were kept, so the policy did not repeat that attempt; it made a different mistake instead. Nothing in the compacted context contradicts the view.py edit, which is why this kind of loss is hard to see from the context alone. Your summary's run is your own measurement.

The check is not the whole verification. Every mode keeps the task message, so the goal and the acceptance check always survive. Of the other facts the policy reads only two, so a summary can pass the check and still leave out which read of status.py is stale, which a later edit would need. The checklist covers what the check cannot. With a model, the same two steps apply, and one run of each version is one observation.

Compact or restart? Run the same file as fresh: the context drops to the task and your handoff, under 1,000 bytes for a 400-byte file, and the newest raw group goes too. Restart when most of the history is stale or contradicts itself, or a phase has ended; compact when the newest results still matter. Either way the next session's first step is to reread the files its edit touches.

docs.title: A skill packages a repeatable procedure
docs.text:
A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md file: YAML front matter with a name (the directory's name) and a description, then a Markdown body. An agent that supports skills keeps only the names and descriptions in view and loads a body when a request seems to need it, so the description decides whether the skill is ever used. The body then enters the context and costs space for the rest of the session, so hold the procedure there and leave longer background in a separate file in the same directory. The workshop uses exactly this format and asks for three body sections: the steps, the judgement a step list hides, and the check. Hosts differ in optional fields and in where they look for skills; verify that for the agent you use rather than assuming it.

---
name: check-label-tools
description: Checks an edited label tool by calling it through the host before the
  change is reported. Use when search_labels or delete_label changed or a call fails.
---
## Steps
1. Read the changed tool definition and predict one call it could break.
2. Run `python label_tools.py` through the course launcher.
3. Make one call of your own with a wrong type, such as `{"query": 5}`.

## Judgement
- If a call you predicted would fail passes, explain why before going on.
- A definition that only mentions `dry_run` is a claim; call the tool to see it.
- If the launcher refuses execution, stop. Do not install dependencies or retry.

## Verification
The `label_tools.py` output matches the table in the notes, and your own call returns
`invalid_argument`.

Write judgement from your own corrections. A step list hides the moments when someone had to step in. Reread one of your own agent sessions, or your P1 trace, and list each place where you corrected or stopped the agent. Each correction is a candidate line for ## Judgement, because the next run will need it too.

Generate, then verify the trigger. A description that says only when ("Use when changing the label tools") can miss "why does search give me no IDs?". One that says only what can fire on every label question. So test it like any other prediction: write three requests in the words people use that should load the skill, and one near miss that sounds similar but needs something else ("rename the label column"). Record your prediction for each before you observe, then observe with an agent session or a classmate who sees only the names and descriptions of the available skills. A near miss that fires means the description is too broad; a missed request usually shares no words with it. Change the description once and recheck only the mismatches.

A context file states project-wide constraints. A skill describes a reusable procedure and its trigger. Neither grants permissions, and any script a skill refers to is code that needs review and launcher execution. In the workshop you write one skill for the tracing method you practiced by hand, trigger-test it, use it once on ci-dashboard and once, read-only, on your candidate contribution project (or a listed repository if you have no candidate yet), and record what changed. A skill nobody has run is a draft.

docs.title: A tool is an interface for a reader that guesses
docs.text:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects an agent's host to servers that expose tools. The agent sees each tool's name, description and input schema, calls it with arguments, and reads the result as data, even when the result asks for something. Whether a tool is reached through MCP or a plain function call, the agent chooses it from that text alone. Design it for a reader that will guess when the text is unclear. Name the effect, not the implementation: search_labels, not handler2. Give the tool no authority beyond its stated purpose. Five rules turn that into checks:

  1. Put every limit in the schema. "enum", "minimum", "maximum", "required" and "additionalProperties": false tell the agent every valid value, and they are checked before your code runs when the server validates each call against the schema, as the workshop's server scaffold does. A limit stated only in a sentence of the description is neither visible as a value list nor checked. When the two disagree, the agent meets rejections that nothing it read accounts for. The MCP specification puts input validation on the server: servers must validate all tool inputs. (tools/model-context-protocol; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2) It is a requirement on the server, not a guarantee that a given server meets it, so check with a call.
  2. Return only what the next step needs. Hand back the fields the next call will use, including the IDs other tools accept, not the stored record. Every extra field is paid for again at each later step, and mirroring the storage layout breaks the tool when that layout changes. If you cut a list short, say so. Anthropic's tool-writing guide gives the same advice: return high-signal fields, and bound large responses with pagination, filtering or truncation and sensible defaults. (tools/anthropic-effective-tools; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)
  3. Report a failure as a result the agent can read. Return a structured error naming what failed and whether trying again could succeed: an unknown ID fails every time, a rate limit clears. A raw exception gives the agent nothing to act on; {"code": "not_found", "retryable": false, ...} tells it whether a retry is worth making. MCP draws this line too: an unknown tool or a malformed request is a protocol error, but a failed input check, such as a value out of range, is a tool execution error, returned in the result with isError: true so the client can hand it to the model to correct. (tools/model-context-protocol; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2)
  4. Say what comes back and where each input comes from. State what the tool returns and which tool produces each ID argument ("a label_id from search_labels"), so the agent can call them in sequence. Name arguments so they cannot be misread: label_id, not label. (tools/anthropic-effective-tools; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)
  5. Guard every irreversible action. Mark the read-only tools as read-only. Give an irreversible tool a dry_run that defaults to true, or split it into preview and commit, so a call that leaves the argument out cannot change anything.

Generate. Below is a course-authored first draft for the request "a search tool and a delete tool for labels", written the way a quick generated answer can look. It looks finished, and it works when the caller already knows the answers.

[{"name": "search_labels", "description": "Search labels. limit can be up to 50.",
  "inputSchema": {"type": "object",
                  "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}, "limit": {"type": "integer"}}}},
 {"name": "delete_label", "description": "Deletes a label.",
  "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"label_id": {"type": "integer"}}}}]

Before reading on, predict what each call in the table does to the draft.

Verify. Reading the definition is not verification; calls are. The worked example applies the published schema as the workshop's server scaffold would: it refuses an unknown or missing argument and checks each argument's type, then its range (true is not an integer), all before the handler runs. It then makes the same four calls against the draft and a revision, each from fresh records. These are its actual outputs, shortened:

Question Call Draft Revision Can the agent chain? search_labels {"query": "red"} ["red-blue", "red-team"]: names, no IDs to pass on label_id and name per label, total, truncated Does a bare delete only preview? delete_label {"label_id": 7} Deleted; label gone dry_run: true, would_delete; label still there Is a bad ID recoverable? delete_label {"label_id": 99} KeyError: 99 traceback not_found, retryable: false, "use search_labels" Does the schema hold? search_labels {"query": "r", "limit": 50} Accepted: the "up to 50" lives only in prose invalid_argument from "maximum": 10

The revision bounds limit (minimum 1, maximum 10, default 5), adds "required" and "additionalProperties": false to both tools, and gives descriptions that name search_labels as the source of label_id, readOnlyHint: true on the reader and destructiveHint: true with a dry_run defaulting to true on the delete. Each row is a check you can rerun; a new rule needs a new call, not a longer description. The workshop applies the same five rules to a different, four-tool ci-dashboard server, and there your own test must make its calls through the protocol, not by importing the handlers.

docs.title: Watch an agent use both servers
docs.text:
The table checks one call at a time. An agent chains calls, so give one request to an agent twice, once with each server:

Delete the label red-team. An old ticket gives its label_id as 21.

There is no label 21; red-team is label 12. Before you look, predict three things for each server: does the agent carry an ID from one result into its next call, does it recover after the ID is not found, and does it preview before it deletes?

The replay steps a fixed policy through each server: the policy picks a call, the tool returns its result, and the policy picks again. The agent is course-written, not a model: five rules, the same for both servers, that never guess an ID. First use the ID the request gives. After a preview of the requested label, commit it. After a delete that deleted something, report it. After any other delete result, look the label up by name once. After a search, delete the ID found for that name, or stop if there is none. Every tool result in the transcript is the real output of label_tools.py.

Draft server Revised server Call 1: delete_label {"label_id": 21} {"traceback": "KeyError: 21"} not_found, retryable: false, "use search_labels" Call 2: search_labels {"query": "red-team"} ["red-team"]: a name, no ID {"label_id": 12, "name": "red-team"} Call 3 None: the agent stops, "no label_id ... I will not guess one" delete_label {"label_id": 12} returns a preview, would_delete Call 4 delete_label {"label_id": 12, "dry_run": false} deletes red-team Carried an ID from a result No: the search returned none Yes: 12, from the search into the delete Recovered after not found No: nothing was deleted Yes Previewed before deleting No: call 1 would have deleted label 21 at once Yes: the bare call only previewed

Now change the ticket's ID to 9 (--ticket-id 9), which is the label release-2. On the draft, the first call deletes release-2 immediately and the agent can only report it. On the revision the same call returns a preview of release-2; the agent sees the name does not match, searches, and deletes red-team after its own preview. The brake did not make the agent smarter. It turned a wrong call into a result the agent could read. --summary prints the three observations; it names the second recovered_from_the_wrong_id, which is true when the first delete hit a missing label or a different one and the run still deleted exactly red-team, so it covers both ticket IDs.

The rules are ours, so the replay shows what the tool design allows, not what a model will do. A model may guess an ID, retry a traceback or ignore an error's message. When available, your instructor shows a run of the same request recorded with the course's hosted model, labelled with its configuration, in the same transcript format; until then, the course replay and its tables are the comparison. A recorded run makes at most four model requests per server, the launcher's per-run cap, so a model that needs a fifth reply stops with step_limit after its fourth reply's calls have run. Compare its transcript with your three predictions, call by call.

docs.title: Brakes, hooks and the sandbox
docs.text: Three layers keep a wrong call from doing harm, and each covers something different. A tool's brake, such as dry_run defaulting to true, makes a call that omits the argument harmless. A pre-call hook checks an event, such as a write path, before the effect happens; the workshop's hook step allows an ordinary edit and rejects an escape. Neither can contain a process that edits or ignores them. The course launcher does that, with copied inputs, no external network and fixed resources. A hook that logs a bad action after it happened has prevented nothing. The optional reading has an in-memory example of a returned note asking for export.

docs.title: Dissect a mature agent's run
docs.text:
The replay agent follows five course-written rules. A mature coding agent wraps a model in a production loop with its own context files, tools, approvals and sandbox. In Week 2 you read a recorded session request by request: what the model was sent. Here you read a run record: what the agent did, and whether its final summary is true to it.

The course uses two command-line agents for this, listed alphabetically. Codex CLI is a coding agent that runs locally in your terminal; its repository is licensed under Apache-2.0 (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5), so you can read the source of the loop you are dissecting. Kiro CLI is the renamed Amazon Q Developer CLI; its software is licensed under the AWS Intellectual Property License (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9). The course endorses neither. Codex CLI is the recorded example; Kiro CLI is a contrast you read from its documentation.

You do not run either tool yourself this term. Each needs credentials inside its own process: an API key or an account sign-in for Codex CLI (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5), an account sign-in for Kiro CLI (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9). The course keeps your key outside the sandbox (Week 0 setup), so you work from a run the teaching team records on ci-dashboard and freezes as a replay record. Until that recording is published, the activity uses a placeholder the course team wrote by hand. No agent or model produced it.

Map the run onto your loop. Every part of your Week 2 and Week 3 loop has a counterpart in a mature agent's run. The Codex CLI column is what the recording should show; the Kiro CLI column comes from documentation only, not from a run.

Your loop Codex CLI Kiro CLI Context. You load the packet into the prompt yourself; no filename acts on its own. Reads AGENTS.md before any work. It builds the chain once per run, from ~/.codex through the project root to the current directory, with later files overriding earlier ones, up to 32 KiB by default. (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5) Steering files in .kiro/steering/ and ~/.kiro/steering/, with the workspace winning a conflict; AGENTS.md is always included. An untrusted workspace's steering files are not loaded. (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9) Plan. A plan in prose grants nothing and restricts nothing. Plan updates are one item type in the run record of codex exec --json. (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5) The documentation card does not cover this; look for a plan or task list in the record. Tool calls and results. Each call has an ID, and its result comes back under that ID. Command executions, file changes and MCP tool calls are item types in the run record; MCP servers are local processes or HTTP addresses. (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5) Tools from MCP servers, local (stdio) or remote (HTTP/SSE); a custom agent's configuration sets which tools it may use. (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9) Approvals and containment. A refused call comes back as data; the brake, the hook and the launcher each contain something different. The sandbox limits writes and network; the approval policy decides when to ask. Turning prompts off does not turn the sandbox off. (tools/codex; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1) codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox by default. (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5) Rules per capability with deny, ask or allow, where deny always wins. A headless run has no one to ask, so --trust-all-tools or --trust-tools grants permission in advance. The documentation lists sandbox execution without per-action prompts for its Web surface only. (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9) Stop. final or step_limit; final ends the conversation and verifies nothing. Read the last events of the record. Read the end of the record.

For each row, ask the same question of the recording: where does this show up, and what does the record leave out? A context file that exists in the repository but that the record does not show being loaded cannot explain what the agent did.

Label the final summary. The agent's closing message is a list of claims, just like the arrows of your repository map. Split it into single claims, then label each one against the record:

  • confirmed: an event in the record shows it; cite the event;
  • refuted: an event in the record shows something else; cite it;
  • cannot tell: no event decides it; say what you would read or run.

Then check every claim again, separately, against the source at your revision, through the launcher where a check needs running. Keep the two labels apart. "Cannot tell" from the record is not "false": the code may well agree. A claim confirmed by the record can still be wrong about the code if the agent read a different revision. For example, take a summary that says "I fixed the bug and all tests pass". If the last test command in the record fails, "all tests pass" is refuted. If the record holds no test command at all, it is cannot tell: name the command you would run, then run it.

Generate, then verify. The agent generated the run and its summary. Before you read the record, predict which claims it will support. Afterwards, label every claim and rerun one check yourself. The point is the same as in the replay: a mature agent's run is evidence, and its summary is a claim about that evidence.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Use the repository-context workshop's tasks for its required pair, boundary check, skill and tool server. The activities rehearse each move on fresh variants of this page's examples in an 80-minute classroom block:

  • 15 minutes: map the project-list path in ci-dashboard.
  • 15 minutes: build a packet of your own for the second question, check it and revise it once.
  • 15 minutes: predict which prompts load check-label-tools, then predict and make three label-tool calls the table does not show.
  • 10 minutes: predict and watch the agent replay on both servers with two new ticket IDs.
  • 25 minutes: start the workshop's Part A.

After the block, Activity 4 practises dissecting a mature agent's run in about 20 minutes, and Activity 5 runs the compaction comparison in about 25 minutes. Both are optional practice outside the published weekly hour estimate: they carry no marks and add nothing you must submit.

The map and the Part A start count towards the workshop's estimated time in its guide. The other 40 minutes use the lecture's examples, which no workshop step covers, so they are class time on top of the workshop's estimate; the published Week 3 estimate covers the week as a whole. At the midpoint, seek help if setup or waiting has prevented progress. These are planning and help checkpoints, not measured completion times or cutoffs for marks or accommodations.

Keep one short work record: your predictions, the packets and answers you checked, your own packet's two check results, the agent observations, verification results and your explanation. Record AI use once and reuse its ID in the repository-context workshop. Write your own no-AI reflection on a prediction error and one change you would test next. Full chats, private environments and unrelated trajectories are unnecessary.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The fixture guide gives the supported launcher commands.

For the context comparison, check that both packets are 639 bytes and that the replay command reports kind: course-synthesised, then a with 0 of 4 and b with 3 of 4. For your own pair, compare the two input-record.json files: same question digest, different packet digests, equal packet_bytes, one call and no repair each. Then check each answer.txt with verify.py in a fresh launcher invocation and report the four field labels, input/output tokens and latency from the minimal trace, keeping missing usage or unknown cost unknown. An unreadable answer, a timeout or a missing report is a failed or unfinished attempt. Preserve order and configuration so that a follow-up can repeat or reverse the pair.

For your own packet, keep the prediction, the packet and the check's output from before and after the one revision. Each run reports packet_bytes within the 400-byte budget and a label per part; a packet over the budget is reported as over_budget and not labelled. Explain any part whose label differs from your prediction from the lines in the packet.

For the compaction comparison, the first line must read agent: course-written policy, not a model. full reports context_bytes: 5283 of budget: 5500 and passes; auto lists message 2 under cleared, edits view.py and fails with two FAIL lines. For your summary, keep the checklist, your prediction and the summary and fresh outputs. A file over 600 bytes is reported with file_bytes and not run. Explain each policy_found value from a line in the context, and each checklist gap the check did not catch.

For the skill, check the structure, then the trigger record: three should-trigger prompts that do not name the skill, at least one near miss, a prediction written before each observation, and a recheck of every mismatch after one description change. A trigger test records what an observer did; it cannot prove the skill fires for every phrasing, and an empty mismatch list is not a better grade than an honest one.

For the tools, run the worked example and confirm each of the four rows for both versions. A rule counts as verified only when a call shows it: the preview leaves the label in place, the bad ID returns retryable: false, the out-of-range limit is refused before the handler runs. Add a call of your own with a wrong type, such as {"query": 5}, as a row in verify() (fixture guide, step 4): both versions should refuse it with invalid_argument, not a traceback. A definition that merely contains dry_run or readOnlyHint is a claim, not evidence.

For the agent replay, the first line must read agent: course-written policy, not a model. Check your three predictions against the transcript, then against --summary, which prints the same three observations computed from the calls and the labels left. When available, the teaching team's recorded model run starts agent: approved model (hosted); read it with the same three questions. Until then, the replay and its tables are the comparison. For LO7, confirm from the transcript that the revised server's bare delete left red-team in place until the explicit dry_run: false, and explain which layer would contain a process that ignored both the brake and the hook.

For a mature agent's run, each claim of the final summary carries two labels, one from the record and one from the source at your revision, and every confirmed or refuted label cites the event or line that decides it. Each row of the mapping table names where it appears in the record, or says that the record leaves it out.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake How to detect it Correction Calling B "better" before running Prediction appears as a measured conclusion Keep prediction and observed results in separate columns Changing more than the packet packet_bytes, model or profile differ between the two records Hold everything but the packet's content fixed, then rerun both Judging an answer against the other packet's answer "B said 401, so A is wrong" Check each answer against the code with the checker Quoting the right lines without their file packet_check.py reports no_file Start each excerpt with a header line that names its file Counting a null as correct, or a confident guess as better than a null Abstained and wrong fields are merged Keep the four labels separate Retrying until the answer passes More than one call or an unlabelled repair Record failure; label any later run separately Reading the replay agent as a model "The agent learned to search" Its rules are course-written; only a recorded model run, when available, shows a model Trusting a summary because the next check passed The checklist has an empty cell in the summary column Check each fact against the transcript as well as rerunning the check Naming a file loosely in a summary "Do not edit the template" without view.py; the next edit lands in view.py Write the path the next edit would use A description that says only when, or only what Requests in users' words never load it, or a near miss does Say what it does and when; rerun the trigger prompts A limit or allowed value stated only in prose An out-of-range call is accepted Move it into the schema; call with the bad value again Returning the stored record Large responses, fields no step uses, no IDs to chain Return the documented fields and the IDs other tools accept A traceback or bare string as the error The agent cannot tell retry from stop Return code, retryable and an actionable message A destructive tool that acts on a bare call Omitting dry_run changes state Default dry_run to true; check the state after the call Testing tools by importing the handlers The test still passes when the protocol layer breaks Call through the protocol, as the agent will Treating a mature agent's summary as its own evidence A claim is labelled confirmed with no event cited Cite the event that shows it, or label it cannot tell Counting a context file in the repository as context the run used AGENTS.md or a steering file is cited, but the record never shows it loaded Name the event that loads it, or say the record leaves it out Reading "no file-change event" as "no file changed" The summary says nothing changed, but the record ran a shell command Check what each command writes, in the source or by running it in the launcher

Use the self-check to explain a correction without consulting an agent.

docs.title: Transfer to a new situation
docs.text:
Packet B's answer gets every field right only after a second call that adds the template file. Can the difference from packet A be attributed to B's content?

Write the expected behavior and the next check before comparing with a partner.

The repository-context workshop produces the map, context record, skill and tool server; you reuse them when selecting M0 scope.

docs.title: Week 3 reading path
docs.text:
Read the objectives and fixed contract in the notes before attempting the first slide question. Use the worked explanation after your prediction. The public fixtures hold the two context packets, the label tools and the agent replay; the required workshop pair uses the repository-context workshop's health task. Revisit the Week 0 setup if you are unsure whether you can run the practices or how to reach the class materials.

There is no extra external reading quota or required product installation this week.
