Optional: for the skills and tool-boundary example, read the Progressive disclosure section of the Agent Skills specification (tools/agent-skills; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1) and the Overview, Features and Security and Trust & Safety sections of the MCP specification (tools/model-context-protocol; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2).

Optional: for the five tool-design rules, read these to see where rules 1 to 4 come from and which of them a server or a schema enforces:

  • The Principles for writing effective tools part of Anthropic's Writing effective tools for agents, especially Returning meaningful context from your tools, Optimizing tool responses for token efficiency and Prompt-engineering your tool descriptions. Read it for rules 2 to 4, then check each piece of advice against your own call table rather than taking it on trust. (tools/anthropic-effective-tools; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)
  • The Error Handling and Security Considerations sections of the MCP Tools page. Read it for rules 1 and 3: who must validate a call, and why a value out of range comes back as a result with isError: true rather than as a protocol error. (tools/model-context-protocol; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2)
  • The note at the top of the MCP reference servers README and the Directory Access Control and Tool annotations (MCP hints) sections of the Filesystem server README, both at a fixed commit. Read them for rule 5 and for who enforces a boundary: sort each boundary into one the server checks (allowed directories), one the client supplies and can change (Roots), and one that only marks a tool for the client (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint). The servers are published as teaching examples, not production code, and you connect none of them. (tools/mcp-reference-servers; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2)

Optional: for the mature-agent dissection, read how each tool loads context and decides permissions, in the documentation pages its factsheet cites. For Codex CLI, read Custom instructions with AGENTS.md and the Permissions and safety and Make output machine-readable sections of Non-interactive mode (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5). For Kiro CLI, read Steering and the How it works and Workspace trust sections of Permissions (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9).

Optional: for the compaction comparison, read LangWatch's The Context Tax: When to Compact Your Coding Agent (studies/langwatch-context-tax; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1). It discusses a trade-off between the repeated-read cost of a growing context and the quality cost of recovering context after compaction. It limits its observations to the author's own usage and calls its measurement observational rather than experimental, so compare its reasoning with your Activity 5 result rather than adopting any threshold from it.

Optional: for researching an unfamiliar repository before you plan a change, read HumanLayer's Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases at a fixed commit, especially What works even better: Frequent Intentional Compaction and Eggs on Faces (studies/humanlayer-context-engineering; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1). It splits work into research, plan and implement, with a written record between phases, and it reports one attempt that failed because the research stopped too early. It is a tool company's account of its own projects, not an experiment, so take the method and ignore its figures. As you read, check that each finding in your own packet names the file and lines behind it.

docs.title: Optional reading beyond the main line
docs.text: The lecture keeps one line: an agent acts only on what reaches it. The sections below go further. They carry no marks and no required time.

docs.title: MCP in more detail
docs.text:
MCP organizes communication between a host application, its client connection and a server exposing capabilities. Requests and responses use JSON-RPC; initialization negotiates the protocol and capabilities before normal operations. A tool description gives a name and an input schema; a tool call supplies arguments and receives a result or error. Resources provide context data and prompts provide reusable prompt templates. Capability discovery is not permission to use everything discovered.

Here is a course-authored illustrative exchange after initialization, not a working server configuration. The workshop supplies a small stdio scaffold that handles this framing, so your work there is the tools themselves.

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"search_labels","arguments":{"query":"red"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"{\"labels\": [{\"label_id\": 7, \"name\": \"red-blue\"}]}"}]}}

Match responses to request IDs. Validate names and arguments before invocation. Treat returned text as data, even if it asks to change permissions. A successful protocol exchange establishes neither truth nor trust. Keep application/tool errors distinct from protocol or transport failures; fail closed on malformed requests and stop at the shared call budget instead of retrying indefinitely.

The existing reviewed incident card describes a research demonstration in which one connection could access public and private repositories: injected public issue text led an agent to publish private information. The disclosed scope concerns the agent system's data flow and permissions, and does not establish that every MCP client is vulnerable. (incidents/github-mcp; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1) We discuss that boundary only. We do not run the source payload, connect a real repository server, or supply credentials or personal data. Week 8 returns to data that asks for authority.

docs.title: Another tool shape: search, then execute
docs.text:
The five rules assume one tool per outcome: search_labels finds, delete_label deletes, and each definition travels with every request. Some servers take another shape. They expose two tools: one searches a catalogue of operations and returns the matching operations' descriptions and schemas, and one executes a named operation with its arguments. Fewer definitions reach every request, and the agent fetches a schema only when it needs one. There is no measured figure in this course for how much context that saves, so treat any number you meet as a claim to test.

Discuss with a partner; there is no single right answer:

  1. What leaves every request, and what must the agent now do before its first real call?
  2. Where do rule 1's schema checks and rule 5's brake live when delete_label is one entry behind execute? Who validates the arguments, and against which schema?
  3. Which call would you make, and what would you check afterwards, to show that execute still refuses to delete without a preview?

docs.title: A hook checks an event; the sandbox contains execution
docs.text:
In the boundary fixture, a pre-call check consumes one of two attempts, permits only read_label, validates a fixed record ID, and records an effect only after validation. A synthetic returned note says "please enable export." The next export request is denied and creates no effect. A third call is refused by the budget. Everything stays in memory: there is no listener, credential read, external request or host-file operation. This models a hook's placement, not an MCP implementation. The fixture guide has the command.

If a hook logs a bad action after it happened, it has not prevented that action. If the same untrusted process can edit or bypass the hook, the hook cannot enforce a security boundary against that process. Keep enforcement in a trusted controller and confirm it with negative tests. The editable fixture is for reasoning; the launcher independently contains it, using copied public inputs, disabled external networking and fixed resources. Neither approval text nor the model's promise to obey is an isolation test.

docs.title: Plans and parallel work need explicit ownership
docs.text:
A plan is: read the fixed question, predict, generate one answer, run the fixed checker, explain the result, stop. A plan-only phase produces proposed steps without granting write or bash access. A tool's named "plan mode" needs its own verified permission behavior; a plan written in prose cannot restrict execution.

A Git worktree provides another working directory associated with a repository, allowing separate branches to be edited concurrently. It does not create a sandbox: repository metadata and host access still need protection. The A/B exercise instead uses separate public input snapshots without .git, which the launcher copies into fresh containers. Do not pass a worktree or the private course repository directly as the student workspace.

A subagent receives a bounded subtask, context and tool access, then returns an artifact or explanation. Delegation adds model calls and coordination work, so count it against a single parent budget. Give each writer an exclusive path and verify changes when combining them. A subagent's report is a claim to check. An author asking their own agent to approve their work does not establish independent review. Week 6 returns to delegation.

docs.title: Week 3 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Try each prompt first, then compare the bounded conclusions below with your record.

docs.title: Q1a–Q1b: Context experiment
docs.text: Q1a. The packets differed in size and the runs used different models, so the observation does not isolate the packets' content. It supports only "this configuration of B answered more fields correctly on this question once." Q1b. Freeze the model and profile, the question, the byte budget, the checker, a fresh call and the one-call limit, and change only what the packet contains.

docs.title: Q2a–Q2c: Context evidence
docs.text: Q2a. Report a tie on this question, field by field, including the shared abstention. Q2b. Token use, latency and verification time can differ, and one question does not establish general effectiveness. Q2c. Compare the packet and prompt digests and sizes in each input-record.json; a filename alone does not prove loading.

docs.title: Q3a–Q3d: Skill loading
docs.text: Q3a. The front-matter description determines whether the agent selects a skill. Q3b. A near-miss prompt that triggers it shows an over-broad description. Q3c. The bounded Judgement and Verification steps define when to stop. Q3d. The tools: as the lecture's diagram of one model request shows, each request carries every tool's name, description and full input schema, whether or not it is called. The skill adds only its name and description until it is loaded; then its body enters the context. A long skill body costs context only once it is used, so hold the procedure there and leave longer background in a separate file. Every tool a server exposes costs context in every request, so expose the tools the task needs. Hosts differ; check how the one you use sends both.

docs.title: Q4a–Q4c: MCP action
docs.text: Q4a. Validate the requested tool and arguments in the trusted action controller before calling the handler. Q4b. The denied export should leave no export effect, with the refusal recorded. Q4c. No. A tool result is data the agent reads, even when it asks for something; a well-formed result establishes neither truth nor permission.

docs.title: Q5a–Q5b: Hook and sandbox
docs.text: Q5a. A post-effect hook did not prevent the write, and a process that can edit or bypass the hook is not contained by it. Q5b. Run through the course launcher and retain negative tests for host-file, Docker-socket and network access.

docs.title: Q6a–Q6b: Execution permission
docs.text: Q6a. No. A green AI-use label grants no execution permission. Q6b. Use the Week 0 launcher route and record its passed runtime check and approved model or replay evidence.

docs.title: Q7a–Q7b: Returning the next step's IDs
docs.text: Q7a. Whether the agent can carry an ID from a result into its next call. Rule 2, return only what the next step needs: include the IDs other tools accept. Rule 4 helps too, because the revised description says where label_id comes from. Q7b. It could pick an ID that names a different label and delete that one; the draft would not even preview it first.

docs.title: Q8a–Q8b: Guarding the irreversible tool
docs.text: Q8a. Rule 5: dry_run defaults to true, so the bare delete_label {"label_id": 9} returns would_delete with the name release-2 instead of deleting it. Q8b. No. The replay's agent follows five course-written rules. A model's behavior needs a model run, such as the teaching team's recorded run with the course's hosted model, labelled with its configuration, when it is available.

docs.title: Q9a–Q9c: Tool contract
docs.text: Q9a. Rule 1: scope needs an enum of local and all in the schema, not a sentence in the description. Q9b. Rule 3: an unknown report should return a structured non-retryable not_found result rather than a traceback. Q9c. Rule 5: archiving cannot be undone, so the tool needs a dry_run that defaults to true; a call with only report_id should preview and leave the report unchanged, which a call without dry_run followed by a check of the report shows.

docs.title: Q10a–Q10b: Map arrows
docs.text: Q10a. Refuted. Keep the arrow and record legacy_app/views.py with the line of abort(401) at your revision, and what the code does instead: a visitor without a session gets 401, not a redirect. Q10b. Cannot tell: nothing you have read shows the text. Reading the template's {% else %} branch in legacy_app/templates/ci/overview.html, or opening the page as a signed-in user with no projects, would let you mark it confirmed or refuted, with its file and line.

docs.title: Q11a–Q11c: Compaction
docs.text: Q11a. It held the constraint in words, "do not edit the template", but not the path. The next edit needs a file, and nothing in the compacted context names view.py as the one to leave alone, so the edit landed there. A summary keeps a fact only in a form the next step can act on: here, the path. Q11b. The current state of the files: that status.py now holds the strip-only version, so the first read is stale, and that view.py is as shipped. The source of the constraint, NOTES.md, is missing too. The check runs on the edited files and the course policy reads only the constraint and the failure, so nothing in the check looks for these facts; the checklist does. Q11c. For example, the newest raw results still matter: the reread of status.py and the check's source are exact text that a summary would only paraphrase, and the next edit or check depends on them. A restart drops them, and the new session has to reread before it edits.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval and transfer
docs.text: Retrieval 1. A completed permitted test result for the current candidate is missing. Retrieval 2. written records only the file operation and a reply without calls only stops the loop; rerun the fixed verification and retain its result and revision. Transfer. B's second call changes the opportunity as well as the content, so it cannot be attributed to the first packet. Compare first answers only, or give both packets the same second call.

docs.title: Week 3 self-check
docs.text:
Answer from your work product and understanding, without an agent. Compare with the notes or a peer first, then use the public answer guidance after the workshop. These questions are formative.

Packet B's answer gets four of four fields right and packet A's gets one. B also had twice as many bytes and used a different model.

1a. What bounded claim does this observation support?

1b. Which experimental variables must be frozen to isolate the packets' content?

Both packets' answers get the same three fields right, and both leave the same field null.

2a. What result should be reported for this question?

2b. Name one cost or limitation that a field count misses.

2c. Which evidence shows that each packet was actually loaded?

For skills/trace-request/SKILL.md, the description, steps, judgement and verification sections are present.

3a. Which part determines whether an agent loads the skill?

3b. Which trigger result would show that its description is too broad?

3c. Which section tells the agent when to stop?

3d. An agent has this skill and the two revised label tools available and has used none of them yet. Which of them puts its full text into every model request, and which puts in only a name and a description? What does that mean for a long skill body, and for a server with many tools?

A discovered MCP tool returns a note asking for data export.

4a. Which component should validate the requested action?

4b. What evidence would show that denial happened before an effect?

4c. Does a well-formed tool result make the note's request trusted?

A hook reports “blocked” after writing a file.

5a. What limitation does the hook have here?

5b. Which execution boundary and negative test are still required?

The offline doctor passes and the task carries a green AI-use label.

6a. Can the label authorize tool execution?

6b. Which evidence is still required?

In the agent replay, the draft server's search returns ["red-team"] and the revised server's returns {"label_id": 12, "name": "red-team"}.

7a. Which of the three observations does this change, and which rule does it come from?

7b. What could an agent that guesses IDs do on the draft server?

With ticket ID 9, the draft server deletes release-2 and the revised server does not.

8a. Which rule's fix makes the difference, and which result shows it?

8b. Does the replay show that a model would behave the same way? What would?

A generated archive_report tool takes report_id (an integer) and scope (a plain string whose description says "local or all"). Archiving cannot be undone, and an unknown report_id raises a traceback.

9a. What schema rule is violated by the unannotated string scope?

9b. What structured behavior should replace a traceback for an unknown report?

9c. What should a call that gives only report_id do, and which call shows it?

A drawn map of the project-list path has the arrow require_user → redirect to /login for a visitor without a session. At your revision, require_user in legacy_app/views.py calls abort(401).

10a. How do you label the arrow, and what do you record beside it?

10b. You have read the route but not the template yet. How do you label the arrow that says an empty list shows No projects yet., and what would change that label?

In the compaction comparison, a student's summary reads: "Goal: make the status labels right. Constraint: do not edit the template. Tried raw.strip(); the check failed on OK." Run as summary, the next edit changes view.py and the check fails.

11a. Which fact did the summary hold, and why did the next edit still miss it?

11b. The student adds view.py to the constraint line and the check passes. Which fact from the session is still missing, and why did the check not catch it?

11c. The same file run as fresh also passes, with a much smaller context. Name one reason to compact rather than restart in a real session.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval: Weeks 1–2 mechanisms
docs.text:
R1. A controller denies a test and the proposer then says “all tests passed.” What observation is missing?

R2. A loop records written after changing a file, and the next reply has no tool calls. What separate observation is required before calling the change verified?

docs.title: Dashboard transfer
docs.text: Packet B's answer gets every field right only after a second call that adds the template file. Can the difference be attributed to B's content, and what check would discriminate that claim?

docs.title: Find the change in an unfamiliar repository
docs.text:
Week 3 · CI dashboard

Which information would change the next proposal?

docs.title: A file on disk is not yet context
docs.text:
The status contract is in the repository, but no request has carried it. Having read only view.py, the model proposes changing the displayed label to passed.

What information would you seek before allowing an edit?

docs.title: Mechanism: Context packet assembly
docs.text:
Each request carries the selected context and the full tool definition to the model; permission remains a controller decision.

Context packet assembly Selected context and the complete tool definitions converge with the request into one model request. A separate controller checks permission before any tool call. request selected context tool definitions (full) one model requestrequest + context + schemas controller policy allowed tool call tool result

docs.title: One idea for today
docs.text:
An agent acts only on what reaches it.

You choose the context it reads, the skill descriptions it picks from, and the tool names, schemas, errors and results it acts on.

Each choice is something you can test.

docs.title: Recall Week 1: where does " OK " first go wrong?
docs.text:
The rule ignores surrounding whitespace and case.

# loader.py
raw = record["status"]
# status.py
label = {"ok": "passed"}.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")
# view.py
render(label)

Name the first line that breaks the rule, and why a template patch is the wrong fix.

docs.title: A real path: the project list
docs.text:
GET /domains/ci_dashboard/
  domains/ci_dashboard.py      overview(): require_user(), query, render
  legacy_app/views.py          require_user(): abort(401) without a user
  legacy_app/templates/ci/overview.html   for ... else: "No projects yet."

The route names what happens. The other two files decide what a visitor sees.

docs.title: A repository map is a checkable claim
docs.text:
For one real path, retain:

  • The checkout revision and entry function.
  • File/function references for validation and output.
  • A test that covers the path, or a stated coverage gap.

A generated map is a proposal: label each arrow confirmed, refuted or cannot tell.

docs.title: Two packets, one question
docs.text:
The same 639 bytes of context, then the same question: status for a visitor with no session, text for an empty list, and the file deciding each.

Packet Content A The route's own file, read on from overview B The API's 401 line, overview, require_user, the template's empty branch

Predict all four fields for each packet.

docs.title: Equal opportunity for each packet
docs.text:
Same question, model, profile and byte budget. One fresh call per packet, no repair, no conversation carryover.

Record digests, usage and every field's result. Check each answer against the code, never against the other answer.

docs.title: Four labels, not a pass count
docs.text:
Label Meaning correct Matches the running dashboard wrong A confident value that does not match abstained An explicit null: the context did not show it missing The field was left out

The key comes from running the app: 401, then No projects yet.

docs.title: A course-written replay, labelled
docs.text:
Packet Status File Empty text File Correct A 302 route file null null 0 of 4 B 401 views.py No projects yet. route file 3 of 4

No model was called: the course wrote both answers to show the checker. Your own pair is the measurement.

docs.title: What one pair can and cannot show
docs.text:
Report the field labels and the usage difference for this question. Do not infer that traced context always wins, or never does.

Reversed order, other questions or repeated runs test a new question. Preserve the first pair as it happened.

docs.title: Your turn: a question with no course packet
docs.text:
A direct POST of a 121-character project title. What status comes back, what is the longest title accepted, and which file decides each?

Build at most 400 bytes from your source and predict what it covers. Run packet_check.py, then revise once.

docs.title: A long session, cut four ways
docs.text:
19 messages, 5,283 of 5,500 bytes. The next check result will not fit.

Mode Carries full every message auto old tool output cleared to stubs summary your summary plus the newest group fresh the task and your handoff only

Which file will the next edit touch after auto?

docs.title: Clearing removed the one instruction
docs.text:
NOTES.md, read once in message 2: "Do not edit view.py". auto cleared it with the other old tool output.

The next edit changed view.py; "queued" showed passed. Nothing left in the context contradicted that edit.

docs.title: Check a summary twice
docs.text:
Against the transcript: each fact the next step needs, with its message. By the next step: the same six-case check on the result.

A passing check covers only what the check reads. Restart instead when the history is mostly stale; reread before editing.

docs.title: A skill is found by its description
docs.text:
---
name: check-label-tools
description: Checks an edited label tool by calling it through the
  host before the change is reported. Use when search_labels or
  delete_label changed or a call fails.
---
## Steps / ## Judgement / ## Verification

The agent sees names and descriptions; it loads a body only when one fits.

docs.title: Would this description fire?
docs.text:
• "Why does search_labels give me names but no IDs?"
  • "I edited delete_label; is it safe to ship?"
  • "Rename the label column in the report."

Predict load or not for each, before anyone answers.

docs.title: Test the trigger like any prediction
docs.text:
Three requests in users' words that should load it. One close-but-wrong request that must leave it unloaded.

Predict, observe, change the description once, recheck the mismatches. A near miss that fires means the description is too broad.

docs.title: MCP: the agent sees names, schemas and descriptions
docs.text:
{"name": "delete_label", "description": "Deletes a label.",
 "inputSchema": {"type": "object",
                 "properties": {"label_id": {"type": "integer"}}}}

This is all the agent has to choose with, and every result it reads is data. Design every field for a reader that guesses.

docs.title: Rule 1: put every limit in the schema
docs.text:
A server that validates calls, as the workshop's scaffold does, checks "maximum": 10 before your code runs. "limit can be up to 50" in prose is not checked at all.

When the two disagree, the agent's calls are rejected for a limit it never read.

docs.title: Rule 2: return only what the next step needs
docs.text:
Return the fields the next step needs, including the IDs other tools accept. Not the stored record.

If you cut a list short, say so: total, truncated.

docs.title: Rule 3: report a failure as a result the agent can read
docs.text:
{"error": {"code": "not_found", "retryable": false,
           "message": "No such label; use search_labels for label_id values."}}

A raw exception gives the agent nothing to act on. This result tells it whether to retry.

docs.title: Rule 4: say what comes back and where each input comes from
docs.text:
"A label_id from search_labels."

State what each tool returns and which tool produces each ID argument, so the agent can call them in sequence without guessing.

docs.title: Rule 5: guard every irreversible action
docs.text:
Readers: readOnlyHint: true. Irreversible tools: destructiveHint: true and dry_run defaulting to true.

A call that leaves the argument out must not change anything.

docs.title: A generated draft: predict four calls
docs.text:
A course-authored first draft of search_labels and delete_label.

search {"query": "red"} · delete {"label_id": 7} delete {"label_id": 99} · search {"query": "r", "limit": 50}

What does each call do to the draft?

docs.title: Verify with calls, not by reading
docs.text:
Call Draft Revision search "red" names, no IDs IDs, total, truncated delete 7, no dry_run deleted preview; still there delete 99 KeyError traceback not_found, retryable: false limit 50 accepted invalid_argument

Each row is a check you can rerun: fixture/label_tools.py.

docs.title: One request, two servers
docs.text:
Delete the label red-team. An old ticket gives its label_id as 21.

There is no label 21; red-team is 12. For each server, predict:

  • Does the agent carry an ID from a result into its next call?
  • Does it recover after the ID is not found?
  • Does it preview before it deletes?

docs.title: The draft server
docs.text:
call p1  delete_label {"label_id": 21}  -> {"traceback": "KeyError: 21"}
call p2  search_labels {"query": "red-team"} -> {"labels": ["red-team"]}
final    no label_id for red-team; I will not guess one

No ID to carry, no recovery, and call 1 would have deleted label 21 at once.

docs.title: The revised server
docs.text:
call p1  delete_label {"label_id": 21}  -> not_found, retryable: false
call p2  search_labels {"query": "red-team"} -> label_id 12
call p3  delete_label {"label_id": 12}  -> dry_run: true, would_delete red-team
call p4  delete_label {"label_id": 12, "dry_run": false} -> deleted

Carried 12, recovered, previewed. Same agent rules, different tools.

docs.title: A stale ID, with and without a brake
docs.text:
With ticket ID 9, which is release-2:

  • Draft: the first call deletes release-2; the agent can only report it.
  • Revised: the first call previews release-2; the name does not match, so it searches.

The brake turned a wrong call into a result the agent could read.

docs.title: The replay agent is not a model
docs.text:
Its five rules are course-written and never guess an ID. A model may guess, retry a traceback or skip the error's message.

When available, the teaching team's recorded run with the course's hosted model (at most four requests per server, the launcher's cap) is the comparison. Until then, the course replay and its tables are the comparison.

docs.title: Brakes, hooks and the sandbox
docs.text:
A brake makes a call that omits dry_run harmless. A pre-call hook rejects an event before its effect.

Neither contains a process that ignores it. The launcher does.

docs.title: Workshop order
docs.text: Part A: the fixed health task for the required pair and boundary check. Part B: your skill, on ci-dashboard and, read-only, on your candidate contribution project. Part C: the ci-dashboard tool server, with your own test through the protocol.

docs.title: Exit: an extra call for B
docs.text:
A's answer gets two fields wrong. B's answer gets one wrong, then a second call adds the template file and B gets all four.

What changed besides the packet? How should the first answers and the later call appear in your record?

docs.title: The repository becomes your course project
docs.text:
Get the ci-dashboard student package in Week 3 and keep it. The repository-context workshop's map and context record help bound your M0 proposal.

Next week: the source can tell us what exists. We still need to discover what a user needs.

docs.title: Workshop and review
docs.text:
Worked notes · Workshop · Self-check

Course case · Week 0 execution route

Use the same work in the linked practice unit or project. No extra report.

docs.title: Week 3 fixtures: context packets, a long session and two tool servers
docs.text: These are course-authored synthetic files. The two packets quote the public ci-dashboard source; nothing here holds personal data or real credentials. The scripts give public formative feedback; they are not a workshop grader or a complete MCP server. Read the Week 3 notes first.

docs.title: Preparation and fixed budget
docs.text:
Use the trusted Week 0 setup and approved route guide. From the course root, resolve the offline profile for every step that makes no model call:

uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json

In the commands below, replace VERSION and DIGEST with version and digest from that result. A model run uses the approved-hosted profile and your key instead: replace HOSTED_VERSION, HOSTED_DIGEST and HOSTED_CONFIG with the values Week 0 setup gives. Do not change model, sampling or resource settings. The resolver's shared contract owns the model and its limits; the launcher policy owns CPU, memory, process, disk, output and execution limits. Save the resolver JSON with your small evidence record so the complete configuration is explicit.

The comparison adds these equal limits to both packets: the same question, 639 bytes of context, one model call, one answer, one check, no automatic retries or repairs. Each packet plus the question is at most 1,022 bytes, within the offline profile's 1,024-byte prompt limit, which the course tests check. The hosted item's own limit is set when that item is enabled; a refusal there is a result to record. The launcher's safety probes add waiting time; count that in your activity time, separately from model-call latency.

Use your editor or file manager to create week3-work under the course root and copy only these public files from this directory into it:

ab-replay.json
agent_replay.py
boundary.py
compaction.py
generate.py
label_tools.py
long-session.json
packet-a.txt
packet-b.txt
packet_check.py
question-2.txt
question.txt
verify.py

Do not copy .git, teacher answers or the private course checkout. Keep the same clean input snapshot for A and B. The launcher copies it into a temporary workspace; it does not mount your host workspace and does not preserve in-sandbox edits. All steps can be completed with a keyboard and plain-text editor.

docs.title: 1. Predict, then check the course replay
docs.text:
Read question.txt, packet-a.txt and packet-b.txt as text. Write what each packet's answer will say for the four fields. Then run the checker over the course-written pair:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python verify.py --replay ab-replay.json

Expect exit_code: 0 and three lines: the record's kind: course-synthesised, its configuration and reproduction command, then a with 0 of 4 correct and b with 3 of 4. No model was called for this record; the course team wrote both answers by hand. If any input file differs from the one the record pins, the checker prints input_changed and exits 2 instead of scoring.

docs.title: 2. Build and check a packet of your own
docs.text:
Read question-2.txt. It has no course packet. From your own ci-dashboard source, create packet-own.txt in week3-work, at most 400 bytes. Copy whole lines, and start each excerpt with a header line that names its file, as packet B does:

legacy_app/views.py (require_user):
def require_user() -> int:

Write your prediction for status and limit, then run:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python packet_check.py packet-own.txt

Expect one line with feedback_only: true, packet_bytes, budget: 400 and a label per part: covered, no_file, browser_only or missing; the notes explain each. The launcher's exit_code is 0 when both parts are covered and 1 otherwise. A packet over 400 bytes is reported as over_budget with no labels, and a file that is not UTF-8 text as unreadable; both exit 2. No model is called. Revise the packet once, run the same command again and keep both outputs.

docs.title: 3. Generate and check your own pair
docs.text:
This step is optional. Each command reads its packet, appends the identical question and makes one call through the launcher's prompt-only broker. It exports the raw answer.txt and input-record.json with the packet, question and prompt digests and sizes. It repairs nothing. Use fresh output directories and trace filenames for each packet. Do not reuse an existing trace or output location, since that would obscure the number of calls or overwrite work.

With your key, from the Week 0 setup values:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version HOSTED_VERSION --digest HOSTED_DIGEST --workspace week3-work --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key --trace week3-a.jsonl --output week3-a-result -- python generate.py a
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version HOSTED_VERSION --digest HOSTED_DIGEST --workspace week3-work --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key --trace week3-b.jsonl --output week3-b-result -- python generate.py b

Without a key, the replay route needs no hosted configuration or key file. Replace REPLAY_FILE and REPLAY_DIGEST with the Week 3 record your instructor names:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version HOSTED_VERSION --digest HOSTED_DIGEST --workspace week3-work --model replay --replay-file REPLAY_FILE --replay-digest REPLAY_DIGEST --trace week3-a.jsonl --output week3-a-result -- python generate.py a
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version HOSTED_VERSION --digest HOSTED_DIGEST --workspace week3-work --model replay --replay-file REPLAY_FILE --replay-digest REPLAY_DIGEST --trace week3-b.jsonl --output week3-b-result -- python generate.py b

Until a Week 3 record exists, the launcher refuses the replay command; use the course replay in step 1 as your comparison. To practise the call itself with no key and no record, use the fake model on the offline profile:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work --model fake --trace week3-a-fake.jsonl --output week3-a-fake -- python generate.py a
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work --model fake --trace week3-b-fake.jsonl --output week3-b-fake -- python generate.py b

The fake model returns a fixed practice string. The checker reports it as unreadable; it is not a measured answer.

Check each answer in a fresh launcher invocation. With your editor or file manager, copy the unchanged verify.py into each result directory. Read answer.txt as text first, then:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-a-result -- python verify.py answer.txt
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-b-result -- python verify.py answer.txt

Expect one line with feedback_only: true, a label per field and the number correct. All four correct exits 0; otherwise 1. An answer that is not one JSON object is reported as unreadable. Record each packet's four labels, tokens and latency from the minimal trace; null usage is missing, not zero, and run.cost_status: unknown stays unknown. Never submit environment dumps or unrelated conversation history.

docs.title: 4. Check a tool definition by calling it
docs.text:
Read the DRAFT definitions in label_tools.py and write down what you expect each of its four calls to do, then run:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python label_tools.py

Expect exit_code: 0 and eight JSON lines, four for draft and four for revised. For the draft: search returns names without IDs, a bare delete_label call deletes (label_still_present: false), the unknown ID returns a traceback, and limit: 50 is accepted. For the revision: IDs with total and truncated, a preview that leaves the label present, a not_found error with retryable: false, and an invalid_argument refusal. The example is in memory with synthetic labels; no server, file or network is involved. Explain which of the five rules each row checks.

The example checks each argument's type before its range, as the workshop's server scaffold would, so a wrong type such as {"query": 5} or "limit": true returns invalid_argument with retryable: false from either version; it never reaches a handler. Only an exception inside a draft handler, such as the unknown ID above, is shown as a traceback entry.

To make a call of your own, add one row to the tuple in verify() in your week3-work copy, after the four rows already there, and run the same command again:

        ("My call", "search_labels", {"query": 5}, None),

A row holds a question, the tool's name, the arguments, and the ID of a label to look for after the call (or None). Each row starts from fresh records, and each version prints one more line per row. Keep the four published rows unchanged, so their output still matches the table in the notes.

docs.title: 5. Watch an agent use both servers
docs.text:
First predict, for each server, whether the agent carries an ID from a result into its next call, recovers after the ID is not found, and previews before it deletes. Then:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python agent_replay.py
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python agent_replay.py --ticket-id 9 --summary

The first line reads agent: course-written policy, not a model. Each server prints the request, every call, every result, the final message and the labels left. With the default ticket ID 21 the draft run ends without deleting anything and the revised run deletes red-team after a preview. --summary adds the three observations as one JSON line per server, computed from the transcript. The tool results are the real outputs of label_tools.py; the agent's choices follow the five rules in policy, which the script steps through one call at a time. It makes no model request. --ticket-id takes any other ID; the activities use 12 and 7.

When available, a run of the same request with the course's hosted model, recorded by the teaching team one server at a time with at most four model requests each (the launcher's per-run cap), is the comparison. It uses the same transcript format, starts agent: approved model (hosted) and is labelled with its configuration. Read it with the same three questions, including any guessed ID, unusable reply, step_limit stop or deleted wrong label. Until then, the course replay and its tables are the comparison.

docs.title: 6. Compact a long session, then check
docs.text:
long-session.json is a 19-message session the course team wrote by hand in the Week 2 message format; no model or agent produced it. compaction.py builds the context the next request would carry in one of four ways, lets a course-written policy pick the next edit from that context alone, and runs the same six-case acceptance check on the result. The notes explain the four modes and the policy's two rules. First read the whole session, with each message's index, role and size:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python compaction.py full --show

Expect the first line agent: course-written policy, not a model, the 19 messages, then one JSON line with feedback_only: true, mode: full, context_bytes: 5283, budget: 5500, next_edit in status.py with status-strip-lower, and check: passed. Fill the checklist in the activity from this output. Then predict and run the supplied compaction:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python compaction.py auto --show

The printed context shows which messages became [cleared: ...] stubs. The JSON line lists kept and cleared message indices, policy_found (the first line the policy found for each rule, or null), next_edit, check and each FAIL line. Then write summary.txt in week3-work, at most 600 bytes, and run it both as a compaction and as a restart:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python compaction.py summary summary.txt
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python compaction.py fresh summary.txt

summary replaces messages 1-16 with your file and keeps the newest group; fresh keeps only the task and your file. The launcher's exit_code is 0 when the check passes and 1 when it fails. A file over 600 bytes is reported with file_bytes and limit and is not run; a file that is not UTF-8 text is reported as unreadable; both exit 2. No model is called and nothing is written. Revise the summary once if you like, and keep each output.

docs.title: Optional: a permission refusal in memory
docs.text:
This belongs to the optional reading.

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week3-work -- python boundary.py

Expect exit_code: 0 and allowed_read, denied_export, budget_enforced all true. The returned note is inert text. The example uses an in-memory dictionary, no sockets, real files, secrets or external services. Explain why the export request leaves the effect list unchanged, and why editing this Python hook cannot disable the launcher.

docs.title: One work record
docs.text:
Use one existing repository-context workshop record, or a plain text note during class:

Profile/version/digest and execution order:
Predictions for packet A / packet B (four fields each):
Own packet: predictions for status / limit, check output before and after the one revision:
Packet and question digests, packet bytes:
Observed A / B: field labels, tokens, latency, cost status, failure category
Agent replay predictions and observations, draft / revised:
Compaction checklist; auto / summary / fresh: next edit and check:
Peer feedback and one visible revision (kept separate from the original pair):
My explanation and no-AI reflection:
AI-use note ID:

If you have no launcher access, a partner can run the commands while you predict, read the outputs and explain them; the activities describe that route.

docs.title: Week 4: Turn a user need into an executable specification
docs.text: This directory holds Week 4 materials. You separate observations from assumptions, decide a feature boundary and write independent acceptance cases; the discovery workshop starts M0.

docs.title: Activity: Which log lines explain the failure?
docs.text:
Time: 10 minutes within class, including feedback and revision. Materials: the text below and a plain-text editor or paper. Format: individual or pairs; pair members each write their own short record. No login, microphone, mouse, personal experience, private repository or real participant is needed. Keyboard-only silent work is a full path through this practice. Timing is a help checkpoint, not a penalty.

S4-B is a fresh case invented for this activity; the lecture has not worked it. Do not recruit anyone or substitute a real anecdote. The complete input is in text; speaking or acting a role is not required. For your own discovery, follow the rules before actual discovery.

docs.title: Input S4-B
docs.text:
A fictional maintainer reads the log of failed run 30 to find what broke it:

Line 1: INFO     Checkout complete
Line 2: WARNING  Option --fast is deprecated
Line 3: WARNING  Cache miss for test data
Line 4: ERROR    test_totals failed: expected 3, got 2
Line 5: INFO     Log upload complete

Supplied fictional event: a "show problems" view displayed lines 2, 3 and 4. The maintainer read both warnings first, then found line 4 and copied it into a bug report. Searching the raw log for the word ERROR was the workaround. There is no evidence here about how long logs usually are, whether a warning ever explains a failure, how often this happens, or any real person's preferences.

Starting question: "Would an AI summary of your logs save you time?" Starting requirement: "Show the problems in a log."

docs.title: Steps and visible outputs
docs.text:
Minutes Action (AI-off throughout) Output and LO 0-2 Read S4-B. Rewrite the leading question to ask about a specific event Original/revised question; LO3 2-4 Use only the supplied event to write one observation, one inference and one unanswered question Your own three short lines labelled S4-B; LO3, LO9 4-6 Write a job statement and a problem statement; avoid prescribing a tool Problem statement with an S4-B reference; LO3 6-8 Write one given/when/then acceptance criterion for a pure function over the log lines. Predict its output for S4-B and give one input on which "problems" and your criterion disagree Criterion, expected result and that input; LO3 8-10 Peer checks one ambiguous clause; solo path uses the checklist below. Revise once and explain what changed Before/after criterion, feedback and brief reason; LO3, LO9

At minute 4, request a hint if you cannot separate observation from inference. Use only the hint needed: (1) underline what happened; (2) circle words introducing your interpretation; (3) ask whether "problem" actually means "error." Extra time or another interaction format should support the same outputs, not require personal disclosure.

docs.title: Feedback checklist
docs.text:
• Does each asserted event exist in S4-B? Label everything else an inference or decision.
  • Does your problem statement describe a difficulty in doing a job rather than a requested technology?
  • Could two implementations disagree about what "problems" means? Replace it with observable behavior. State input assumptions, the output order and one empty or boundary result.
  • Is your record labelled as practice and written by you without AI?
  • If this had been real research and consent were withdrawn, which evidence would you stop using, and who would check removal and replacement arrangements?

Record all outputs in one small work record. Add one AI-use note ("No AI used in this activity") and a short AI-off reflection. Do not fill maintenance metadata or create a disclosure file. This is practice, not one of your two M0 discoveries.

docs.title: Staged delegation round
docs.text:
Time: 25 minutes within class. Materials: AC1 from the notes, the public example and the exact launcher commands. Format: individual or pairs; each person keeps their own record. Output: one short delegation record.

Take AC1 to a candidate in five stages and stop after each one. At every stage you may act as the agent yourself or use an approved assistant through the route in Week 0 setup; the checkpoints are what you are practising. Implement uses the three course candidates, or optionally one more that you generate with the model command; Test uses the launcher. Write down your decision at every stop: continue, narrow, go back, or stop.

Use the course-written research-codebase skill for Research and plan-change for Plan. End each stage with its file (research.md, then plan.md) and start the next stage from that file alone.

Minutes Stage Do this Checkpoint you record 0-4 Research Read README.en.md, acceptance.py and run_example.py without editing. Write three findings, each with file and function Strike any finding you cannot point to 4-8 Propose Write two ways to meet AC1 within the non-goals, each with what changes and what could break Your choice and one sentence on why 8-13 Plan List the steps. Next to each, write the AC1 clause it serves and the check name from acceptance.py Every clause has a step; every step has a check 13-18 Implement Read candidate_a.py, candidate_b.py and candidate_c.py as text against your plan. Optional: read the prompt in run_example.py, predict, then generate one more with model Accept or reject each candidate before it is tested; anything beyond failed_ids is rejected 18-23 Test Run each candidate in the launcher. Record the launcher JSON exit_code and the first failing check/output or the one all-pass summary; later checks are not run after a failure One candidate passes Test and still breaks the bound: which one, and why did Test not catch it? Accept, or go back to the named stage 23-25 Stop line One line: where you stopped or narrowed the task, and why Peer reads it and asks one question

At minute 13, swap plans with a partner (or use the checklist below on your own). Find one step whose check would still pass with a wrong implementation, and revise it. One example: a plan that checks only AC1-mixed would accept a function that always returns [9].

  • Does every finding name a file and function you opened?
  • Did you choose the option, or accept the first one offered?
  • Was each check written from AC1 before the candidate existed?
  • Did the candidate stay inside the bound you set?

If execution is unavailable, do the text trace and mark it not executed; ask for a supported execution opportunity. Do not substitute host execution or claim that a text trace or FAKE output is a completed real model run.

docs.title: Where the specification lives
docs.text: Optional discussion (5 minutes): discuss one concrete repository arrangement for your project: where will the feature specification, staged plan and decision record live (for example, docs/specs/, plans/ and a decision log)? Explain how a code change updates the relevant specification and acceptance checks, where an agreed requirement change is logged, and what the next agent session must read to recover that context. This discussion adds no separate submission.

docs.title: Carry the round into M0
docs.text:
Outside class, about 45 minutes. Run one round for your personal ci-dashboard project:

  1. Pick one acceptance criterion, by its AC-n ID, from your personal M0 feature specification, and the smallest part of the feature that it constrains, for example one function or one view. Pick a slice other than the worked overview example in the notes.
  2. Research: run the course research-codebase skill on that slice, with or without an approved agent. Keep only findings that name a file and function you have opened. Name paths and function names only; do not paste code, signatures or key: value lines into the work record.
  3. Propose: write at least two options, with trade-offs, and pick one.
  4. Plan: list steps, each with the check derived from your criterion that shows it is done. Check each acceptance criterion against the specification yourself. Then ask the approved model, in a fresh context, for a bounded review of the criterion and your planned checks only (never participant notes), and mark each finding confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with your own evidence. If model review is unavailable, ask a TA. Do not execute those acceptance tests in this round.
  5. Implement only if the first step is small and bounded, inside the launcher on your copy of the project. Otherwise stop after Plan and say so: the reviewed change itself is M1 work.
  6. Test: run the M0 smoke command python3 -I launch.py smoke through the launcher and record its observed result. Acceptance tests are not executed in this round; after a stop, record not run.

Write the round into your personal M0 work record, under Artifact and decision: the criterion's AC-n ID, one line per stage, and a last line saying where you stopped or narrowed the task. The specification itself stays as it is; there is no separate submission. Reuse the work record's AI-use note ID.

docs.title: Your contribution project
docs.text: Confirm your contribution project this week: keep the candidate you used in the Week 3 skill transfer or choose another from the approved list, or propose one that meets the same conditions. A project takes at most five students at a time, so keep a second choice. Read its contribution guide and AI-use rules, then find the small, complete fix (a defect, a test or documentation) you will make as the C1 warm-up contribution, due in Week 6. See the syllabus for the rules and the course-hosted route.

docs.title: Return to the dashboard
docs.text:
Critique an interview question, distinguish an observation from an assumption and write an executable acceptance condition.

Reuse relevant discovery in the discovery/specification workshop and M0 under the established consent/equivalence route. The workshop's remaining(capacity, requested) function is an optional warm-up; the M0 feature specification and this failure filter are separate contracts.

Before leaving, decide whether to accept the change, narrow the task, obtain one missing observation or stop. Explain what evidence could change that decision.

docs.title: Week 4: Requirements, user discovery and specification-driven development
Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, you can:

  • LO3: replace a leading question with a question about a concrete event; distinguish an observation, an inference and an unanswered question.
  • LO3: connect discovery evidence to a problem statement, a small product requirements document (PRD), an acceptance criterion and an executable test.
  • LO9: explain when evidence may be used, what must be removed, and why a synthetic exercise cannot prove real participation or approved equivalence.
  • LO3, LO9: diagnose a generated implementation against the agreed criterion, revise it after feedback, and explain both the verification and its limits.
  • LO3: carry agreed acceptance criteria into a staged delegation (research, propose, plan, implement, test), decide at a checkpoint after each stage, tie every plan step to a check derived from a criterion, and record where you stopped or narrowed the task.

The activity and self-check map each output to these outcomes. Every scenario and data value in this lesson is invented for teaching; none of it is discovery evidence for M0.

docs.title: The continuing dashboard case
docs.text: A fictional maintainer wants to isolate failed runs. Scenario S4-A below supplies the event, input and workaround. The classroom implementation returns unique failed IDs in ascending order; this ordering is an explicit exercise decision, not a participant preference. Use the same contract through the worked example, tests and first repair. The slide's later first-occurrence ordering question is a new agreed requirement, not the original oracle. "Latest per pipeline" would require additional fields and a separate product decision.

docs.title: Discovery before a feature request
docs.text:
Fitzpatrick's Mom Test teaching guidance emphasizes improving questions and recognizing biased data. Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD), as described by Ulwick, focuses on the underlying job a customer wants to accomplish rather than the product. (studies/user-discovery; as_of: 2026-09-08; Source 1; Source 2)

Use these course interview practices to apply that focus:

  1. Ask about a specific past event: "Walk me through the last time you checked a run."
  2. Ask what happened, what the person tried and what remained difficult. Avoid pitching a solution or asking for predictions such as "Would you use our smart dashboard?"
  3. Listen and follow up without supplying the answer. A compliment does not establish a requirement. Keep contradictions and uncertainty in your own notes.

Scenario S4-A: A fictional project maintainer checks run results before deciding which failed job to investigate. The supplied run list is [(12, "passed"), (9, "failed"), (11, "running")]. In the fictional event, a "not passed" filter displayed runs 9 and 11. The maintainer opened run 11, found it still running and returned to the list. A handwritten list of failed run IDs was the workaround. The maintainer wants to inspect failures; there is no evidence of a need for notifications, user tracking or automatic retries.

Do not add personal experiences, real repositories, screenshots, recordings or participant details to this practice.

Evidence step Our worked example What we still cannot conclude Observation S4-A The fictional filter included a running job How common this is in real work Inference Mixing running and failed jobs may distract from investigating failures Whether a separate filter is the preferred interface Follow-up question "What did you do after opening the running job?" Whether alerts would help JTBD frame (course wording) When checking run outcomes, I want to identify failures so I can choose a job to investigate That every maintainer has the same job Problem statement P1 The fictional maintainer cannot isolate failed runs because the current filter also includes running runs That a particular technology is needed

Generate the statement by hand, then verify each clause against S4-A. Remove "everyone needs instant alerts": neither "everyone" nor alerts has supporting evidence. This is also the boundary for M0's yellow AI rule: the student owns the problem statement and its reasoning; use AI only within the actual assignment's specified assistance scope. Discovery notes and reflection remain AI-off throughout.

docs.title: A small PRD and one criterion
docs.text:
A PRD records the problem, intended user, desired result, scope and unresolved choices. It is a decision document, not a list of tools. This course example needs only:

  • P1 / evidence: S4-A, explicitly synthetic; one fictional maintainer's task.
  • Outcome: obtain the IDs of failed runs to support manual investigation.
  • In scope: a pure function failed_ids(runs) over a list of (id, status) pairs.
  • Agreed assumptions: IDs are integers; status is passed, failed or running. Each pair describes an input observation. Repeated failed IDs appear once in output.
  • Non-goals: a web UI, login, notifications, network access, retries, persistence and validation of malformed input. These need separate requirements if adopted.
  • Open question: what order best supports the user's next decision? For this example we choose ascending ID order as a deterministic design decision, not an interview finding. Record that distinction and revisit it with appropriate evidence.

AC1: Given any list satisfying those input assumptions, when failed_ids is called, then it returns the ascending, duplicate-free list of IDs whose status is exactly failed. It returns [] if there are no failures and leaves the input unchanged.

AC1 replaces the ambiguous "show jobs needing attention." It specifies observable behavior; it does not prescribe an algorithm. Acceptance tests can check this function contract but cannot establish that the product is useful or that consent exists.

docs.title: Generation, failure, diagnosis and repair
docs.text:
First predict the result for S4-A without executing anything. A plausible generated candidate uses the wrong predicate:

return sorted({run_id for run_id, status in runs if status != "passed"})

It returns [9, 11]; AC1 requires [9]. The problem is the interpretation of "needs attention," not Python syntax. Repair the predicate to status == "failed" and run the same test again. Also test empty input, no failures, ordering, repeated IDs, a different ID and input preservation. The public example contains the complete failing and repaired implementations and executable checks. Use only the launcher commands in Verification to execute them.

Trace the decision: S4-A -> P1 -> AC1 -> AC1-mixed -> predicate repair. The sorting/duplicate rules are explicit design choices. A passing test of those choices does not retrospectively turn them into interview evidence.

docs.title: Spec Kit and specifications as source
docs.text:
Spec Kit documents a workflow of principles, specification, plan, tasks, implementation and convergence against the artifacts. Its optional analysis reads the specification, plan and tasks and reports conflicts, gaps and ambiguities without editing them. (tools/spec-kit; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4)

Use the constitution -> spec -> plan -> tasks sequence to organize this example:

Artifact Course example Verification before moving on Constitution No personal data; no network; changes need behavior checks Confirm input provenance and launcher boundary Spec P1, input assumptions, AC1 and non-goals Trace the problem to S4-A; label design choices Plan Pure function plus public checks; no service or database Check that the plan can implement every AC1 clause Tasks Write counterexample; implement filter; verify; explain limits Every task names an artifact and its check

Then generate the small implementation and compare code, tests and spec. We practice the artifacts here without installing a Spec Kit integration or adding an unapproved model. Tool-specific setup belongs to the approved environment for the actual practice unit.

"Specifications as source" means versioning intent and reviewing its changes alongside tests and code. A requirement change should identify affected tests and implementation; a code change should still satisfy the current requirement. Record each agreed change under the Change log heading of the feature specification template: the changed clause, the acceptance cases and tests it affects, the reason and who agreed. Prose is not automatically executable, complete or true. A mistaken spec can produce consistent but unwanted code. An AI consistency report is a review input, not a proof of correctness or authorization.

docs.title: Delegating against the specification in stages
docs.text:
AC1 says what must be true. It does not say how to hand the work to an agent. One request such as "implement AC1" asks the agent to research, choose, plan, write and judge in a single step, and you only see the end. Split the delegation into five stages instead: research, propose, plan, implement, test. Different workflows name these stages differently; the names matter less than the stop after each one. At every stop a person reads what the stage produced and decides: continue, narrow the task, return to an earlier stage, or stop. An agent can draft the output of every stage. It cannot make those decisions for you, and it cannot be the one who checks its own result.

Use the course-written research-codebase skill for Research and plan-change for Plan, here and in your M0 round. They return the located claims and the plan tables this lesson checks; the stops stay yours.

Each stage hands the next one a file. End every stage with a short written artifact: research.md holds the located claims you kept, plan.md the step-to-check table. Start the next stage in a fresh session that reads only that file and the paths it names, not the conversation that produced it. The next session then starts from what you checked rather than from every guess and dead end along the way, and the file is something a partner can review. The order matters too. A wrong research claim becomes a wrong option, then a wrong plan step and wrong code, so striking it at the first stop is the cheapest repair in the round.

Choose the least elaborate delegation that still leaves you an independent check. A direct prompt fits a small change in code you already know when one acceptance case can check the result. Start with a plan when the change is bounded but you need to agree the files and checks first. Research before planning when the repository or call path is unfamiliar and the acceptance case can be made concrete after the map. Use repeated research-to-plan rounds when the scope or boundary is still uncertain and several acceptance cases must be negotiated. The last two levels use research-codebase followed by plan-change; stop and narrow whenever the next check is not yet observable.

Delegation level Use it when ci-dashboard example Handoff Direct prompt The edit is small, the code is familiar, and one acceptance case can check it Rename the label in a known status component and run its existing rendering check One bounded request and its result Plan first The edit is bounded, you know the area, and one acceptance case can check the planned files Add the empty-state branch to a familiar builds view and map each step to its check plan-change output before implementation Research then plan The path crosses unfamiliar files, and one acceptance case can be made checkable after tracing Trace the /projects/<id>/builds status filter, then plan a change to its handler and template research-codebase record, then plan-change Multiple research → plan rounds The boundary is uncertain, you know little of the path, or several cases must be agreed Trace status filtering and the permission boundary, revise the scope, then plan each bounded slice A checked research record and a revised plan at each stop

Here is one round for the failure filter. The agent, whether a model or you playing its part, reads only the public example directory, and generated code runs only through the launcher.

Stage What you ask for What must come back Your checkpoint Research "Read README.en.md, acceptance.py and run_example.py. Change nothing. Report what already exists for AC1, citing file and function." Claims with locations, such as "acceptance.py CASES has six cases; verify also fails if the input changes" Open each cited location. A claim without one is a question, not a finding Propose "Give two or three ways to meet AC1 within the non-goals; for each, what changes and what could break." Options with trade-offs You choose and write down why Plan "List the steps for the chosen option. Name the AC1 check that shows each step is done." Steps, each with an observable check Every AC1 clause has a step; every check existed before the code Implement "Write only failed_ids in one new file. No imports. Do not edit acceptance.py." One bounded change Read the diff as text; reject anything outside the bound, even if it passes Test Run the existing checks in the launcher Launcher JSON exit_code plus the first failing case/output, or the one summary line after all cases pass Record the failure and the stage to revisit; checks after a failure are not run, not passed

repaired already implements AC1 and remains the worked reference; the delegation round must preserve that oracle while it evaluates a new candidate.

At Propose, suppose the agent offers three options. (A) Change the predicate inside broken: smallest diff, but it removes the counterexample the class relies on. (B) Add a separate failed_ids checked by the same verify: one new function, and the counterexample stays. (C) Add a status option to the run list screen: a web UI is a non-goal. You choose B. Rejecting C is a scope decision from the PRD, not a technical judgment, so write it down as one.

At Plan, each step points to a check written from AC1 before any code existed:

Step AC1 clause Check Keep only status exactly failed "whose status is exactly failed" AC1-mixed, AC1-no-failures Return each ID once "duplicate-free" AC1-duplicate Sort ascending "ascending" AC1-sort Handle no runs "returns []" AC1-empty Use the input, not fixed values the whole criterion AC1-other-id Do not change the input "leaves the input unchanged" the input was modified assertion

Use the feature specification template for this plan: list each permitted changed file with its relevant line number (or new), and list each test separately against its acceptance case. Implementation may change only those files; revise and check the plan before adding another file.

If a step has no check, you either write the check first or drop the step. The plan is where you narrow: if ordering were still disputed, you could take only the first two rows now and record the ordering question as open.

At Implement, the bound is part of the request. The model mode of run_example.py sends exactly such a bounded request; read its prompt and check that it names every clause in your plan. It exports candidate.py and stops. Without a model, the three course candidates are what you read at this stop. Read the candidate as text before starting Test with the separate launcher command below. A failure tells you where to go back. A wrong predicate returns you to Implement. A clause the plan never covered returns you to Plan. A misread requirement returns you to Propose or Research. Do not repair a failure by editing the check.

Record the round in a few lines: the brief for each stage, what came back, your decision at each stop, and where you stopped or narrowed the task. Stopping after Plan because the first step is not yet small enough is a legitimate result.

docs.title: A worked round on ci-dashboard
docs.text:
The failure filter fits on one screen. Here is the same round on the project repository, ending in a stop after Plan. The course wrote this record; no model was called. Line numbers refer to the course's starting capstone/legacy/ci-dashboard, so open each one before you accept a claim. This slice is the worked example; choose a different one for your own M0 round.

AC-W (written for this example): given a signed-in owner with one active and one archived project, when the owner opens the overview, then the active project is listed and the archived one is not. The archived project's own page still opens.

Research with research-codebase returns four claims:

Claim Location After opening it R1. overview selects the caller's projects WHERE owner_id=? ORDER BY id and renders ci/overview.html domains/ci_dashboard.py:28-38 Keep R2. The template prints one row per project with an Archived or Active label; its {% else %} branch prints No projects yet. only when the list is empty legacy_app/templates/ci/overview.html:17-24 Keep R3. archive_project flips archived and redirects to the overview; it deletes nothing. The Unarchive button is on the project page domains/ci_dashboard.py:96-106; legacy_app/templates/ci/project.html:6-8 Keep R4. "The overview query already skips archived projects, so only the label needs to change." domains/ci_dashboard.py:34 Strike: the query has no archived condition

If R4 had survived, the plan would have changed only the label, and the archived project would still be listed.

Propose. (A) Add AND archived=0 to the overview query at domains/ci_dashboard.py:34. (B) Keep the query and wrap each row of the template loop at overview.html:17-23 in {% if not project.archived %}. B touches only the template, but for an owner whose projects are all archived the loop still receives rows, so the {% else %} branch never runs and the table is blank. Choose A, and record that B was rejected for a case you could name before any code existed.

Plan. Changed files: only domains/ci_dashboard.py:34. Tests to write, one per clause:

Test AC-W clause Expected result test_overview_hides_archived the active project is listed and the archived one is not the active title appears; the archived title does not test_archived_project_page_opens the archived project's page still opens status 200 for that project's page

Stop. Writing the tests exposes a case AC-W never names: an owner whose projects are all archived. With A, that owner reads No projects yet. (overview.html:24), which is untrue, and the only way back to the Unarchive button is to type the project's URL. Neither is a code question. The round stops after Plan: record both questions against AC-W and take them back to the specification before anyone edits code.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Complete the 10-minute, AI-off discovery activity in activities.en.md. It uses a fresh case, S4-B, so you practise these moves on input you have not seen worked. Work from the provided text, individually or in pairs. Produce a question revision, your own short observation/inference record, a problem statement and one acceptance criterion. A silent keyboard-only path uses exactly the same input and outputs. No personal disclosure or real participant recruitment is required.

Use another 25 minutes within class for the staged delegation round: take AC1 through research, propose, plan, implement and test, stop at each checkpoint, and run the launcher checks. Get peer feedback on one plan step whose check is weak and revise it. At Implement you read the three course candidates as text, or generate one through the optional hosted route; Test then runs them in the launcher. Ask for help after five minutes without an explainable failure. If setup is unavailable, trace the cases on paper or in text and label them not executed.

Then carry one round into your personal M0 project outside class (about 45 minutes). Pick one acceptance criterion, by its AC-n ID, from your personal M0 feature specification and the smallest slice of the ci-dashboard feature that it constrains, other than the worked overview slice above. Research uses research-codebase, as in class. Implement only if the first planned step is small and bounded; otherwise stop after Plan and say so, because the reviewed change itself belongs to M1. Write the round into your personal M0 work record, citing the criterion by its ID. The specification itself stays as it is, and the round is not a separate submission.

The M0 feature specification holds AC-1 through AC-3 as Given/When/Then criteria, each traced to exactly one [interview:ID]. The workshop's remaining(capacity, requested) function is an optional warm-up, not the M0 task. Reuse discovery IDs where the actual topic is relevant and consent covers both uses.

docs.title: Before actual discovery or reuse
docs.text: Before any activity with a real participant, follow the course participation rules and the discovery workshop's input and privacy rules. Obtain active consent first, collect only what the task needs, and write and de-identify your notes yourself, without AI. Participant material, de-identified or not, never goes into a model prompt. If someone withdraws, stop using their material and remove it with your teacher. An approved alternative keeps the same learning outcomes, analysis steps and maximum score.

docs.title: Run the public example inside the launcher
docs.text:
Use the approved hosted or replay route in Week 0 setup. Run code only after that page's check shows you can run the practices. Independent assessments remain AI-off.

From the trusted course root, resolve the course profile:

uv run --locked python scripts/hosted_profile.py --profile approved-hosted --json

Replace VERSION and DIGEST below with the returned version and digest. They are explicit placeholders, not additional model settings. Use the public example directory alone; never mount the private course checkout, teacher answers or credentials. These commands preserve the launcher's network, filesystem, CPU, memory, process and timeout limits.

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace lectures/week-04/example -- python run_example.py broken
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace lectures/week-04/example -- python run_example.py repaired

The first invocation is expected to fail: AC1-mixed: expected [9], got [9, 11]. The repaired invocation must have container exit_code: 0 and AC1: all public checks passed; this is practice feedback, not a grade. Read the launcher's actual JSON result; a printed success line alone is insufficient. Safety probes take time on every invocation. A safety failure stops execution; do not change the limits or switch to host execution to finish the exercise.

docs.title: Implement and Test without a model
docs.text:
The three course candidates are versions of failed_ids that the course wrote; no model was involved. At the Implement stop, read each one as text and decide whether it stays inside the bound before you test it. Then run Test on each:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace lectures/week-04/example -- python -c 'from candidates.candidate_a import failed_ids; from acceptance import verify; verify(failed_ids)'

Replace candidate_a with candidate_b or candidate_c for the other two. Record each JSON exit_code and the first failing check or the all-pass line next to the decision you wrote before running it.

docs.title: Optional live generation
docs.text:
With your own key on the hosted route, generate one more candidate. Choose a new output directory for each attempt:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key --workspace lectures/week-04/example --output week4-candidate-01 -- python run_example.py model
