Without a key, the course candidates above are your Implement and Test material. If your instructor names a Week 4 replay record, replay it by replacing --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key with --model replay --replay-file REPLAY_FILE --replay-digest REPLAY_DIGEST.

Generation sends only the supplied synthetic specification through the broker's course_llm call and saves a candidate. It does not ask AI to write discovery notes. The separate Test invocation reports syntax errors, truncated responses, incorrect behavior or timeouts as failed attempts. Inspect the emitted candidate as text before starting Test; never execute exported code on the host. The launcher writes the output directory only on success; a failed attempt keeps the emitted artifact in its bounded JSON result. Inspect it as text through the course's supported feedback route, or ask for help. To run Test after the pause, put only candidate.py and the public acceptance.py in week4-repair using your editor:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week4-repair -- python -c 'from candidate import failed_ids; from acceptance import verify; verify(failed_ids)'

Explain which predicate changed and retain the failing/passing evidence. Do not reroll until a success without recording why the earlier candidate failed.

docs.title: Inspect the evidence
docs.text:
Check Evidence to retain in the existing work record LO3: traceability S4-A/P1/AC1 IDs, including which clauses are design decisions LO3: execution Predicted result, actual exit/output, current spec/test/code revision and one new boundary case LO3: delegation The brief and output of each stage, your decision at each checkpoint, the plan step-to-check table, and where you stopped or narrowed the task LO9: responsibility Synthetic label; for actual work, current teacher reference and permitted data only LO3, LO9: explanation Why the first predicate failed, what was revised after feedback, what passing tests cannot prove

Add one AI-use note to this record: no AI, or actual tool/model and purpose; reuse its ID in the discovery/specification workshop and M0. Keep the approved hosted or replay profile version/digest with any generation result. No full chat export or separate disclosure document is required. Your own short reflection is AI-off.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake How to notice it Correction Asking "Would you like our feature?" The answer supplies approval but no concrete event Ask about the last occurrence and workaround Treating a design choice as a user finding No observation supports sorting or duplicates Label the decision and state how to revisit it Equating not-passed with failed A running item appears in AC1 output Use the exact agreed status predicate Writing tests from the implementation only Both repeat the same wrong interpretation Derive expected results from AC1 and critique a fresh case Delegating all five stages in one request You first see the agent's work when the tests run Stop after each stage and record a decision before the next Accepting research without locations A finding names no file or function you can open Treat it as a question and ask for, or find, the location A plan step with no check You cannot say what would show the step is done Derive a check from a criterion clause, or drop the step Letting the implementation widen The diff touches checks, other files or non-goals Reject the change, restate the bound and narrow the plan Fixing a failed check by editing it The check changes in the same diff as the code Go back to the stage the failure points to; change the requirement only by agreement Treating tests as complete validation Nothing checks consent or whether P1 matters Review provenance and usefulness separately Letting AI write or polish discovery notes The submitted account is no longer your own record Write and de-identify notes yourself; keep AI in permitted work Counting S4-A as a real or approved equivalent activity There is no actual participation/approval record Label it practice and obtain the required arrangements Keeping withdrawn notes or lowering an alternative's ceiling Old confirmation is reused or fewer marks are available Stop use, follow removal, and preserve equal assessment limits

docs.title: Transfer to a new situation
docs.text:
The filter returns the right records but sorts them differently from the agreed display order. Is the requirement satisfied?

Write the expected behavior and the next check before comparing with a partner.

Use the relevant discovery and specification evidence from the discovery/specification workshop and M0 by reference.

docs.title: Optional reading after the exercise
docs.text:
The notes and supplied scenario contain everything needed for the class exercise. No purchase or extra pre-class reading is required; these sources support the specific concepts used this week, not a general product survey.

  • Question critique and JTBD: the discovery factsheet links Fitzpatrick's "Recommended teaching topics" and Ulwick's "Learning Jobs-to-be-Done Theory." Compare an event-based question with a proposed solution, then describe the job independently of that solution. (studies/user-discovery; as_of: 2026-09-08; Source 1; Source 2)
  • OpenSpec: read the Specs, Delta Specs and Archive sections of the concepts page at a fixed commit. It keeps the current specification apart from proposed changes and writes each requirement with Given/When/Then scenarios. Compare its scenarios with your acceptance checks, and notice that its optional verify step is described only as checking that the implementation matches the specs: a scenario becomes evidence once a test runs it. (tools/openspec; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)
  • Spec Kit: read the Spec-Driven Development section of the README and the /speckit.analyze and /speckit.converge sections of the command reference, both at a fixed commit. Read them to map the week's constitution -> spec -> plan -> tasks table onto a published workflow, then identify which of our artifacts expresses intent and which check supplies execution evidence: analysis compares the documents with one another, which is not a test run. This is conceptual reading, not permission to install an integration or use an unapproved model. (tools/spec-kit; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4)

The scenario, PRD, sentence frame and checks used in class are course originals.

docs.title: Week 4 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Separate observations, requirements and hypotheses in your record.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: For example: "Walk me through the last time you checked whether a run had failed." Its answer can establish one person's account of that event: what happened, what they tried and what stayed difficult. It does not show that alerts would save time or that anyone else has the problem.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: Opening a running job is an observation. Calling it a distraction is an inference; claiming every maintainer needs alerts is an unsupported generalization.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: The agreed output is [3, 7]: keep the failed IDs 7, 7 and 3, remove the repeat, then sort. A predicate that also keeps running ID 2 gives [2, 3, 7]. Add another failed ID and an empty-input case to guard against a hardcoded result.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: Review the changed requirement and its change-log entry, the affected tests, the code and the regressions together. Internal consistency alone does not establish usefulness.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: Withdrawal stops use of the participant material for the unapproved purpose. Check the consent and withdrawal record, remove linkable raw material and retain only permitted deletion evidence.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: An equivalent discovery route needs explicit approval and must preserve the learning outcome, analysis steps, criteria and score ceiling. The work and explanation remain individual.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: Only inside the course launcher. Agreeing to take part does not permit running generated code on your own machine, and it does not let a model write your discovery notes or see participant material.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: Three clauses have no step: return [] when nothing failed (AC1-empty), use the input rather than fixed values (AC1-other-id), and leave the input unchanged (the input-modified assertion). The three listed rows are sound. Add a step and its check for each missing clause before you leave the Plan checkpoint.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: Stop after Plan when the first planned step is not yet small and bounded (one function or one view), when a step has no check yet, or when the criterion leaves a case open, as in the worked ci-dashboard round. Record where you stopped and why; the reviewed change itself is M1 work.

docs.title: Q10
docs.text: A direct prompt is enough here: you already know the handler, the edit is one small branch, and a single acceptance case gives you a check that does not depend on the agent. Research before planning if you cannot yet name the files and functions the status value passes through, for example if it also feeds a template or permission check you have never read. Without that map you could not write an acceptance case that tests the right place, so you would have nothing to check the edit against.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval and transfer
docs.text:
Retrieval 1. The dispatcher constrains requests; the external launcher contains process, filesystem, network and resources. Retrieval 2. A near-miss trigger means the skill description is too broad; inspect the trigger result and its bounded verification.

Dashboard transfer. No: a different sort order fails the agreed requirement until the implementation or the specification is changed by agreement. The smallest discriminating check is AC1-sort: [(8, "failed"), (3, "failed")] must give [3, 8].

Sufficient evidence. For the checked cases you can accept the behavior: failed-only selection, ascending order and one entry per ID, on the [3, 7] case, running-only input and empty input, with the bounded diff read. Whether users prefer ascending order remains a separate claim: it is a design decision that no observation supports, and these checks do not test it.

docs.title: Week 4 self-check
docs.text:
After the workshop, use the public answer guidance.

Answer without AI, then compare your reasoning during feedback. These questions are practice, not a graded quiz. Public answer guidance is linked above.

  1. LO3: Rewrite "Would our smart alerts save you time?" as a question about a concrete recent event. What can the answer to your version establish?

  2. LO3, LO9: In S4-A, which of these is an observation rather than an inference: "opened a running job", "running jobs distracted the maintainer", "all maintainers need alerts"?

  3. LO3: For [(7, "failed"), (2, "running"), (7, "failed"), (3, "failed")], what output should AC1 produce?

  4. LO3: What evidence must be reviewed when the agreed output order changes?

  5. LO9: A participant withdrew after consenting to the workshop but not a public demonstration; may the notes be used for M0?

  6. LO3, LO9: When a student cannot recruit safely, what approval boundary governs a substitute discovery activity?
  7. LO9: A participant has agreed to take part in your discovery. Where may a generated acceptance test run?
  8. LO3: An agent returns this plan for AC1. Which AC1 clauses have no step?
Plan step Check Keep status exactly failed AC1-mixed Return each ID once AC1-duplicate Sort ascending AC1-sort

  1. LO3: When is stopping after the Plan checkpoint the correct M0 result?

  2. LO3: You know the ci-dashboard status handler, the change is one small branch, and one acceptance case can check it. Which delegation level should you choose? Give one situation that would make you research first, and explain why.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval: Weeks 2–3 context and boundaries
docs.text:
Answer these two short prompts after the workshop. They revisit an earlier decision so that the evidence, not a memorized label, is carried forward.

R1. Retrieval 1. A dispatcher accepts only a fixed verification command. Why does the external launcher still matter?

R2. Retrieval 2. A skill description triggers on a near miss. What does that say about the description, and what evidence should be checked next?

Use the same evidence-first format as the questions above.

docs.title: Dashboard transfer
docs.text:
The filter returns the right records but sorts them differently from the agreed display order. Is the requirement satisfied?

Name the expected behavior, the smallest discriminating check and what its result would let you decide.

docs.title: A decision with sufficient evidence
docs.text:
Another person derives [3, 7] from the agreed ascending/deduplicated rule; the current filter passes that case, running-only and empty input, with an inspected bounded diff. What behavior can you accept for these checks, and what user-preference claim remains separate?

State the checked scope before naming a remaining limit.

docs.title: Turn a user need into an executable specification
docs.text:
Week 4 · CI dashboard

What should the program do, and why?

docs.title: Code cannot settle an unclear requirement
docs.text:
Last week we located a behavior in source. This week the request is: "Show jobs needing attention."

Does that mean failed, running, or something else?

docs.title: A fictional maintainer's recent task
docs.text:
Run 12: passed
Run  9: failed
Run 11: running

A "not passed" filter displayed 9 and 11. The maintainer opened 11, saw it was running and returned. A handwritten list of failures was the workaround.

Course-authored scenario S4-A, not a participant observation.

docs.title: What did we observe?
docs.text:
Classify each sentence:

  • The maintainer opened run 11 and returned.
  • Including running jobs may distract from finding failures.
  • All maintainers need notifications.

Which statement can S4-A directly support?

docs.title: Observation, inference and unsupported claim
docs.text:
Sentence Status Opened 11 and returned Supplied event Running jobs may distract Interpretation to investigate Everyone needs notifications Unsupported generalization

A useful problem statement stays close to the user's task.

docs.title: Mechanism: From observation to a check
docs.text:
An observed event becomes a bounded criterion, then an independent check decides what the evidence supports.

From observation to a check An observed event becomes a bounded criterion, then an independent check decides what the evidence supports. observed eventcriterionacceptance caseindependent check

docs.title: A question that does not supply its answer
docs.text:
Would our smart alerts save you time?

Rewrite this to ask about a concrete recent event. What could the response help you learn?

docs.title: An event-based follow-up
docs.text:
What did you do after opening the running job?

This can reveal a workaround or another obstacle. It does not ask the participant to endorse our proposed interface.

Your own discovery notes and problem reasoning remain AI-off.

docs.title: A bounded product decision
docs.text:
For the classroom exercise, return IDs of runs whose status is exactly failed.

Inputs are (integer ID, status) pairs, with statuses passed, failed or running.

A UI, notifications and automatic retries are outside this small task.

docs.title: Ordering is an explicit design choice
docs.text:
For this exercise, output IDs are ascending and duplicate-free.

That convention makes the result precise. S4-A did not establish it as the fictional maintainer's preference.

Selection, duplication and order each need an agreed rule.

docs.title: An acceptance example before implementation
docs.text:
[(7, "failed"), (2, "running"),
 (7, "failed"), (3, "failed")]

Write the exact output using the agreed rules. Which input checks more than simple filtering?

docs.title: Deriving the output
docs.text:
Select failed:  7, 7, 3
Remove repeats: 7, 3
Ascending:     [3, 7]

Each step follows a specification clause. The candidate implementation does not supply the expected answer.

docs.title: The proposed predicate
docs.text:
ids = {run_id for run_id, status in runs if status != "passed"}
return sorted(ids)

A generated implementation might look reasonable and still interpret "failed" incorrectly.

docs.title: One case that exposes the disagreement
docs.text:
Which input makes status != "passed" disagree with status == "failed"?

Give the input and expected output before reading the repair.

docs.title: Running does not mean failed
docs.text:
Input:    [(2, "running")]
Required: []
Proposal: [2]

The repair changes the predicate to status == "failed". Keep the duplicate/order case and an empty-list check as regressions.

docs.title: A testable criterion
docs.text:
Given valid run pairs, calling failed_ids returns the ascending, duplicate-free IDs whose status is exactly failed.

assert failed_ids([(2, "running")]) == []
assert failed_ids([]) == []

Finite checks support these cases. They do not establish that users prefer the feature.

docs.title: A small specification connects the decisions
docs.text:
S4-A: difficulty isolating failures
  -> problem statement
  -> failed-only selection, explicit order/non-goals
  -> input/output examples
  -> implementation and unchanged verification

An assistant may propose implementation within the assignment's rules. The student owns discovery and the expected behavior.

docs.title: One request hides five decisions
docs.text:
"Implement AC1" asks an agent to research, choose, plan, write and judge in a single step.

You see its work only when the tests run.

docs.title: Five stages, a stop after each
docs.text:
Research -> stop -> Propose -> stop -> Plan
         -> stop -> Implement -> stop -> Test -> stop

At every stop a person decides: continue, narrow, go back or stop. The agent cannot check its own result.

docs.title: Each stage hands the next one a file
docs.text:
research.md -> fresh session -> plan.md -> fresh session -> candidate

The next session reads only the checked file and the paths it names. A wrong research claim becomes a wrong plan and wrong code: strike it at the first stop.

docs.title: Choose the delegation level
docs.text:
Level Use it when Direct prompt Small edit, familiar code, one case checks it Plan first Bounded edit in an area you know Research, then plan The path crosses files you have not read Repeated research and plan The boundary is still uncertain

Pick the least elaborate level that still leaves you an independent check.

docs.title: Research returns locations
docs.text:
acceptance.py, CASES: six cases. verify also fails if the input changes.

Open each cited location before moving on. A claim without a file and function is a question, not a finding.

docs.title: Three options come back
docs.text:
• A: change the predicate inside broken
  • B: add failed_ids, checked by the same verify
  • C: add a status option to the run list screen

Which option does the specification rule out, before any code?

docs.title: Ruling out C is a scope decision
docs.text:
A web UI is a non-goal in our small PRD. A removes the counterexample the class relies on.

Choose B and write down why. The choice is yours, not the agent's.

docs.title: Which clauses have no step?
docs.text:
Plan step Check Keep status exactly failed AC1-mixed Return each ID once AC1-duplicate Sort ascending AC1-sort

Compare with AC1 before reading on.

docs.title: Every clause gets a step and a check
docs.text:
Missing step Check Return [] when nothing failed AC1-empty Use the input, not fixed values AC1-other-id Leave the input unchanged input-modified assertion

Each check was written from AC1 before the code existed.

docs.title: Implement inside a bound
docs.text:
Only failed_ids, in one new file, with no imports. acceptance.py stays unchanged.

Read the candidate as text: the model's, or one of the three course candidates. A change outside the bound is rejected even when every check passes.

docs.title: A failed check points to a stage
docs.text:
Failure Go back to Wrong predicate Implement A clause the plan never covered Plan A misread requirement Propose or Research

Do not repair a failure by editing the check.

docs.title: Record where you stopped
docs.text:
One line per stage, a decision at each stop, and where you narrowed or stopped the task.

Stopping after Plan because the first step is still too large is a legitimate result.

docs.title: ci-dashboard: which claim do you strike?
docs.text:
AC-W: the overview lists active projects, not archived ones.

Claim Location R1 overview selects projects by owner_id domains/ci_dashboard.py:28-38 R2 {% else %} prints No projects yet. for an empty list ci/overview.html:17-24 R3 archive_project flips archived, deletes nothing domains/ci_dashboard.py:96-106 R4 The overview query already skips archived projects domains/ci_dashboard.py:34

Open each line before you answer.

docs.title: Option A, planned line by line
docs.text:
• A: add AND archived=0 at domains/ci_dashboard.py:34
  • B: wrap each template row in {% if not project.archived %}; an owner with only archived projects gets a blank table

Plan for A: change only line 34, and write test_overview_hides_archived and test_archived_project_page_opens.

docs.title: Stop after Plan
docs.text:
The tests expose a case AC-W never names: every project archived.

No projects yet. would be untrue, and Unarchive is reachable only by URL. Take both questions back to the specification before anyone edits code.

docs.title: Class practice and actual discovery
docs.text:
The activity gives you a fresh case, S4-B, to practise on.

Actual discovery for the discovery/specification workshop and M0 needs the established consent or an approved equivalent route. Do not relabel a fictional case as participation.

docs.title: Transfer: the ordering decision changes
docs.text:
A new agreed requirement says "retain first occurrence order." The same failed IDs arrive as 7, 7, 3.

What output now follows? Which specification, check and code need review before accepting the change?

docs.title: A change of requirement needs a new oracle
docs.text:
The new expected output is [7, 3]. The previous [3, 7] expectation belongs to the old rule.

Record the change in the specification's change log: the clause, the superseded check and why. A consistent specification and test can still need validation with users.

docs.title: Exit: "latest failure" is a new question
docs.text:
A user asks for the latest failed run per pipeline. Our inputs contain only ID and status.

Name one missing piece of information and a question that would let another person derive the expected output.

docs.title: M0 supplies the next change's contract
docs.text:
Keep the problem, agreed criterion, evidence and open questions together. Record one staged round for your personal ci-dashboard slice in the M0 work record.

Next week you will change existing code while protecting the behavior its callers already rely on.

docs.title: Workshop and review
docs.text:
Worked notes · Workshop · Self-check

Course case · Week 0 execution route

Use the same work in the linked practice unit or project. No extra report.

docs.title: Synthetic failure-filter example
docs.text:
Use the launcher commands in Week 4 notes. This directory contains only the public worked example and its public acceptance checks. It can be selected as a launcher workspace. Never select the whole course checkout or copy instructor answers into it.

  • acceptance.py holds the six public cases and verify.
  • run_example.py runs the two worked versions. broken deliberately includes running jobs; repaired is the explained worked example. model requests one candidate through the launcher's host-side broker and exports it after the Implement pause; run the separate verification command in the notes after reading candidate.py. The model prompt is a course-authored specification, not student discovery notes.
  • candidates/ holds three versions of failed_ids that the course wrote for the Implement and Test stages when you do not generate one. No model wrote them. Each file starts with a one-line label comment; read everything below it as the candidate.

No dependencies are installed and no private data is used. Malformed output, test failure or timeout is a failed Test attempt, not a reason to weaken the test or execute the candidate on the host.

These checks are transparent teaching examples, not a secure grading harness. A candidate can read public tests or print misleading success text; inspect its code and add a fresh case. Official assessment needs its own approved grading boundary.

docs.title: Public files
docs.text:
• candidate_a.py
  • candidate_b.py
  • candidate_c.py

docs.title: Week 5: Deliver a small change without breaking callers
docs.text: This directory holds Week 5 materials. You protect existing behavior, inspect dependencies and complete an explainable first change for M1; CP1 follows practice this week.

docs.title: English materials
docs.text:
• Notes and safe execution commands
  • Slides
  • 20-minute code-reading activity
  • Practice: a context file, a hook gate and a hand-off
  • Self-check
  • Reading paths

The public fixture is synthetic preparation, not CP1 material.

docs.title: Read before changing: 20 minutes
docs.text:
This activity uses only the course-original synthetic status formatter and its public characterization cases. There is no real user data, private repository input or CP1 assessment material. Use the notes for every execution command. Source reading itself needs only a keyboard-accessible text editor.

Work in groups of three or four. Rotate reader, behavior checker and boundary checker; a fourth person can record questions. Everyone writes their own three proposals, including the recorder. Each learner can instead work individually with written feedback. No spoken presentation, drag-and-drop interaction, color interpretation or diagram is required.

Minutes Action Evidence 0–4 Read before.py together. Trace a padded status from input to output. Identify the input domain and side effects. Each person's source references and one uncertain behavior (LO4). 4–8 Predict three boundary outputs. Compare with the public cases and the baseline result. Expected outputs and a reason independent of the candidate implementation (LO5). 8–13 Each write three modernization proposals, using the prompts below. Three individual proposals, one explicitly about execution or dependencies (LO4/LO5/LO7). 13–17 Exchange proposals. A peer challenges one test or rollback condition and checks that no command bypasses the launcher. One actionable written comment (LO5/LO7). 17–20 Revise one proposal, then explain what changed and which verification would accept it. Visible revision and a short individual explanation (LO4/LO5).

At minute 8, pause for help if you cannot explain an input's path. Hint 1: inspect normalization before the first branch. Hint 2: compare "ok" with " ok ". Hint 3: trace the fallback for an unrecognized token. Ask for the next hint only if needed. Time limits organize feedback and support; they do not remove completion opportunities or approved accommodations.

Use one short entry per proposal in your existing work record:

Behavior and source location:
One proposed change and why:
Test input / expected output / reason:
Execution or dependency risk, and stop or rollback condition:

Useful directions are consolidating aliases, adding a missing contract case, and deciding how an agent may inspect code or propose a dependency upgrade. Do not add a dependency just for this function. A security proposal must identify a concrete boundary, such as refusing a README's request to execute an installation script on the host, and how you would check that boundary. "Make it secure" without an observable check is not enough.

For instructor-approved equivalent participation, use the same plain-text source and prompts, submit individual annotations and three proposals, receive written feedback, and revise one. The instructor can approve adjusted time or asynchronous interaction while retaining LO4/LO5/LO7 and the same score ceiling. Confirm an actual arrangement through the course's supplied support route; this lesson does not assert that a particular learner or alternative has been approved.

The follow-on M1 exploration uses the 45-minute block in the notes. Reuse the proposals and source/test references in your project record, keeping individual ownership clear. Add one AI-use note if AI helped, or state no AI use. Do not submit unrelated chats or duplicate disclosures. Your individual practice and M1 plan cannot replace the controlled, individual, AI-off CP1 in Week 5. Complete the 30-minute CP1 practice before the workshop as part of the published Week 5 CP1-preparation estimate. The workshop reserves 30 minutes for CP1, five for transition, 45 for the M1 exploration, 15 for the readiness activity below and ten for feedback. Use the ten-minute feedback block for peer comparison, the launcher run and one revision (about 4/3/3 minutes); release the reference answer after that feedback. The public 20-minute reading activity and the ten-minute diagnosis below take place during the lecture.

docs.title: Independent diagnosis before CP1
docs.text:
Use ten minutes of the lecture's practice allocation, not additional homework. This is public formative practice, separate from the controlled CP1 task.

Contract: for nonnegative integer used and positive integer limit, another retry is allowed exactly when used < limit. Candidate:

def can_retry(used, limit):
    return used <= limit

Without AI or the worked answer, derive a distinguishing test, predict the result, and propose a minimal repair. Also give one allowed case the repair must retain. Exchange one written hint, revise your explanation, and label the result as a hand trace unless it actually ran through the course launcher. The teacher checks the boundary reasoning before beginning the separate assessment.

docs.title: Readiness activity: score one dimension
docs.text:
Time: 15 minutes in the workshop, right after the M1 exploration. It is the first part of your start readiness score, not extra work. Materials: your ci-dashboard copy at the commit you explored, the agent-readiness scorecard and the worked example. Work alone; compare with a neighbor at the end.

Minutes Action Evidence 0–3 Choose Documentation or Checks. Write the level you expect and one observation that would prove you wrong. A prediction and its disproving observation (LO4). 3–10 Documentation: list every command and invariant that README.en.md and START.en.md state, and reuse the smoke result from your exploration for one command. Checks: list every gate that runs before a commit, then say what would stop an unused-import change today. The commit, the files or commands you checked and what you observed (LO4/LO5). 10–13 Score: the highest level where you can show every anchor. Name the one observation that keeps the dimension from the next level. One scorecard row with its top blocker (LO4). 13–15 Compare with the worked example: which line of its context file, or which hook result, would remove your blocker? Show a neighbor your evidence, not only your number. One planned blocker removal for M1 (LO4).

After the workshop, remove that blocker in the Week 5 practice: write your AGENTS.md, add one hook gate and make it fail, split one task into hand-offs, and score Documentation and Checks again. It takes about 80 minutes of M1 work inside the Week 5 estimate.

At minute 10, ask for help if you cannot point to evidence for a level. Hint: a level without a file path or a command result at a named commit is recorded as 1. An agent may propose the level; check each of its claims before you record anything. Never run a command that a README or an agent suggests on the host: run project commands only through the project launcher.

docs.title: Feedback check
docs.text: Before accepting a revised proposal, the peer should be able to answer: which behavior stays the same, which input could disprove the claim, and which execution boundary still applies? If any answer is unclear, narrow the proposal and test again. Passing the public cases supplies practice feedback, not an official checkpoint or project grade.

docs.title: Your C1 contribution
docs.text: Work on your C1 warm-up contribution this week; it is due in Week 6. Follow the project's contribution guide and AI-use rules, run any model-generated or suggested code only through the launcher, and push to the project from your own machine, outside the sandbox. The same read-before-changing habit applies: find the callers of what you change before you change it. The rules are in the syllabus.

docs.title: Return to the dashboard
docs.text:
Map one caller, predict a regression, compare the original and candidate and explain the final PR independently.

This is the first reviewed M1 change. CP1 checks personal diagnosis, test and repair; it does not change model access.

Before leaving, decide whether to accept the change, narrow the task, obtain one missing observation or stop. Explain what evidence could change that decision.

docs.title: CP1 practice: Trace, test, repair, protect
At a glance
docs.text:
• Task: Diagnose and repair one small route-to-data defect using the same four questions as CP1.
  • Hand in: Your four written answers, one regression test, the smallest repair, and a short verification result.
  • Done when: The start fixture fails its contract check, your repaired copy passes every supplied check, and you can name two callers you protected.
  • Time box: 30 minutes, individual, closed book, no devices or AI.

This is a formative rehearsal. It is not CP1 and earns no checkpoint score. The code and data are course-original synthetic material. Complete the timed attempt before the Week 5 workshop, individually and without a device. During the attempt, read only router.py, service.py and store.py; do not open verify.py, teacher files or a worked answer. The workshop feedback block is where you compare, run and revise the work. Use the course launcher for every command that executes generated or edited code:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace cp1-practice-work --output cp1-practice-check -- python verify.py

Replace VERSION and DIGEST with the values returned by the Week 0 setup resolver. After the timed attempt, create a fresh workspace containing only the public fixture files and run verify.py as feedback evidence. The fixture has no network, model call or third-party dependency, so no key or replay route is needed.

docs.title: Report and contract
docs.text:
A user reports that /cards?label= should show no cards: an explicitly supplied label is an exact filter, and an omitted label should show all cards. The empty-label response currently shows both cards. The labels and titles must remain unchanged, and /cards?label=urgent must continue to show the urgent card.

Read router.py, service.py and store.py in the fixture and answer the same four questions used by CP1. Open verify.py only after the timed attempt, during feedback:

  1. Locate and explain (3 marks). Name the file, function and line where the value first departs from the contract. Trace the request from the route to that line and explain why the empty value takes the wrong branch.
  2. Regression test (3 marks). Write one pytest test that fails on the starting code and passes after your repair. Quote the contract sentence that determines the expected result.
  3. Minimal repair (2 marks). Give the smallest change that distinguishes an omitted label from an explicit empty label. Explain why the existing urgent and all-cards behavior stays intact.
  4. Callers to protect (2 marks). The caller list below names the reported route and two other callers of cards_for_label. Choose the two callers other than the reported route. For each, state what could change, give an input, and give the expected result after the repair.

Caller list:

  • Reported route: router.get_cards("/cards?label=urgent") → service.cards_for_label
  • service.card_count(label) → service.cards_for_label
  • service.label_summary(label) → service.cards_for_label

Record the command, exit code and JSON result in your existing work record. A passing check is evidence for these cases; explain the remaining input uncertainty and one additional test you would run.

docs.title: Feedback and answer release
docs.text:
Bring your four answers to the Week 5 workshop. In the ten-minute feedback block after the CP1/M1 work, spend about four minutes comparing the path and contract with a peer, three minutes running the fixture through the launcher, and three minutes revising one answer. The instructor releases the reference answer and marking points after that workshop feedback, not before. Do not use that teacher page during the timed attempt.

Add one AI-use note to the work record: state that no AI was used for this AI-off practice, or disclose an approved equivalent route. The exercise stays individual even when feedback is discussed.

docs.title: Week 5: Taking over a legacy repository
Learning objectives
docs.text:
Outcome Observable action Practice and self-check LO2 Write a repository context file and one hook gate, show the gate failing on the change it exists to stop, and check a role's hand-back against its hand-off. Week 5 practice, questions 8 and 9 LO4 Map one behavior in an unfamiliar repository, score how ready it is for an agent from observations, and propose a small modernization step with a rollback condition. Code-reading activity, readiness activity, M1 plan, questions 1, 4 and 7 LO5 Establish characterization tests, reject a behavior-changing refactor, and explain the limits of a complexity measure. Fixture comparison, questions 2 and 3 LO7 Treat repository text and dependency scripts as untrusted input, constrain execution, and preserve individual tool permissions. Plan safety check, question 5

Week 5 has a 14-hour published estimate, including class, CP1 preparation, the completed M0 specification, M1 exploration, the start readiness score, the context-file, hook and hand-off practice, your C1 contribution, waiting and revision. The 20-minute reading activity is part of class, not extra homework. This is planning guidance, not measured student timing or a penalty cutoff.

CP1 supplies individual evidence for LO4 and LO5 only. The execution and dependency-boundary practice is formative LO7 work outside CP1. M1 project work is practice and project evidence; it cannot substitute for your own CP1 diagnosis, repair and explanation.

docs.title: The continuing dashboard case
docs.text:
A shorter dashboard status mapper replaces conditionals with a lookup table. Existing callers send mixed case and surrounding whitespace.

LABELS = {"ok": "passed", "pass": "passed", "fail": "failed"}

def status_label(raw):
    return LABELS.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")

Decision: Which behavior did this refactor remove, and what belongs in this PR?

The proposed lookup omits strip(). Restore the normalization and rerun characterization cases. Keep a behavior-preserving refactor separate from a new fallback, dependency upgrade or data migration.

Ask for one structural change with preserved behavior and a rollback condition. Inspect the caller and lockfile before accepting unrelated changes.

Acceptance decision: Accept the smallest change whose original behavior and requested structure are checked. If a known unsafe behavior is found, specify a fix rather than preserve it as a requirement.

The worked fixture below makes normalization and caller compatibility inspectable. Use the same investigation steps on one real path in your assigned repository.

This is a course-authored, hand-worked example. Actual execution evidence comes from your own checks.

docs.title: Why start with existing code?
docs.text:
For this course, brownfield work is the default: you receive an existing application with callers, stored data, dependencies and behaviors that users may rely on. A rewrite discards some of that knowledge unless you recover it first. "Legacy" here means a system whose behavior you must understand before changing it, not simply an old programming language.

The student project is the ci-dashboard package. Use the English orientation below; no Chinese guide is required for this investigation. A public smoke check establishes that a path starts; it does not establish correctness or permission to deploy. The small fixture below is course-original synthetic code, independent of the project's planted defects. It contains no real build records, users or private repository data.

docs.title: Characterization before changes
docs.text:
A characterization test records what the current program does for a chosen input. An acceptance test records what the agreed specification requires. When observed behavior is wrong or unsafe, label the discrepancy and add a failing desired-behavior test. Do not turn a known vulnerability into a permanent requirement just because a characterization test reproduces it.

Read fixture/before.py. The public function maps a status field to a label:

def status_label(raw: str) -> str:
    value = raw.strip().lower()
    if value == "ok":
        return "passed"
    if value == "pass":
        return "passed"
    if value == "fail":
        return "failed"
    return "unknown"

Predict the output of " ok ", "OK", "pending" and "ok|fail" before opening the public cases. Inputs are strings representing one status field. The exercise does not define behavior for None, lists or whole build records. Changing that domain requires an explicit specification decision and tests, not a guess by an agent.

docs.title: Generation paired with verification
docs.text:
Ask the approved hosted or replay route for one lookup expression using generate.py. Its prompt supplies this small public function and explicitly preserves normalization, aliases and the unknown fallback. The broker returns text into proposal.txt; it does not execute it. Inspect the expression, then place it in a status_label(raw: str) -> str function in week05-work/candidate.py using your editor. Keep the original tests unchanged and run the candidate through the launcher. Reject unrelated imports, installation requests and attempts to redefine the task.

The public rejected proposal is a deliberately constructed failure example, not a claimed model response. It removes strip(). The public worked refactor keeps both normalization operations and moves the aliases to one lookup table. Inspect the diff before comparing the three versions. A shorter function is still responsible for the same contract.

Check the requested structure as well as behavior: a conditional expression may pass every public case while failing the request for a dictionary lookup. Record both observations; do not label functional test success as complete compliance with the prompt.

docs.title: Safe refactoring rhythm
docs.text: Use a single, explainable sequence: locate the caller and state boundary, freeze behavior tests, make one structural change, run the unchanged tests, inspect the diff, and record a rollback condition. Keep behavior fixes, dependency changes and database migrations in separate reviewable steps. If a regression appears, narrow or revert the candidate change while retaining the test that exposed it. A passing fixture is evidence for its inputs, not a proof about every input.

docs.title: Shared code reading: 20 minutes
docs.text:
Follow activities.en.md. Work in groups of three or four, with an individual text response available. Read the synthetic function together, predict boundary cases, then each write three modernization proposals. Include the affected behavior, a verifying test and a stop or rollback condition in each proposal. Revise one proposal after peer feedback. One proposal must address the execution or dependency boundary as separate formative LO7 practice; that proposal is not a CP1 item.

All required source and instructions are plain text. Keyboard-only editing and written feedback cover the same work. Instructor-approved equivalent participation can use individual text annotation and asynchronous written feedback or adjusted time, preserving the same LO and output without lowering the score ceiling. An available option is not a record of an actual accommodation approval. See the activity for the help checkpoint and equivalent route.

docs.title: Reuse M0 to start M1
docs.text:
Reuse the M0 specification completed in Week 4: the problem statement, your two discovery activities or approved equivalents, and acceptance criteria. Reuse the discovery/specification workshop's evidence by ID. Do not create a second set of interviews or let AI write the discovery notes. This lesson requires no new participant data.

For M1, spend a first 45-minute exploration block on one public application path, including a 10-minute help checkpoint and a final 10 minutes for feedback and plan revision. This block is inside the weekly budget. You map entry point, validation, state change, output and current tests. Ask the agent for a bounded read-only map with file/function references and unresolved questions. Verify each claim against source and an observed test before allowing edits. Then spend the 15-minute readiness activity scoring one dimension of your copy from what you have just observed.

docs.title: English project orientation for the M1 investigation
docs.text:
This is an original source-reading guide for the bounded Week 5 task. The existing Chinese project manuals are optional background, not prerequisites. All identifiers below are in public Python source; a browser or Chinese-language interface is unnecessary for this investigation.

Project Product and domain orientation Public source to inspect ci-dashboard A workspace for synthetic projects, pipelines and build reports. Follow the project-list request GET /domains/ci_dashboard/: current user, database query, then the overview template. domains/ci_dashboard.py, function overview; domains/model.py, load_fixture, for sample records.

For the required first investigation, select GET /items. The public smoke includes an observed check for this shared record-list path. Open legacy_app/views.py, function items, in the ci-dashboard source. Trace require_user, the optional q query and length check, the owner-bound database query, and the call to render_template("items.html", ...). Map those steps before running the check below. The domain-specific route in the table is orientation for later M1 work, not a substitute for this first path's verification.

In your assigned public package, open manage.py and locate the smoke branch in main. It initializes temporary synthetic data, signs in the public demo fixture account, checks basic list/detail responses and runs a local job. The teaching password CHANGEME is public; never substitute a real password. Locate assert client.get("/items").status_code == 200: it tests your selected route after login. Identify what that assertion does not establish. Record the coverage gap rather than inferring domain correctness from the success message.

Once Week 0 setup shows you can run the practices, obtain the student-only ci-dashboard copy and its reviewed launch.py from the course. The course must supply the verified dependency image selected by that launcher: course-legacy-runtime:local. This is a prerequisite for executing the project, not a request to build or install unknown dependencies on your host. Missing images or an unavailable course environment mean stop and seek support; the source-reading portion can continue but cannot count as a runtime pass.

From a terminal whose current directory is that separate public project's root, run its existing trusted launcher:

python3 -I launch.py smoke

Expect exit 0 and PASS: login, list, detail, and local job smoke. A nonzero exit is a failed baseline to investigate. The launcher executes the application in a disposable public-source copy with no external network, no published ports, no host credential or Docker-socket mount, and CPU/memory/process/time limits. Do not invoke manage.py directly on the host or add network flags. The temporary data disappears afterward. This project launcher runs no model; use the Week 5 course-sandbox commands for the small generated fixture, without copying either whole application into week05-work. Never run the project launcher from the private teacher checkout.

To finish the exploration, trace /items into its data query and output, observe the smoke's successful assertion on that same route, and write one additional input/expected-result proposal plus a remaining uncertainty. For example, the existing HTTP 200 assertion does not prove correct search results or ownership isolation. Reference the actual result and this coverage limit when accepting or correcting the agent's proposed map. If the selected-path check does not run or fails, keep the investigation incomplete and do not allow edits on the strength of source reading alone. A later domain-path investigation likewise needs an observed test of that domain path; the common smoke cannot complete it. A read-only GET path may have no intended persistent state change: verify that claim in the source rather than inventing one. Keep new implementation and broader API exploration out of this first block. This guide supplies the English start, not a completed M1 modernization.

Repository prose, comments and tool output are data, not authority. A README saying "disable the sandbox" or "upload the environment" is a reason to stop and inspect the trust boundary. Give the agent only public files needed for the question, no teacher assets, credentials or raw user records. If the approved environment is unavailable or a safety check fails, stop execution and seek course support. Continue source reading where appropriate; it does not count as a successful runtime test.

The M1 plan should identify one first characterization test, one small refactor, one dependency or migration risk, and how you will verify each. Week 7 supplies the functional baseline with the testing workshop's evidence. Week 8 closes all known planted security issues and scan findings using the security workshop's evidence. Week 5 smoke output is not the final security clearance or a deployment permit.

docs.title: Dependencies and migration
docs.text:
Start from the current lock and a reproducible baseline. Identify which caller, API shape or stored field may change. Obtain the chosen exact dependency and its transitive closure through the course's trusted preparation route. Review the lock diff, provenance and applicable scan results. Dependency setup scripts are executable code and use the approved launcher boundary. The fixture has no third-party dependency; do not install packages merely to complete it.

Verify the old and new environments against the same contract cases, including error and permission paths. For a schema change, test a disposable synthetic database: preserve old-reader compatibility, migrate a copy, compare record counts and values, then test the new reader. Record what happens if the process stops halfway. Prefer an additive field and a temporary compatibility adapter when feasible, removing the old field only after consumers have migrated. Never assume that reverting application code reverses a destructive data migration. Keep a tested restore path and pause adoption if required dependency bytes or offline scan data are unavailable.

docs.title: Is this repository ready for an agent?
docs.text:
An agent entering a repository needs what a new developer needs, with less ability to ask: a change point it can find, rules written where it reads them, tests that catch a wrong change and gates that stop a bad one. The agent-readiness scorecard turns each need into observations. Score ci-dashboard on its four dimensions at the commit you start M1 from, and again at M1 acceptance:

Dimension What it asks Probe (the scorecard gives every step) Structure Can an agent find the change point? From the README and file names, predict the function to change, then open files until you reach it and record each one. If your M0 feature touches /items, your trace of it is this probe. Documentation Are the rules written where an agent reads them? Give a fresh session only the context file. Ask how to run and test the project and what must never change, then run every command it gives you. Tests Fast, repeatable, covering what you will change Run the full test command twice, search the tests for hidden inputs and break one path you will change. The package has no test command yet, so expect a 1 here. Checks What must an agent's change pass? List every gate before a commit or merge. Make an unused-import change and a canary change, and record what stops each.

Each dimension has four levels, and the scorecard gives the observable anchors for each level. Give the highest level where you can show every anchor. A dimension with no evidence link is recorded as 1, whatever you believe about it. An agent may propose a level, but treat its answer as claims to check, as the scorecard shows. The score is a to-do list, not a grade: the lowest dimension names the blocker to remove first.

Demonstration. In the lecture, the teacher works the ci-dashboard example for the two dimensions a context file and a hook can raise today; Tests waits for a test command. The package has no AGENTS.md. The example's context file states the run and test commands and three invariants, each with the check that protects it. A fresh session is asked one question at a time and sees only the section of that file that should answer it: how to run and test the project, then what must never change. Every command in its answers is run. Each section fits in one 1024-byte launcher prompt with its question; a rule too long for that is too long for a newcomer to keep in mind. Then a pre-commit hook in the style of the Week 3 hook runs lint. It stops a proposal that imports a module it never uses (exit 2) and passes the revision (exit 0).

Practice. In the workshop, the 15-minute readiness activity scores one dimension of your own copy at its start commit. Record the level, commit, evidence and top blocker in the existing M1 work record, then finish the start scorecard as M1 work. A repository that scores well is also easier for the people who work in it, which is why this work is worth doing even when no agent is involved.

docs.title: A context file, a hook gate and a hand-off
docs.text:
The score names blockers. Three small files remove the two that ci-dashboard starts with, and the third makes delegation checkable.

The context file is the hand-off every session receives. Agent tools read a repository context file when a run starts. Codex, for example, reads AGENTS.md files from its global folder down to the current directory before it does any work; files nearer the current directory come later and override earlier ones, and it stops adding files at a size limit (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5). Kiro also reads AGENTS.md and always includes it (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9). Whatever the file says reaches every session, so it must be short and true at the commit. It says four things: what to run to verify a change, which rules must hold and which check protects each, which files not to touch, and what to report at the end. Verify it in two ways. Run every command it lists, as written. Then compare what a session does on one bounded task with and without the file.

A hook turns a rule into a gate. A Boundaries line asks a session not to change pyproject.toml in a feature change. A pre-commit hook that stops any commit listing that file makes the rule hold even when a session ignores it. It also gives the session a runnable pass/fail signal of the kind the guidance on agentic coding recommends (tools/claude-code-best-practices; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1). A gate counts as evidence only after you have seen it fail on the change it exists to stop, with its own reason, and pass on a good change. An exit 2 because the hook refused its input is not the rule firing.

A hand-off divides one task between roles. A subagent is a fresh session with one role and only the context that role needs. Some tools let you define such a role in a configuration file that sets its tools, permissions and context (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9). The division holds only if each hand-off says what the role may change, what it must run and what it hands back. Check each hand-back against the diff and the launcher results, not against the role's own summary. A reviewer that receives the implementer's notes judges the plan it has read instead of the change that was asked for.

The Week 5 practice does all three on your copy, offline with course-written replays, in about 80 minutes of M1 work. It ends with a second score for Documentation and Checks.

docs.title: LLM wiki and documentation discipline
docs.text: An LLM wiki is a navigable explanation generated from repository material. It is a draft index, not an extra source of truth. For this exercise, one paragraph in the existing M1 record is enough: "At commit X, caller A invokes B; test C checks input D; error behavior E is still unverified." Replace X/A/B/C/D/E with actual evidence. A model's confident prose cannot establish an invariant. Update the paragraph with code changes, keep uncertainty explicit, and remove stale claims. Avoid duplicating entire files or adding a documentation platform. Review any suggested command before running it through the launcher.

docs.title: A fresh public diagnosis before CP1
docs.text: Use the retry-boundary exercise to derive a new test and repair without the worked answer. It changes the input rule from whitespace normalization to a retry limit. Preserve an allowed case as well as the distinguishing equality boundary. The teacher provides feedback before the separate assessment; this public hand-trace exercise is not a CP1 bank item.

docs.title: CP1: personal diagnosis, test and repair
docs.text: CP1 is a 30-minute individual AI-off diagnosis, test and repair in week 5, worth 10 points. Practise on the public fixture; the assessment uses a different task. Receive targeted feedback before the permitted equivalent resit for a failed component. The current syllabus defines the 50% replacement cap and preservation of original records. CP1 does not change model access.

docs.title: Supported execution
docs.text:
First use the trusted Week 0 setup and approved route guide. Run these commands from the course root. The resolver is the sole configuration source:

uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json

Substitute its version for VERSION and digest for DIGEST below. Create week05-work with your editor and copy only the five public .py files from lectures/week-05/fixture/ into it. Never give the launcher the whole private checkout or an instructor directory. Each output directory must be new; for a repeat use a new name. The launcher copies public inputs into a bounded temporary workspace, reruns its safety checks, and returns the actual exit code and bounded output.

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-work --output week05-before -- python verify.py before
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-work --output week05-rejected -- python verify.py rejected
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-work --output week05-refactored -- python verify.py refactored

For one deterministic proposal rehearsal, use the keyless FAKE broker. This path runs offline and does not produce a real model response.

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-work --output week05-proposal --model fake -- python generate.py

Read exported proposal.txt as text. If it is missing, truncated or off-task, record that failure and discuss the public worked refactor. Do not increase the frozen model limits or call a different provider to force success. After inspecting the proposal, save candidate.py inside week05-work using your editor, alongside verify.py. Then run:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-work --output week05-candidate -- python verify.py candidate

FAKE broker practice can use --model fake without a key, but cannot stand in for actual model generation. No full chat export is required. Record the actual profile/version/digest, which proposal you adopted or rejected, the tested artifact, launcher result and a short causal explanation in the existing work record. Add one reusable AI-use note. Public verifier output is feedback, never an authoritative grade. If a candidate changes the verifier, recover the trusted verifier before testing.

docs.title: Reading the fixture comparison
docs.text:
The fixed Python 3.12 fixture has ten named input/expected-output pairs and no randomness or third-party dependencies. verify.py also counts Python AST If nodes across the selected module, a deliberately narrow branch-structure complexity proxy, not cyclomatic complexity or a maintainability score. Reproduce the following with the three launcher commands above:

Version Passing cases Regression cases Module if statements Before 10/10 0 3 Rejected proposal 7/10 3 0 Worked refactor 10/10 0 0

The rejected proposal should return nonzero and fail the three padded known-status inputs. Both shorter implementations have zero if statements, but only one preserves the tested behavior. The lookup table still contains decisions. These results describe this synthetic fixture only; they are not industry statistics or an improvement estimate for the project repository.

Add one case before accepting your own candidate, justify it without consulting the candidate's output as an oracle, and rerun the before/candidate comparison with identical tests. Explain one remaining uncertainty. Peer feedback should challenge your expected output and rollback condition; revise and rerun. Use selfcheck.en.md unaided to prepare for CP1.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Detection Correction "Tests pass, so the specification is correct." Only copied current outputs, no desired behavior or safety check. Separate characterization from acceptance and record known discrepancies. One large modernization patch. A failure cannot be attributed to refactor, upgrade or migration. Separate steps and retain a testable rollback boundary. Fewer branches proves better code. Rejected proposal has the same low count as the worked version. Check behavior, readability, test coverage and remaining risks together. The wiki overrules code. A claim has no matching commit, function or test. Verify against source and refresh or remove stale text. A dependency fix needs host installation. Proposed command downloads or executes unreviewed scripts outside the launcher. Use trusted acquisition and isolated execution, or stop when unavailable. An agent's readiness level goes straight into the scorecard. The level has no command output or file path at a named commit. Run the probe, record what you observe and score only what the commit shows. A hook counts as a gate because it exists. No run shows it stopping the change it is for, with its own reason. Run the bad event, keep the failing result, then the passing one. A role's hand-back is the record of what it did. Its list of changed files was never compared with the diff. Check the hand-back against the diff and open each launcher result. Project work stands in for CP1. Individual competence is inferred from an AI-assisted project change or a peer's answer. Each student completes their own diagnosis and repair; model access follows Week 0. A resit supplies unrestricted extra points. The replacement cap is omitted. Preserve both attempts; use max(original, min(resit, 5)) for CP1.

docs.title: Transfer to a new situation
docs.text:
The author also changes unknown statuses to "failed" because that seems safer. Is it still only a refactor?

Write the expected behavior and the next check before comparing with a partner.

This is the first reviewed M1 change. CP1 checks personal diagnosis, test and repair; it does not change model access.

docs.title: Make your copy ready for an agent: a context file, a hook gate and a hand-off
docs.text:
The workshop's readiness activity scored one dimension of your ci-dashboard copy at its start commit. This practice removes the blockers that the worked example found in two dimensions, Documentation and Checks, this time on your own copy and at your own commits. You write an AGENTS.md, add one hook gate, split one task into hand-offs, and score again. Every part has a generation step and a verification step, and only the verification counts as evidence.

Time: about 80 minutes of M1 work, inside Week 5's published estimate: 25 minutes for the context file, 25 for the hook, 20 for the hand-off and 10 for the new score.

Route: everything below works offline with the course-written replays. A real agent session is optional and is used only where a part says so.

You need: your copy at the commit you scored in the workshop, the agent-readiness scorecard, the M1 description and the files in example/. Everything in example/ is course-written for teaching; none of it is a captured model response.

Resolve VERSION and DIGEST as in the notes and run each sh scripts/course-sandbox command from the course root, as Week 0 setup explains. Run launch.py commands from the root of your ci-dashboard copy. Create each workspace with your editor.

docs.title: Part 1: write an AGENTS.md and check that it changes something (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Generate. Write AGENTS.md at the root of your copy. You may start from agents-example.txt, or ask an agent to draft it from README.en.md, START.en.md, manage.py and your exploration notes. Either way, treat every line as a claim about your copy at this commit. Keep five short sections:

Section What it must say Run and test Every command a newcomer needs, exactly as it is typed, and the result that means it worked Before every commit The hook command from Part 2 and what its exit codes mean Invariants At least three rules that must not change, each naming the check that protects it Boundaries The files a feature change must not touch, and what a session must never do, such as install a package Report What a session hands back at the end: files changed, commands run with exit codes, and what it did not check

The whole file should fit on one screen. A rule that needs a paragraph to explain is a rule a session will half-follow. Keep the Run and test and Invariants sections short enough for the worked example's fresh-session probe, which refuses a section that does not fit in one launcher prompt.

Verify that every command runs. Copy each command from the file and run it as written, through the launcher it names. Write down the exit code and the first line of output. A smoke result from your exploration counts only if it is from the same commit. If a command fails as written, fix the line in the file and run it again; do not fix it in your head. Then run each invariant's check, including the deliberate violation, and restore the file afterwards with git restore.

Verify that the file changes what a session does. example/replay/ holds one bounded task given to two fresh sessions, one without the context file and one with it. The task, in handoff.json, is to add a skipped status to domains/labels.py. Each session's hand-back is in without.json and with.json, and what git diff --name-only printed afterwards is in without-diff.txt and with-diff.txt. Read both hand-backs and predict which one meets the hand-off.

Then check each one with check_handoff.py. It reads the hand-off, the hand-back and the diff, and never runs a command from them. Create week05-check in the course root and copy check_handoff.py and the five files from example/replay/ into it. Then run:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-check -- python -B check_handoff.py handoff.json without.json without-diff.txt
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-check -- python -B check_handoff.py handoff.json with.json with-diff.txt
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-check -- python -B check_handoff.py handoff.json without.json

Expect exit_code 2 for the first command, with eight findings. The first is the session's list of changed files against the diff, which also contains pyproject.toml. The last is did not hand back 'not_checked' as a non-empty list. Expect exit_code 0 for the second command and PASS: the hand-back matches the hand-off; changed files taken from the diff. The third command checks the same hand-back without the diff. Its output no longer mentions pyproject.toml, because the checker can then compare only the session's own claims.

For each finding in the first run, name the line of the context file that removed it in the second run. The session without the file did reasonable things: it wanted a test, found no test command and installed one. It had no way to know that a dependency change is its own reviewed change. Then name what the file could not fix. The with session's exit codes are still its own claims until you open each launcher result, and its two not_checked items are now your next checks.

Optional, with an agent. On a scratch branch of your copy, give the same task to two fresh sessions of your approved agent, one with your AGENTS.md and one without it. Run any command a session proposes only through the launcher. Write each hand-back in the same JSON shape and check both with the commands above.

docs.title: Part 2: add one hook gate and make it fail (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Your Boundaries section says which files a feature change must not touch. A rule that only a session reads is a request. A hook that stops the commit is a gate.

Define the bad change first. Write down the event that the gate must stop: a commit whose changed files include a protected file. In the worked example, that is {"event":"before_commit","paths":["domains/labels.py","pyproject.toml"]}. Write down the good event too, one your gate must let through: {"event":"before_commit","paths":["domains/labels.py"]}.

Generate. Copy pre_commit.py into a new workspace, week05-gate. If your Boundaries list differs from the example's, give an agent the hook and your Boundaries section and ask it to change the protected set to match. Ask it not to read or run the files it checks. You can also make the edit yourself. Compare the result with the course hook's PROTECTED set and protected function, and read every changed line before you run it.

Verify: has it ever failed? A gate you have only seen pass has not been shown to stop anything. Copy labels_revised.py into the workspace as domains/labels.py. Predict each result, then run the bad event, the good event, and the bad event with the protected path spelled another way:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-gate -- python -B pre_commit.py '{"event":"before_commit","paths":["domains/labels.py","pyproject.toml"]}'
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-gate -- python -B pre_commit.py '{"event":"before_commit","paths":["domains/labels.py"]}'
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-gate -- python -B pre_commit.py '{"event":"before_commit","paths":["./pyproject.toml"]}'

With the course hook, expect exit_code 2 and pyproject.toml: protected by AGENTS.md; change it in its own reviewed change for the first command. Expect exit_code 0 and PASS: no protected file and no unused import in 1 file(s) for the second. Expect exit_code 2 again for the third.

Read the reason, not only the exit code. A line that starts with REFUSED: means the hook rejected its input, and that is not your rule firing. A lint-only hook refuses pyproject.toml as "not an ordinary .py file": it exits 2, but for the wrong reason, and it would let launch.py through if the file were present. Your first run must print your rule's own line. Keep all three launcher results.

The hook runs two checks today: protected files, then lint. The test step waits for a test action in the project launcher; launch.py has no test action yet.

docs.title: Part 3: split one task into hand-offs (20 minutes)
docs.text:
A subagent is a fresh session with one role. It gets only the context that role needs and a hand-off: the task, the files it may change, the commands it may and must run, and what it hands back. Your AGENTS.md is the hand-off every session receives. A role's hand-off narrows it to one job. Here is a division of the skipped task:

Role Receives May change Runs Hands back Explorer The task and AGENTS.md Nothing Nothing; it only reads files callers: each path:line that calls status_label; open_questions Implementer The task, AGENTS.md and the explorer's callers domains/labels.py The hook and the smoke test changed, ran, not_checked Reviewer The task, the implementer's hand-off, the diff and the implementer's hand-back Nothing Nothing findings: each with a path:line and the check that would confirm it

The reviewer does not receive the explorer's notes or the implementer's reasoning. It judges the change against what was asked and what ran, not against a plan it has already read.

Generate. Choose your own first M1 change, or the skipped task if your change is not settled yet. Write three hand-offs in the shape of handoff.json, one per role. An explorer's or reviewer's hand-off has "may_change": [] and "run": []. Name the extra fields it hands back in hand_back, for example ["callers", "open_questions"]. You can ask an agent to draft them; you decide what each role may touch.

Act it out. Play each role yourself or give it to a fresh session. Do the implementer's work on a scratch branch, write its hand-back in the shape of with.json, and save what git diff --name-only prints as diff.txt. A read-only role's diff should be empty.

Verify. Create week05-roles and copy check_handoff.py into it, with each role's hand-off, hand-back and diff under names of your choice. Run the checker on each role as in Part 1, with your file names. Then do by hand what the checker cannot. Open each path:line the explorer returned. Rerun each check a reviewer finding names. Compare each ran entry with the launcher result you kept. A role that changed a file it was not given, or handed back nothing for a field, has broken the division. Narrow its hand-off and run it again.

In Week 6 you run a planner, an implementer and a reviewer as separate launcher runs on a real review task. This week's hand-offs are the contracts those runs need.

docs.title: Part 4: score again (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Score Documentation and Checks with the scorecard at the commit that adds your AGENTS.md and hook. Use the same probes as at the start and give the highest level where you can show every anchor.

Dimension Start End Evidence Blocker removed Documentation your start level The AGENTS.md path at the end commit, each command's result and each invariant's check Checks your start level The hook's failing and passing results, and the line in AGENTS.md that requires the hook before every commit

The worked example's file and hook reach 3 in both dimensions; your copy may score differently. The protected-file rule enforces a line of your Boundaries section, but it does not by itself move Checks: the scorecard's Checks anchors ask what stops an unused-import change and, at level 4, a secret scan that stops the canary. Write down what still keeps each dimension from level 4.

docs.title: What to keep
docs.text:
Put these in your existing M1 work record, linked by evidence ID:

  • the AGENTS.md commit and each command result from Part 1, plus your line-by-line answer for the replayed pair;
  • the hook's protected set, the three launcher results from Part 2 and the line in AGENTS.md that requires the hook;
  • your three hand-offs, the implementer's hand-back, diff.txt and the checker results;
  • both scorecard rows.

If an agent helped, add one AI-use note and reuse its ID. No transcript is needed.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake How you notice What to do The context file describes the plan, not the copy. A listed command fails when copied at the commit. Fix the line and run it again before scoring. The gate has only ever passed. You have no failing run that prints your rule's line. Run the bad event and keep the result. An exit 2 is counted as the rule firing. The output starts with REFUSED:. Fix the event or the workspace until your rule's line appears. A hand-back is taken at its word. No diff was given to the checker. Give it the git diff --name-only output; open the launcher results yourself. A reviewer gets the implementer's notes. The reviewer repeats the plan's reasoning. Hand it only the task, the hand-off, the diff and the hand-back.

docs.title: Week 5 reading paths
docs.text:
No additional external reading is required. The lesson uses course-original synthetic code and local, reproducible evidence rather than industry productivity claims. Reading time is included in the weekly budget.

  • Read the notes and public before version for the shared code-reading activity. Inspect the public cases after predicting outputs.
  • Use Week 0 setup for the supported launcher and hosted profile startup for the shared profile contract. These operational guides own configuration and readiness; this lesson does not duplicate them.
  • For M1, use the English project orientation to inspect the named public functions and run the reviewed smoke entry in your assigned ci-dashboard package. It provides the product context, source map, prerequisites, command and expected result. Chinese project manuals are optional background. You do not need teacher defect maps, solutions or hidden tests.
  • For the readiness score, use the agent-readiness scorecard and the ci-dashboard worked example: a context file with three invariants checked by a fresh-session probe, and a lint hook with a failing and a passing case.
