  • For the Week 5 practice, optional and short: how one tool reads AGENTS.md files and where it stops adding them, in Custom instructions with AGENTS.md (tools/codex-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5); how another treats AGENTS.md and defines a custom agent's tools, permissions and context, in its Steering and Custom agents pages (tools/kiro-cli; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4; Source 5; Source 6; Source 7; Source 8; Source 9); and why an agent needs a runnable pass/fail check, in Best practices for Claude Code (tools/claude-code-best-practices; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1). Read them for the mechanism. Your own AGENTS.md, hook and hand-offs are checked by running them, not by what a guide says.

The course's structural and assessment authority is SYLLABUS.md, particularly the Week 5 row, the LO4/LO5 mapping for CP1, the separate formative LO7 safety practice, M0/M1 milestones and CP1 rules. The notes state the required student-facing rules in English. No Chinese reading or industry report is an extra prerequisite for this unit.

docs.title: Week 5 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Tie each conclusion to the stated contract and revision.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: Map one public entry point through validation, state access and output. Collect callers, tests and source references before editing.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: status_label(" PASS ") returns passed under the normalization contract. Characterization records observed behavior; desired-behavior tests encode the requirement.

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: Review the candidate that retains normalization, aliases, fallback and contract cases. Fewer if statements or ten examples do not prove the domain.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: Freeze the old code, data and lock; test old and new readers, partial migration, restore and safe restart. Reverting source cannot restore dropped data.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: Refuse host-environment export and unpinned install scripts. Use trusted preparation and the course launcher; a failed safety check cannot be bypassed.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: Keep the first observation and later correction as separate records. A correction does not erase the initial result.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: Give a fresh session only the context file and run every command it returns. Level 3 also needs at least three invariants, each naming the check that protects it. ci-dashboard starts without an AGENTS.md, so the scorecard's level-1 anchor applies; even if you count the README as the context file, it writes down no invariant, so the level cannot reach 3 whatever the claim. Record the commit, the file and each command result. The top blocker is no context file (or, if you count the README as one, no invariant written down).

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: No. Exit 2 with REFUSED: means the hook rejected its input; the rule never ran. A lint-only hook gives the same result. Run the bad event with a Python file the hook can read, such as domains/labels.py and pyproject.toml, and look for the rule's own line: pyproject.toml: protected by AGENTS.md; ... with exit 2. Then run the good event without the protected file and expect exit 0. Keep both results.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: Without a diff the checker compares only the session's own claims. Give it the output of git diff --name-only for the same change: a file the session changed but did not list, such as pyproject.toml, then shows up as a finding. The checker cannot see exit codes either, so open the smoke test's launcher result and confirm exit 0 at that commit.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval and transfer
docs.text: Retrieval 1. A single pass supports only that recorded case and configuration; inspect context composition and digest. Retrieval 2. “Make it fast” lacks a measurable limit and check. Mapping unknown to failed changes behavior and needs a product decision and regression.

docs.title: Week 5 self-check
docs.text:
After the workshop, use the public answer guidance.

Answer unaided, then compare uncertain answers with the notes or a peer first and raise what is still unclear in the workshop. Use your existing work record, without a separate report or transcript. These are public preparation questions, not the CP1 assessment. They do not award marks or tool access.

  1. LO4: In an unfamiliar repository, which application path should you map first?
  2. LO5: What output should status_label(" PASS ") produce under the contract?
  3. LO5: With both candidates free of if statements, which one should proceed to review?
  4. LO4/LO5: What compatibility check is required when a dependency changes the persisted status format?
  5. LO7: What should you refuse when a wiki requests host environment variables and an unpinned install?
  6. LO4/LO5: How should an initial result and a later corrected result be recorded?
  7. LO4: An agent reports "Documentation: 3. The README explains how to run everything." Which observation could disprove that level, and what do you record instead?
  8. LO2: Your new hook exits 2 on {"event":"before_commit","paths":["pyproject.toml"]}. Its output is REFUSED: 'pyproject.toml' is not an ordinary .py file inside this workspace. Has the protected-file rule been shown to work? What run would show it?
  9. LO2: An implementer's hand-back lists one changed file, domains/labels.py, and says the smoke test exited 0. The checker prints PASS when given only the hand-off and the hand-back. What has not been checked yet, and how do you check it?

docs.title: Spaced retrieval: Weeks 3–4 context and specification
docs.text:
Answer these two short prompts after the workshop. They revisit an earlier decision so that the evidence, not a memorized label, is carried forward.

R1. Retrieval 1. Two contexts both pass one public case, but only one records the context digest. What bounded claim is supported?

R2. Retrieval 2. A proposed plan says "make it fast" without a measurable check. What acceptance clause is missing?

Use the same evidence-first format as the questions above.

docs.title: Dashboard transfer
docs.text:
The author also changes unknown statuses to "failed" because that seems safer. Is it still only a refactor?

Name the expected behavior, the smallest discriminating check and what its result would let you decide.

docs.title: A decision with sufficient evidence
docs.text:
The lookup refactor retains normalization, aliases and fallback and passes unchanged contract cases on the reviewed current revision. Can that bounded refactor proceed? Name what would change your decision if the dependency lock also changed.

State the checked scope before naming a remaining limit.

docs.title: Deliver a small change without breaking callers
docs.text:
Week 5 · CI dashboard

What must a refactor preserve?

docs.title: The requirement is already in use
docs.text:
Week 4 made desired behavior explicit. Now a caller depends on a working implementation.

The task is to replace conditionals with a lookup table, while preserving this function's behavior.

docs.title: The original function
docs.text:
def status_label(raw):
    value = raw.strip().lower()
    if value == "ok":
        return "passed"
    if value == "pass":
        return "passed"
    if value == "fail":
        return "failed"
    return "unknown"

Public Week 5 fixture. Its contract adds the pass alias to Week 1's example.

docs.title: What do callers receive?
docs.text:
Inputs are strings naming one status. Predict:

Input Output " PASS " ? "pending" ? "ok\|fail" ?

What would be a different task from this refactor?

docs.title: The observable behavior to protect
docs.text:
" PASS " becomes passed. "pending" and "ok|fail" become unknown.

Supporting non-string input or changing unknown to failed would change the contract. It needs its own decision and checks.

docs.title: Mechanism: A safe brownfield change
docs.text:
Protect callers by freezing a baseline, making one bounded edit, and checking the unchanged contract before accepting it.

A safe brownfield change Protect callers by freezing a baseline, making one bounded edit, and checking the unchanged contract before accepting it. caller mapbaselinebounded editregression check

docs.title: Characterization and acceptance
docs.text:
A characterization test records what the existing code does. An acceptance test states what the agreed requirement demands.

They can disagree. An existing security defect is a defect to repair, not a behavior to preserve indefinitely.

docs.title: A proposed refactor
docs.text:
LABELS = {"ok": "passed", "pass": "passed", "fail": "failed"}


def status_label(raw):
    return LABELS.get(raw.lower(), "unknown")

This is the public, course-authored rejected candidate.

docs.title: Which existing behavior disappeared?
docs.text:
Compare the original and candidate on " PASS ".

Name the lost operation and a regression assertion. Would removing if statements alone justify acceptance?

docs.title: A structural change can preserve the rule
docs.text:
return LABELS.get(raw.strip().lower(), "unknown")

The lookup now retains normalization and aliases. Rerun the original cases unchanged, then inspect the diff.

A behavior check and the requested dictionary structure answer different questions.

docs.title: One path through the real repository
docs.text:
GET /items -> current-user check -> query -> template

The notes locate items in ci-dashboard's legacy_app/views.py. Trace the input and owner filter before editing.

An HTTP 200 smoke result does not establish the returned records are correct.

docs.title: A wiki paragraph needs evidence
docs.text:
The list is isolated to the current user and handles every search correctly.

The only cited check asserts HTTP 200 after login.

Which claim is still untested? Propose one input and expected result.

docs.title: Is ci-dashboard ready for an agent?
docs.text:
Score Structure, Documentation, Tests and Checks from observations, not belief.

Demo: a fresh session reads one AGENTS.md section per question; run every command it gives back. Then a lint hook stops an unused import (exit 2) and passes the revision (exit 0).

The lowest score names the first blocker to remove.

docs.title: The context file every session reads
docs.text:
AGENTS.md says what to run, which rules hold and which check protects each, what not to touch, and what to report.

Verify it twice: run every command as written, then compare one task done with and without the file.

docs.title: Has this gate ever failed?
docs.text:
Paths in the event Output domains/labels.py, pyproject.toml pyproject.toml: protected by AGENTS.md; ... exit 2 domains/labels.py PASS: no protected file and no unused import ... exit 0 domains/label.py (a typo) REFUSED: ... exit 2

Which runs show the rule working? Which exit 2 is not evidence?

docs.title: A hand-off is a contract
docs.text:
Role May change Hands back Explorer nothing callers, open questions Implementer domains/labels.py changed, ran, not checked Reviewer nothing findings, each with its check

Check each hand-back against the diff and the launcher results, not its summary.

docs.title: A bounded first PR
docs.text:
Record the caller, candidate revision and protected behavior. Ask for one structural change, with no dependency upgrade.

The review needs the original failure or baseline, the actual retest, and a rollback condition tied to a regression.

docs.title: A dependency change introduces another boundary
docs.text:
A new dependency may change API shape or persisted data. Compare locked old/new environments against the same behavior cases.

Installation scripts are executable code. Use the trusted preparation and launcher routes from the notes.

docs.title: Reverting code may not restore data
docs.text:
A migration replaces stored status names with numeric codes. Old code still expects names. The new deployment is rolled back.

What must a recovery plan restore or keep compatible?

docs.title: Compatibility needs its own check
docs.text:
Test old and new readers on a disposable migrated copy. Check interrupted migration as well as the completed path.

An additive field can keep old readers working during transition. A destructive transformation needs a tested restore path.

docs.title: Independent diagnosis before CP1
docs.text:
A retry is allowed exactly when used < limit. Inputs: nonnegative integer used, positive integer limit.

def can_retry(used, limit):
    return used <= limit

Derive a test, predict the fault and propose a repair independently. Keep one allowed case. Use the activity's ten-minute practice block.

docs.title: Three proposals in the reading activity
docs.text:
Use the existing 20-minute activity:

  • One behavior-preserving structural change.
  • One missing contract check.
  • One concrete execution or dependency risk.

For each, state a test and a stop or rollback condition.

docs.title: Feedback that narrows the change
docs.text:
A peer asks whether your PR also changes the unknown fallback.

Revise the scope or split the behavior decision from the refactor. Explain which original checks stay unchanged and why.

docs.title: Exit: a "safer" fallback
docs.text:
The author changes unknown statuses to failed in the same PR.

Is this still only a refactor? Give one input that distinguishes the old and new behavior and name the decision still needed.

docs.title: CP1 and the first M1 change
docs.text:
CP1 is the separate 30-minute individual AI-off session in the workshop. Use public practice for preparation; the assessment uses a different task.

The first M1 PR reuses your bounded investigation. Next week, a model reviews it and you verify each point it raises.

docs.title: Workshop and review
docs.text:
Worked notes · Workshop · Self-check

Course case · Week 0 execution route

Use the same work in the linked practice unit or project. No extra report.

docs.title: Worked example: a context file and a pre-commit hook for ci-dashboard
docs.text:
The student ci-dashboard package arrives with a README but no agent context file and no check before a commit. This example removes one blocker in each of two readiness dimensions, Documentation and Checks, and shows how to verify each removal. Score with the agent-readiness scorecard; the notes introduce the dimensions. Every file here is course-written for teaching. None is a captured model response.

File What it is agents-example.txt A context file for ci-dashboard, to save as AGENTS.md: run and test commands, three invariants each with the check that protects it, boundaries and how to report probe.py The fresh-session probe: sends one question and the one section of the context file that should answer it, and exports the answer pre_commit.py A pre-commit hook that stops a change to a protected file, then runs lint; exit 0 lets the commit continue and exit 2 stops it labels_proposed.txt A proposed helper, as text, that imports a module it never uses labels_revised.py The same helper after revision check_handoff.py Checks what a session handed back against the hand-off it was given, and against the diff replay/ One task as a hand-off, and the hand-backs and diffs of two fresh sessions, one without the context file and one with it

The Week 5 practice uses the last two files, the hook's protected-file rule and the context file's Boundaries and Report sections.

Resolve VERSION and DIGEST as in the notes and run the course launcher commands below from the course root. Run the launch.py commands from the root of your own ci-dashboard copy.

docs.title: Where the package starts
docs.text: Dimension Observation at the start Level Documentation No context file such as AGENTS.md, which is the scorecard's level-1 anchor. README.en.md and START.en.md are guides for people: they list launcher commands but write down no invariant or the check that protects it, so even counted as a context file they would not reach 3. 1 Checks No gate runs before a commit. An unused import can be committed. 1

docs.title: Part 1: the context file
docs.text:
Generate. You could ask an agent to draft AGENTS.md from README.en.md, START.en.md and manage.py. agents-example.txt is a course-written draft of that kind. Treat it as a list of claims, like any agent output: the commands it lists, and three invariants, each with a check.

Verify with a fresh-session probe. A session that has read nothing else shows what the file alone tells a newcomer. The probe asks one question per run and sends only the section of AGENTS.md that should answer it. run sends "Run and test" and asks how to run and test the project. rules sends "Invariants" and asks what must never change and which check protects each rule. A launcher prompt holds at most 1024 bytes, so the probe refuses a section too long to send and says how far to shorten it.

  1. With your editor, create week05-probe in the course root. Copy probe.py into it, and copy agents-example.txt into it under the name AGENTS.md. Add nothing else; the script refuses any other file, so the answer can come only from the context file.
  2. Run the probe once for each question. These commands rehearse it offline with the FAKE model, which returns a fixed placeholder rather than an answer:

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-probe --output week05-probe-run --model fake -- python probe.py run sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-probe --output week05-probe-rules --model fake -- python probe.py rules

With a key on the API route, ask the real model the same questions. Week 0 setup explains the key file and HOSTED_CONFIG:

sh sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key --workspace week05-probe --output week05-probe-run-api -- python probe.py run sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key --workspace week05-probe --output week05-probe-rules-api -- python probe.py rules

Without a key, the FAKE rehearsal checks only the mechanics. Use the real answers from the lecture demonstration for this file. For your own AGENTS.md, do the probe by hand: read only that file, write down every command and rule it gives you, then run them. 3. Read probe-answer.txt in each output directory. An output directory must be new, so a repeat run needs a new --output, such as week05-probe-run-2. Every command in the run answer must be one the section states, word for word, and each invariant in the rules answer must come back with its check. A command the answer invents, or a rule it misses or misreads, is a finding about the file: rewrite that line and probe again. probe-record.json holds the digest of AGENTS.md, the section that was sent and the size of the prompt in bytes. 4. Run every listed command through the launcher it names and keep each result. Then run each invariant's check, including the deliberate violation for I3, and restore config.toml afterwards with git restore config.toml.

The results the source code leads you to expect are below. Record what you actually observe, not this table.

Invariant Check Expected result I1 The main user path works python3 -I launch.py smoke exit 0 and PASS: login, list, detail, and local job smoke I2 Synthetic data is reproducible python3 -I launch.py sample --seed 7 --count 12, twice, outputs compared the two outputs are identical I3 The app stays local host = "0.0.0.0", then python3 -I launch.py init-db exit 2 and ERROR: invalid local configuration or application files; after restoring, PASS: database initialized

Score. If every listed command ran as written and each check behaved as its invariant says, Documentation is 3. It is not 4: nothing runs the documented commands automatically, so a command that goes stale would not fail any check. If a command from the probe answer fails when you copy and run it, the level stays at 2 until you fix the line that misled the probe.

docs.title: Part 2: the pre-commit hook
docs.text:
Generate. You ask an agent for a small helper that maps a raw build status to a label. labels_proposed.txt stands in for its answer. The helper works, but it imports re and never uses it.

Verify. pre_commit.py follows the Week 3 hook: one JSON event, exit 0 to allow and exit 2 to stop. It parses each named Python file and never imports or runs it. Create week05-hook in the course root and copy pre_commit.py into it. Save the text of labels_proposed.txt there as labels.py with your editor. Predict both results, then run the hook once on the proposal:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week05-hook -- python -B pre_commit.py '{"event":"before_commit","paths":["labels.py"]}'

Expect exit_code 2 in the launcher result and labels.py:3: unused import 're' in its output. That is the failing case: the hook stops the change. Delete the import line and the blank line below it, so that labels.py matches labels_revised.py exactly, and run the same command again. Expect exit_code 0 and PASS: no protected file and no unused import in 1 file(s). That is the passing case. Keep both launcher results.

This part shows the lint check. The hook also stops a change to a protected file; the Week 5 practice makes that rule fail and pass. The test step waits for a test action in the project launcher; launch.py has no test action yet.

Score. Before the hook, Checks is 1. With the hook written into AGENTS.md as the step before every commit, one offline command runs the project's only pre-commit gate and stops the unused-import change: Checks 3. This is not the scorecard's level-2 state, where gates can be run by hand and nothing requires them: the context file that every session reads makes the hook a required step before each commit, and you keep its launcher result with each commit. If a commit lands without that result, Checks falls back to 2. It is not 4: the hook does not yet run where the agent works before it offers a commit, and no secret scan stops the canary.

docs.title: The scorecard rows
docs.text:
Dimension Start End Evidence Blocker removed Documentation 1 3 AGENTS.md at the end commit, probe-answer.txt with probe-record.json for run and for rules, each command's result and each invariant's check No context file: AGENTS.md added with commands and three invariants, each with its check Checks 1 3 Both hook results: exit 2 on the unused import, exit 0 after revision No gate before a commit: the lint hook

In M1, write your own context file and hook for your copy at your own commits, and record your own results. Your levels may differ from this example; score what your commit shows.

docs.title: Week 6: Review and delegate a bounded change
docs.text:
This directory holds Week 6 materials on delegating to roles whose context you control, a model review whose every point the student verifies (confirmed, refuted or cannot tell), PR hygiene and the explain gate. Workflow types and parallel worktrees are optional reading.

The third classroom activity, Review what a background agent hands back, checks a replayed issue-to-pull-request run offline: the diff against the issue, the claimed tests, the description's claims and the agent's permissions.

docs.title: Review, hand off and revise
docs.text: This page has three classroom activities. Activities 1 and 2 use the same synthetic fixture. Activity 1 (45 minutes) is the individual review, handoff and revision. Activity 2 (35 minutes) runs the same change as an unattended issue run; a model reviews it in a fresh context against the review rules, and you verify each point it raises. Activity 3 (25 minutes) has its own page: you review what a background agent handed back for a dashboard issue before anything merges. The M1 project work that carries Activities 1 and 2 onto ci-dashboard is in the notes.

docs.title: Activity 1: Review, hand off and revise
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes within the class, including feedback and revision. Format: pairs, with individual first reviews; a solo or asynchronous text exchange is an equivalent participation option when approved by the instructor. Materials: the synthetic fixture, a text editor, the launcher commands, one existing work record and, for execution, a device that passed the Week 0 setup check. No private repository, real participant, credentials, mouse-only interface or paid account is needed.

The teacher can demonstrate one fresh candidate generation and one model review during the lecture; students do not run that demonstration. The shared activity uses the bundled candidate so every pair reviews the same input. Identify that candidate as course-created, not a captured model response. Keep any live generation's candidate/results separate. The course-written comparison below is the same for every pair; it is not a real-model acceptance or a substitute for P2's actual individual assessment requirements.

Minutes Action Observable output 0-5 Read the contract and predict behavior for an inactive owner and your completion time, without AI One personal prediction (LO5, LO9) 5-13 Each person reviews the candidate independently, before seeing model or partner findings Location, input, expected/observed result, consequence or justified no-finding (LO5) 13-20 Exchange findings with your partner; run the supplied checks through the launcher and write the handoff note below A reproducible finding and a handoff note (LO2, LO5) 20-28 After saving first reviews, examine the labelled synthetic comparison below, and the instructor's live model review if one was shown Each claim marked confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with its evidence, plus anything the review omits (LO5, LO9) 28-38 Give peer feedback, revise the candidate and explanation, rerun unchanged checks using a fresh output directory Visible before/after diff and actual retest (LO2, LO5) 38-45 Each person answers the four causal questions and writes a brief AI-off prediction/actual reflection One work record with AI-use note and evidence references (LO9)

At minute 20, ask for help if the failing input or execution boundary is unclear. Do not spend the remainder installing an unapproved tool. Hint ladder: trace the inactive-owner input; then parenthesize the role expression; then check the active requirement on both paths. Feedback must name a reproducible claim, not "looks good." Each person revises at least one finding/explanation in the same record after feedback. If a safety check fails, stop execution and retain the safe failure category. Text tracing remains possible but must be labelled unexecuted.

docs.title: Before opening the worked explanation
docs.text: Use the contract and candidate first. Save the review during the slide's first challenge before the teacher reveals the arrangement or repair. If you already read the worked explanation, mark this as informed practice; do not label a remembered finding an unseen diagnosis. P2 retains the first review of your actual new candidate before the assistant comparison, under the assignment's rules.

docs.title: Synthetic comparison, opened after your own review
docs.text:
This is a course-authored review fixture, not measured AI output:

A1: The active staff example returns true, so the access check is correct.
A2: The function must parse the string "false" as False before checking access.

Mark each claim confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and write the contract clause and input that decide it. What does the review omit? The claims are labelled A1 and A2 so that they are not confused with the review rules R1 to R4 in Activity 2. If the instructor showed an actual AI review, compare its real claims too; do not replace them with A1/A2 or assume it has the same weaknesses. A model finding is not a grade or an authorship judgment.

docs.title: Handoff note
docs.text: Write a short handoff note in your record: the base and candidate revision, the check command and its result, each review claim with its outcome, and one unresolved question. Someone who reads only this note should be able to rerun your check. Parallel worktrees are optional reading.

docs.title: Activity 2: An unattended issue run and a model review
docs.text: Time: 35 minutes, after the 10-minute contract review. Format: pairs or solo. Each student is the issue author and the person who decides whether to merge; the model reviewer must not see the plan, the prompt or the drafted description. Save your own review before opening the plan. Materials: issue-example.txt, delegate.py, review-rules-example.txt, the public checks and the launcher commands. The review step runs delegate.py review, not the course review-diff skill: the skill reads a Git working tree, and this reviewer's workspace holds only the issue, the diff, the evidence and REVIEW.md. Without a key, take the replay route: the review the teaching team recorded or, until it is published, the course-written sample run for every model output, labelled as such; it is not a run of your own. Size the issue within the launcher limits. If the issue stage times out or reaches a limit, keep the refusal as evidence and continue with the replay route rather than rerunning it.

docs.title: Set up the practice repository
docs.text:
Do this once before minute 0; it takes about three minutes. The issue needs a real base commit, and the proposal needs a branch to land on. From the course root, make a separate practice repository that holds the original fixture:

git init w6-practice
cp lectures/week-06/fixture/access.py lectures/week-06/fixture/check_access.py w6-practice/
git -C w6-practice add access.py check_access.py
git -C w6-practice commit -m "Add the original Week 6 fixture"
git -C w6-practice rev-parse --short HEAD

The last command prints the base commit. Use it for BASE_SHA in issue.md and in the branch command in the notes. If Git asks who you are, set user.name and user.email for this repository only with git -C w6-practice config. Never give w6-practice to the launcher as a workspace: it holds .git, which the launcher refuses. Copy plain files from it into each launcher workspace instead.

docs.title: Run, check and review
docs.text:
Minutes Action Observable output 0-5 Author: copy the example issue to issue.md, replace BASE_SHA with the commit the setup printed, and predict whether an unattended run will stay inside the issue's scope issue.md and one written prediction (LO2, LO9) 5-12 Author: run delegate.py issue through the launcher; note the model requests and the time waited from the launcher result Exported proposal, draft description and run record (LO2, LO9) 12-18 Author: apply the proposed file on the issue branch in w6-practice; run the checks through the launcher; save the launcher JSON as evidence.txt Actual check result (LO5) 18-25 Student: save your rule-cited review; then run delegate.py review in a fresh workspace with only the issue, diff, evidence and example rules in REVIEW.md Your review, the AI review.txt and its run record (LO2, LO5) 25-32 Student: mark each point of the model review confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with its evidence; then read the issue for anything the diff lacks, and say what the reviewer caught that the plan missed, or why it caught nothing Each point with its outcome and evidence (LO5) 32-35 Author: decide whether a person should merge, and write the cost note Decision and cost note in the work record (LO9)

At minute 12, ask for help if the launcher refuses the issue: read the refusal, correct the issue and record that you did. A FAKE run is not a refusal of your issue. With --model fake, every stage stops with "FAKE checks the launcher connection only", the planner included, because FAKE writes no plan, change or review. Keep that result as your connection check and continue on the API route or the replay route. Do not rerun the issue stage to get a nicer proposal; one run is the exercise. If the proposal fails the checks, that failure is your evidence and the AI reviewer still receives it. Verify the output against the rules file, not the plan; if you have seen the plan, say so in your record.

You answered the four explanation questions for this change in Activity 1. Update those answers after class only if this run changed what you verified.

The cost note names the model requests, the minutes waited and the minutes spent reviewing, and whether the output was kept. It answers one question: for this small, clearly specified change, did running unattended save anything?

Optional, 3 minutes, if you finish early. Take the example rule whose check was hardest to apply, or one that produced a refuted point, and rewrite it with its source and a check that a reviewer can apply to a diff or a run. Or turn "code should be clean" into such a rule. Keep both wordings in your record. This step carries no marks.

docs.title: Activity 3: Review what a background agent hands back
docs.text: Time: 25 minutes, after Activity 2. Format: solo, or pairs with individual records. A label on an issue starts a background agent; it returns a branch, a pull request description and a run report while nobody watches. You are the maintainer who checks them before anything merges: the diff against the issue, the claimed tests run again through the launcher, each claim in the description, and what the agent's token allowed it to do. The run is a course-written replay, so the activity needs no key and no network. Follow the steps on the activity page.

docs.title: Participation and evidence boundaries
docs.text:
All material and results can be read in a text editor or terminal using the keyboard. The full contract and code are plain text. No diagram, color distinction, voice recording, drag gesture or live spoken turn conveys unique information. The instructor can approve additional time, a written asynchronous exchange, a screen-reader text transcript or a supported device with the same individual review, evidence analysis and revision goals. Actual accommodation approval and equipment availability must be arranged, not inferred from this example. A text-only execution transcript supplied for an approved arrangement must identify its source and actual run; do not claim to have run it yourself.

Model access, keys and the launcher check follow Week 0 setup. Independent assessments remain AI-off.

The output is one existing record containing the candidate/diff, your first review, comparison, verification reference, revised explanation and one honest AI-use note. Share minimal synthetic snippets only. No raw chat, personal data, private source or duplicate disclosure file is needed. Write your reflection yourself without AI. This rehearsal cannot replace individual P2 evidence. The weekly self-check is formative.

docs.title: Practitioner guest
docs.text: A practitioner from a partner organization joins the first class this week for up to 45 minutes to describe how their organization reviews agent work and decides what to delegate; the rest of the class runs as usual. Before class, write one question for the guest. After class, write one sentence comparing one claim the guest made with this week's evidence, such as your first review or the model review points you confirmed or refuted. Keep both in your Week 6 work entry. The talk is not assessed and adds no time outside class. A guest speaks about their own organization's practice; the course endorses no product. The talk is recorded only with advance notice and the consent of those present. If no guest is available, the class runs as usual.

docs.title: C1 and the C2 proposal
docs.text: Submit your C1 warm-up contribution this week. At the end of the week, submit your C2 proposal: the project, the issue and the scope of one feature or non-trivial fix, in one or two pull requests. The teacher approves the project, issue and scope before Week 7; if the proposal cannot be approved, the teacher assigns one from the approved list. Before you submit C1, review your own pull request the way this page reviews a change: against what its issue asks for, before you read anyone else's review. See the syllabus.

docs.title: Return to the dashboard
docs.text:
Review a small diff, reproduce one finding and revise your explanation after peer feedback.

P2 is your individual contract review, change review, reproducer and explanation. The project reuses the repaired PR.

Before leaving, decide whether to accept the change, narrow the task, obtain one missing observation or stop. Explain what evidence could change that decision.

docs.title: Review what a background agent hands back
docs.text:
A background agent works on an issue while nobody watches. Something starts it, such as a label on the issue. It runs in a workspace of its own and comes back with a branch, a pull request with a description and a report of what it did. The first time a person looks at the work is when the pull request arrives. This activity is that moment: you are the maintainer, and nothing merges until you have checked what came back.

Time: 25 minutes in the second class, after Activity 2. Route: offline, with no key. The agent's run is a course-written replay. A real pipeline of this kind needs a hosted repository and a token, which the course does not provide. In Activity 2 you ran one issue through a model or replayed that run; here you review what a whole pipeline hands back.

Everything in the background/ folder is written by the course team to look like one run of such a pipeline on a small part of the dashboard. None of it is a captured model response. Hosted code platforms and agent tools offer background agents in several forms; this page describes the mechanism, not any product.

docs.title: The files
docs.text:
File What it is issue-42.txt The issue a maintainer labelled for the agent: the files it may change, the check to run, the acceptance criteria and what is out of scope pipeline-example.txt What starts the agent, where it runs and what its token may do (grants G1 to G4) base/durations.py and base/test_durations.py The two files at the commit the agent started from replay/durations.py and replay/test_durations.py The same two files on the agent's branch replay/pr-description.txt The pull request description the agent wrote replay/report.json The agent's run report, in the hand-back shape from Week 5 handoff.json The issue written as a Week 5 hand-off: the files the agent may change, the command it must run and what it must hand back

You also need check_handoff.py from the Week 5 practice. Resolve VERSION and DIGEST as in the notes and run each sh scripts/course-sandbox command from the course root, as Week 0 setup explains. Create each workspace with your editor.

docs.title: Minutes 0-3: set up the repository and replay the agent's push
docs.text:
The trusted Git commands below make a practice repository at the base commit, then put the agent's two files on its branch, as the pipeline would have pushed them:

git init w6-bg
cp lectures/week-06/background/base/durations.py lectures/week-06/background/base/test_durations.py w6-bg/
git -C w6-bg add durations.py test_durations.py
git -C w6-bg commit -m "Add the duration summary"
git -C w6-bg rev-parse --short HEAD
git -C w6-bg switch -c agent/42-running-builds
cp lectures/week-06/background/replay/durations.py lectures/week-06/background/replay/test_durations.py w6-bg/
git -C w6-bg commit -am "Fix #42: skip running builds in the duration summary"

The rev-parse line prints the base commit; use it for BASE_SHA below. As in Activity 2, never give w6-bg to the launcher as a workspace, because it holds .git. Copy plain files out of it instead.

docs.title: Minutes 3-6: read what came back and predict
docs.text: Read the issue, then the pipeline, then the description and the report, in that order. The description says the tests pass, and the report says the check exited 0. Before you check anything, write one prediction in your work record: if G4 had merged this pull request when its check passed, would the default branch now hold only what issue 42 asked for?

docs.title: Minutes 6-12: does the diff match the issue?
docs.text:
Look at the change itself, not at the description of it:

git -C w6-bg diff --stat BASE_SHA HEAD
git -C w6-bg diff BASE_SHA HEAD

File level. Create week06-bg-check in the course root and copy into it check_handoff.py, handoff.json and replay/report.json. Save the changed file names as diff.txt, then check the report against the hand-off and the diff:

git -C w6-bg diff --name-only BASE_SHA HEAD > week06-bg-check/diff.txt

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week06-bg-check -- python -B check_handoff.py handoff.json report.json diff.txt

Expect exit_code 2 with two lines: did not hand back 'not_checked' as a non-empty list and STOP: the hand-back does not match the hand-off. The checker finds nothing wrong with the files: both are ones the issue allows. It also takes the report's exit code 0 at its word.

Hunk level. The checker cannot read a hunk, so you do. For each hunk in git diff, name the acceptance line it serves or the out-of-scope line it breaks. Two hunks need a closer look. One changes format_duration, which the issue puts out of scope. The other rewrites the expected value of an existing test, test_format_minutes, which the issue says to keep as it is. A file list that passes is not a diff that stays in scope.

docs.title: Minutes 12-18: were the claimed tests run, and do they say what was claimed?
docs.text:
Run the agent's own check on the agent's branch. Create week06-bg-branch and copy durations.py and test_durations.py from w6-bg into it:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week06-bg-branch -- python -B test_durations.py -v

Expect exit_code 0 and, in stdout, Ran 6 tests and OK. The check passes, but read what ran: six tests, one of them with an expected value the agent rewrote.

Now run the checks as they were at the base against the agent's code. Create week06-bg-base-tests with durations.py from w6-bg and test_durations.py from lectures/week-06/background/base/:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week06-bg-base-tests -- python -B test_durations.py -v

Expect exit_code 1, with FAIL: test_format_minutes, AssertionError: '3:05' != '3m 05s', Ran 5 tests and FAILED (failures=1). The existing check catches the display change; the agent's branch passed only because the same change rewrote that check.

Finally, run the issue's own reproducer on the agent's code, not the agent's test of it:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week06-bg-branch -- python -B -c "from durations import median_duration; print(median_duration([{'duration': 60}, {'duration': None}]))"

Expect exit_code 0 and 60 in stdout. On the base code the same line raises TypeError, as the issue says.

docs.title: Minutes 18-22: is each claim in the description true?
docs.text:
Mark each claim confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, with the evidence that decides it, as you did for model review points earlier this week:

Claim The description says Where to look B1 Running builds (duration None) are left out of median_duration The reproducer run; the issue's acceptance lines B2 Two regression tests were added The test file's hunks B3 No change to how durations are displayed The format_duration hunk; the base-tests run B4 python -B test_durations.py -v: 7 tests, all passed The Ran ... tests line of your branch run, and which test file it ran B5 The overview panel now shows the median for a mix of running and finished builds What your workspaces contain

A cannot-tell entry names what is missing and the run that would decide it. Then answer: what did the description leave out that the issue asked for?

docs.title: Minutes 22-25: what could the agent do, and where should the pipeline stop?
docs.text:
Read the grants in pipeline-example.txt again and write four short answers:

  1. Which grants does the agent need to hand back a branch and a pull request?
  2. Follow this run through G3 and G4. The required check runs the test file on the agent's own branch, and G3 lets the agent edit that file. What would have merged, with nobody looking?
  3. What do you change? Name the grant you remove, the grant you narrow and where the required check takes its test file from.
  4. Even with those changes, why should the pipeline stop at a person's review before anything merges?

Then write your decision for this pull request: merge, ask for changes, or close. Give the evidence for it.

docs.title: What to keep
docs.text:
Put these in your existing Week 6 work record. This is not a new submission:

  • your prediction and whether it held;
  • the git diff --stat output, the checker's result and your note on each hunk;
  • the three launcher results, with exit_code and the lines that matter;
  • B1 to B5, each with its outcome and evidence;
  • your four answers on the grants and your decision.

No AI use is needed for this activity. If you used any, add one AI-use note and reuse its ID.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake How you notice What to do Taking the report's exit code as a run Your record has no launcher result of your own Run the check yourself and keep the launcher JSON Running only the branch's tests Every check you ran came from the agent's branch Run the base's test file against the agent's code too Counting a file-level PASS as in scope You have no note on each hunk Read each hunk against the acceptance and out-of-scope lines Forcing B5 into confirmed or refuted No run you made renders the panel Mark it cannot tell and name the run that would decide it Letting a green check merge The check runs a file the agent can edit Take the check's test file from the base and leave the merge to a person

docs.title: Week 6: Review and delegate a bounded change
Learning objectives
docs.text:
This week has one main line: review a change against what was asked, using roles whose context you control. A model reviews; you verify each point it raises. By the end of the lesson, you can:

LO Observable action Practice and self-check LO2 Assign a bounded task, context, permissions and verification; run a planner, an implementer and a reviewer in separate contexts Activities 1, 2 and 3; M1 delegation run; questions 6 and 12 LO3 Review a request before the change: find a clause with two readings, give an input that separates them and the question for the request's owner, or show the search behind a no-finding Contract review before Activity 2; question 9 LO5 Review a short change yourself, reproduce a failure, mark each point of a model review confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with its evidence, and explain a revision Activities 1, 2 and 3; questions 1, 2, 3, 7 and 12 LO9 Keep minimal source/AI-use evidence, respect another person's access and participation boundaries, calibrate your time prediction and judge what an unattended run costs Activity evidence note; issue-run record; Activity 3 merge decision; questions 4, 5 and 8

Estimated time this week is about 13 hours. This includes the classes, P2's three hours (workshop, verification and short explanation included), Activity 2's 35 minutes and Activity 3's 25 minutes in class, about two hours 15 minutes of M1 project work (45 minutes to write your review rules and 90 minutes for the delegated change and the verified model review, including waiting and checks), and finishing your C1 contribution and C2 proposal. Activities 2 and 3 are part of the scheduled class time, not additional projects. These are course estimates, not measured completion times. Ask for help at the checkpoint rather than widening the task or buying model access. Workflow types and parallel worktrees are optional reading; optional extensions do not affect the attainable grade.

Before the first review, use only the permission contract and candidate on the slides. Save your finding before opening the worked explanation here. If already exposed, identify informed practice; P2 uses the first review of your actual new candidate before the assistant comparison.

docs.title: The continuing dashboard case
docs.text:
The dashboard allows owners or staff to edit active builds. An agent proposes an authorization expression and a reviewer checks only a staff account.

allowed = is_owner or is_staff and not archived

Decision: Can an owner edit an archived build under this expression?

Python's operator precedence puts and before or. An owner can satisfy the first term even when archived. The required policy is (is_owner or is_staff) and not archived; verify the role/archive combinations independently.

Write your own review before consulting the agent. Ask it for claims tied to inputs and code references, then mark each claim confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with its evidence.

Acceptance decision: Merge only after the repaired expression passes every role and archive combination on the exact revision you will merge. A model's review or explanation does not establish who may edit.

The public permission fixture below supplies a compact review target. Relate its parentheses to the dashboard role policy; do not infer permission from a model explanation.

This is a course-authored, hand-worked example. Actual execution evidence comes from your own checks.

docs.title: The synthetic change
docs.text:
Use the fixture contract. An account can edit a document exactly when active is true and at least one of owner or staff is true. Inputs are booleans. The bundled candidate is course-written, deliberately faulty, and has this body:

return owner or staff and active

Predict the result for an inactive owner before testing. The expression allows that owner to edit: owner alone can make the result true. The contract requires the active check on both role paths. A proposed revision is:

return active and (owner or staff)

Do not accept the revision just because it looks clearer. Verify inactive accounts, active outsiders, each permitted role and overlapping roles. This is an access decision exercise with synthetic booleans, not a production authentication system.

docs.title: Prepare the accepted launcher
docs.text:
Model access, keys and the launcher check follow Week 0 setup. From the course root, run the trusted configuration query:

uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json

In the commands below replace VERSION with version and DIGEST with digest from that output. The offline profile runs without a key. Do not change profile parameters to make a run pass.

With your editor/file manager create week6-work inside the course root, as Week 9 does with week09-work. Copy only access.py and check_access.py from lectures/week-06/fixture into it. The commands use week6-work from the course root; the launcher refuses any workspace path that contains ... Exclude .git, teacher material, keys, private code, raw interviews and unrelated personal data. The launcher copies these inputs into its bounded temporary workspace and exports only explicitly emitted files. Host files are not mounted into student execution. Do not run these scripts on the host, in an editor terminal without the launcher, or in the Dev Container directly.

Launcher limits. This is the one place this week states them. Each launcher run has a 30-second wall-clock limit including model time, at most four model requests, 64 KB of total output (including JSON prompt frames and base64 artifact frames) and 1 MB of aggregate input. The fixture's delegate.py also rejects any single input file over 32 KB. For the two-request issue stage, keep the target file around 12 KB; when plan and implement run separately, a target around 20 KB fits each run. A timeout or limit refusal is a recorded result. Keep its record; do not rerun for a nicer output, raise a limit or move to another tool. If a target is too large, narrow the issue.

docs.title: Review, check and revise the bundled candidate
docs.text:
Every student reviews the same bundled candidate. In the lecture the instructor may also generate one fresh candidate and request one model review of it through the launcher with the fixture's workflow.py; you do not run that script. Keep a live candidate and its results apart from the bundled one.

Write your own review before reading any AI review. Name a location, a concrete input, expected versus observed behavior and consequence. If no defect appears, explain the cases you checked and the limits of that conclusion. Then execute the public checks:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week6-work --output week6-check-before -- python check_access.py -v

For the bundled candidate, test_inactive_owner and the inactive case in test_overlapping_roles fail. Record the actual result; do not copy this prediction as your observed output. The launcher JSON includes the container exit_code, combined output in stdout and model request count. Read those fields rather than treating creation of an output directory as success. Each invocation also runs the launcher's actual safety suite, including deliberate limit probes; include this waiting in your time record.

Save your review in the existing work record, then compare it with the course-written review claims A1 and A2 in Activity 1, or with the instructor's live review if one was shown. Verify each claim against the contract and inputs. An AI review is a hypothesis source: it may identify a useful boundary, miss a defect, or invent a requirement. For example, a demand to accept strings such as "false" is outside this boolean-only contract. A human can also miss an operator-precedence defect, follow the model's suggestion too readily or misunderstand the specification. Your own first review and a reproducer make both more useful; neither is a correctness guarantee.

Revise only the necessary code in your editor. Rerun the same checks with a fresh output directory, week6-check-after, and compare before/after behavior and the actual diff. For the proposed revision all seven checks should pass, covering the eight boolean combinations. Inspect the copied test source against the course version too: a candidate can alter its own writable sandbox. Public self-check results are practice evidence, not an isolated hidden grader, trusted score or automatic merge authorization.

docs.title: Review the request before you delegate it
docs.text:
Contract review: 10 minutes, AI-off. A review judges a change against what was asked, so check what was asked first. An unattended planner fills a gap in the request with a guess, and a review point that depends on a clause with two readings cannot be confirmed or refuted. Suppose the first draft of this week's issue had this acceptance line:

Only active owners and staff can edit.

Before reading on, write four things in your work record: the clause, two readings of it, an input that the two readings treat differently, and the question you would ask the person who owns the request. If you find no clause with two readings, write your search instead: the clause you examined most closely, the two readings you tried, and an input both readings treat alike.

One answer: "active" can apply to both nouns or only to the first.

  • Reading A: owners and staff must both be active.
  • Reading B: owners must be active; staff can edit whatever their status.
  • Separating input: an inactive staff member, can_edit(active=False, owner=False, staff=True). Reading A denies it; reading B allows it.
  • Question for the person who owns the request: "Must a staff member's account be active to edit, as an owner's must?"

The words group two ways, just as owner or staff and active does. The answer was reading A. The fixture contract records that answer ("Inactive accounts cannot edit, including inactive owners and staff"), and so does the example issue's first acceptance line. Until such a question is answered, the issue states which reading it implements or the change waits. A review point that depends on the open reading is cannot tell. P2 asks for the same four parts on its own contract.

docs.title: Plan, implement and review in separate contexts
docs.text:
Delegating one change to an agent hides three jobs: deciding what to do, doing it, and checking it. Give each job its own launcher run and its own workspace, so that each role sees only what it needs. The fixture's delegate.py runs one role per invocation. It reads only the files it names and sends them to the model as data. It never executes the model's code or the issue's verification command, and it exports text for you to inspect.

Role Workspace holds Exports You do next Planner delegate.py, issue.md, the target file plan.md Read the plan; strike anything the issue does not ask for Implementer delegate.py, issue.md, your edited plan.md, the target file proposed-<file>, change.diff, pr-description.md Apply the file on a branch; run the checks Reviewer delegate.py, issue.md, change.diff, evidence.txt, REVIEW.md review.txt Verify each point: confirmed, refuted or cannot tell

The issue is a short plain-text file. Copy issue-example.txt to issue.md and replace BASE_SHA with the base commit that the practice repository setup prints. It names one target file, the acceptance criteria, the verification command and what is out of scope. Every run also exports run-record.json, which lists each file that went into the prompt with its SHA-256 digest and the number of model requests. Keep these records: they show what each role could see.

The reviewer's context is the point of the exercise. Its workspace holds the issue (the specification), the diff, your check output and your review rules, and nothing else. It never sees the plan, the implementer's prompt or the drafted description. A reviewer that has read the plan inherits the plan's assumptions; one that sees only what was asked, what changed and what ran has to judge the change against the request. The script refuses to review when the workspace holds any other file, before it reads or sends anything.

With VERSION and DIGEST resolved as above, create the workspaces with your editor and run each role with a fresh output directory:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace w6-plan --output w6-plan-out --model fake -- python delegate.py plan
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace w6-impl --output w6-impl-out --model fake -- python delegate.py implement
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace w6-check --output w6-check-out -- python check_access.py -v
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace w6-review --output w6-review-out --model fake -- python delegate.py review

Between the second and third commands, make w6-check hold check_access.py and the exported proposed-access.py saved as access.py. Copy the third command's launcher JSON, with its exit_code and stdout, into evidence.txt for the reviewer's workspace. Each model run makes one request. A refusal or an incomplete response is a result to record, not a reason to rerun until something appears.

As written, with --model fake, these commands check only the launcher connection: every stage refuses the FAKE placeholder and writes no plan, change or review. For a real run, take the API route. Resolve the approved-hosted profile and hosted configuration as Week 0 setup describes, and use its options in place of --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --model fake, for example:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile approved-hosted --version HOSTED_VERSION --digest HOSTED_DIGEST --model api --hosted-config HOSTED_CONFIG --key-file ~/.config/course/hosted-key --workspace w6-plan --output w6-plan-out -- python delegate.py plan

Without a key, take the replay route below.

docs.title: The model reviews; you verify each point
docs.text:
A model, not another student, reviews your change, and you verify what it says. Fresh context is not independence. The same model may share the implementer's blind spots, and a reviewer that sees only a diff cannot notice a change that is missing from it. So call its output a model review, never an independent review, and treat every point as a claim.

  1. Before you read the review, write your own short review against REVIEW.md: one input you expect to fail, or a no-finding with the inputs you checked.
  2. Run the reviewer on your change in a fresh workspace, as above.
  3. Give every point in review.txt exactly one outcome:
  4. Confirmed: a reproducer shows the problem. It is an input with its actual result, a diff line, or a line of the evidence, and someone else can rerun it.
  5. Refuted: runnable evidence shows the point is wrong: the input passes, or the rule it cites is met. Or the contract or issue shows the requirement it asserts does not exist.
  6. Cannot tell: the files you have cannot decide it. Write what is missing and why. Never record it as confirmed or refuted. P2 calls this outcome unverified.
  7. Read the issue again for anything the diff should contain and does not. The reviewer could not see it, so record it as your own finding.

Cannot tell is the usual outcome for a point about code outside the reviewer's files. Suppose a review says that a caller in another file may rely on the old behavior. The issue, the diff and the evidence do not hold that caller, so the reviewer was guessing, and from those files you cannot decide it either. Mark it cannot tell and name the file and the call that would decide it. In your own repository you can then look: search for the changed function's callers, for example with git grep -n "can_edit(", and read what each one passes and expects. With that evidence the point becomes confirmed or refuted, and the callers you checked go into your review record.

Record each point, its outcome and its evidence under ## Review evidence in the PR. Fix each confirmed point, or record why it waits for a later change. Keep refuted points with the evidence that refutes them. Whether the reviewer caught something or nothing, write which inputs it considered and whether your own checks already covered them.

Without a key. You may take the replay route without giving a reason. Replay the model review that the teaching team recorded with the approved configuration on the course sample change, using the replay command in Week 0 setup, and verify each of its points in the same way. Until that record is published, verify the course-written comments in the sample run and label them course-written. For your own M1 change, write your own review against REVIEW.md, note under ## Review evidence that no model review ran, and ask a TA, as the PR template says.

docs.title: Review rules you write and check
docs.text:
An AI reviewer and a human reviewer drift toward different concerns unless you state what matters. Write a short REVIEW.md in your project repository: three to six rules, each with the source that justifies it and a check that a reviewer can apply to a diff or a run. Derive the rules from your M0 specification and from defects you have already met, such as a CP1 repair or an M1 regression. The fixture's review-rules-example.txt shows the shape for the document-edit guard.

R3  Inputs stay Python booleans; the change adds no parsing and no new input type.
    Source: contract "Inputs are booleans"; issue out of scope "Parsing strings".
    Check: the diff adds no str handling, conversion or default argument.

"Code should be clean" is not a rule: nobody can show that a diff breaks it. The review role reads REVIEW.md and cites a rule ID for each point; cite the same IDs in your own review. A point that cites a rule is still a claim, and a reproducer decides its outcome, not the rule ID. Change the rules by PR, like code. When a rule keeps producing refuted points, rewrite or remove it and record why. REVIEW.md tells reviewers what to check; it enforces nothing. The launcher and your merge rule enforce.

docs.title: From an issue file to a PR description
docs.text:
The handoff can become a pipeline: an issue describes a bounded task, a trigger starts an agent, and the agent returns a pull request. The issue run does this locally and unattended. One launcher invocation plans and implements with no person between the two steps:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace w6-issue --output w6-issue-out --model fake -- python delegate.py issue

As above, --model fake checks only the launcher connection: the run stops at the planner with the FAKE message. A real issue run uses the API route options. w6-issue holds delegate.py, issue.md and the target file. The run makes two model requests and exports the plan, the proposed file, change.diff, pr-description.md and its run record. The draft names the branch and base and lists the acceptance criteria. It leaves the four explanation questions as the template's prompts, so the explanation check reports them incomplete until you answer them yourself.

An issue is data from whoever could write it. Its wording cannot widen what the run may do; the script's structure decides that. The script refuses an issue that leaves BASE_SHA unreplaced, names more than one target, names a check or test file as the target, uses a path containing .., or contains a line that is not a known field. It cannot create a branch, push, reach the network or run the verification command. A model can still return a wrong or over-scoped change from a well-formed issue. The course-written sample run shows a plan that added string parsing nobody asked for, and a change that still passed all seven checks.

The proposal then goes through the same gate as any other change. In the practice repository from the Activity 2 setup, create the branch from the recorded base with trusted commands, save the proposed file over w6-practice/access.py with your editor, and inspect the staged diff:

git -C w6-practice switch -c issue/inactive-owner BASE_SHA
git -C w6-practice add access.py
git -C w6-practice diff --cached

Run the checks through the launcher as above, then let the model review the change and verify each point as described. Answer the four explanation questions from your actual result. Only a person merges.

docs.title: PR hygiene and the explanation gate
docs.text:
Before submitting a small PR, inspect git status --short and git diff --cached in the practice repository. Stage explicit files. Keep unrelated formatting, dependency changes, artifacts and private data out. Give the base and candidate revision, scope, observed failure, changed behavior and unresolved limitations. A changed candidate needs fresh verification and a fresh review.

A context file, such as the Week 5 AGENTS.md, tells each role what to do, and a hook, such as the Week 5 lint hook, checks an event such as a commit. Neither is isolation: the launcher enforces the execution boundary. Treat a suggested change to a rule file or a hook as reviewable code, not as permission for the author to widen their own access.

The existing explanation guide supplies the four-question PR template:

  1. What changed? Identify the boolean guard and the affected behavior.
  2. Why? Connect the guard to the active-account requirement.
  3. Which inputs are likely to fail? Include inactive owners and overlapping roles.
  4. What did you personally verify? Reference your actual launcher result and version.

These hints are not completed student answers. Write your own causal account. The explanation check looks only for completeness, so a complete answer can still be false; the guide explains how staff check the answers. Another student's explanation does not prove your understanding, and no one may infer authorship or grades from writing style.

docs.title: When unattended runs help
docs.text:
An unattended run helps when the task is independent and has an exclusive file, its acceptance criteria and verification command are written down, waiting would otherwise dominate, and someone is free to review the result when it returns. It does not help when the task is ambiguous, because an unattended planner fills gaps with guesses, or when review is already the bottleneck.

Unattended runs have costs that attended work makes visible. Every run uses model requests from the same budget whether you keep its output or not. An over-scoped or failed run costs review time. Rerunning until the checks pass selects an output; it does not verify one. For each run, record the model requests from the launcher result, the time you waited, the minutes spent reviewing, and whether you kept or discarded the output. Compare these with doing the same change attended. This course runs these steps locally inside the launcher. It provides no hosted agent service and no CI trigger that holds credentials; the issue file, run records and review record practice the same decisions.

docs.title: A background agent: what its token allows and who merges
docs.text: A background agent takes the issue run one step further. A trigger, such as a label on an issue, starts the agent in a workspace of its own, and it hands back a branch, a pull request with a description and a run report. Nobody watches in between. Two questions decide whether such a pipeline is safe to use. First, what can the agent's token do: push which branches, change which files, and can it merge? Second, what decides the merge? If the required check runs a test file that the agent may edit, a green check shows only that the agent's change agrees with the agent's tests. Take the check's test file from the base commit, keep the agent's grants to what the issue needs, and stop the pipeline at a person who reviews the pull request against the issue. The description and the run report are claims, like any model review point: run the checks yourself and read every hunk. The background-agent activity is a replay of one such run on a dashboard issue; it needs no key.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Complete the 45-minute review and handoff activity. You will first predict one result and review individually, exchange a reproducible finding, then revise and retest. Use the supplied synthetic candidate for the same comparison so every student has the same input. Keep any real-model candidate and its results clearly separate. The instructor may show one live generation and model review during the lecture; you do not run that demonstration.

Then do the 10-minute contract review and complete the 35-minute issue-run activity on the same fixture: write the issue, run it unattended, apply and check the proposal, let the model review it in a fresh context against the example rules, and verify its points. Finish with the 25-minute background-agent activity: review a replayed pull request from a background agent as its maintainer, then decide what the agent's token should allow and where the pipeline stops.

M1 project work (individual, required). Carry the same steps onto one change you are making to ci-dashboard for M1. Each step says what to do on the API route and without a key; both routes reach the same M1 evidence.

  1. Write your REVIEW.md from your M0 specification and the defects you have met, commit it by PR, and use its rule IDs in every review from now on.
  2. Write the change as an issue whose target is the one file it edits, copied into the workspace at its repository path, for example domains/metrics/search.py. On the API route, for an attended handoff run plan, inspect and approve the plan, then run implement in its separate workspace. The unattended issue stage has no approval pause and must export the complete target file within one run. Size the target within the launcher limits. Without a key, no model plans or implements your change: write the plan yourself in plan.md, check each step against the issue, and make the change yourself on the issue branch. On both routes, apply the change on the issue branch and run your existing checks for that behavior through the launcher; the checks need no key.
  3. Write your own review against REVIEW.md before you read any other review. On the API route, run the model reviewer in a fresh workspace with the issue, the diff, the check output and REVIEW.md. Without a key, no model reviews your change: verify the replayed review of the course sample change, or the course-written sample comments until it is published, and ask a TA to review your change. On both routes, mark each point you receive confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with its evidence.
  4. Read the issue again for anything your diff should contain and does not, and record it as your own finding. Keep the reviewer blind to the plan on every route. If a launcher timeout or limit refusal occurs, preserve its record and continue with the replay or TA route; do not rerun the issue stage.

Put this evidence in the M1 reviewed-change PR and the existing work record. It is not a new submission. A TA checks this review evidence for M1.

Evidence API route Without a key Request issue.md issue.md Plan and change The approved plan.md, change.diff and each role's run-record.json Your own plan.md and the diff of your change Checks The launcher JSON of your checks on the issue branch The same Review Your own review; each model-review point with its outcome and evidence Your own review; each point of the replayed or course-written sample review with its outcome and evidence; the TA's points with theirs; a note under ## Review evidence that no model reviewed your change On both routes Anything missing from the diff, the four explanation answers, and any timeout or limit refusal record The same

Retain one small work record: candidate/version, your finding and comparison, verification reference, four causal answers and one AI-use note. Reference that record from your PR and project explanation rather than copying it. A synthetic example of a note is:

Record W6-example: AI used through the course broker for one unattended issue run and
one model review. Tool/model: record the actual resolved identity. I wrote the first
review independently and checked the before/after results referenced in this record.

If you used no AI, write that in the note and identify the supplied synthetic artifact and your own verification. Do not invent a session or claim the course-authored fixture was your generated output. A zero-AI declaration does not waive a practice unit's model-execution requirement where one exists; P2 has none, because its comparison uses a supplied review.

The activities rehearse P2, whose assessed work is individual and has two halves. The specification half reviews the change request's contract: one clause with two readings, an input that separates them and the question for its owner, or the search behind a no-finding. The code half is your own line-by-line review of the change, saved first, then a comparison with a supplied review for omissions and refuted claims, plus a live AI review where your instructor offers one. AI generation is allowed; AI cannot write or replace that first review. Follow P2's own instructions for the assessed work. The weekly self-check is formative retrieval practice. The project artifact cannot replace P2's first individual review and explanation, or later independent assessments. Write your brief calibration/reflection yourself without AI, using one prediction difference, verification reference and improvement.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Use the exact launcher commands above with resolved identity and fresh output directories. Evidence should let another reviewer answer: which candidate, which inputs, which actual result, what changed after feedback, and what remains uncertain? Inspect the test file, candidate diff and the actual result together. If execution fails, retain the safe failure category and ask for supported help; do not enable network, add a host mount, enlarge a resource limit or move execution to another tool. Reading the fixture as text remains possible but is not an execution pass.

For the delegated change, check the run records before the outputs. The reviewer's run-record.json should list exactly issue.md, change.diff, evidence.txt and REVIEW.md as its inputs, with digests matching the files actually reviewed. Plan text pasted into evidence.txt, or no review record at all, is evidence that the review was not fresh; stop and record that limitation. Each confirmed or refuted point needs evidence that someone else can rerun, and each cannot-tell point names what is missing. The drafted PR description is not verified until the four answers are yours and the explanation check reports them complete. One failure case to recognize: the issue run exports a change whose checks pass but whose diff adds behavior the issue ruled out of scope.

Map evidence to the objectives: LO2 uses scope/permissions, a reproducible handoff and the three role records; LO3 uses your contract review, with the clause, both readings, the separating input and the question, or the search behind a no-finding; LO5 uses your first review, the reproducer, each verified review point and the retest; LO9 uses honest attribution, minimal disclosure, accessible participation, prediction versus actual time and the cost record of the unattended run. Use self-check questions after the activity and revise one answer after comparing with these notes or the answer guidance.

Only synthetic snippets needed for this comparison belong in the prompt or your PR. No raw interview, private source, credential, real account, unrelated personal data or full environment dump is needed. Save only the comparison excerpt and checks relevant to this task; no generic chat export or additional log quota applies. A required excerpt that cannot be safely exported uses contemporaneous, checkable equivalent evidence through the course's announced process. Never fabricate an earlier conversation.

docs.title: Common mistakes
