docs.text: Mistake How to detect it Small correction Reviewing the change before the request A review point depends on a clause with two readings Write both readings and a separating input, ask the request's owner, and mark the point cannot tell until it is answered Trusting a green public test run Test source changed or edge cases absent Compare the test snapshot and reproduce the boundary input Calling AI findings your own review Your first review appears only after the AI response Keep stages separate; acknowledge actual assistance and seek required remediation Letting the reviewer read the plan Plan text appears in evidence.txt, or the review record is missing Stop and record the non-fresh or incomplete review; use a new workspace with only the issue, diff, evidence and rules Calling a model review independent review The record says "independent", or a point is accepted without your evidence Label it a model review and mark each point confirmed, refuted or cannot tell with evidence Forcing every point to confirmed or refuted A point is decided without the input or file that could decide it Mark it cannot tell and name what is missing Trusting a reviewer's "no finding" The issue asks for a change the diff does not contain Read the issue against the diff yourself and record the missing change Rerunning an unattended pipeline until the checks pass Several run records, one kept and unexplained Report every run; fix the issue or the plan instead of resampling Letting a background agent's green check merge The required check runs a test file the agent could edit Run the base commit's checks against the agent's code, and leave the merge to a person

docs.title: Transfer to a new situation
docs.text:
A dashboard issue asks the edit guard to deny archived builds and to log every denied edit. The model reviewer saw only the diff and reports no finding. The diff repairs the guard but adds no log call. What does that "no finding" establish, and which check would decide acceptance?

Write the expected behavior and the next check before comparing with the answer guidance.

P2 is your individual contract review, change review, reproducer and explanation. The project reuses the repaired PR.

docs.title: Read only what the exercise needs
docs.text:
There is no added external reading requirement or product comparison in this lesson. These links revisit course-authored material within the Week 6 budget:

  • Fixture contract and shared context: use during the activity to distinguish required behavior from an invented review requirement (LO2, LO5).
  • Week 0 setup and fallbacks: revisit only if you need the accepted launcher, resolver or current equipment-availability boundary (LO2, LO9).
  • Four-question explanation guide: use its existing template and evidence references for the handoff (LO5, LO9).
  • Course-written sample issue run and example review rules: use in Activity 2 to classify review comments against checkable rules (LO2, LO5).
  • Background-agent activity and its example pipeline: use in Activity 3 to check a replayed pull request and decide what the agent's token should allow (LO2, LO5).

docs.title: Optional primary sources
docs.text:
Start with one study of model-written review comments in real use. Read the abstract and sections 4.2, 4.3 and 6 of Vijayvergiya et al., AI-Assisted Assessment of Coding Practices in Modern Code Review (about 20 minutes) (studies/autocommenter-code-review; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1). Read it because Activity 2 asks you to classify review comments. The authors had raters judge each comment by whether it was correct and whether the author could act on it, had to suppress comments based on outdated practices, and report that a promising offline evaluation was not enough: evaluation in real use and system changes were essential for deployment. Ask those two questions of every comment you accept, and treat the paper's figures as one organization's results, not targets.

The remaining readings, in alphabetical order, support review and delegation decisions in the workshop:

  • Anthropic, Writing effective tools for agents (tools/anthropic-effective-tools; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1) — use its prototyping and evaluation guidance when deciding what evidence a delegated tool change must produce.
  • Chroma, Context Rot (studies/chroma-context-rot; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1) — use the controlled input-length discussion when deciding what a review context should hold constant.
  • Claude Code, Best practices (tools/claude-code-best-practices; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1) — use its verification guidance to check that a delegated run produced a readable pass/fail signal before acceptance. This is one tool's documentation; the verification principle carries over to the course launcher and other tools, while its product commands are not required.
  • GitHub Blog, How to review code effectively: A GitHub staff engineer's philosophy (studies/github-code-review-philosophy; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1) — read Ask questions and To approve or not before writing your review rules. One engineer separates preferences from blocking problems and prefers a test as the answer to a review question; give each blocking comment you keep a check that fails before the fix.
  • LangWatch, The Context Tax: When to Compact Your Coding Agent (studies/langwatch-context-tax; as_of: 2026-10-07; Source 1) — use this bounded case study to discuss compaction trade-offs and evidence limits when deciding what context a reviewer session can afford.
  • Superpowers, README at a fixed commit (tools/superpowers; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1) — read The Basic Workflow beside "Plan, implement and review in separate contexts": an open-source skills library that can send each planned task to a fresh subagent and review after each one. Its README calls the workflows mandatory, but they are written as skills for the model to follow; for each one, say what would enforce it, or mark it "cannot tell".

docs.title: Optional: workflow types and parallel worktrees
docs.text:
This section is optional reading. The week's required work does not depend on it, and it does not affect the attainable grade.

Choose a workflow by its handoff. These are conceptual roles, not claims that a named product has a particular feature. An IDE workflow keeps selection, editing and local feedback beside the code. A CLI workflow makes the command, inputs and exit result explicit. A cloud workflow delegates a bounded task to a separately provisioned environment and returns a change for review. For each, ask what context it receives, where code executes, how work stops, and how someone else reproduces the result. A remote interface alone proves none of those properties. The course runs only the accepted local launcher path.

A synchronous handoff resolves one question while the result is visible, at the cost of both sides waiting for the same operation. An asynchronous handoff leaves a bounded change and evidence for later review. It must pin the base and candidate revision, the scope, the unfinished questions and the verification commands. A stale branch can pass its own tests yet break after integration.

Parallel worktrees and one integration step. A Git worktree gives a task a separate working directory and branch. It is a version-control arrangement, not a security boundary: never pass a worktree with repository metadata to the launcher, and copy only the intended plain files into an execution directory. In a separate synthetic practice repository, these trusted commands start two branches from one recorded base:

git worktree add -b w6-implementation ../w6-implementation BASE_SHA
git worktree add -b w6-review-tests ../w6-review-tests BASE_SHA
git worktree list

Branch separation cannot prevent incompatible assumptions. If one branch repairs the guard and the other changes a test to allow inactive owners, each can report green under its own expectation. Resolve the conflict against the contract, bring the reviewed commits into one candidate, recopy its files and rerun the checks on the combined snapshot. Test success on either old branch leaves the combined result unverified. For a change as small as this week's, sequential work usually costs less than a second worktree; record whether parallelism removed waiting or only added integration work.

docs.title: Week 6 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Use these explanations after your first attempt and keep each claim tied to recorded evidence.

docs.title: Q1a–Q1c: Verifying a model review
docs.text: Q1a. Run the inactive-owner input on the reviewed revision: the contract requires False and the candidate returns True. A check that fails before the fix and passes after it confirms the point. Q1b. The contract says inputs are booleans and the issue puts string parsing out of scope; cite that clause and the rule whose check the diff meets. The point asks for invented scope, so it is refuted. Q1c. Mark it cannot tell when the caller is not among the files you were given. Record which file and which call would decide it, and why you could not check it; do not call it confirmed or refuted.

docs.title: Q2a–Q2c: Boolean contract
docs.text: Q2a. An inactive owner is a distinguishing input. Q2b. The contract denies it; the unguarded expression can allow it through the owner term. Q2c. A matrix covering owner/staff and active/inactive cases falsifies a wrong revision.

docs.title: Q3a–Q3c: Review evidence
docs.text: Q3a. The review never tries an inactive account, so it omits the inactive-owner defect. Your own reproducer shows it: can_edit(False, True, False) returns True where the contract requires False. Record it as your own finding; it is not one of the review's points. Q3b. Run the reproducer on the same revision: a reproduced problem confirms the point, and a passing input or a met rule refutes it. Q3c. No; a public pass cannot authorize a merge or grade.

docs.title: Q4a–Q4c: Participation
docs.text: Q4a. Take the replay route without giving a reason: replay the review the teaching team recorded, or the labelled course-written sample until it is published, and verify each point. For your own change, write the plan and the change yourself, review it against REVIEW.md and ask a TA. Q4b. Record the route, the passed launcher check and the same verification evidence. Q4c. Shared work cannot replace an individual's review or explanation.

docs.title: Q5a–Q5c: Responsible records
docs.text: Q5a. Remove private chat, raw participant notes and unsupported authorship claims. Q5b. Record zero AI use explicitly when that is the case. Q5c. Count waiting for the launcher and the model as actual time spent, and record it apart from your hands-on review minutes, as the cost note does.

docs.title: Q6a–Q6b: Review scope
docs.text: Q6a. Keep the file list, context digest, revision and completed run record. Q6b. A fresh prompt can inherit the same missing caller or scope assumption, and a diff-only reviewer cannot see a change that is missing from the diff.

docs.title: Q7a–Q7c: Review comments and rules
docs.text: Q7a. The string-parsing comment is confirmed: the diff adds a str branch that the boolean-only contract rules out. Q7b. For the string parsing, cite the added diff lines. For the inactive-staff denial, test_inactive_staff ran and passed on the current revision, which refutes that comment. Q7c. A checkable rule names where it comes from and how a reviewer applies it to a diff or a run. For example: "R5 The change edits only the issue's target file. Source: the issue's Target line. Check: every path in change.diff is that target." Any rule with a source and a check that someone else can apply will do.

docs.title: Q8a–Q8b: Repeated runs
docs.text: Q8a. Record every run, request count, waiting time, review time and retained output. Q8b. Repetition does not add a new requirement check or explain what changed.

docs.title: Q9a–Q9c: Reviewing a request
docs.text: Q9a. Reading A: the owner of the document being edited. Reading B: any account that holds an owner role, for example one that owns a different document. Q9b. An account that owns document 7 asks to edit document 9: reading A denies it, reading B allows it. can_edit receives owner as a boolean, so the caller decides this input when it computes owner; no boolean test of can_edit alone separates the readings. Q9c. Ask: "Does 'owner' mean the owner of this document, or anyone with an owner role?" The fixture contract answers it with "the document owner".

docs.title: Q10a–Q10c: Handoffs (optional reading)
docs.text: Q10a. The synchronous handoff names the decision needed now, current context, permission state and stop condition. Q10b. The asynchronous handoff names the bounded command, inputs, expected artifact, deadline and evidence to return. Q10c. Verify the passed launcher check, allowed files, model or replay route, resource budget and stop status before remote execution.

docs.title: Q11a–Q11d: Worktrees (optional reading)
docs.text: Q11a. Resolve the guard and test-contract conflict against the requirement. Q11b. Rerun the combined revision, including the inactive-owner cases. Q11c. A worktree separates edits but does not contain a process or host. Q11d. A context file states instructions but cannot enforce a sandbox boundary.

docs.title: Q12a–Q13b: The background-agent pipeline
docs.text: Q12a. Only what the agent reports: a check on its own branch, which ran a test file the agent had just edited. You have not run anything yet. Run the test file from the base commit against the agent's code through the launcher. A failing existing test, such as one whose expected display value the agent rewrote, refutes the claim. Q12b. Cannot tell. Record what is missing, the page and a launcher run that renders it, and do not mark the claim confirmed or refuted. Q13a. Remove the merge grant: a person merges. Narrow the file grant to the files the issue names, and run the required check with the test file from the base commit, so the agent cannot edit what judges it. Q13b. Everything the pipeline hands back was written or chosen by the agent: the description, the report and the branch the check ran on. A check sees only what it tests, so an out-of-scope change can pass it. Deciding whether the diff matches the issue, and accepting it, is the maintainer's job.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval and transfer
docs.text:
Retrieval 1. Review the changed requirement, tests and implementation together. Retrieval 2. A new product decision and acceptance cases are required before mapping unknown to failed.

Transfer. The "no finding" establishes only that the reviewer found nothing in the diff it was given. The issue asks for a log call that the diff does not contain, so the reviewer could not see what is missing. Record the missing log call as your own finding. Accept only when a check on the revision you will merge shows that an edit to an archived build is refused and that the refusal is logged.

docs.title: Check your workflow reasoning
docs.text:
After the workshop, use the public answer guidance. Answer in your existing notes and revise one answer when the evidence changes. These questions are formative. Questions 10 and 11 cover the optional reading.

A model reviews the bundled candidate owner or staff and active and raises three points: the guard lets an inactive owner edit; the function should accept the strings "true" and "false"; a caller in another file may rely on the old behavior.

1a. What evidence would let you mark the first point confirmed?

1b. What evidence would let you mark the second point refuted?

1c. When must you mark the third point cannot tell, and what do you record?

For owner or staff and active, the fixture contract requires an owner or staff member to be active.

2a. Give an input that distinguishes the unguarded expression from the contract.

2b. What are the expected and observed results for that input?

2c. Which test would falsify a proposed revision?

A review of the bundled candidate says an active staff case passes and asks for string parsing.

3a. What did the review omit, and which input shows the omission?

3b. What evidence distinguishes a confirmed point from a refuted one?

3c. Can a passing public test authorize a merge or grade?

A student has no key for the approved model.

4a. Which supported route applies to the model review?

4b. What evidence is needed before execution?

4c. Can shared work replace the individual's first review or explanation?

A change record contains private chat, raw participant notes and a style-based authorship claim.

5a. Which material must be removed or corrected?

5b. How should no-AI use be recorded?

5c. How should time spent waiting be recorded?

A reviewer receives only declared files and context, with digests showing what was seen.

6a. What run evidence demonstrates that scope?

6b. What blind spot can remain even with a fresh prompt?

A sample run reports a missing inactive-staff denial and alleged string parsing.

7a. Which comment is confirmed?

7b. Which evidence settles each comment?

7c. Rewrite "code should be clean" as a rule a reviewer could check: give its source and its check.

After three green reruns of one change:

8a. Which execution costs belong in the record?

8b. Why is the third green run not, by itself, verification?

A draft request for the guard says only: "Owners can edit."

9a. Give two readings of "owners".

9b. Which input separates the two readings, and where in the code is that input decided?

9c. What do you ask the person who owns the request, and which words of the fixture contract answer it?

docs.title: Optional reading: workflow types and worktrees
docs.text:
A synchronous task needs discussion now; an asynchronous command-line task will be reviewed tomorrow.

10a. What belongs in the synchronous handoff?

10b. What belongs in the asynchronous handoff?

10c. Which execution, context, permission and stopping boundaries must be checked before remote execution?

Two worktrees start at the same revision. One changes the guard; the other changes the test expectation to allow inactive owners. Both report green tests.

11a. What must be resolved before the branches are combined?

11b. Which revision must be rerun after combining them?

11c. Why does a worktree fail to establish a sandbox boundary?

11d. Why does a context file fail to establish a sandbox boundary?

docs.title: The background-agent pipeline
docs.text:
A background agent's pull request for a dashboard issue says the tests pass, and its run report says the required check exited 0. The same change edited one existing test's expected value.

12a. What does the reported exit code establish, and which run would you make before believing the description's claim that nothing visible changed?

12b. The description also says a dashboard page now renders correctly, and no file you were given renders that page. Which outcome do you give that claim, and what do you record?

The pipeline's token may push agent/ branches, open a pull request, change any file and merge when the required check passes on the agent's branch.

13a. Which grant would you remove, and which would you narrow?

13b. After those changes, why should the pipeline still stop at a person's review before anything merges?

docs.title: Spaced retrieval: Weeks 4–5 specification and change safety
docs.text:
R1. A specification changes output order. Which requirement, tests and implementation evidence must be reviewed together?

R2. A refactor passes existing tests but changes an unknown status to failed. What new contract decision is required?

docs.title: Dashboard transfer
docs.text: A dashboard issue asks the edit guard to deny archived builds and to log every denied edit. The model reviewer saw only the diff and reports no finding; the diff repairs the guard but adds no log call. What does that "no finding" establish, and which check would decide acceptance?

docs.title: Review and delegate a bounded change
docs.text:
Week 6 · CI dashboard

What decides whether a review point holds?

docs.title: A small PR can hide a consequential case
docs.text:
Last week we protected caller behavior. This week we review an access decision before trusting the change.

Write your own first review before seeing an assistant's review.

docs.title: The permission contract
docs.text:
An account may edit exactly when it is active and is an owner or staff member.

Inputs are booleans. All other combinations must deny.

In the dashboard analogy, an archived build is inactive. The public fixture consistently names that state active.

docs.title: The proposed guard
docs.text:
return owner or staff and active

The reviewed example uses an active staff account and passes.

Course-authored candidate from the public fixture.

docs.title: Your first review
docs.text:
Choose a case the active-staff check does not cover. Write its inputs, required result and predicted candidate result.

Then identify the expression responsible. Do this independently before comparing findings.

docs.title: Operator precedence changes the policy
docs.text:
owner or (staff and active)

For owner=True, staff=False, active=False, the candidate returns True. The active requirement should apply to the owner too.

The finding has a cause and a specific unauthorized result.

docs.title: Mechanism: Delegation with an evidence handoff
docs.text:
A bounded issue moves through isolated work and a model review; you verify each point before anyone merges.

Delegation with an evidence handoff A bounded issue moves through isolated work and a model review; you verify each point before anyone merges. scoped issueisolated workmodel reviewyou verify

docs.title: A repair to challenge
docs.text:
return active and (owner or staff)

Do not stop at visual clarity. Which allowed and denied cases could falsify this repair?

docs.title: Both role paths need coverage
docs.text:
Active Owner Staff Required False False False Deny False True False Deny False False True Deny False True True Deny

Inactive state blocks every role combination.

docs.title: Authorized work must still succeed
docs.text:
Active Owner Staff Required True False False Deny True True False Allow True False True Allow True True True Allow

A deny-all repair would fail the legitimate cases.

docs.title: A reproducible finding
docs.text:
Location: access guard in candidate revision
Input: owner=True, staff=False, active=False
Required: deny; hand trace of candidate: allow
Cause: owner bypasses the active condition
Consequence: inactive owner's edit can be allowed

Add actual execution evidence when the check runs.

docs.title: Comparing an assistant's review
docs.text:
After saving your own finding, inspect these authored review claims:

A1: Active staff passes, so the guard is correct. A2: It must also parse the string "false".

Mark each confirmed, refuted or cannot tell. What decides it?

docs.title: Both claims are refuted
docs.text:
A1: the inactive-owner input is allowed. One passing case cannot establish the policy.

A2: the contract says inputs are booleans; string parsing is invented scope.

For a real assistant response, assess its actual claims; do not assume it made the same mistakes as this exercise.

docs.title: A bounded review request
docs.text:
Review this guard against the supplied boolean contract. For each finding, give a source location and distinguishing input. Do not change the implementation or expected results.

An assistant's finding remains a hypothesis until reproduced.

docs.title: Three outcomes for every review point
docs.text:
Confirmed: a reproducer shows it. An input and its actual result, a diff line or an evidence line.

Refuted: runnable evidence shows it is wrong, or the contract or issue shows the requirement it asserts does not exist.

Cannot tell: the files you have cannot decide it. Name what is missing.

docs.title: The workshop review cycle
docs.text:
Save your first review; reproduce one finding. Then compare the assistant review, revise and rerun unchanged checks.

Use the existing 45-minute activity and one record.

docs.title: Four questions about your PR
docs.text:
What changed, and why does the contract require it?

Which input could fail? What did you personally verify on this revision?

Completeness of an explanation does not make its claims true.

docs.title: Exit: a new state in the guard
docs.text:
The candidate adds suspended. The agreed policy says suspended accounts cannot edit, even when active and staff.

Give one distinguishing input and the check needed before acceptance.

docs.title: Review the request before you delegate it
docs.text:
A first draft of the issue says:

Only active owners and staff can edit.

Write two readings, an input that separates them and the question you would ask the request's owner.

docs.title: Words can group two ways, like operators
docs.text:
A: owners and staff must both be active. B: only owners must be active.

can_edit(active=False, owner=False, staff=True): A denies, B allows.

Ask before delegating. Until it is answered, a review point that depends on it is cannot tell.

docs.title: Three roles, three contexts
docs.text: You read the plan before anything is implemented.

docs.title: The reviewer sees the request, the change and the evidence
docs.text:
Its workspace holds issue.md, change.diff, evidence.txt and REVIEW.md. Nothing else: no plan, no implementer prompt, no drafted description.

The script refuses any other file; the run record lists what the reviewer saw.

docs.title: What can a fresh-context reviewer still miss?
docs.text:
It runs on the same model and sees only the diff.

Name one kind of defect it cannot catch from those inputs.

docs.title: Fresh context is not independence
docs.text:
Shared model, shared blind spots. A change that is missing from the diff is invisible in the diff.

So you verify each point, and you read the issue for what the diff lacks.

docs.title: Review rules a reviewer can check
docs.text:
R3  Inputs stay Python booleans; no parsing, no new input type.
    Source: contract "Inputs are booleans"; out of scope "Parsing strings".
    Check: the diff adds no str handling, conversion or default argument.

Every rule has a source and a check. "Code should be clean" has neither.

docs.title: Confirmed, refuted or cannot tell?
docs.text:
The sample change passes all seven checks.

C1 (R3): lines +6 and +7 add string parsing for active. C2 (R1): no check denies an inactive staff member.

Which evidence decides each comment?

docs.title: A reproducer decides, not the rule ID
docs.text:
Run the input, point at the diff line, or cite the evidence line.

A comment that cites a rule is still a claim. Rules that keep producing refuted points get rewritten by PR.

docs.title: No key? Replay the recorded review
docs.text:
The teaching team records a model review of the sample change. Replay it and verify each point the same way; until it is published, verify the course-written sample comments.

For your own M1 change, write the plan and the change yourself, review it against REVIEW.md and ask a TA.

docs.title: An issue is data, not authority
docs.text:
The issue names one target, the acceptance criteria and the check to run.

The script refuses an unpinned base, a test file as target, .. paths and unknown lines. It cannot branch, push, reach the network or run the check.

docs.title: The pipeline drafts; you explain
docs.text:
The unattended run exports a proposal, a diff and a draft PR description.

The four explanation questions stay as template prompts. The explanation check reports them incomplete until you answer from your own run.

docs.title: When to run unattended
docs.text:
Helps: independent task, exclusive file, written acceptance and check, time to review.

Costs: requests for every run you discard, review time, stale bases. Rerunning until green selects an output; it does not verify one.

docs.title: A background agent hands back a pull request
docs.text:
A label on an issue starts the agent in its own workspace. It returns a branch, a description and a run report.

Nobody watched the run. You are the first person to look.

docs.title: What would have merged?
docs.text:
The token may push agent/ branches, change any file and merge when the check passes on the agent's branch.

The agent's change also rewrote the expected value of test_format_minutes. What did the green check show?

docs.title: Checks the agent cannot edit; a person merges
docs.text:
Run the base commit's tests on the agent's code: FAIL: test_format_minutes.

Remove the merge grant. Narrow the files to what the issue names. Review every hunk and every claim before anyone merges.

docs.title: P2 and M1 carry this week's work
docs.text:
P2 has two halves: a review of its contract, then your first review of the change, a reproducer and the comparison.

M1 carries the delegated change, your review rules and each review point you verified.

Next week: even a careful review relies on tests. How do we find out which faults those tests can miss?

docs.title: Workshop and review
docs.text:
Worked notes · Workshop · Self-check

Course case · Week 0 execution route

Use the same work in the linked practice unit or project. No extra report.

docs.title: One change, one contract
docs.text:
This is a course-created synthetic exercise. No real account, document, participant or model session appears here. The bundled candidate deliberately needs review. It is not a captured AI response. workflow.py is the instructor's live demonstration: it requests a fresh candidate through the approved launcher, and separately requests review text after students have saved their own reviews.

Contract: inputs are Python booleans. An account may edit exactly when it is active and is either the document owner or a staff member. Inactive accounts cannot edit, including inactive owners and staff. An active outsider cannot edit. Overlapping roles are allowed. Return a Python boolean. Parsing strings and checking identity against a database are outside this small function's contract.

Files: access.py is the candidate, check_access.py contains public checks, and workflow.py generates text without executing the returned code. delegate.py runs one delegation role per launcher invocation (plan, implement, review, or the unattended issue run), reading only the files it names. Every stage of both scripts refuses the launcher's FAKE placeholder, which checks the connection only. issue-example.txt is an issue to copy to issue.md, review-rules-example.txt is a set of review rules to copy to REVIEW.md, and sample-run.en.md is a course-written sample of an issue run for review on the replay route. See the complete launcher instructions. Copy only the files a step names to your separate exercise directory, never the private repository or teacher answers.

Each launcher run works within the launcher limits. The issue stage uses two requests in one run and must return the complete target file. A timeout or limit refusal is evidence to record; do not rerun it to seek a better proposal. Without a key, use the replay route described in the notes.

Before opening an AI review, write your own finding with input, expected/observed behavior, location and consequence. Then run the public checks through the launcher. A passing test report from this workspace is practice evidence: the candidate can modify files in its own sandbox, so this harness is not a trusted grader or a source of formal scores.

docs.title: Shared context example
docs.text:
You can include this plain text in your existing context file. It states an agreement for each role, not an installed product configuration or permission enforcement:

Task: active account AND (owner OR staff) may edit.
Roles: implementer edits access.py; reviewer records findings in a separate file.
Tests: check_access.py is public; verify unchanged checks against the input snapshot.
Execution: course-sandbox only; no network, dependency install or private inputs.
Budget: one generation and one later review request; stop on a safety refusal.
Handoff: base revision, candidate diff, check results, four answers, AI-note ID.
Conflict: stop and recheck the contract before changing it or the test expectations.

A context file helps each role know the intended work. A permission policy enforces allowed operations, while a hook can provide a reminder or a check at an event such as a commit. Neither prose nor a hook replaces sandbox isolation. In this exercise the trusted launcher enforces the execution boundary; no new hook or tool adapter needs installing.

docs.title: A sample issue run to review
docs.text: Everything on this page is written by the course team to look like the output of one unattended run of delegate.py issue on issue-example.txt. It is not a captured model run. Use it until the teaching team's recorded review is published if you take the replay route, or to compare with your own run. Read it in the order a reviewer would receive it.

docs.title: The issue
docs.text: issue-example.txt, with Base set to the recorded base commit.

docs.title: The plan the run wrote (the reviewer does not see this)
docs.text:
1. Make the active check apply to both role paths.
2. Keep the function signature and return type.
3. Accept "true"/"false" strings for active, since callers may send form values.
Inputs to check: inactive owner, inactive staff, active outsider, active owner.

docs.title: change.diff
docs.text:
--- a/access.py
+++ b/access.py
@@ -3,4 +3,6 @@

 def can_edit(active: bool, owner: bool, staff: bool) -> bool:
     """Decide whether a synthetic account may edit a synthetic document."""
-    return owner or staff and active
+    if isinstance(active, str):
+        active = active.lower() == "true"
+    return active and (owner or staff)

docs.title: evidence.txt
docs.text: The author applied the proposed file on the issue branch and ran python check_access.py -v through the launcher. Course-written summary of that record: exit_code 0, seven checks run, all passed. If you can execute, apply this diff to your own copy and run the same command to see your actual result.

docs.title: Two review comments to classify
docs.text:
The course team wrote these in the style of an AI review that was given review-rules-example.txt as REVIEW.md:

C1 (R3) Lines +6 and +7 add string parsing for active. The contract allows booleans only.
   can_edit("false", True, False) now takes a code path the contract does not define.
C2 (R1) No check denies an inactive staff member. Input: can_edit(False, False, True);
   required: False.

Mark each comment confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and give the evidence that decides it: an input you run with its actual result, a diff line, or a line of the evidence. For cannot tell, name what is missing. Then answer: what did the reviewer catch that the plan and the implementer missed? Where did the extra scope come from?

docs.title: Week 7: Challenge the tests
docs.text: This directory holds Week 7 materials. You use a surviving mutant to choose a property and a reproducible fuzz input, then strengthen your M1 tests in the testing workshop.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Duration: 55 minutes, including verification, feedback and revision, within the budget for the Week 7 workshop and the testing workshop. Materials: notes, the public fixture, a keyboard-accessible text editor and terminal, and, for actual execution, a device that passed the Week 0 setup check. Grouping: pairs rotating driver/observer roles, or individual work with the same feedback checkpoint. Output: your changed assertions, actual failure/pass evidence and a short explanation of their relation to the contract. This is formative practice.

Each launcher command first repeats the launcher's safety checks, including a 30-second time-limit probe, so expect about 40 seconds per command. The table needs about twelve of your own runs, roughly eight minutes of waiting in total. Start a run, then read or write while it finishes. The instructor shows the pristine mutation, fuzz and replay runs on screen in class, so you do not rerun them here.

Minutes Action Evidence and LO 0-7 Read the contract and weak assertions in notes. Individually explain why each of the three assertions cannot distinguish an incorrect integer result. Three blind spots and proposed replacements (LO5) 7-15 Run weak, unit and property checks on the supplied candidate (three runs). Explain why a passing property does not settle rejection behavior. Actual outcomes, expected versus unexpected exception (LO5) 15-25 Write three meaningful replacements in weak_checks: an expected value, a boundary case and an invalid-input check. Keep the contract fixed. Rerun on the broken candidate before proposing a repair (one run). A demonstrated red test, then a length/ASCII repair proposal (LO4/LO5) 25-31 Switch roles. Run the mutation command on your revised checks (one run) and compare with the instructor's pristine result of weak 0/3, strong 3/3. Named survivor, or all three killed, and the distinguishing input (LO5) 31-39 Apply the repair to candidate.py. Rerun your changed checks, then unit, property, seeded fuzz and both replays on the repaired workspace (six runs). Repaired results; the "" and "12" replays now pass (LO5) 39-48 A peer points out one oracle blind spot or unsupported success claim. Revise a test or explanation and rerun the relevant case. Before/after evidence and visible revision (LO5) 48-55 Individually write what belongs in the M1 baseline and which security items remain open. Answer self-check Q4. Functional snapshot and individual attribution; Week 8 closure boundary (LO4/LO5)

At minute 15, offer help: (1) compare the asserted value with the contract; (2) try "9" and "12"; (3) use unit_checks and property_checks as public worked support. Keep the original public files separately so the published 0/3-versus-3/3 comparison can be reproduced. Your revised weak suite may produce different counts; report its actual revision and counts. verify_demo.py describes the original fixture, so run it on that original copy. It intentionally detects changed expected fixture behavior.

If time is consumed by setup, arrange supported continuation or the text exercise. Do not increase limits or use host execution. The testing workshop's four-hour and Week 7's 12-hour budgets are design/help checkpoints, not grading penalties. Extending the fuzz harness is optional and does not lower attainable marks when omitted.

docs.title: Execution route
docs.text:
Complete Week 0 setup before using the following execution route.

Run these trusted preparation commands from the reviewed course root. They copy only public synthetic files and resolve public configuration; they execute no exercise code on the host. The two workspaces are intentionally separate:

  • week07_pristine_work: keep an unmodified original copy for the demonstration
  • week07_repaired_work: use this one for student edits and repaired validation

Use distinct names and keep these variables for the subsequent commands.

week07_pristine_work=$(mktemp -d ./week07-pristine.XXXXXX)
week07_repaired_work=$(mktemp -d ./week07-repaired.XXXXXX)

cp lectures/week-07/fixture/candidate.py lectures/week-07/fixture/demo.py lectures/week-07/fixture/verify_demo.py "$week07_pristine_work/"
cp lectures/week-07/fixture/candidate.py lectures/week-07/fixture/demo.py "$week07_repaired_work/"
week07_profile=$(uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json)
week07_version=$(printf '%s' "$week07_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["version"])')
week07_digest=$(printf '%s' "$week07_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["digest"])')

The workspace contains only these files and your exercise edits. Never copy the whole private course checkout, teacher answers/tests, .git, credentials or user data. Use your editor for modifications. The launcher copies input into a bounded temporary workspace; no host workspace is mounted, no package installation is needed, and each invocation reruns the actual safety checks, about 40 seconds per command.

Run each command separately so an expected nonzero result does not hide the next case. Keep all baseline commands on the pristine workspace. Run these three yourself:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_pristine_work" -- python demo.py weak
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_pristine_work" -- python demo.py unit
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_pristine_work" -- python demo.py property

Expected: weak and property exit 0; unit exits 1 with IndexError.

The instructor runs the remaining pristine commands on screen in class. You do not need to rerun them during the activity; run them afterwards on your own pristine copy if you want your own record:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_pristine_work" -- python demo.py mutation
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_pristine_work" -- python demo.py fuzz --seed 7
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_pristine_work" -- python demo.py replay --text ''
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_pristine_work" -- python demo.py replay --text '12'
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_pristine_work" -- python verify_demo.py

Expected on the unmodified fixture workspace: mutation exits 0 and reports weak 0/3, strong 3/3; fuzz exits 1 with 109 cases and findings; the two replays exit 1 with unexpected_IndexError and accepted_invalid_input; verify_demo.py exits 0 with six checks. These are predicted synthetic fixture outputs, not a transcript of a model run. Inspect actual launcher results when executing.

First edit demo.py's weak_checks in $week07_repaired_work and use the changed-test commands before repairing the parser. Then edit candidate.py in that same mutable workspace and rerun regression checks in that repaired workspace. Keep public test expectations unchanged and do not move verify_demo.py to this workspace. Select --implementation candidate to exercise your edited candidate.parse_level; the name identifies the module, even after you repair it.

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_repaired_work" -- python demo.py unit --implementation candidate
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_repaired_work" -- python demo.py property --implementation candidate

All repaired regression commands should exit 0 on that revised workspace. fuzz with seed 7 should report no findings in the given corpus, which is not a proof. Replay successes show your revised invalid-input regression behavior is enforced. Leaving candidate.py unchanged still fails unit, fuzz and both replay checks. For an optional worked comparison, select the supplied demo.repaired function on the pristine workspace:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_pristine_work" -- python demo.py unit --implementation repaired

That comparison does not test your edits. Keep each run's output with its workspace, command and candidate revision; these commands do not export or overwrite files. No invocation calls a model: these supplied proposals are course-authored practice. For optional actual agent generation, use only the Week 0 model/broker route, give the contract and public fixture, and inspect its response as text before editing. All proposed tests, repairs, dependencies and harnesses still require launcher execution. Do not label a scripted proposal or FAKE response as an actual model experiment.

docs.text:
After replacing the assertions in weak_checks, run this on the mutable workspace before repairing its parser. It executes your new checks, not the original unit suite:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_repaired_work" -- python demo.py weak --implementation candidate

Keep that actual failure. After repairing candidate.py, rerun the same command. Then compare what your revised checks detect in the supplied mutant set:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week07_version" --digest "$week07_digest" --workspace "$week07_repaired_work" -- python demo.py mutation

The report's weak field now refers to your revised weak_checks; identify that revision. Its count can differ from the pristine fixture's published result. If an unexpected exception interrupts a mutant run, diagnose it; do not count every process failure as a kill.

If you cannot run the practices yet, annotate this synthetic text walkthrough: input "3" returns 3; input "12" returns 1 in the faulty parser despite the contract; input "" attempts indexing and raises IndexError. Predict which assertion or property distinguishes each case, then explain the proposed repair and M1 boundary. This text exercise provides learning support, not actual execution evidence.

docs.title: Week 7: Testing and verification with agents
Learning objectives
docs.text:
• LO4: preserve a legacy module's intended behavior during a repair, connect its regression evidence to your offline gate command, and explain what an M1 functional baseline establishes.
  • LO5: challenge generated tests with an independent oracle, a property, a mutation and a reproducible fuzz input; explain the limits of each result.

The activity and self-check map to both outcomes. LO4 is assessed individually in CP1 and the individual defense. LO5 is assessed individually in P2 and through CP1/CP2. The testing workshop feeds M1. A green run does not replace your own explanation of each failure and pass, and project work does not replace checkpoint work.

M1 timing: Week 7 produces a reproducible functional baseline snapshot showing the state of characterization tests, defect repairs, dependency upgrades and your CI result. This is not final M1 acceptance and does not establish that security work is complete. After the Week 8 security teaching and the security workshop, close all known planted vulnerabilities and scanner items, then undergo M1 security closure and final acceptance.

CI result in this course means the exit status and summary output of your own offline gate command: the one command your agent-readiness Checks row names, run on the baseline revision. If you do not have a gate command yet, record the test command you ran and say that no gate command exists yet. If a command could not run, record "not executed" and the reason instead of a result.

docs.title: The continuing dashboard case
docs.text:
The dashboard level field accepts exactly one ASCII digit and rejects every other string with ValueError. The supplied candidate passes the ordinary input "3" and the current happy-path test:

def parse_level(text: str) -> int:
    if text[0] in "0123456789":
        return int(text[0])
    raise ValueError("Invalid level")

Decision: What rejected input can distinguish the candidate from the product contract?

For "12", the candidate reads only the first character and returns 1. For "", indexing crashes with IndexError instead of the required ValueError. These are two different defects. Derive rejection cases from the single-ASCII-digit contract; valid-input properties alone miss this boundary. The exit variation later considers a different candidate, int(text), under this same contract.

Generate a test for an independently stated invariant. Mutate a correct candidate, inspect surviving mutants and choose an input that can distinguish the changed behavior.

Acceptance decision: Accept a test improvement when it detects a meaningful fault while preserving valid behavior. Explain the mutant denominator; a score by itself does not identify the remaining risk.

The integer-parsing fixture represents the level field in the continuing case. Keep its deliberately narrow input contract fixed when judging candidate tests.

This is a course-authored, hand-worked example. Actual execution evidence comes from your own checks.

docs.title: Specify the oracle before asking for code
docs.text:
This is a course-authored synthetic slice of the dashboard level field. A legacy configuration field represents a level. Its input domain is Python strings; callers are responsible for supplying a string. Its contract is:

requires: text is a string
accepts:  exactly one of "0", "1", ..., "9"
ensures:  an integer with the corresponding value, with no state changes
rejects:  every other string by raising ValueError

Thus "3" maps to 3; "12", "", whitespace and a non-ASCII digit are rejected. Exception message wording is deliberately unspecified. This lightweight specification is precise enough to make examples and properties executable. It is not a formal proof. A test explores selected executions; even complete enumeration of the ten accepted strings does not cover the infinite rejected-string domain.

Before generating a repair, write assertions for "3", "" and "12". Inspect the supplied candidate as text:

def parse_level(text: str) -> int:
    if text[0] in "0123456789":
        return int(text[0])
    raise ValueError("Invalid level")

Characterize the intended "3" behavior, but do not preserve acceptance of "12" merely because the old implementation does it. Record that disagreement as a defect against the explicit contract. For a real legacy ambiguity, seek a requirement decision before changing the oracle. An agent cannot settle the requirement by copying the code.

docs.title: Red, generate, green, then challenge green
docs.text:
Run all commands through the activity's launcher route. First run demo.py unit against the supplied candidate: it fails on the empty string with IndexError, where the test expects ValueError. In class the instructor replays "12" separately to show silent acceptance rather than a crash. A failed test due to an import or missing dependency is a setup problem, not a demonstrated behavioral defect.

Now propose a repair in your editor: check the length before indexing, and require one ASCII digit. Test the proposal through the same launcher. The public repaired function in demo.py supplies a worked comparison when you need help. It is teaching support, not a hidden testing workshop solution. Rerun the original tests unchanged. Then ask which defect could still pass them and add a distinguishing test. Only after this evidence should a refactor be considered; rerun again on the refactored revision.

This is agent TDD: the person fixes the intended behavior and reviews the tests before generation; the agent may propose tests or an implementation; actual execution judges the proposal. These supplied proposals are synthetic AI-style examples, not recorded model outputs. If you use an agent through the Week 0 route, give it only this public contract and fixture, and execute its test, harness and repair proposals through the course launcher. Do not give it private teacher tests, credentials, real user data or unrestricted shell/network access.

docs.title: Three assertions that cannot distinguish a wrong result
docs.text:
The following course-written sample represents an AI-style weak test. For the supplied integer-returning candidates, all three assertions pass even when the result is wrong:

result = parser("3")
assert result == result
assert parser
assert result or True

Explain each assertion's blind spot before replacing it. The call can still crash; these assertions do not make a program immune to exceptions. The activity asks for three meaningful replacements and evidence that each checks the contract rather than echoing the implementation. An agent's confident explanation is not that evidence.

docs.title: A property describes a family of inputs
docs.text:
For every integer n from 0 through 9, parsing str(n) must return an actual integer in range and round-trip to str(n). The public property_checks enumerates this whole small valid domain. It detects a constant-return parser that one happy-path example misses. It still passes the faulty candidate: rejection behavior needs its own checks.

In a larger property test, choose generators from the input domain, define invariants or relations independently of the implementation, and retain counterexamples. A round-trip between two equally faulty functions can agree for the wrong reason; here the independent numeric enumeration supplies the expected values. The classroom uses standard-library enumeration to expose the principle. It does not replace the course's selected property-testing tooling or the testing workshop's required explained property.

docs.title: Mutation tests ask whether a defect would be noticed
docs.text:
Our bounded mutation demo changes a correct original in three ways: return zero for all accepted strings, return zero only for "9", and accept trailing characters. First require the original to pass. Then run the same suite separately against each mutant. A mutant is killed when an assertion detects its changed behavior. A survivor shows a change the suite cannot see. It stays a survivor until a test kills it or a written contract reason shows that it is equivalent.

For this fixed classroom set, the weak suite kills 0 of 3, and the unit-plus-property suite kills 3 of 3. These are reproducible course fixture counts, using Python 3.12 and demo.py mutation through the launcher. They are not industry statistics, a testing workshop feedback goal or a course grade. The report names every mutant and its outcome.

In a real report, state the tool/configuration, original revision, tests, selected mutants and denominator. Investigate timeouts, invalid mutants and infrastructure failures separately; do not relabel them as behavioral kills. For this contract, a mutation changing only a ValueError message is equivalent and is excluded with that reason. The testing workshop's project fixes its denominator the same way: its public mutant_manifest.json, beside the mutants.json configuration, gives each equivalent or control entry a kind and a reason. Its scorer also reports a feedback_score, which is formative feedback only and never enters the course mark. Do not remove a surviving non-equivalent mutant just to improve that number. Line coverage records execution; mutation evidence asks whether a particular change was detected. Neither proves general correctness or security closure.

docs.title: Fuzz the boundary, then replay the input
docs.text:
The supplied fuzz function generates nine explicit boundary inputs plus 100 strings from a fixed alphabet with maximum length four, using a caller-specified seed. It compares observations with a separate mapping of accepted strings to values. Expected ValueError on an invalid string is normal; unexpected exceptions, accepted invalid strings and wrong results are findings. Catching every exception and returning success would hide the defect this harness is meant to discover.

In class the instructor runs demo.py fuzz --seed 7 on the unmodified fixture. The first finding is the boundary seed "" causing unexpected_IndexError. This is seeded discovery, not a claim that random search discovered it. It is already minimal by string length. The instructor replays it with demo.py replay --text ''; keep the exact input and add it as a regression before repair. "12" is replayed too: fuzzing must detect an incorrect result as well as crashes. You rerun both replays on your repaired workspace. For a longer finding, delete characters while preserving the same failure category; save the reduced input even when you also retain the seed. A seed alone may not reproduce a changed generator or runtime version.

An agent can propose an additional harness input or oracle, but independently check both and verify the harness on a known-bad and a repaired target. Extending this supplied harness is optional. The bounded random run is not exhaustive, coverage-guided fuzzing or a proof that no other defect exists. It uses only synthetic strings.

docs.title: Let the agent propose the harness, then verify it dynamically
docs.text:
An approved model can propose a property strategy, a mutation command or a small fuzz harness for the ci-dashboard validation boundary. Treat that response as a list of claims and candidate code. Inspect the oracle and run the proposal through the launcher; never let the proposal choose its own score or mutate the scoring tool. The locked course mutator changes the validation implementation from a fixed seeded configuration and reruns the submitted tests, while the course's standard-library property helper supplies bounded, reproducible examples. Dynamic results decide whether a claim survives. Week 3's mature-agent dissection applied the same rule to an agent's final summary: "all tests pass" stays a claim until a test result in the record, or your own launcher run, shows it.

For each surviving non-equivalent mutant, record the mutant, the missing observation and the model claim it challenges. Keep equivalent changes (such as an unspecified error-message wording change) outside the denominator with a written reason. A timeout, missing dependency or launcher failure is infrastructure evidence and is not a kill. Add one property with an independent expectation, then replay the same seeded fuzz input against the repaired revision. This is the verification loop of the testing workshop's agent-generated tests step. Without a key, start from its frozen replay response, a fixed proposal that you inspect and score the same way.

The workflow reflects the role of generated harnesses in current fuzzing practice; see the registered tool cards (tools/oss-fuzz-gen; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) and (tools/fuzzingbrain; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1). Those cards are context for the method, not performance claims about this course fixture.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Use the 55-minute activity, including peer feedback and visible revision. Keep one work product with its verification and short explanation, and add AI use once (or state no AI use). Reuse that evidence in the testing workshop and M1 where relevant; no second report or full conversation export is required. Personal reflection stays AI-off. Optional harness extensions do not change the full-mark requirements.

Week 7's published estimate is 12 total hours, including about two hours on your C2 contribution; the testing workshop's four-hour time box includes its workshop, verification and explanation. The activity fits within that work rather than adding another assignment. These are help and design checkpoints, not measured durations, penalties or automatic stopping rules. Ask for support if setup consumes the time box; do not move execution onto the host to catch up.

The main line of the testing workshop is mutation testing against its published feedback goal, one explained property and running the supplied fuzz example to explain a planted defect. Its own assignment supplies its feedback tool and feedback goal; this lecture invents neither. Reuse your test changes and failure/pass evidence in your M1 repository. The Week 7 baseline records commit, locked environment, commands, CI result (your offline gate command's result, defined above) and open security items. Week 8 teaching and the security workshop precede closure of all known planted vulnerabilities and scanner items and M1 final acceptance.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The execution route contains complete copyable commands, resolves the offline profile and copies only public fixture files. Every test, mutation and fuzz invocation stays inside scripts/course-sandbox, with no external network, host credentials or teacher assets. Complete the Week 0 launcher check first.

Read the launcher's actual exit code and bounded output, not just a printed success label. Expected candidate results: weak passes, valid-domain property passes, unit fails, fuzz fails, empty-input replay fails. Expected repaired results: unit/property pass, fuzz has no findings in its stated corpus, and both replays pass. Mutation counts are 0/3 weak versus 3/3 strong. verify_demo.py checks these expectations, seed reproducibility, invalid strings and oracle failures inside the launcher.

If a student changes the public checks to print success, that proves nothing about the parser. These are editable formative tools, not an authoritative scorer. Keep the contract and expected outputs fixed during repair, inspect the diff, and rerun the tests on the exact candidate used for the baseline. Preserve an unexplained failure as unresolved. Failures of launcher safety checks stop execution entirely.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake How to notice it Corrective action Generate implementation and derive all expected values from it Wrong result equals the same wrong result Write the contract oracle first; use explicit counterexamples Preserve a planted defect as characterization "12" is accepted despite the requirement Separate observed behavior from approved behavior Claim properties prove correctness Valid digits pass but empty input crashes Include invalid-input obligations and report tested domains Count any failed mutation run as a kill Missing dependency or timeout replaces an assertion Diagnose infrastructure separately and report every disposition Swallow fuzz exceptions Known-bad target reports no findings Check the harness against known-bad and repaired targets Treat a green gate run as security evidence or as your explanation Security items remain open, and the run does not say which behavior each test checks Record what the gate runs, explain your test changes, label the Week 7 functional baseline and finish security closure in Week 8

docs.text:
A property checks that parsed values are non-negative for generated digit strings. Does it cover negative or decorated inputs?

docs.text:
Before class, read the learning objectives and fixed contract in the notes. Attempt the first slide question before opening the worked explanation. After class, use the worked sections, activities and self-check. If you already saw a solution, mark the next attempt as informed practice.

The course case explains how this week connects to the product.

docs.title: One focused external reading
docs.text: • A generated input is not a verified finding (about 12 minutes, optional): read FuzzingBrain CRS — README, especially “What a run leaves behind”, to distinguish candidate harnesses or patches from crash reproduction, regression tests and other dynamic evidence. (tools/fuzzingbrain; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1)

docs.title: Week 7 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Compare these explanations with the contract and the evidence you recorded.

docs.title: Q1a–Q1c: Oracles
docs.text: Q1a. Compare each result with the explicit contract and a meaningful expected value, not a truthy or non-empty value. Q1b. For example, parser("3") returning 0: all three weak assertions still pass, but assert parser("3") == 3 fails. Another is parser("12") returning 1, which a check that "12" raises ValueError detects. Q1c. Yes. A better assertion still needs an execution result and an exception or timeout check.

docs.title: Q2a–Q2c: Mutation
docs.text: Q2a. nine_to_zero and accept_trailing survive; all_zero is killed by parser("3") == 3. Q2b. For n in 0..9, require parser(str(n)) == n; this kills nine_to_zero. Q2c. Require parser("12") to raise ValueError; this kills accept_trailing.

docs.title: Q3a–Q3c: Fuzz evidence
docs.text: Q3a. The contract requires ValueError for empty input, so IndexError violates the fixture contract. Q3b. Keep the exact input "" and the command demo.py replay --text '' through scripts/course-sandbox. On the pristine workspace it exits 1 (shown in class, or your own later run); with --implementation candidate on your repaired workspace it exits 0. Retain both results with the input and revision. Q3c. A clean 109-case run does not prove untested inputs or absence of a different defect.

docs.title: Q4a–Q4c: Security completion
docs.text: Q4a. For each known security item (every scanner finding and every planted vulnerability you know of), a negative test or local reproduction that fails before the fix and passes after it, plus a rerun of the scanner and your offline gate command on the same revision. Green functional tests and locked dependencies say nothing about these items. Q4b. Run the Week 8 local attack and defense regressions. Q4c. Explain the chosen property, mutant, reproducer and verification in the personal record.

docs.title: Q5a–Q5c: TDD
docs.text: Q5a. A test for "12" must go red when only one ASCII digit is allowed. Q5b. Add the requirement test, implement the smallest change, then rerun the old and new cases. Q5c. Execute generated code and tests through the course launcher.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval
docs.text: Retrieval 1. Refuse the unpinned host script and environment export at the launcher boundary. Retrieval 2. Add the reviewed diff, input contract, reproducer and completed check.

docs.title: Dashboard transfer
docs.text: No. The generator produces only digit strings, so a negative input such as "-1" or a decorated one such as " 3" or "+3" is never tried. A discriminating check calls the parser on those inputs directly and requires ValueError for each. Even if they were generated, non-negativity is the wrong oracle for them: a parser that wrongly returns 3 for " 3" still passes it.

docs.title: Exit question: int(text)
docs.text: int(text) accepts many strings this contract rejects: "12" gives 12, " 3" and "+3" give 3, "٣" (a non-ASCII digit) gives 3, and "-1" gives -1. A check that the result is non-negative exposes only the negative case; every other example returns a non-negative integer and passes. Check rejection directly: each of these inputs must raise ValueError.

docs.text:

R2. A review has only an agent report, not the diff. What evidence must be added before treating the finding as actionable?

docs.text:
Week 7 · CI dashboard

Would our tests notice a meaningful fault?

docs.title: A passing check still has a boundary
docs.text:
Week 6 required evidence for a review claim. This week we inspect the checks themselves.

The dashboard's level field accepts exactly one ASCII digit.

docs.title: The parser contract
docs.text:
Input: a Python string.

Exactly "0" through "9" return the corresponding integer. Every other string raises ValueError.

Exception-message wording is unspecified. There are no state changes.

docs.title: The actual public candidate
docs.text:
def parse_level(text):
    if text[0] in "0123456789":
        return int(text[0])
    raise ValueError("Invalid level")

parse_level("3") == 3 passes.

docs.title: Two invalid strings, two different failures
docs.text:
Trace "12" and "" through the candidate.

For each, state the required behavior and the predicted behavior. Keep the exception type precise.

docs.title: Acceptance and rejection are both behavior
docs.text:
Input Contract Candidate hand trace "12" ValueError Returns 1 "" ValueError Raises IndexError

The first silently accepts invalid input. The second fails through an unintended exception.

docs.title: Mechanism: Red, generate, green, then challenge green
docs.text:
You fix the contract and tests first. The agent only proposes; a launcher run on the unchanged tests decides.

Red, generate, green, then challenge green The person fixes the contract and tests. A red run shows the empty string raising IndexError. The agent proposes a repair. A launcher run with the tests unchanged decides: still red sends the proposal back for revision; green leads to a challenge with a mutant, a property or a fuzz input. A new distinguishing test is added and the suite is rerun with the earlier tests unchanged. contract + testsfixed by you red run"" → IndexError agent proposesa repair (generate) launcher runtests unchanged greenon this suite only still red: revise the proposal challenge greenmutant, property, fuzz add a test thattells the defect apart rerun: earlier tests unchanged You: the contract, the oracle, the testsAgent: proposed tests or codeExecution: judges every proposal

docs.title: A length check before indexing
docs.text:
if len(text) == 1 and text in "0123456789":
    return int(text)
raise ValueError("Invalid level")

Keep the rejection tests and valid cases unchanged during repair. Then challenge what the green suite might still miss.

docs.title: Which assertion compares with the requirement?
docs.text:
result = parser("3")
assert result == result
assert parser
assert result or True

Could all three pass if the result were 0? What could still make the function call fail?

docs.title: An oracle supplies an independent expectation
docs.text:
assert parser("3") == 3

The contract supplies 3; the candidate does not. The weak assertions can accept a wrong integer, though the call can still crash.

Replace them with a value check, a boundary case and a rejection check.

docs.title: A property covers a family of inputs
docs.text:
For each integer n from 0 through 9:

result = parser(str(n))
assert type(result) is int
assert result == n

Here the valid domain is small enough to enumerate completely. The rejected-string domain is still untested by this property.

docs.title: Deliberate faults test the tests
docs.text:
A mutant is an intentionally changed implementation. A behavioral assertion failure kills it.

Does the suite notice a deliberate fault? A correct original must pass the suite first. Apply one mutant and rerun the same suite. If an assertion fails, the mutant is killed. If every test passes, it survived: add a test that kills it, or write the contract reason it is equivalent. A timeout or setup failure is infrastructure evidence, not a kill. correct originalmust pass the suite first apply one mutanta deliberate change rerun the same suitethrough the launcher an assertion failskilled every test passessurvived timeout or setup failureinfrastructure, not a kill add a test that kills it, orwrite the contract reason it is equivalent

docs.text:
The only assertion is parser("3") == 3.

Mutant Deliberate change all_zero Every valid input returns 0 nine_to_zero Only "9" returns 0 accept_trailing Accept a digit followed by extra text

Predict killed or survived for each.

docs.title: Survivors point to missing cases
docs.text:
all_zero is killed by "3". nine_to_zero survives; "9" -> 9 distinguishes it. accept_trailing survives; "12" -> ValueError distinguishes it.

A survivor shows a change the suite cannot see. It stays a survivor until a test kills it or a contract reason shows it is equivalent.

docs.title: The denominator has a meaning
docs.text:
Report which mutations were selected and each outcome.

An error-message-only change is equivalent under this contract. A missing dependency or timeout is infrastructure evidence, not a behavioral kill. The testing workshop's scorer reports a feedback_score: formative feedback only, never a course mark.

Do not discard an unexplained survivor to improve the score.

docs.title: Fuzzing searches beyond the chosen examples
docs.text:
A harness generates inputs and compares each observation with the independent contract.

The supplied harness combines explicit boundary seeds with bounded random strings. It accepts a reproducible seed.

Expected ValueError is normal; unexpected acceptance is a finding too.

docs.title: A finding must survive replay
docs.text:
input: ""
reason: unexpected_IndexError

Why is this a defect? What is the regression expectation? Does a saved random seed alone identify this exact input forever?

docs.title: The input and failure category make replay useful
docs.text:
Retain the exact string and expect ValueError after repair. The empty string is already minimal by length.

For a longer input, remove characters while retaining the same failure. Keep the generator/runtime version as well as its seed.

docs.title: An agent proposes a harness; execution verifies it
docs.text:
Give the approved model one M1 contract and ask for tests, a property and a bounded fuzz input.

Run the proposal through the launcher, then let the locked, seeded course mutator change domains/validation.py and rerun the tests. The course mutator is a local, standard-library tool; (tools/oss-fuzz-gen; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3) and (tools/fuzzingbrain; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1) are context for the model-proposed harness pattern, not tools used by this run.

Record each surviving mutant, the claim it challenges and the independent property you added.

Steps and a no-key frozen replay: agent-generated tests.

docs.title: Workshop: improve your own checks
docs.text:
Replace the weak assertions, run your changed suite on the faulty candidate, and retain the failed result before repair.

Then compare the repaired behavior and the supplied mutation/fuzz runs. Keep the pristine fixture separately for its published comparison.

docs.title: Feedback on an untested domain
docs.text:
A peer observes that your property generates only valid digits.

Add an invalid-input obligation and explain why it reaches behavior that the original generator never visited.

docs.title: Exit: conversion is not this contract
docs.text:
A fresh proposal simply returns int(text).

Give an input it accepts that this contract rejects. Would checking only that the returned value is non-negative expose it?

docs.title: M1 has a functional baseline
docs.text:
The testing workshop's explained checks support the Week 7 functional baseline. Week 8 and the security workshop address the remaining known security items.

Next week we ask whether a refused action could still cause an effect.

docs.title: Workshop and review
docs.text:
Worked notes · Activity · Self-check

Testing workshop · Course case · Week 0 execution route

Use the same work in the testing workshop and M1. No extra report.

docs.title: Public files
docs.text:
• candidate.py
  • demo.py
  • verify_demo.py

docs.title: Week 8: Protect the agent and the application
docs.text: This directory holds Week 8 materials. You separate data from authority, reproduce an inert local attack and check that permitted work still succeeds; the security workshop closes M1 security issues.

docs.title: Purpose and materials
docs.text:
Proposed duration: 120 minutes within existing practical work. Materials: notes, public fixture guide, text editor, terminal and the course-supported execution route. Mode: individual work with an optional written comparison. Output: one existing work record containing the candidate, actual verification and your own short explanation (LO5, LO7).

Minutes Action Evidence 0-10 Read the contract and prepare only public files. State the permitted input, output and boundary. 10-20 Predict from the contract and displayed candidate excerpt before opening full fixture comments or checks. Input, expected result and proposed result. 20-40 Run the public check, propose one repair and rerun the same check. Preserve the actual original failure, your change and the rerun, including denied_unlisted. 40-70 Run the FAKE agent replay, harden the policy and inspect every decision. Dangerous effects are absent while health still passes. 70-110 Complete the 40-minute triage drill. One disposition per finding, the repaired verifier run and one wrong agent claim. 110-120 Record your evidence and decision, then read the handoff. Regression evidence, remaining limits and your accept/narrow/observe/stop decision.

The generation packet in the execution route is optional and sits outside these 120 minutes.

If preparation consumes the first ten minutes, ask for support and start the text trace. Do not spend the whole session repeatedly retrying setup. During the repair block, use the contract hint in the notes if the repair is still unclear; do not replace individual explanation with copying a solution. Timing is a help checkpoint, not a penalty.

Save your own expected results from the fixed contract before opening the worked explanation or public checks. If you already saw the answer, identify this as informed practice.

docs.title: Execution route
docs.text:
Use Week 0 setup for access and execution requirements. These preparation commands copy only public course files; they do not run the exercise on the host. Start from the reviewed course root. Use a new directory name if this one already exists; do not overwrite another attempt.

mkdir week08-work
cp lectures/week-08/fixture/candidate.py week08-work/
cp lectures/week-08/fixture/exercise.py week08-work/
cp lectures/week-08/fixture/demo.py week08-work/
cp lectures/week-08/fixture/verify_demo.py week08-work/
week08_profile=$(uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python infra/hosted/resolve_profile.py --profile offline --json)
week08_version=$(printf '%s' "$week08_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["version"])')
week08_digest=$(printf '%s' "$week08_profile" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["digest"])')

Run the public check, then use the identical command after editing only candidate.py in your editor:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week08_version" --digest "$week08_digest" --workspace week08-work -- python exercise.py

Expected fixture behavior: the unchanged starter's public check exits 1; a contract-correct repair should exit 0 with every named check passing. Compare these predictions with your actual launcher and exercise results. No model is called by these commands.

Optional, outside the 120-minute plan: the generation-plus-verification route repeats the same contract as a generated packet. It uses the same launcher and a fresh output file. Generate the synthetic packet first, then verify that unchanged packet after editing only candidate.py:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week08_version" --digest "$week08_digest" --workspace week08-work -- python demo.py > week08-demo-launcher.json
python3 -c 'import json; from pathlib import Path; envelope=json.loads(Path("week08-demo-launcher.json").read_text()); assert envelope["exit_code"] == 0; Path("week08-work/generated.json").write_text(envelope["stdout"])'
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version "$week08_version" --digest "$week08_digest" --workspace week08-work -- python verify_demo.py generated.json

The first command is generation, not a model run. The second is verification. The starter is expected to exit 1 because denied_export and denied_unlisted observe an effect; after a bounded repair it should exit 0.

An exercise assertion/report mismatch is different from a launcher safety or preparation failure. If the launcher refuses execution or reports a safety failure, stop and use the course support route; do not change the executor, mount private assets, weaken limits or run the proposed code on the host. Missing exercise output is not evidence that the candidate passed.

docs.title: Agent-loop injection and hardening
docs.text:
