"own_check": {
  "finding_id": "own-<short-name>",
  "kind": "new-defect",
  "requirement": "R<n>",
  "disposition": "confirmed",
  "evidence": {"check": "<check>", "args": {<its keys>}, "command": "<printed command>"}
}

"own_check": {
  "finding_id": "own-<short-name>",
  "kind": "scope-check",
  "requirement": "R<n>",
  "result": "no-defect-observed",
  "scope": "<the range you checked>; <the boundary that stays unchecked>",
  "evidence": {"check": "<check>", "args": {<its keys>}, "command": "<printed command>"}
}
  • new-defect: an input that no recorded claim and not the worked row is about, whose observation breaks a frozen requirement; or
  • scope-check: such an input whose observation shows no defect, with a sentence naming the checked range and its boundary.

When the five rows and the own check are filled, run the verifier. Use a fresh output name on every retry:

sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST \
  --workspace week12-audit-work --output week12-audit \
  -- python verify_audit.py --submission student-audit.json

docs.title: Your M3 timeline
docs.text:
When What you do By the end of Week 11 Tag a clean revision of your project, check the tag and push it, as in Tag your M3 snapshot After the tag deadline The teaching team runs the model audit on your tag and sends you a copy of its output and run record; keep the copy unchanged Week 12 workshop, last 25 minutes Start your own record: label the tag, write a plan line for every finding and run the first check Rest of Week 12 Verify every finding and add your own check; plan about five hours for it Published M3 deadline Submit your verification record

Week 12's published estimate is nine hours. The class, the user test scheduled this week and the self-check take most of the rest.

Your own audit follows the same steps as the drill. Check out the tag in a separate worktree, so that every observation comes from the frozen revision, and run each check through the launcher as in the project workshops:

git -C PROJECT_REPO worktree add ../m3-check m3-freeze-12

For each finding in your copy, write the requirement from your project's acceptance criteria, then the check, input and expected observation. The M3 instructions say what each disposition needs: a test that fails on the tag or a repeatable reproduction to confirm, runnable evidence against the claim to refute, or the missing input named for cannot tell. Split a finding whose parts differ. Your own check probes a path the audit did not cover, or bounds a clean range.

docs.title: Tag your M3 snapshot
docs.text:
In a real M3 audit the model reads only your frozen snapshot. The M3 instructions require that it holds only your own work: no participant material, including de-identified notes, and no credentials, session logs or unrelated personal data. By the end of Week 11, confirm the tree is clean, create an annotated tag and record the commit it names:

git status --porcelain       # empty output
git tag -a m3-freeze-12 -m "M3 snapshot"
git rev-parse m3-freeze-12^{commit}

List every path the tag contains; the audit receives exactly these:

git ls-tree -r --name-only m3-freeze-12

Then scan the tagged tree, not your working copy. From the course root, with PROJECT_REPO replaced by your checkout, copy the security workshop's scanner and the tagged files into a new workspace and run the scan through the launcher:

mkdir -p m3-scan-work/tagged
cp -R capstone/security-workshop/student/scan m3-scan-work/scan
git -C PROJECT_REPO archive m3-freeze-12 | tar -x -C m3-scan-work/tagged
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST \
  --workspace m3-scan-work -- python scan/run_scans.py --target tagged

In the report, which is the launcher's stdout, the secret entry under counts must be 0, or each secret finding must be an sk-EXAMPLE value you recorded as an exception. If a path holds participant material or a real credential, do not submit that tag: revoke a leaked key with its provider and tell the teaching team. Otherwise push the tag by the end of Week 11, because a plain git push does not send tags:

git push origin m3-freeze-12

The M3 rubric shows how your verification is marked. Keep the user tests scheduled across Weeks 11-13 going while the audit runs; M4 needs all three (preparing user tests).

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
verify_audit.py exits zero only when all five recorded claims and the own check have reproducible evidence. It accepts exactly these meanings:

  • confirmed: the runnable observation demonstrates the stated defect on this snapshot;
  • refuted: the runnable observation contradicts the stated defect; or
  • undetermined: the snapshot lacks the input or configuration needed to decide, and the missing item is named.

The verifier holds each claim as the check and inputs it is about and as its reach: one input, some input, every input, or each member of a listed set. That is the question, not the answer. It checks the snapshot, the check name, the arguments and the canonical command, then runs the deterministic check and derives the supported disposition from the observation. Arguments must be exactly the keys the check takes, with private a JSON true or false and role either viewer or owner, so the verifier judges the same input the check ran.

It rejects an input that does not test the claim, a disposition the observation does not support, an observation that cannot decide the claim's reach, an item with no evidence, an empty undetermined reason, a claim about a listed set without one part per member, a different command and a missing own check. Each rejection names the key, the command or the observation it used. It does not call a model and model output never enters a scoring path.

Evidence conflicts go to the human integrity process; an automatic authorship detector does not decide responsibility.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a hand prediction as a run.
  • Running the first check that looks related instead of the input the claim describes.
  • Recording the launcher-prefixed command, or spaced JSON arguments, instead of the command the check printed.
  • Refuting a claim about some input because the inputs you tried behaved.
  • Confirming a claim about every input from one input that showed the problem in one place.
  • Marking a claim with an overstated scope with one word instead of splitting it.
  • Calling a claim cannot tell because a search was unfinished, when the snapshot holds what decides it.
  • Calling a false positive confirmed because its wording sounds plausible.
  • Using a different revision or changing the evidence arguments after the run.
  • Calling missing production configuration a defect, or "deciding" it with a check of a different path, instead of undetermined.
  • Forgetting to probe one path the recorded review did not mention, or failing to bound a clean path.
  • Reusing evidence from a repaired revision to close a finding on the frozen revision.

docs.title: Week 12 readings
docs.text: Before class, read the notes, label the frozen snapshot with its requirements R1–R6 and answer the first slide question: which of the review's claims can this snapshot decide, and with which input? After class, use the workshop and self-check to revisit one evidence row. The public fixture in lectures/week-12/fixtures/ is the only required example; it is synthetic and contains no model call.

docs.title: Week 12 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Keep each audit conclusion tied to a frozen snapshot, a requirement, the exact command and the observed state. Read the claim's wording first: it sets what one run can decide.

docs.title: Q1
docs.text: A hand trace is a prediction, not an observation. Write the prediction, mark execution as unavailable and leave the disposition empty. The row can carry a disposition only after a check runs on the frozen tag through the launcher and you keep its printed command and output. It is not undetermined either: the snapshot holds what decides the claim; it has just not been run.

docs.title: Q2
docs.text: refuted. The claim is about every file type, so one refused type is a counterexample. Keep the bound in the scope sentence: "Checked report.exe on the frozen tag: refused. This refutes acceptance of any file type; it does not show that every disallowed type is refused."

docs.title: Q3
docs.text: Both are wrong. The claim is about some query, so queries that behave show only where the problem is not; they cannot make it refuted. It is not undetermined either, because the snapshot holds the search code that decides it. Read the rule the query builder applies, for example which fields it matches and how it combines the owner filter with the search terms, and try queries at that rule's edges. Keep each query you tried. One query that lists another user's report makes the claim confirmed.

docs.title: Q4
docs.text: Build the input at the requirement's edge: a test that failed on one revision and passed on the next, and never both on the same revision. By the requirement it is stable, but a scorer that only looks for a pass and a fail anywhere in the history would rank it flaky. Run the scorer on that history. If it ranks the test as flaky, the claim is confirmed. If not, try the next edge, such as runs of one revision recorded under two build numbers, before you decide anything.

docs.title: Q5
docs.text: Split the claim into three parts, one per handler, each with its own evidence: the handler that skips the check is confirmed, and the two that call it are refuted. A single refuted would hide the handler that really skips the check. A single confirmed would assert that the other two skip it, which your evidence contradicts.

docs.title: Q6
docs.text: The scan read the tagged tree, not the deployment settings, so it does not test the claim. A clean result there says nothing about a file it never read. Mark the row undetermined and name the missing input: the deployment settings. Do not close it with evidence about a different input, and do not mark it confirmed because of a different defect.

docs.title: Q7
docs.text: A green suite shows only the paths its tests exercise, and it may hold no test that requests another user's export as a viewer. Passing tests do not refute the claim. Write a check that makes that request on the frozen tag and records what comes back, then mark the claim by that observation. If you tried only some exports, bound the conclusion to those.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text: Probe a sibling the audit did not cover: another export format built by a different function, with an input that tests the same requirement the audit checked on export_csv. If it shows a defect, the own check is a new defect with its command and output. If it is clean, the scope sentence names what you checked, for example "the PDF export with these names", and the boundary you did not check, such as the remaining formats.

docs.title: Q9
docs.text: Only your own work: no participant material, including de-identified notes, and no credentials or unrelated logs. List the tag with git ls-tree -r --name-only m3-freeze-12 and scan the tagged tree for secrets before you push it by the end of Week 11. Send an evidence conflict to the human integrity process, not an automatic authorship detector.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval
docs.text: Retrieval 1. Add a JSON contract, parser checks, malformed and missing-field cases, an Unknown route and regressions. Retrieval 2. A timeout could hide a completed job or a job that never started; inspect persisted state by operation key and verify the current result.

docs.title: Check your reasoning
docs.text:
These questions use situations outside the workshop fixture, so you apply the method rather than recall the drill. Use the notes and answer before you read the public answer guidance.

  1. In your own project you read a filter function and conclude by hand that it drops the last row, but the launcher is down and nothing has run. What do you write in that finding's row today, and what must happen before the row can carry a disposition?
  2. A review says: "The upload endpoint accepts any file type." Your requirement allows only .csv and .json. You send report.exe and the endpoint refuses it. Which disposition does that one run support, and what scope sentence keeps the conclusion within what you checked?
  3. A review says: "Some search query makes the results page list another user's reports." You try three ordinary queries and each lists only your reports. One classmate wants to mark the claim false, another wants to mark it as impossible to decide. What is wrong with each, and what do you do next?
  4. A review says, with no function or input named: "The flaky-test scorer can rank a stable test as flaky." Your requirement says a test is flaky only if it both passed and failed on the same revision. Turn the claim into a check: which input would you build first, and which observation would decide the claim?
  5. A review says: "Every handler in routes.py skips the permission check." The file has three handlers. Your check shows that two call the permission check and one does not. Write the record for this claim, and say what a single-word record would lose.
  6. A review says the deployment settings store a database password in plain text. Those settings are not in your snapshot. A classmate runs the secret scan on the tagged tree, sees no secrets and wants to close the finding. What is wrong with that evidence, and what does the row say instead?
  7. In your own project every test passes, and a model claims that a viewer can download another user's export. A classmate dismisses the claim because the suite is green. What is wrong with that, and what would you run instead?
  8. The audit of your project examined export_csv and reported nothing about the other export formats. Which path would you probe for your own check, and what must a clean result say to count as a scope check?
  9. Your M3 tag is due at the end of Week 11. Which files may it contain, how do you check them before you push it, and where should an evidence conflict go?

Keep one revised answer beside the launcher output. Do not submit a generic transcript.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval: Weeks 10–11 evaluator and recovery
docs.text:
Answer these two short prompts after the workshop. They revisit an earlier decision so that the evidence, not a memorized label, is carried forward.

R1. Retrieval 1. A scorer accepts a scalar answer but the contract changes to JSON. Which parser and malformed cases must be added?

R2. Retrieval 2. A timeout leaves no persisted-state observation. Name two possible histories and the next discriminating check.

Use the same evidence-first format as the questions above.

docs.title: Verify a model audit with reproducible evidence
docs.text:
Week 12 · LO7, LO9

Which of the review's claims can this snapshot decide, and with which input?

docs.title: M3 is individual verification
docs.text:
You push a frozen tag by the end of Week 11; the teaching team records one review of it.

You mark every finding confirmed, refuted or cannot tell, and add one check.

The model text is evidence to inspect, never a score.

docs.title: Freeze before reading
docs.text:
snapshot: week12-audit-snapshot
feature: report view, status, export, archive and scoring
requirements: R1-R6
source revision: <frozen revision>
inputs: <the check and input you chose for each claim>
outside scope: production-only configuration

A clean label keeps evidence attached to the intended revision.

docs.title: Frozen requirements
docs.text:
• R1 access: a viewer or an owner reads a public report; no role reads a private body
  • R2 status: only ready and queued are accepted
  • R3 paths: every exported or archived path stays under /srv/reports
  • R4 secrets: no export configuration exposes a secret directory
  • R5 scoring: the private-count scorer gives 1 only for the right count
  • R6 root: the report root is written once, as REPORT_ROOT

Judge each claim against these, not against the review's wording.

docs.title: A review is a hypothesis
docs.text:
A plausible sentence is not an observation.

Preserve the requirement, input, expected effect and protected state.

Run the exact question before saying confirmed.

docs.title: Why over-assertion happens
docs.text:
A salient token can trigger a shortcut.

The review may miss an allowlist, a guard that covers only one branch, or a sibling that does it right.

Run the exact input and state before accepting the claim.

docs.title: Why omissions happen
docs.text:
A named route is only one path.

Probe a sibling path, boundary value or protected-state change.

A clean result is bounded by the range you checked.

docs.title: The recorded review: five claims
docs.text:
Security, evaluation and maintenance claims, each with an id.

Most point at a function. One is prose only.

No check, input or answer is given: you choose them.

Course-authored practice record; no model wrote it.

docs.title: One worked row
docs.text:
Claim (not in the review): an owner can read the body of a private report.

  • Requirement: R1
  • Check and input: private-report-view, {"private": true, "role": "owner"}
  • Prediction: if the claim holds, the body is visible
  • Observation: deny, body_visible: false
  • Disposition: refuted, for this one input

docs.title: What one run can decide
docs.text: The claim is about One run can one input confirm or refute it some input confirm it, with a witness every input refute it, with a counterexample each member of a listed set decide that member only something outside the snapshot show it cannot be read

docs.title: An unfinished search is not a disposition
docs.text:
Inputs that behave do not refute a claim about some input.

The snapshot still decides it, so it is not cannot tell either.

Read the rule the code applies; probe its edges; keep every input you tried.

docs.title: Turn a prose claim into a check
docs.text:
1. Name the requirement it says is broken.
  2. Find the check that exercises that behaviour.
  3. Write the input that would show the problem, and the expected observation.
  4. Choose inputs at the rule's edges, not typical values.

docs.title: Split an overstated claim
docs.text:
"Every function does X" often holds for one function and not another.

Record one part per member, each with its own evidence and disposition.

One word would either hide a real defect or assert a false one.

docs.title: Bound the unknown
docs.text:
A claim about something outside the snapshot cannot be decided from it.

Disposition: undetermined; name the missing input.

A check of a different path does not decide it.

docs.title: Add an own check
docs.text:
Probe a path that no claim is about: a sibling of the one the review followed.

A defect: record the input, command and observation.

Or: “I checked this range; no defect was observed; this boundary remains outside scope.”

docs.title: Evidence record
docs.text:
finding_id    the id in model-audit.json
requirement   R1-R6
disposition   confirmed | refuted | undetermined
evidence      the check and args you chose, and the printed command
parts         one per member, for a claim about a listed set
missing       required for undetermined
scope         the range checked and what stays outside

docs.title: Run one check
docs.text:
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST \
  --workspace week12-audit-work \
  -- python audit_packet.py --check private-report-view --args '{"private":true,"role":"owner"}'

Copy the command the check prints: it starts at python and uses compact, sorted JSON.

docs.title: A runnable command has identity
docs.text:
The verifier checks:

  • frozen snapshot
  • check name and arguments
  • that the input tests the claim
  • canonical command
  • observation against the disposition

Changing an argument changes the question.

docs.title: The verifier is deterministic
docs.text:
The verifier derives the supported disposition from the public observation.

No model output enters a scoring path.

docs.title: Run through the approved launcher
docs.text:
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST \
  --workspace week12-audit-work --output week12-audit \
  -- python verify_audit.py --submission student-audit.json

Use resolver values and a fresh output directory.

docs.title: What the verifier rejects
docs.text:
• an input that does not test the claim
  • a disposition the observation does not support
  • an observation that cannot decide the claim: choose another input
  • a listed-set claim without one part per member
  • missing evidence or an empty reason for undetermined
  • a changed command, or missing, extra or wrongly typed argument keys
  • a missing own_check

docs.title: Your M3 timeline
docs.text: When You End of Week 11 push the frozen tag After the deadline receive a copy of the audit Week 12 workshop plan every finding; run the first check Rest of Week 12 verify every finding; add your own check M3 deadline submit the record

docs.title: Tag one version for M3
docs.text:
By the end of Week 11:

git status --porcelain   # keep the output empty
git tag -a m3-freeze-12 -m "M3 snapshot"
git rev-parse m3-freeze-12^{commit}  # record this revision

Run the evidence against this tag, then keep the tag and output together.

docs.title: Check the tag, then push it
docs.text:
git ls-tree -r --name-only m3-freeze-12   # every path the audit receives
git push origin m3-freeze-12              # a plain push does not send tags

Scan the tagged tree for secrets before you push.

docs.title: Protected state matters
docs.text:
A response can say deny while still changing a report or path.

Record the state as well as the response.

docs.title: Real M3 boundaries
docs.text:
The audit reads only your frozen snapshot: your own work.

No participant material, including de-identified notes; no credentials or unrelated session logs.

docs.title: Evidence conflict
docs.text:
An evidence conflict goes to the human integrity process.

An authorship detector does not decide responsibility from style.

docs.title: Workshop sequence
docs.text:
0–10 freeze · 10–20 plan · 20–40 run · 40–50 mark and split

50–60 own check · 60–65 verify · 65–90 start your own M3 record

docs.title: Exit question
docs.text:
A claim says some input breaks a rule, and your first three inputs behave.

What do you write, and how do you choose the fourth input?

docs.title: Transfer to M3
docs.text:
Your tag was pushed by the end of Week 11.

Verify every audit finding, split any whose parts differ, and add one check the review missed, or bound a clean range.

Keep the model record separate from the evidence you submit, and keep your user tests going.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
Notes · Workshop · Self-check

Public fixture in lectures/week-12/fixtures/ · Week 0 execution route

M3 instructions · M3 rubric

docs.title: Public audit-verification fixture
docs.text: This is a course-authored synthetic snapshot. audit_packet.py is the frozen public surface; it has no network, package installation, credential, or personal-data path. Run it and verify_audit.py only through the Week 0 course launcher.

docs.title: Frozen requirements
docs.text:
Every disposition is judged against these requirements, not against the wording of the review:

R1 access: a viewer or an owner can read a public report; no role reads a private report body.
R2 status: the status endpoint accepts only the labels ready and queued.
R3 paths: every exported or archived report path stays under /srv/reports.
R4 secrets: no export configuration exposes a secret directory.
R5 scoring: the private-count scorer gives 1 only when the answer's first word is the number of private sample reports; every other answer scores 0.
R6 root: the report root is written once, as REPORT_ROOT; no function repeats the literal path.

Production configuration is not part of this snapshot, so no check here can read it.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
• audit_packet.py is the snapshot's report feature and its deterministic evidence checks. Run it with no --check to list each check and its argument keys. A run prints the args it used, the observation and the canonical command to record as evidence. It refuses a missing, extra or wrongly typed argument: private is a JSON true or false, and role is viewer or owner.
  • model-audit.json is a recorded review with five claims about security, evaluation and maintenance. Each has an id, an area and, for most, the function it cites. It names no check, input or answer; you choose the check and input for each claim. It is course-authored practice material; no model wrote it.
  • student-audit.json is an empty starter record. Students add one verification for each recorded claim and either a new defect check or a bounded clean-scope check. The notes show a filled row, the parts shape for a claim about each member of a listed set, and both own-check shapes.
  • verify_audit.py recomputes every named check, checks the exact reproducible command, checks that the input tests the claim and derives the supported disposition from the observation. It accepts only confirmed, refuted or undetermined; an undetermined row must name the missing input or why it cannot be decided.

The verifier tests the evidence supplied by the student. The recorded review is not a model score and its text is never sent to a grader. A hand trace is not an observation; retain the launcher output with the frozen snapshot identifier. An own check must probe a new input or state a checked range and its remaining boundary.

docs.title: Week 13: Respond to findings and improve usability
docs.text: This directory holds Week 13 materials. You turn each Week 12 audit result into an M4 response, observe a user try a task and verify the interface change that follows.

docs.title: A finding becomes a bounded iteration
docs.text: Use the complete case packet, the fixture, a keyboard-accessible text editor and one existing work record. Save an independent prediction before the worked explanation. A previously seen solution is informed practice. Pair discussion can also use written feedback; each learner keeps their own explanation.

docs.title: Activity sequence
docs.text:
Minutes Action Retained work 0-8 Observe a partner try the task on a page they have not seen, from the --view output for rehearsal.html; record only actions and words. If your partner opens a control, read them what is inside it from rehearsal.html, and record the action and their words One observation, one hypothesis and one question 8-15 Predict whether the task check completes on rehearsal.html and name the output line you expect to decide it; run it The prediction beside the output, and one step where the check's keyboard walk and your partner's actions differ or agree 15-25 As a pair, choose one fixture variation; write the output line you expect to change, then run the check on your copy The variation, the predicted line and the output 25-38 Write the repair test in a copy of the Week 12 fixture and run it through the launcher on the frozen snapshot. If the test failed on the snapshot, fix the function from R1, rerun the test and rerun the other three cases of the rule; if it passed, recheck the disposition before changing code The snapshot output; if the test failed, the output after the fix and the three case observations, each with its revision 38-45 Write the M4 response records for your F1–F5 results and your own check; exchange one with a partner and revise one claim independently One response record per record or part, and one for your own check

If you did not run the task check on current.html and the two proposals in class, run those three commands from the execution route first. Continue actual M4 work and the three scheduled user tests during remaining practical time, using the session checklist. Use real de-identified records only under the established arrangements. The supplied rehearsal does not count as a participant or approved equivalent session.

docs.title: Execution route
docs.text:
Start from the reviewed course root. The task check reads HTML as text and never runs it, so the unchanged course file runs on the host with the locked course tools:

uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py --view lectures/week-13/fixture/rehearsal.html
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/rehearsal.html
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/current.html
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/proposal-a.html
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/proposal-b.html

Expected behavior: --view prints the Tab order and the rows shown, with no result. The current page and proposal A exit 1 with result: NOT COMPLETED; proposal A's output also shows fields the dashboard ignores: state. Proposal B exits 0 with result: COMPLETED. If an output differs from your prediction, keep both and find the line of the page or of the check that you misread.

For a variation, change only a copy of a page, never check_task.py or dashboard.py:

mkdir week13-ui
cp lectures/week-13/fixture/proposal-b.html week13-ui/
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py week13-ui/proposal-b.html

The repair test runs student-edited code, so it runs only through the launcher. Replace VERSION and DIGEST with the resolver values from Week 0. Copy the Week 12 packet into a new workspace, so that your Week 12 record keeps its frozen snapshot, and save the test from the notes there as test_private_report.py:

mkdir -p week13-repair
cp lectures/week-12/fixtures/audit_packet.py week13-repair/
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST \
  --workspace week13-repair -- python test_private_report.py

Keep that output with the label week12-audit-snapshot. If the test failed on the snapshot, edit private_report_view in week13-repair/audit_packet.py so that it follows R1, then run the same launcher command again and keep the second output with a label for your repair. If it passed, go back to the notes before you change any code. After a repair, rerun each of the other three cases by ending the same launcher command with:

-- python audit_packet.py --check private-report-view --args '{"private":false,"role":"viewer"}'
-- python audit_packet.py --check private-report-view --args '{"private":false,"role":"owner"}'
-- python audit_packet.py --check private-report-view --args '{"private":true,"role":"owner"}'

Each prints its observation; compare its status with the table in the notes.

docs.title: Organization practice
docs.text:
After class, after you have read Agents across an organization. Parts 1 and 2 take 15 minutes and are this week's after-class practice, inside the week's hour estimate. Parts 3 and 4 take 20 more minutes; they are optional practice and sit outside the estimate. Work alone, then compare with a partner.

Each part has the same two steps. Generate: a course-authored file stands in for what an organization's agents and services produced, and its agent_summary is a replayed claim, as if an agent had reported on its own work. Verify: check the records by hand and write your answer and the result: line you expect, then run the check and compare. Everything in the four files is synthetic: the sessions, runs, units, review minutes and evaluator results are invented for practice, the route names are placeholders and no model, portal or gateway was used. A unit is a course-made number, not a price.

Minutes Action Retained work 0-8 Part 1, the portal: in org-portal.json, match each call to the grant that allows it or mark it denied, then list what each grant can reach; run portal. Narrow the grant you found to the task's repositories in your copy, predict which call changes and run it again The over-broad grant, the call outside the task it allowed, whether the agent's summary is true, and the narrowed grant with its owner, reason and the denied call that tests it 8-15 Part 2, the gateway: in org-gateway.json, replay the policy over each run by hand, adding each request's reservation before it is sent as the Week 11 ledger did, and search the sandbox-side lines for the key; run gateway Each run the policy should have refused or capped, with the request where it should have stopped, and the line that holds the key 15-25 Part 3, optional, cost per accepted change: from the table below, compute it by hand, then run cost Your calculation beside the output, and one sentence on why it differs from the trace total of run a3 25-35 Part 4, optional, routing: in org-routes.json, decide for each task whether the chosen route passes every case the current route passes, on the revision in use; run route Supported or not for each task, with the deciding line, and what a route choice cannot be trusted on even with a supported result

The runs and reviews behind four changes, as recorded in org-changes.json:

Change Runs (units) Decision Review minutes fix-118 a1 6 (checks failed), a2 6 accepted 20 fix-119 a3 3 accepted 10 fix-120 a4 3, a5 2 rejected 15 fix-121 a6 2 (timed out, retried), a7 2 accepted 15

docs.title: Organization route
docs.text:
The commands run the copies in your workspace, which you may change, so they go through the launcher like the repair test above. Replace VERSION and DIGEST with the resolver values from Week 0, then copy the check and its four files into a new workspace:

mkdir week13-org
cp lectures/week-13/fixture/org_check.py lectures/week-13/fixture/org-*.json week13-org/
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week13-org -- python -B org_check.py portal org-portal.json
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week13-org -- python -B org_check.py gateway org-gateway.json
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week13-org -- python -B org_check.py cost org-changes.json
sh scripts/course-sandbox --profile offline --version VERSION --digest DIGEST --workspace week13-org -- python -B org_check.py route org-routes.json

For the narrowed grant in Part 1, edit only week13-org/org-portal.json and run the portal command again. Expected behavior: each check prints one line per call, run, change or task and ends with a result: line. The launcher reports exit_code 1 for portal on the supplied file and 0 once the grant reaches only the task's repositories, 1 for gateway and route, and 0 for cost. If an output differs from your prediction, keep both and find the field that you misread.

docs.title: Demo rehearsal (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Use the Week 13 fixture as the course-authored preview, or your own approved de-identified artifact. Do not add participant identities, raw recordings, private code or model transcripts. Each student keeps an individual outline even when pairs exchange feedback.

Minutes Rehearsal move Output 0-8 State the need, finding and separately labelled hypothesis Opening outline 8-16 Show the generated change and what stayed unchanged Bounded diff or request 16-24 Show expected checks before their output Verification handoff 24-28 Partner asks one changed-condition question Input, expected effect and decision 28-30 Revise one sentence and name the remaining limit Updated response record

The demo arc is need, finding, change, verification, decision and limit. This rehearsal prepares your expo demonstration; it is not a second test, an oral-defense instance or evidence of a participant session. A written or keyboard-only exchange is an equivalent route to spoken feedback. Captions or a text transcript must be available for any recorded demonstration, and no one must disclose a sensitive experience.

This rehearsal is for the expo, not the oral defense. If your defense appointment falls in Week 13, work through the first 32 minutes of the Week 14 defense rehearsal before it.

docs.title: Practitioner guest
docs.text: A practitioner from a partner organization joins the first class this week for up to 45 minutes to describe how agents are run at organization scale, including gateways and cost; the rest of the class runs as usual. Before class, write one question for the guest. After class, write one sentence comparing one claim the guest made with what this week's notes and your own runs show, for example on portals, gateways, cost and routing. Keep both in your Week 13 work entry. The talk is not assessed and adds no time outside class. A guest speaks about their own organization's practice; the course endorses no product. The talk is recorded only with advance notice and the consent of those present. If no guest is available, the class runs as usual.

docs.title: Finish C2
docs.text: Your C2 contribution is due at the end of this week (Friday 23:59 course time) or the day before your defense, whichever comes first. It is marked with the same explanation check, verification evidence and AI-use note as your other open work, plus your upstream collaboration: issue discussion, revisions after review and following the project's rules. A merge or a maintainer reply is not required. See the syllabus.

docs.title: Transfer
docs.text: Take one control you change on your own page for M4. Which line of the own-page cross-check would show that its value reaches the view, and what would that line still not show about the people who use the page?

docs.title: Evidence and support
docs.text:
At the first feedback checkpoint, ask for a hint if the input, required effect or next observation remains unclear. Planned times organize support rather than penalize extra time or approved participation arrangements. Keep actual runs and participant records distinct from authored examples. All execution follows the Week 0 route.

Use the same evidence in M2/M3/M4 where relevant. No duplicate report is required.

docs.title: Week 13: Respond to findings and improve usability
Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this session you can:

  • separate a raw observation of a user task from a hypothesis and a bounded interface change;
  • verify an agent's proposed interface change with one executable task check, and show when a plausible-looking change did not help;
  • turn each Week 12 audit disposition into an M4 response: repair, defer, no change or investigate; and
  • say what tool portals, model gateways, cost per accepted change and routing add when a whole organization uses agents, and which check would reveal each one failing (LO3, LO5, LO9).

This packet is a 60-minute lecture followed by a 30-minute demo rehearsal. All examples below are course-authored synthetic practice. They are not M3, M4 or oral-defense instances, and a rehearsal record is never evidence of a real user test.

docs.title: Route and timebox
docs.text: Minutes Purpose Student output 0-8 Name the interface, task and raw observation One observation with no inferred cause 8-16 Separate a hypothesis and request a bounded change One falsifiable hypothesis and a change request 16-32 Verify two agent proposals with one task check A prediction and the check's result for each page 32-46 Carry the Week 12 audit into M4 One response per finding, with its evidence 46-54 Agents across an organization For each piece, the problem it solves and the check that would reveal it failing 54-60 Accept the iteration within its evidence A decision tied to a revision and a remaining question 60-68 Rehearse a demo opening Need, scope and evidence in one outline 68-82 Rehearse the change and verification Generation and verification shown as separate moves 82-90 Take questions and revise the handoff One answer that names an input, expected effect and limit

docs.title: Interface, task and raw observation
docs.text:
Course-authored interface: visible controls are Overview | Options | Refresh. Inside Options, State offers All, Failed and Running. The page shows the two most recent builds. The synthetic task is "Find the most recent failed build in pipeline Alpha." The page is current.html in the fixture. A supplied record says:

The user opens Overview, then returns.
The user selects Refresh twice.
The user asks where failed builds are shown.
The task is not completed before the rehearsal ends.

Write an observation, a hypothesis and a candidate change before reading on. The record contains no real participant, timestamp or population-level finding. The query returns the correct failed records, so behavior correctness and locating the control are different questions.

docs.title: A hypothesis becomes a bounded change
docs.text:
"Options may not communicate status filtering" is an interpretation. Exposing Status: All is one plausible change to test, not a proven solution. Request that small interface patch while retaining selection, order, permission and keyboard operation. An assistant may propose code within the assignment's rules; you own the discovery records and the interpretation of evidence.

Unchanged query tests remain relevant to the query. A different control now supplies the filter value, so check that the request still carries the field name and value the query reads, then row order, focus, accessible label and keyboard selection. Repeat the neutral task on the new revision under the actual consent/equivalence arrangement. The old session cannot show that the new label is understandable. Retain minimal de-identified observations rather than names, raw media or unrelated personal details.

docs.title: Keep an evidence ledger
docs.text:
Write the three layers in separate fields before asking an assistant for a patch:

Layer Example from this packet What would make it stronger Observation The user opened Overview, returned and asked where failed builds were shown. The same action is recorded on the affected revision and task. Hypothesis The word Options does not reveal that status filtering is inside it. A neutral task can distinguish locating the control from query correctness. Change Expose Status: All while keeping the existing filter and ordering. A diff and an explicit acceptance check show the intended scope.

The table is a reasoning aid, not a claim about a population. If the observation and hypothesis are written in one sentence, split them before implementation. If the change is larger than the hypothesis, narrow it or record why a product owner must decide.

docs.title: Generate, then verify
docs.text:
Generation is the request for a bounded patch. The fixture records this request:

Add a visible Status: All control to the existing build page. Preserve the current query contract, result order, permission check and keyboard operation.

agent-replay.json holds two replies. They are a course-authored replay that stands in for an agent; no model wrote them. Both replies say that a labelled, keyboard-operable Status control now puts failed builds one step away. Proposal A adds a new select and leaves Options unchanged. Proposal B moves the existing select out of Options. Compare each page with current.html, then predict: will the task complete on each page?

Verification is one task check. check_task.py tries the task the way a keyboard user would, with one narrow strategy. It presses Tab from the top, opens a menu or chooses an option only when its text shares a word with the task, follows no links, and then presses the first submit button it reached. The unchanged query answers whatever the form sends. The task is completed when the first row shown is #121, the most recent failed build in pipeline Alpha, and every control reached has an accessible name. The check reads HTML as text and never runs it, so the course file runs on the host with the locked course tools:

uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/current.html
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/proposal-a.html
uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/proposal-b.html

The current page and proposal A exit 1; proposal B exits 0. Proposal A prints:

page: proposal-a.html
task: Find the most recent failed build in pipeline Alpha.
unchanged query check: pass; query(pipeline=alpha, status=failed) returns #121, #119
keyboard walk from the top of the page:
  1. link "Overview": not followed; the strategy does not follow links
  2. select "Status": chose "Failed"
  3. disclosure "Options" (closed): not opened; no task word
  4. button "Refresh": submit button
not reached: select "State" inside closed disclosure "Options"
reached controls without an accessible name: none
request sent: pipeline=alpha&state=failed&status=all
fields the dashboard ignores: state
fields sent more than once: none
rows shown: #123 running, #122 passed
expected first row: #121 failed
result: NOT COMPLETED - the first row shown is #123 running, not #121 failed

Proposal A is the change that looks right and does not help. Its diff is small, its control is labelled and reached by keyboard, and the unchanged query check passes. The selection never reaches the query: the new select sends state, the dashboard reads status, and the old State select inside Options still sends all. That runnable observation refutes the reply's claim that failed builds are one step away. Proposal B sends status=failed, shows #121 first and completes the task. If a page sends the same field twice, the dashboard reads the first value, and the check lists the field under fields sent more than once.

Each check answers a different question. The unchanged query check shows that the query still returns #121 and #119. The request line shows what the page actually sends. The keyboard walk shows that a named control is reached without opening a menu. None of them shows that a person can find the control without a hint; only a new authorized task observation on the accepted revision can show that. The check matches words literally, so a person may succeed where it fails, or fail where it succeeds. A green task check cannot certify a label, and a successful task observation cannot certify an unchanged permission boundary.

docs.title: Carry the check to your own page
docs.text:
check_task.py reads only the fixture's pages and asks only the fixture's dashboard. It cannot read your ci-dashboard templates, whose options come from template loops, or the view that answers them. For the page you change in M4, cross-check the same three things as text. git grep reads tracked files and runs nothing, so these commands run on the host. Replace PROJECT_REPO with your repository and TEMPLATE with the page's template, for example legacy_app/templates/ci/builds.html:

git -C PROJECT_REPO grep -n -E 'name="' -- TEMPLATE
git -C PROJECT_REPO grep -n -E 'request\.(args|form)\.get\(' -- '*.py'
git -C PROJECT_REPO grep -n -E '<label for=|<details|<summary| id="' -- TEMPLATE

Then write one line for each comparison:

  1. Form names against view reads. Every field the form sends is a name the view reads, and every name the view reads comes from a control on the page or has a stated default. A name on only one side is the proposal A defect. A read through a helper, such as request.args.get(name, ...), needs the call that passes the name.
  2. Label pairs. Every <label for="..."> matches the id of exactly one control, and every control you changed has a label.
  3. Reach. The control you changed is not inside a <details> that starts closed, unless its <summary> names what is inside.

If the template builds names or ids in a macro, or you cannot tell which view answers the form, use the manual route instead: write the page's Tab order from the template, mark each closed disclosure, write the request the form would send after a user chooses the task's option, and find each of its field names in the view that answers the form. Either route is text evidence about the revision you read. It is not a task run and not a participant session. To observe the rows the view returns, write a test that sends that request through your framework's test client and run it through the launcher like your other project tests.

docs.title: Carry the Week 12 audit into M4
docs.text:
In Week 12 you marked each recorded finding confirmed, refuted or cannot tell (undetermined in the record) and added one check of your own: either a new defect or a scope check that observed no defect. M4 turns each of those results into a response. The findings came from a model. Where a finding came from is no reason to accept or dismiss it; the Week 12 evidence decides.

Week 12 result M4 response What the response must show confirmed repair, or defer with an owner Repair: a test that fails on the frozen snapshot and passes after the fix, and the other cases of the rule rerun. Defer: who owns it, why it waits and what reopens it. refuted no change The refuting command and its output, kept with the snapshot label cannot tell (undetermined) investigate The missing observation, named, and the next check that would supply it Own scope check, no defect observed no change The command, the checked range and the remaining boundary, and what would reopen the question

Apply the table to your own F1–F5 results from the Week 12 drill: one response per record, one per part where you split a record, and one for your own check. Your disposition chooses the response; this step does not reopen it. If writing a response shows that your evidence does not support the disposition, go back to the Week 12 check and change the input, not the response.

A repair is written from the frozen requirement, not from the finding's wording. Requirement R1 of the Week 12 fixture reads:

R1 access: a viewer or an owner can read a public report; no role reads a private report body.

For a record you confirmed against R1, test the case the record is about before you touch the code. In a copy of the Week 12 fixture, test_private_report.py can be:

from audit_packet import run_check

observed = run_check("private-report-view", {"role": "viewer", "private": True})
assert observed["status"] == "deny" and observed["body_visible"] is False, observed

Run it through the launcher on the frozen snapshot first; the workshop's execution route gives the full commands. A confirmed defect makes the assertion fail there, and that failing output is your evidence before. If the test passes on the frozen snapshot, it does not reach the defect or the disposition needs another look: settle that before you change any code. Then fix the function from the rule in R1, not from the test alone, run the same test again and keep both outputs, each with its revision. Finally rerun the other three cases of the rule with the same private-report-view check, so that the fix neither blocks a permitted reader nor lets anyone else through:

Arguments Required observation {"private": false, "role": "viewer"} allow {"private": false, "role": "owner"} allow {"private": true, "role": "owner"} deny

A fix that only makes the one assertion pass can still break a case it does not cover. A test that has only ever passed cannot show that it would catch the defect.

Keep one response record per finding:

Finding ID and Week 12 result (disposition, or no defect observed)
M4 response: repair | defer | no change | investigate
Evidence before: frozen revision, command and output
Evidence after (repair): repair revision, the same test and its output
Owner and reopening trigger (defer), missing observation and next check (investigate),
  or checked range, boundary and reopening change (scope check)
Remaining question

A label such as "fixed" or "won't fix" alone does not explain the engineering judgment. Do not turn a cannot-tell item into "no change" because nothing has failed yet, and do not change code for a refuted finding to make the record look busier. Your own M3 record follows the same mapping, including your own check: a new defect is confirmed and repaired or deferred, and a scope check keeps its range and boundary with no change. The user-test iteration above joins them in one M4 record.

If you have an approved route, you may dispatch the repair of one confirmed finding as a background task: write the issue as in Week 6, let the agent return a change, and review it through the explanation gate. A plain-text issue and a hand-made change earn the same credit.

docs.title: Agents across an organization: portals, gateways, cost and routing
docs.text:
Week 11 described one gateway you can read in full: the launcher's host broker keeps the key outside the work, fixes the destination, caps each run and keeps a minimal record (the Week 11 gateway jobs). It also compared a cheaper route against your frozen evaluator cases before trusting it. When a whole organization adopts agents, those jobs move into shared services. Four pieces recur. Each solves a real problem and each concentrates authority, so each needs a check that would reveal it failing. This course runs none of them as a shared service; you are asked to recognize them and to say what would test them.

Tool portal. One service lists which tools exist, who may call each and with which arguments, and it records every grant. The Week 3 hook checked one tool call before its effect. The launcher's tool session is the course's one-person version: it knows four tools (read, write, verify and bash) with fixed argument names, it accepts only the exact call that the model's reply proposed, in order, within a per-run limit, and the program in the sandbox cannot add a tool or change a call. A portal applies that idea to everyone at once, so one review or revocation reaches every agent, and so does one mistaken grant. Tools that an agent discovers through MCP do not grant themselves permission. In one public demonstration, an agent's single GitHub MCP connection could reach both public and private repositories; injected text in a public issue led the agent to write private information into a public pull request, and the disclosers recommend limiting repository access (incidents/github-mcp; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1). Checking each call against the grant is therefore not enough: when the grant itself reaches more than the task needs, every call passes the check. Compare what each grant can reach with what the task needs as well. Treat each grant like code: it has an owner, a reason and a test showing that a call outside the grant is denied and leaves no effect.

Model gateway. A shared gateway holds what individual developers should not: keys, budgets, rate limits and request logs. In LiteLLM, for example, virtual keys control model access and track spending, key settings can bound budgets, budget periods and request and token rates, and one logging setting keeps message content away from logging providers while request metadata is still tracked (tools/litellm; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2). Those are the Week 11 broker's jobs at organization scale. Check them the same way: replay the policy over the gateway's own records, so that a request over a cap or on an unlisted route shows up as refused before it was sent, and a log on the sandbox side holds neither the key nor prompt text.

Cost per accepted change. A trace total such as course-llm cost measures one run. At organization scale the useful number is what an accepted change cost: every run that led to it, including failed and retried attempts, plus the time people spent reviewing it. Runs spent on changes that were rejected count too, because the organization paid for them. Divide the total of all runs by the number of accepted changes, and report review minutes beside it in the same way rather than converting them into a price. Cost per token rewards cheap output that nobody can merge.

Routing. A routing policy sends each task to the cheapest route that passes the evaluator and escalates when a check fails. Week 11 made that decision once, for one step of your M2 feature: a cheaper route is good enough only if it passes every frozen case that the current route passes. A policy makes the decision for many tasks at once, and a rule such as "passes 90% of the cases" can hide the one case a route loses. The frozen evaluator cases must also be rerun whenever a route or a model changes; a model's name does not guarantee unchanged behavior. Even a fresh, complete pass says nothing about inputs that are not among the frozen cases.

The organization practice checks all four pieces on replayed, course-authored records: a portal's grants against one agent session, a gateway policy against six runs, the cost of three accepted changes and three route choices.

Rolling model access out to a whole organization brings a gateway's failure modes with it. For each risk, name the check that would detect it:

Risk Check that would reveal it Keys copied into repositories and CI instead of held by the gateway Secret scanning and key rotation; the gateway is the only holder Groups bypass the gateway with personal tools, so caps and logs miss that work Compare model use you can see with the work being delivered Logs quietly become a store of prompts holding code or customer data Minimal records by default, like the course trace One cap for everyone either blocks real tasks or protects nothing Set caps per task from measured runs; every refusal says what to do next A gateway or provider outage stops everyone at once A tested fallback, such as replay or a no-model path Adoption is judged by usage rather than results Evaluator results and incident records, not token counts

Because each piece concentrates authority, apply the Week 8 boundary tests before trusting it: a denied call stays denied through every route, and permitted work still succeeds.

docs.title: Accept the iteration within its evidence
docs.text: If proposal B's page passes the task check, the unchanged query check and the affected keyboard checks, and an authorized new session completes the task without a navigation hint, accept the iteration for that checked scope. Record the revision, the inputs and the observed results. Do not claim that all users will now succeed.

docs.title: Run each scheduled user test
docs.text:
The three user tests scheduled across Weeks 11-13 use one checklist. Prepare it before each session and fill it in yourself during the session.

Before the session:

  • Consent route. Confirm the consent or approved equivalent route you set up under the Week 4 participation rules. The person may stop at any time; if they withdraw, follow the same rules for their material.
  • Neutral task. Write the task as a goal, as in Week 11, and give it exactly as written, aloud or on paper. It names no control and does not ask whether anything is easy.
  • Revision. Note the commit the person will use. A session on another revision is evidence about that revision only.

During the session:

  • Actions and words. Record what the person did and said, in order. Put no cause on this line; the hypothesis goes on its own line afterwards.
  • Hint rule. Give no navigation hint. You may repeat the task or ask "What would you try next?" If the person cannot go on without a hint, give the smallest one, record its exact words and when you gave it, and record the task as completed with a hint.

Record these fields for each session:

Session: S<n> (no name), date, revision
Consent route: the Week 4 arrangement it uses
Task, as given
Actions and words, in order
Hints: none, or the exact words and when
Task result: completed | completed with a hint | not completed
Hypothesis, separate from the observation
Next check or change

Keep names, raw media and unrelated details out of the record. Session notes never enter a model prompt, even after you remove names.

docs.title: Demo rehearsal: a short walk-through of evidence
docs.text:
The expo demonstration is a communication exercise, not a second test or a substitute for the individual defense. Rehearse with the Week 13 fixture as the course-authored preview, or with your own approved, de-identified work; do not paste participant identities, raw recordings, private code or model transcripts into what you show.

Oral defense appointments start this week. If yours falls in Week 13, work through the first 32 minutes of the Week 14 defense rehearsal before it, with a partner or on your own with the public practice packet.

docs.title: A compact demo arc
docs.text:
Use this order and give each move a visible artifact:

  1. Need (one minute): state the user task and the agreed requirement. Name the evidence source without claiming more than it shows.
  2. Finding (one minute): show one observation and label the hypothesis separately.
  3. Change (two minutes): show the smallest generated change and say what stayed unchanged. If an assistant proposed it, say what you inspected yourself.
  4. Verification (two minutes): run or show the affected behavior, integration and accessibility checks on the same revision. Give the expected result before the output.
  5. Decision (one minute): say repair, defer, no change or investigate, with the requirement and remaining question.
  6. Limit (one minute): state what this evidence supports and what still needs a new test, user observation or product decision.

docs.title: Question drill
docs.text:
The partner asks one changed-condition question: “What would you check if the label changed again?” Answer with the new input, expected effect and decision that would move. If the existing test cannot see the changed condition, name the different check. A good answer can be brief; it must be specific enough for another person to run.

End the rehearsal by revising one sentence in the response record. Keep the demonstration separate from the three scheduled user tests and from your individual defense evidence.

docs.title: Hands-on exercise
docs.text:
Work through the activity; it adds no separate report.

  1. Observe one rehearsal of the task on a page your partner has not seen. Your partner tries it from the --view output for rehearsal.html while you record only actions and words. If your partner opens a control, read them what is inside it from rehearsal.html, and record the action and their words. Write the observation, a hypothesis and one question.
  2. Predict whether the task check completes on rehearsal.html, run it, and compare its keyboard walk with what your partner did.
  3. With your partner, make one fixture variation: write the output line you expect to change, then run the check on your copy.
  4. Run the repair test on a copy of the Week 12 fixture through the launcher, fix from R1 and rerun the other three cases. Then write one M4 response record for each of your F1–F5 results and for your own check.
  5. Continue your actual M4 work: respond to your own verified M3 findings, carry the check to your own page, and continue the three scheduled user tests with the session checklist, using real de-identified records only under the established arrangements.
  6. After class, check the replayed portal and gateway records in the organization practice; its cost and routing parts are optional.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Run the task check on the page you would accept:

uv run --project infra/hosted --locked python lectures/week-13/fixture/check_task.py lectures/week-13/fixture/proposal-b.html

Expected evidence: exit 0, with request sent: pipeline=alpha&status=failed, rows shown: #121 failed, #119 failed and result: COMPLETED - the first row shown is #121 failed. Keep the output with the page it checked.

Failure case: the same command on proposal-a.html exits 1 with fields the dashboard ignores: state and result: NOT COMPLETED, although its keyboard walk reaches a named Status control and the unchanged query check passes. When a change passes the query check but fails the task check, read the request line first: it shows exactly what the form sent.

For an M4 repair, the evidence is a test that fails on the frozen revision and passes on the repair revision, with both outputs kept beside their revisions. For your own feature, observe the new interaction under the actual consent or equivalence arrangement and retain the affected revision; a task check on a fixture is not a participant session.

All execution follows Week 0 setup. The classroom packet is authored practice; actual runs and participants need their own evidence.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake How to detect it Correction Writing an interpretation as the observation The observation line names a cause or a feeling, such as "could not recognize the filter" Rewrite it as what was done and said; move the cause to the hypothesis line Accepting a UI change because its diff, label and query check look right No task check output exists for that page, or nobody read its request line Run the task check and read request sent and fields the dashboard ignores Treating a completed task check as proof that people understand the label The usability claim cites only the script Limit the claim to the scripted strategy; observe a new authorized session on the same revision Counting a rehearsal or an old-label session as evidence for the new label The session's revision differs from the accepted one, or the record says rehearsal Record a new authorized session on the accepted revision Repairing a confirmed finding without a test that failed first The repair record shows only passing runs Run the new test on the frozen snapshot, keep the failing output, then fix Turning a cannot-tell item into "no change" The response names no missing observation Name the missing observation and the next check, and keep the item open Changing code for a refuted finding The diff touches the path the refuting command exercised Revert that change and keep the refuting command and output Quoting one run's trace total as what a change costs The figure leaves out failed, retried and rejected runs and review time Divide all runs and all review minutes by the accepted changes

docs.title: Week 13 readings
docs.text:
Before class, read the learning objectives and fixed contract in the notes. Attempt the first slide question before opening the worked explanation. After class, use the worked sections, activities and self-check. If you already saw a solution, mark the next attempt as informed practice.

The course case explains how this week connects to the product.

docs.title: Two focused external readings
docs.text:
• Separate assisted practice from independent evidence (about 15 minutes, optional): read Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics, especially “Experimental Design” and “Main Results”, to decide which of your repair explanations and verification steps still need to be completed without generated prompts. (studies/bastani-pnas-2025; as_of: 2026-09-05; Source 1; Source 2; Source 3; Source 4)
  • Listed is not granted (about 8 minutes, optional): read Introducing the MCP Registry, the preview announcement on the MCP project blog, especially “Public and private sub-registries” and “Community-driven mechanism for moderation”, beside the notes section on portals, gateways, cost and routing. A registry entry is information the server's maintainer reports, and moderation removes a bad entry only afterwards. Say which checks a tool portal must still make before it grants an agent a call. The post describes a preview, so do not take it as the registry's current state. (tools/mcp-registry; as_of: 2026-10-09; Source 1)

docs.title: Week 13 self-check answer guidance
docs.text: Keep observations, hypotheses and decisions in separate sentences.

docs.title: Q1a–Q1b: Observation and hypothesis
docs.text: Q1a. The record shows Overview opened, a return, two Refresh selections and a question about failed builds; the task ended before completion. Q1b. “Options may hide the status filter” is a hypothesis to test, not a fact about the user's motivation.

docs.title: Q2a–Q2b: Integration
docs.text: Q2a. Evidence about the unchanged query contract remains useful when tied to the relevant revision. Q2b. Repeat the UI-to-query check: the request still carries the field name and value the query reads. Then check result ordering, focus, accessible label and keyboard operation.

docs.title: Q3a–Q3b: A plausible change that did not help
docs.text: Q3a. request sent: pipeline=alpha&state=failed&status=all and fields the dashboard ignores: state: the new select sends state, the query reads status, and the old select still sends all. Q3b. It refutes the claim that failed builds are now one step away. The unchanged query check and a label-and-keyboard check alone would both have passed.

docs.title: Q4a–Q4b: Acceptance
docs.text: Q4a. Accept the checked behavior for that interface revision and authorized session. Q4b. The observation does not establish success for every user, task or future label.

docs.title: Q5a–Q5b: Old label
docs.text: Q5a. The old-label session is evidence about the old revision only. Q5b. Run and record a new authorized observation for the new label.

docs.title: Q6a–Q6b: Confirmed
docs.text: Q6a. Repair. The test submits an empty name and requires a rejection with nothing saved; it fails on the frozen revision, where the empty name is saved, and passes on the repair revision. Then rerun the criterion's other cases: names of 1 and 80 characters are saved, and a name of 81 characters is rejected. Q6b. Defer only when the repair is outside this iteration; the record names the owner, why it waits and what reopens it, and keeps the risk visible.

docs.title: Q7: Refuted
docs.text: Q7. Nothing changes in the code. Keep the refuting command and its rejection output with the snapshot label, and the scope sentence that names the file you tried.

docs.title: Q8a–Q8b: Cannot tell
docs.text: Q8a. Investigate: name the missing observation, the deployed runner settings, and the next check that would supply it. Q8b. No observation has shown the claim false, so "no change" would treat a missing input as a refutation.

docs.title: Q9: Scope check
docs.text: Q9. No change. Keep the command, the checked range and the boundary that remains unchecked, and name the change or input that would reopen the question. A scope check is not a confirmed defect, so there is nothing to repair.

docs.title: Q10a–Q10b: Permission portal
docs.text: Q10a. Test concentration risk: one mistaken grant reaches every agent, so a denied scope must remain denied through every route. Q10b. A call outside the grant gets a structured refusal and leaves no effect.

docs.title: Q11a–Q11b: Cost per accepted change
docs.text: Q11a. 30 units ÷ 3 accepted changes = 10 units of model use per accepted change, and 45 ÷ 3 = 15 review minutes per accepted change. The rejected change's runs count, because they were paid for. Q11b. It leaves out failed and retried runs, the runs behind the rejected change and the review time.

docs.title: Q12a–Q12b: Routing by the evaluator
docs.text: Q12a. Not supported: find the case the cheaper route fails, which the current route passes, and check that both results are for the routes' current revisions. A pass share alone hides the lost case. Q12b. Inputs outside the frozen cases, and behavior after the route or its model changes, until the cases are rerun on the new revision.

docs.title: Spaced retrieval
docs.text: Retrieval 1. A different build with the same key should be rejected without creating or mutating a job. Retrieval 2. Keep minimum synthetic or de-identified evidence and its digest; remove raw participant notes, identifiers, credentials and session material from model input.

Week 13 · CI dashboard

docs.title: What the task check cannot show
docs.text:
It follows one literal strategy, not a person. A person may succeed where it fails, or fail where it succeeds.
